[h3] Bond is back! [/h3]
I'm a lifelong Bond fan, so I was hopefully optimistic for this game. Surprisingly, I was rewarded with something that felt like a love letter to the franchise, whilst also reminding me of the great era of singleplayer games that have since been lost to the modern open-world 200hr+ repetitive content slop games.

I will admit that there were some technical issues, but luckily for me the game ran smoothly at 60fps in 4k. The things I encountered were mainly glitches to do with movement and my controller. I see a lot of hotfixes being thrown out that look to combat these sorts of things.

- In terms of gameplay, I thoroughly enjoyed the escalations for the mode of play (stealth, hand to hand and licence to kill), and when you go balls-to-the-wall you really do feel like John Wick in places. 
- The puzzles were fun, and I found myself using actual algebra in a notebook on my desk to crack one of the codes.
- Story-wise it felt like a Bond Film. Sure, some of the dialogue was cheesy etc, but that's Bond in my opinion.
- The references and easter eggs weren't in-your-face or superficial, instead they felt crafted into the game in a meaningful way. To me, this was one of the most enjoyable things about this game.
- The characters and voice cast were incredible. I would happily watch an actual Bond film with all of them. I think this Moneypenny is my favourite.

Finally, most of the hate I see online is complaints over ~20 hours of gameplay (which is what it took me to finish the story) for the price tag. In my opinion, this is just plain wrong. People have become dependent on £50+ games being 100+hrs of 'content' but this 'content' is just open world repetitive side missions vaguely disguised as 'worldbuilding'. I'd much rather 20 hours of well-crafted and engaging story than 100 of meaningless running around/side quests.

TL;DR - You *should* buy this game if:
- You're a Bond fan.
- You miss the old days of singplayer story-centric games.
- You wanna be John Wick.

You *shouldn't* buy this game if:
- You like Ubislop style games where everything is open world and repetitive.
- You don't like things that are good.

Maybe the best introduction you could expect for Bond in the modern era. It hits the notes you expect: you get to dress up and enjoy exotic locales, do casual stealth infiltrations, and then (more rarely but also more meaningfully) get the bombast of "Licence to Kill" shoot-outs. You also get the back-and-forth dialogue pacing that is as laced with innuendo as it is with bite and wit. Good stuff, fun stuff, all that double-O jazz.

It is a lot more singular than IO's previous Hitman trilogy and, perhaps as a consequence of its pacing, a little limiting at times. When the engine is working well, you don't really notice these little seams. However, over the course of 10-ish hours, there were little hiccups. Fairly early on, I caught up with a person I was meant to chase but not catch quite yet and so the game had to just let Bond linger until the next trigger was hit. Another time, a boss fight short-circuited after realizing I had a weapon (when I was expected to play fair with fists, even with a bomb timer lingering in the background). This is not Hitman; cleverness is always limited to expected outcomes (usually involving your gadget watch). But this more cinematic styling is not entirely negative either; it, on the contrary, helps the flashier moments really glitter, especially since the core systems here are so much more natural than Hitman's.

Everywhere you look, you can basically taste the polish. The melee combat is no longer just a quick-time event; it is the centerpiece of Bond's action sandbox. There are punches and kicks, throws, grabs, and plenty of items and emptied weapons to pitch. It is immense fun and helped along considerably by the clarity of enemy indicators (arms out means grab; don't get grabbed!). The gunplay is less robotic and clean as Agent 47's, adding to the drama a constant need to improvise. You can miss with automatic weapons easily, and the lighter aim assist makes sniping the greatest pleasure of all.

It's not always perfect, though. There are plenty of "filler" sections, where you just need a key and can't do anything besides listen to NPCs for the necessary information to progress. Sometimes the way forward demands such a particularly minute solution that you feel less like Bond and more like a toddler ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ themselves. Sometimes, especially in boss fights, it can feel less like Bond is outwitting an opponent and more like an opponent is just waiting for you to do your part so the plot can progress. But the vibe is, across the whole experience, neatly maintained, in a way that only Bond fans could fully appreciate (considering Bond's up-and-down filmography). Overall, First Light has its rails, but as long as you can follow them, you will have a very enjoyable time. The dialogue is fun and appropriately severe when it wants to be; the gameplay is flashy and surprisingly deep; the characters are wonderfully well realized, friends and enemies alike. Much like Machine Games' Indiana Jones a few years ago, it is a remarkably fun and expansive look into a film franchise long past its prime, a game that can (by virtue of being a game) escape the horror of expanding the franchise by more traditional means.

Praising everything without critique is how we get mediocre games. While 007 - First Light shows flashes of brilliance, it ultimately fails to live up to expectations after its first few chapters. Buy it during a sale, not at full price.

Story & Writing: Frustratingly Predictable
The narrative kicks off with a great sense of mystery, but it quickly devolves into a repetitive mess.

[spoiler] The plot features an unnerving dystopian scenario where billionaire families push a malfunctioning AI while covering up their tracks and disappearing whistleblowers. A few years ago, this would have been a fun, albeit cliché, story. Today, it’s just the reality we live in, which drains the excitement out of it with no fault of the game itself. [/spoiler]

The writing relies way too heavily on constant twists right up until the endgame. What some might call "exciting," I call poor writing.

[spoiler] Everyone at MI6 except James is written as incredibly naive. James is vindicated at every turn, which could have been fixed if the writers actually let him make mistakes. Instead, you watch a 25-year veteran like Greenway act completely blind during the telescope ship spotting section, and Moneypenny blindly follow protocol even when people are actively trying to kill you.

James's friends are killed or crippled so early on in their first mission that I forgot their names by the end of the review. Worse, their deaths don't affect Bond at all. He’s right back to cracking quirky jokes, rendering the time spent establishing their friendship completely pointless. [/spoiler] 

The game has an identity crisis in the Gameplay department.
They tried to mix up their classic Hitman formula, but the gameplay loop is all over the place.

The Good: The gunplay is extremely fun, and taking down enemies is highly creative. When a combat section started, I genuinely rejoiced. The social stealth chapters with large crowds feel great and reminiscent of Hitman.

The Bad: There are no disguises. You are either in a safe area or a restricted one. In restricted areas, you can sneak, bluff, or comply, but it doesn't matter if you're wearing a clown costume. It just doesn't feel very spy-like.

Mind-numbing puzzles make up nearly half the game. Like the annoying puzzle missions in Spider-Man, these are mandatory roadblocks. There is only ever one solution, which usually involves tedious pipe-climbing or railing-scaling. [spoiler] The inclusion of Rhys's "secret" UV logos to guide you was hilarious. There’s only one linear path to take anyway, so why bother marking it? [/spoiler]

The Cutscenes: The action sequences feel incredibly rushed and poorly put together, especially during and after the [spoiler] Vietnam chapter. A cutscene involving a cottage fire cuts away so fast it's accidentally hilarious. Another scene with a collapsing crane has so much screen shake that you literally cannot see the choreography, even the character model shakes. [/spoiler]

Beautifully lit framed pictures instantly turn pitch black the second you pick them up to examine them. Even worse, there isn't a basic "read" button for text documents.

For some reason, the TacSim is treated as an entirely separate game mode. To leave it, you have to exit to the main menu, even though you can visually see Q’s lab and the elevator right next to you. Why this wasn't integrated seamlessly into the lab is odd.

On the bright side, the voice acting is great, and the protagonist is well-portrayed. The environments look nice at a glance, but if you look at the distant background details, they still don't match the quality of a 2016 game like Uncharted 4.

I do hope they take these things into account when they eventually will develop the sequel. Bon'ds character is charismatic and fun to follow. I had my expectations higher than the almost Ubisoft class of game delivered is all.

After more than a decade without a truly great James Bond game, 007 First Light finally delivers the experience fans have been dreaming about. Developed by IO Interactive, the studio behind the modern Hitman trilogy, this isn't just a fantastic Bond game—it's one of the finest action-adventure titles of the decade. From its globe-trotting espionage story to its cinematic set pieces, memorable characters, and outstanding performances, 007 First Light earns every bit of its perfect score.

The biggest triumph of the game is its portrayal of a young James Bond. Rather than simply imitating any previous actor, Patrick Gibson creates a version of Bond that feels fresh while honoring the character's legacy. His performance brilliantly combines the wit and effortless charm of Roger Moore, the dangerous edge of Timothy Dalton, the confidence and sophistication of Pierce Brosnan, and the emotional vulnerability and physical intensity of Daniel Craig. Yet Gibson never feels like a copy of any of them. He successfully creates a Bond that belongs entirely to this generation.

The story is equally impressive. By focusing on Bond's early days in MI6 and his journey toward earning the famous 007 designation, the game gives players a side of the character rarely explored in either film or gaming. The narrative feels like a perfect blend of classic Ian Fleming espionage and modern blockbuster filmmaking, constantly surprising players with twists, betrayals, and spectacular action sequences.

Gameplay is where IO Interactive truly shines. The stealth systems, investigative mechanics, social infiltration, gadgets, and freedom of approach create the feeling of actually being James Bond. Whether you're sneaking through a heavily guarded facility, charming information out of a target at a lavish gala, or escaping a high-speed chase, every mission captures a different aspect of the Bond fantasy. 

Visually, 007 First Light is stunning. Exotic locations, detailed environments, gorgeous lighting, and cinematic presentation make every mission feel like a playable Bond film. The soundtrack captures the spirit of the franchise while establishing its own identity, and the supporting cast helps make the world feel alive and believable. 

Perhaps the most exciting aspect of First Light is what it sets up for the future. IO Interactive has openly discussed ambitions for multiple Bond games and potentially a trilogy following this younger incarnation of 007. If future installments build upon the strong foundation established here, Bond fans could be witnessing the beginning of the greatest video game adaptation the franchise has ever received.

Patrick Gibson deserves enormous credit for carrying the iconic role. Taking over a character made famous by so many legendary actors is no easy task, but his performance feels authentic, charismatic, and unforgettable. By the time the credits roll, it becomes impossible to imagine anyone else playing this version of Bond.
Final Verdict: 10/10
007 First Light captures everything that makes James Bond special—style, danger, intelligence, humor, action, and heart. Patrick Gibson delivers a definitive new interpretation of 007, while IO Interactive has created a thrilling origin story that honors the past while boldly charting the future. If this truly is the beginning of a new trilogy, then Bond's gaming future has never looked brighter. **The name is Bond. James Bond. And he's back.**

I'd probably give this one a neutral review if it were possible but if I have to land one way it's Negative unfortunately.

Where the game shines is in its production values. The game looks and sounds great, with the kind of highly populated, fantastically detailed and believable environments IO became known for with their Hitman series. Character models look good and animation is decent. No issues here. Story? It's fine I guess and the performances are very good.

But the gameplay...oh man. Most people know by now that this isn't Bond flavoured Hitman. It's very much a cinematic stealth action game, full of set pieces and scripted events. What people may not be expecting is just how much of a stranglehold the game has on the player throughout the experience. Walk when we tell you, use your gun when we allow you, let us take control from you for while etc. This game could make Uncharted look like Deus Ex. In principle some of the levels have multiple approaches but even then it's a very guided affair (overhear an opportunity and the game will guide you through the execution steps). The stealth gameplay is very basic stuff; the game has the now ubiquitous X-Ray vision and knee high invisibility grass as well as the "press X to stealth button" to insta-kill/knock out opponents. You've done it all before in other games, the only wrinkle here is that you have Q gadgets you can take on missions, but none of them are that interesting. The melee is a kind of Arkham-lite system that feels a bit iffy at times and the gunplay is bare bones too, though you'll often go long stretches without using a gun anyway.

People are saying this is the best Bond game ever but production values don't make a game. First Light is nowhere near as much fun to play in 2026 as Goldeneye was 1997. Goldeneye is still mentioned often today and I suspect it will continue to be discussed long after First Light has faded from memory. It's a game that feels authentically Bond, perhaps more than any other, but the actual gameplay experience is shallow as a puddle.

I bought this game because I'm a James Bond fan. Unfortunately, after several hours, I can only describe it as one of the most boring AAA games I've played in recent years.

The gameplay feels trapped somewhere between a Lara Croft clone and a walking simulator. Most of the time you're not being a secret agent - you're climbing pipes, squeezing through windows, crawling through vents, shimmying across ledges, and slowly walking from one scripted sequence to another. Every mission feels almost identical to the previous one, just with different scenery.

The lack of action is astonishing. This is James Bond, yet the game constantly avoids letting you actually do anything exciting. There are occasional shooting sections, and the gunplay is decent enough, but they are far too rare. The game seems determined to interrupt every potentially fun moment with another climbing puzzle or traversal sequence.

The gadgets are a massive disappointment. For a franchise famous for iconic spy technology, the gadgets here are unimaginative, forgettable, and often completely useless. It feels as if the developers added them simply because a Bond game is expected to have gadgets, not because they had any interesting gameplay ideas for them.

Then there is the enemy AI. For a game released in 2026, it is embarrassing. Guards appear both blind and deaf. Even on the highest difficulty, enemies provide almost no challenge. Stealth sections become laughably easy because the AI is incapable of reacting in a believable way. There is no tension, no need for planning, and no feeling that you're outsmarting professional security personnel.

What makes this even more frustrating is that games solved these problems decades ago. Remember No One Lives Forever from 2000? That game had creative gadgets, memorable weapons, varied missions, humor, challenging enemies, interesting locations, and constant action. More than 25 years later, a €70 James Bond game somehow feels less creative, less exciting, and less engaging than a spy shooter released at the beginning of the century.

The story isn't enough to save the experience either. Bond games should make you feel like a sophisticated spy operating in dangerous situations. Instead, I spent most of my time wondering how much longer I would have to climb, crawl, and slowly walk before something interesting happened.

The biggest criticism I can give is this: I have replayed some of the weakest Hitman games multiple times because they were still entertaining. With 007 First Light, I struggle to find the motivation to finish it even once.

For €70, I expected an exciting spy thriller packed with action, memorable missions, clever gadgets, and replay value. What I got instead was a repetitive, slow-paced, heavily scripted experience with outdated AI and surprisingly little imagination.

As a product, 007 First Light is perfectly fine. I can't honestly call it a bad game. It's gorgeous, technically impressive, and the budget is visible in every aspect of the presentation.

At the same time, this game is the embodiment of everything that makes me roll my eyes at modern AAA game design.

- The combat looks great, but it gets repetitive very quickly. What you see after the first few hours is pretty much what you'll be doing until the credits roll
- Enemy AI is shockingly dumb. During larger fights, it's not uncommon to see enemies simply stand around doing nothing while their friends are actively shooting at you or shouting "HE'S RELOADING, LET'S GET HIM" and remaining to stand still
- The "open" levels have almost no depth. Nearly all of them follow the same formula: overhear a conversation, follow the marker, press the interaction button, move on
- The "linear" levels are basically "hold forward and follow the yellow paint."
- Bond constantly talks to himself to explain what he needs to do next, apparently because the player can't be trusted to figure it out
- Your sidekick in the earpiece feels the need to tell Bond to "focus" ten times per mission, just in case you forgot you're playing a video game
- There are far too many boring, lazy quick-time events
- The puzzles feel like pure time-wasting filler. "The gate is closed. Climb the ladder marked with a giant icon, pull the lever, climb another ladder, pull another lever, go back to the car." Riveting stuff
- The game tricks you into choosing dialogue options under pressure but they don't matter at all, they lead to the same outcome no matter what you choose

The story is fine. Not good, not bad. I'll probably forget most of it within a few months, but I had some fun.

If you're the type of person who enjoys action movies like John Wick, you'll probably have a good time. If you're looking for any meaningful gameplay depth, you're likely going to bounce off it hard.

I pushed through to the end, but if I have to choose between Recommended and Not Recommended, I'm going with Not Recommended.

007 First Light is one of the best experiences I've had in a long time.

The gameplay is tight, offering a solid stealth experience with some challenging puzzles. The gadgets at your disposal make for a pretty fun sandbox, and when mixed with the bluffing mechanic, it really delivers that secret spy fantasy. But let's be honest, a solid stealth game was a given considering IO Interactive developed the Hitman franchise.

What actually surprised me most is the action part of the game.

Because 007 First Light isn't just one of the best James Bond games I've played, it's also the best John Wick game we currently have. The game mixes solid gunplay—with weapons that sound great and really pack a punch—with excellent CQC (Close Quarters Combat).

The limited ammo capacity and the fairly inaccurate weapons at long range, combined with a gunplay and CQC system that seamlessly transition into one another, really give you that "gun-fu" feeling.

You're constantly moving, shooting, and throwing your weapon at an enemy only to perform a takedown, catching their weapon mid-air to shoot another foe in slow-mo right before getting into a fistfight with yet another enemy. It really is an addictive gameplay loop, and I don't think I've played a game this satisfying since Max Payne 3.

The story is good if you like the 007 franchise, and the pace is great—there is never a dull moment. You're always traveling around the globe to unexpected locations, and the game constantly gives you incentives to carry on. I must say that I found the villains a bit weak and lacking, but all of that is compensated for by the charisma of Bond and the desire to see where the game will take you next, given how gorgeous each location looks.

Overall, 007 First Light is a GREAT game. It's an amazing 15-20 hour experience, and I bet it's a game that I'll replay multiple times and go back to regularly for the gameplay alone.

It really is a breath of fresh air to have such a tightly crafted experience that respects your time and wallet in today's market. I hope the success of this title will push the industry in this direction, instead of towards the battle pass, time-and-money-consuming machines we've been fed for the past few years.

Overall I think this is a very solid 8/10 game, if you want a James Bond adventure you will absolutely get it here.


The main accomplishment: This feels just as valid an entry in the franchise as a movie. Patrick Gibson's Bond especially is a highlight. Fully committing to a floating timeline, where 007 would've been born around 2000 and he's working/competing with modern technology before his spy career even starts is a bonafide adrenaline shot for the franchise. "What if James Bond was Gen Z" sounds like a setup to a bad joke, but they genuinely could not have done better than this, every ounce of his personality is preserved [i](though he's less cynical/world weary, because this is an origin story)[/i] while still adapting him into a new context.


One of the smartest ideas is how contextual your actions are. Most stealth game protagonists have their full moveset available at all times, but Bond essentially has three modes: A restrained mode for behaving himself in public, an unrestrained mode where he can do stealth, unarmed combat and all of his gadgets, and License to Kill when he can use guns. This means, unlike Agent 47, Bond can't gun down civilians or awkwardly crouchwalk around in front of people.

Thankfully, these modes are implemented in a pretty smart, well paced manner. There really weren't situations where I wanted to use a gun and couldn't, and not having guns helps highlight the gadgets much more/avoid the issue of a silenced pistol being too overpowered in stealth. Plus, there are segments esp. later on in the game where you have License to Kill in stealthable segments and genuinely can use your whole arsenal.


In terms of gameplay design, a special shoutout for me goes to the melee combat. It's not particularly complicated or deep, but the ability to throw enemies towards stuff, and use this functionality in stealth, allows for some very creative gameplay and takedowns, and throwing the gadgets in as well, people are going to do some nuts stuff with this gameplay, and I cannot wait.


I do understand if some people feel that the level design is a bit too restrictive. As a World of Assassination superfan, this game definitely feels very linear, but this is a licensed game where a lot of people who don't normally play games will be playing it, and I've seen a handful of Uncharted fans say they actually felt it bordered on TOO open which IMO seems like the correct balance has been hit. This is an an action-adventure first and foremost, stealth game second, and after three WoA games + Freelancer, IMO making for the single overall best stealth game of all time, I think IO has given the stealth genre enough to have earned a break. You just need to adapt to seeing Mission Stories not as the "training wheels" you want to break out of, but as the objectives in and of themselves.

Really, the only thing I think the campaign consistently fails on are boss fights, which IMO are all varying degrees of misfire without a single one I enjoyed, unfortunately. Far too gimmicky on the whole, and there were many encounters with normal enemies that IMO stood out more. Thankfully, there are not many of them, and they are over quickly, but I wish they were done better.



My main complaint with the game as a whole is the current TacSim content available. TacSim is the main replayable mode outside of the campaign which IO will be supporting over time. Unfortunately they have put some baffling limitations on it:

[list]
[*]Why aren't all the major mission segments in Tac Sim?? If I want to replay an old mission, and I do because the game's best unlocks are all in those mission challenges, there is thankfully a very robust mission/segment select, but I need to create a whole new savefile for it and more importantly can't use any unlocks as you can in normal TacSim. I do understand IO will probably need some work to adapt the more cinematic/scripted elements of the missions into TacSim, but if this game ends support without any effort to implement this feature it'd be ridiculous. Nobody cares about the lore/realism issues of Bond finding physical collectables within TacSim (the collectables make almost no effort to be diagetic anyway) or TacSim recreating things that should never have been recorded.

[*]Why doesn't TacSim have the game's whole arsenal of guns? I understood this limit in Hitman: WoA because 47 ultimately doesn't have much use for most guns, but this is a game with gunfights as a core gameplay pillar, so I really don't see why weapons like the silenced SMG or burst fire pistol are excluded here. In particular, the decision to limit pistol options to only the MI6 Service Pistol and a silenced variant, leaving the Golden Gun as a mere reskin, feels like actual blasphemy!

[*]For whatever reason, IO have tripled down on Escalations as core content when the Hitman community have been fed up with them for *checks notes* a decade. I don't mind Escalations that are fully different scenarios in each stage, but when it's just "now do it again, but take no damage" come on, implement that as an optional Challenge for a single core gameplay scenario instead of this blatant padding. I would much rather take MGS-esque VR missions in a generic, themeless virtual space over Escalations.
[/list]


TacSim will get more content, but I am mostly just asking for content that's already in the game to be reused in TacSim in order to flesh it out. This is my main gripe with the game and keeps its gameplay from shining on its own as it stands currently.


Overall, First Light is not a generational accomplishment like I feel the WoA trilogy is. It's like an 8/10 very solid action adventure game, with potential to rise to a 9 if IO execute all future DLC/updates absolutely perfectly (which they didn't for WoA frankly, so likely won't here).

For a lot of people I imagine that will be a miss, but if this is the kind of adventure/genre you want right now, and especially if the James Bond license is a plus or full selling point for you, I have no reservations in recommending First Light.

Probably the best movie license adaptation into a game. It's gorgeous, and the dialogue, the music, the ambiance, the locations.. It all matches what you'd expect to see in a Bond movie. Not only that, but there is a ton of optional dialogue to flesh out the world..

We even have a gorgeous full title sequence in the same style as the movies, of appropriate length too.

IO Interactive also didn't forget to treat us to a fair bit of time in MI6, seeing the politics, the research, the intel collection/analysis.. Some NPCs even say words of encouragement etc, it's really well fleshed out.

The game however does suffer from a bit of "content padding", as-in, parkour/travel sequences that are needlessly long and feel like time wasters more than anything else. Which is a confusing choice for a game that really wouldn't be too short without them anyway. (I count 2 or 3 hours of padding over 18 hours of gameplay in total for the base story)

We also have an extra gameplay mode with challenges, XP, unlocks, etc... Both to enjoy the game even more, and to get better at it, very well designed too.

Overall, it's a glowing recommendation from me. It's a VERY expensive game, but it is perhaps the first time that I can say with confidence that you can see a level of quality and polish that justifies the price point.

Summary: 
Combat is satisfying, missions and narrative flows surprisingly well (compared to Hitman games). Great balance of storytelling/diegetic segments and satisfying combat, as well as very exciting blockbuster set piece segments (but not much interaction). A very successful aspect of the game is how it introduces new gameplay elements/mechanics that are relevant to the story, characters, and narrative, while making you feel like you're in control. Often times, I caught myself seeing something interesting, then wondering: "Maybe I'll use that later" or "maybe that'll become a new enemy type later" - and then it happens. It's fun, but a bit short (15-20 hours) and there is not much replayability compared to Hitman WOA.

Pros:
- The most fun aspect is definitely the combat - ONCE YOU GET USED TO IT. I had to rebind keys multiple times and dial in my controls over the course of a few levels to get Bond to do things I wanted, when I wanted. When you do get the hang of combat, gunfights completely change - They are no longer about shooting from behind cover and only running when grenades are thrown at you. It's all about about forward momentum - I run, shoot, and when I'm out of ammo, I don't reload - I throw the gun at the nearest guy and take his gun. Out of ammo again? Bond can kick up dropped guns into his hands while still sprinting, without losing any momentum. Enemies behind cover? I can vault over and kick the gun out of a guy's hands and catch it in mid-air, all in one smooth sequence. The action just flows very well - of course, on the highest difficulty you have to really use your gadgets wisely and choose your shots carefully (there are a bit too many explosive barrels placed very conveniently than I would like), but still - switching to your enemy's gun is faster than reloading.

- The story feels VERY 007. Lots of witty dialogue, doesn't take itself TOO seriously, lots of a big set-pieces, lots of over-dramatized stuff, but still grounded somehow. I like how it's set in 2026, and is not shy about talking about issues with AI and modern technology. It was a bit predictable at times, but that's the thing - a lot of Bond movies are like that! It really did feel like it had the soul of a Bond movie. A little bit of cheesiness, a little bit of campiness - but not enough to take me out of the story.

- Adding on to the witty dialogue - Bond is casted and written very well. Lots of good, borderline cheesy lines. Lots of witty flirting, lots of good character moments. All the characters were written quite well, although I wish some got more screen time.

- There is a great balance of problem-solving, combat, and character development. The overall pacing of the story, gameplay, and cutscenes was quite good. Although, there were a couple sections that I feel dragged a bit too long, and a couple location transitions that were a bit abrupt. I reloaded the game once thinking I missed some dialogue or a cutscene because I may have exited the level too quickly, but no. It was just immediately on to the next location, no dialogue or explanation of how Bond got there or how much time had passed.

- The way they introduce new plot points and gameplay mechanics is a little bit on-the-nose, but just the right amount in my opinion. A lot of "Chekhov's Guns" - you're shown something (or someone), and you should expect them to be relevant to gameplay or story later. I will say, the payoffs were mostly decent, but some were pretty underwhelming/underutilized or came in too late into the game.

Cons:
- Some bugs still - sometimes I start floating in the air when doing specific movements (mostly jumping stuff in combat and ziplines), but I quickly get teleported back to a checkpoint (without reloading progress).

- A bit short - I know it's mainly a story-driven game, but I would have preferred some side-quest-y stuff that wasn't Escalations, especially during segments of the game where it really feels like you're in a "hub" area.

- Some segments are a bit too linear - This is very minor, but I feel like the most fun parts were the larger combat levels with lots of verticality where I could choose to go loud or stealthy. Funnily enough, some of the most satisfying levels were the capture-the-flag exercises in the training grounds - which weren't "real".

- Vehicles are a bit underused. I was very excited during the first real driving sequence, but then the rest felt very "on-the-rails", even though they were clearly big spectacle set-pieces. I want more freedom to drive around, more paths to take, maybe one that requires driving in another direction other than "forward". The one time you DO get to drive in any direction you want, you are literally stuck in a room. Some driving sequences really felt like they should have been cutscenes - you'll probably know which one I'm talking about.

- Not much replayability outside of Escalations and certain combat-heavy levels. Not many options to tackle objectives like in Hitman. Hitman usually has more than 1 target and maybe a side-objective per level, with 3-4 "scripted" ways of dealing with each target, as well as challenges (SASO, Sniper Assassin, etc). This game usually only has 2-3, and sometimes there is no way to accomplish an objective without using "hint-tracking" (Mission Stories), and there are challenges, they are very limited.


Notes:
Although the game does a fairly decent job at introducing the combat mechanics, the game really skips out on the hand-to-hand combat tutorials - it is actually a lot more in-depth than people may realize. I suggest going into the Tac-Sim and doing the Advanced Close Combat escalations as soon as they become unlocked. You also get to practice in a more sandbox-y like space to really nail the combat and the transitions from ranged to melee or vice-versa.


Hitman Comparison:
It's a lot less sandbox-y as Hitman, but still has a bit of Hitman DNA. The "Eavesdrop" and story hint mechanics are very similar to the "Mission Stories" of Hitman WOA. The detective/spy-like levels are definitely a lot smaller and more compartmentalized compared to Hitman's sprawling levels (Sapienza, Mumbai, even Paris). Some iconic parts of Hitman's sandbox nature is still there though - you can distract enemies by tampering with objects like generators,  radios, etc. to isolate them for a takedown or sneak past them. You also have an inconspicuous refillable emetic poison dart gun (like the Sieker 1 in HItman), as well as a laser that can temporarily blind people. Despite there being no disguises, you can "bluff" non-enforcer type enemies if you are trespassing - which in my opinion, is very realistic, and something I've always wished for in a Hitman game. Replacing Hitman's tossable coins, you can also use your voice to lure enemies to your position. Although, unlike Hitman, the consequence of you literally punching and shooting your way through the entire game is next to nothing.

Although it does have many hallmark Hitman elements, this game is NOT a Hitman game. You have way less freedom in how to tackle levels. You're only able to engage in non-lethal combat in very specific zones, and gunfights are usually only allowed in scripted segments or when certain conditions are met. This means that you can't knock out civilians that might catch you trespassing (you're forced to sneak or bluff them), and you literally can't take out your gun in any of the Hitman-like segments. Additionally, although you can replay the Hitman-like segments to tackle situations differently, this game is a story-driven, linear game, similar to the Uncharted games - just with a bit of Hitman sprinkled in. I don't think it's very replay-able - I would only replay some combat stuff because it's satisfying.

As someone who grew up loving action movies and spy thrillers, this is actually my first time reviewing a story-driven action-adventure game, so take this more as a fan sharing his experience rather than a professional critique.

I'm also a huge 007 fan. I've followed James Bond from Sean Connery all the way to Daniel Craig, watching every film and enjoying every era of Bond in its own way.

When I first heard that a new 007 game was being made, I was honestly a little skeptical. Bond games have always been hit or miss, and I wasn't sure what to expect. But the moment I found out that IO Interactive was developing it, my excitement immediately took over. As a longtime Hitman fan who has been playing since the very beginning, I knew there was a good chance they would understand what makes a spy game special.

And thankfully, they absolutely delivered.

From the moment I started playing, it felt like stepping into a James Bond movie. The gameplay captures the perfect balance of action, espionage, and style that the franchise is known for. Whether you're sneaking through enemy territory, gathering intel, or diving into intense action sequences, everything feels unmistakably Bond.

What surprised me the most was how invested I became in the story. I wasn't just completing missions. I was genuinely excited to see what would happen next. The entire experience felt cinematic, like I was playing through my own Bond film.

The presentation is also top notch. The cinematics are stunning, the environments look beautiful, and if you've played Hitman before, you already know the level of detail IO Interactive brings to its games. The sound design and music do an excellent job of building tension and making every moment feel bigger and more memorable.

Most importantly, I had fun. A lot of fun.

At the end of the day, that's what matters most to me. This game reminded me why I fell in love with the James Bond franchise in the first place. It made me feel like a kid again, imagining what it would be like to be the world's greatest spy.

Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it, and if this is the future of James Bond games, then I can't wait to see where the series goes next. I'm already looking forward to the next adventure.

As someone whose first ever video game purchased on release day was 007: Everything or Nothing over 20 years ago, someone who's been an avid fan of 007 for quite literally as long as I can remember, and as somebody who would consider 007: Nightfire one of their personal Mt. Rushmore games, 007: First Light is absolutely worth the hype, as long as you understand what you're in for.

The Bond franchise, whether it's the movies, or the books, or the games, is almost never the trendsetter. The experience you'll get is almost always more of a celebration of whatever happens to be popular at the time. Whether it's blaxploitation like Live and Let Die, the Star Wars craze of Moonraker, the Hitchcock love letter that is From Russia With Love, the 90's high-energy action wave GoldenEye rode, or the obviously Batman Begins-influenced Casino Royale, 007 wears its' influences on its' sleeves, and ironically helped influence and create most of the things they borrow from.

The games have always been the same way. GoldenEye 007 was revolutionary at the time, but it wouldn't have gotten there without Sega's Virtua Cop and Doom. Agent Under Fire and Nightfire, two of my favorites, both captured the essence of FPS games at the time. Halo was an obvious influence, and both Halo and Agent Under Fire both have heavy roots in Quake, with Halo taking the arena shooter genre to consoles, and Agent Under Fire doing something similar while also running on id Tech 3 (Quake III.) They also relied on the Need For Speed developers for the in-game driving levels. EA Black Box was releasing arguably the best NFS games while also working on Everything or Nothing's driving levels.

The point I'm trying to make here is that everybody who seems to hate on this game goes into it expecting essentially Hitman but with James Bond instead. It is not. It's a bit of a salad mix of Hitman, Metal Gear Solid, Uncharted, Watch Dogs, and Payday (specifically the nightclub mission,) and that's FINE. That's what Bond has always done. First Light essentially bounces between the more linear style of first-party PlayStation games like Uncharted and God of War- a lot of slow exposition heavy segments with platforming and massive setpieces which lead to chaotic action, and the more free-form gameplay of games such as Cyberpunk, Payday (the License to Kill mechanic while lore accurate is essentially the same as when your cover is blown in Payday and your mask is forced on,) and Hitman when the game calls for Bond to do actual spy work. 

From a Bond game, it's everything I could've wanted it to be, and more. It celebrates a lot of staples in modern gaming, all of which in return were influenced in some way by James Bond's adventures on the big screen. It has fantastic writing, Patrick Gibson absolutely nails it as 007, and the final few missions are undeniably some of my absolute favorites out of any Bond game ever. If you like story driven linear games which give you freedom of choice and multiple different options when it comes to how you complete almost any objective, First Light is absolutely worth it.

Absolutely Fantastic – The Best James Bond Experience in Years

This game is simply fantastic. From the very first hour, it throws you straight into the James Bond atmosphere and keeps you there for hours on end. It genuinely feels like you're living your own 007 adventure rather than just playing a video game.

One thing I really love is the level design. It's easy to understand, even for idiots like me. The objectives are clear, and there are usually multiple ways to approach every situation. You can take your time, explore, enjoy the story, and immerse yourself in the world, or you can play like a real secret agent—fast, precise, and efficient.

There is something here for almost everyone. Stealth fans, action fans, and people who just want to experience a great James Bond story will all find something to enjoy.

The only downside is performance. If you don't have a good PC, your experience may suffer quite a bit. I highly recommend having an NVIDIA graphics card or at least a strong AMD GPU. Otherwise, you might end up playing at around 30–40 FPS, and honestly, that takes away from the experience.

Overall, this is one of the best games I've played in a long time. It captures the spirit of James Bond perfectly. At times, it genuinely feels like you are James Bond himself.

Highly recommended

007:First light review from a random chud


[h1] Combat [/h1] 

The combat in this game was extremely fluid, reactive, and fun all throughout the story. The combos you could do, to the environmental attacks, it really did feel freeing. When bond struck his opponents, it really did FEEL painful. Awesome design all around.


[h1] The Story [/h1] 

I'm always blinded by gameplay to really think about the story, But the story was actually not bad. the pacing felt fine, and there was no real Endgoal for most of the game (which actually works here, as the game is supposed to depict bond's introduction to the 00 program, and not have some big overarching goal to achieve.) You do finally have an endgoal nearing the end of the game, but even leading up to it made sense. Characters are memorable and fun. (anybody who says DEI or woke is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by the way). Overall, the story did have more ups, than downs, which helps it make a strong, modern introduction to the bond franchise.


[h1] Cast [/h1] 

My oh my, Patrick Gibson IS James Bond to me. He absolutely nailed it! from his quips, humor, and charming personality. Patrick really does have potential to be the new modern Daniel Craig.

MoneyPenny and the other supporting cast do very well, and aren't just NPCs to advance the story. Lennie James does wonders as Greenway, and captures that older veteran who doesn't take ♥♥♥♥ from anybody, PERFECTLY. 


[h1] Visuals [/h1] 
I don't care for visuals in games so this wont be a long section. even on a 5060Ti (8 gb version!) and a ryzen 5 5600g, on medium settings, DLSS targeting 120 fps on 1440p, the game ran very well, except for a few stutters, and it looked amazing. No complaints here


[h1] Misc [/h1] 

Things like the stealth system was integrated very well. I loved the bluffing feature, the things Bond says make sense, and its so in line for him. You can move past an entire restricted area just by talking out of your ass LOL. The gunplay was nice, the animations for picking up guns were fast, but cool. Bond kicking the gun up, to him grabbing it midair, it was good. The amount of weapons to use was average, and the sounds weren't terrible.

overall, the game was worth the 110 CAD to me. story took about 15 hours, and I haven't even touched TacSim yet, so im excited to hop into that. if your not big on games like this, most definitely wait for a sale. But if you don't mind the price tag, buy it!

[b]RATING -> 8/10 (Currently 7/10 but when I play more ik its going to get better for me so...)[/b]

[h2]Intro[/h2]
Before reading, I played on Purist mode or the hardest difficulty and I am just going to go through the chapters and saying what I liked and what I didn't (more stuff about the negatives because when the game is good its amazing).

Another FYI, bond is amazing, the femme fatales are amazing, the side characters (except M and the villains, they are just fine) are amazing. The story is gripping and I love the dialogues as well.
[b](BTW is it just me or does bond look like B.J Novak sometimes)[/b]

I have divided the game into sections I love and sections I dont like as much.

[h2]Goated Section[/h2]
The prologue plus the first couple of chapters (till lets say chapter 3 and some parts of 4) are outstanding. This game has one of the best tutorial sections and the story moves along nicely, I like all the characters and Bond feels like BOND.
Chapter 3 being the highlight of this section, start to finish masterpiece of a level.

[h2]Its Good but not Amazing Section[/h2]
Chapter 4 is where it beings to falter a bit. The start of the chapter is spectacular with so many cool possibilities but then you are subjected repetitive stealth or melee (depending on what you want to do) areas. This part of the chapter just feels like a rehash of the "advanced training" level. But the end is fine with some cool sceneries, so overall its a good chapter but definitely a level below the previous stuff. 

[h2]Bad Section[/h2]
Chapter 5 and 6 is where the game is at its worst for me. Chapter 5 starts with just a long and tedious
section of traversal which could've been made better with a tighter and better inclusion of gadgets, but it just feels boring and useless as it currently is. Which is then followed by a series of fire fights which is cool but to me this is where the biggest nitpick I have with the game comes into play, THE AMMO SCARCITY. In earlier and further "license to kill" sections the ammo isn't a big issue as the enemies are grouped up and its easy to go from one enemy to the next in a fluid manner combining gadgets, gunplay and cqc. But here I was constantly out of ammo and there were no resources near by for me to regen them and use the gadgets. The firefight section is separated into mini firefights each connected by a rest period. This is fine but the distance between the mini firefights is too long imo so the trifecta isn't fluid and it feels like I need to constantly run, hide and search for ammo to kill all the enemies (I have only played through the level once, so maybe when I do the challenges for the level I will get a better appreciation for it but as it stands this is my opinion).

Chapter 6 for is a nothingburger of a level. I find the end sequence and the start (end of chapter 5 ig) amazing. But there is a huge portion in the middle which just feels like a rehash of chapter 3. Some of the next chapters also contain parts of chapter 3 but the environments are hugely different so it feels different and unique but for chapter 6 it just feels the same. Chapter 6 also includes one of the worst boss fights in the game. The first time I started this I felt this could be similar to the Mr. Freeze boss fight from the Arkham game but alas its not. You just run around wait for the boss to come to a location and use a gadget (this is where bond not carrying a gun in most of the missions becomes really annoying) and boom boss takes some damage. You cannot engage with the boss in cqc at all even though you already fought him before and lowkey whopped some ass. So this chapter has some highlights but most of it is just okay to atrocious.

[h2]Another Goated Section[/h2]
But now comes chapter 7 which is as expected one of the best parts of the game (it really is personification of the meme). From the start to finish its gripping, funny and the trifecta combat is the best in this section. I had so much fun playing this level and weaving from one style to another. It also helps that this level introduces my favorite gadget. 

7 followed by 8 is another amazing chapter the atmosphere and the environment is amazing the mini quests before the main fight/stealth section is fun (the bond girl as well :))). But the biggest improvement, WE FINALLY GET A SILENCED PISTOL. The following fight section is new and so cool, followed by a much better mini boss fight in the middle, followed by some of the coolest action set pieces in the game followed by another solid boss fight to end the level. (Also the ending of this chapter, beautiful). Just two amazing chapters which shows how good IOI can be.

[h2]Good, the Bad and the Ugly Section[/h2]
But, Then comes chapter 9 and 10. I have the same issue with both chapters. It starts out great there is some really cool and fun sections in the middle and then the end is just bad or average. [spoiler] Spoilers from now on for the last two levels. As soon as we had to face the android enemy my interest levels went down considerably, the whole game play loop is run around if an android comes close stun it or call the ball to destroy it, its just boring and repetitive. [/spoiler] The chapter has a nice end to it with a solid and cinematic chase sequence but the android enemeies leave a sour taste in my mouth. Similarly, chapter 10 starts out with a bang. Keeps building into some of the best fight sequences in the game. Blasting through the enemies is challenging but so fun. [spoiler] Then when we get our gadgets the chapter becomes a lot easier but it feels so fresh to spam gadgets on enemies, its just a funny section before the end. But the issues start as soon as we get into the car. The car sequence is nothing to write home about idk if we can even die in this sequence its just boring, also I hoped we could drive the car but was so disappointed that it was just a batmobile fight sequence. Then it is followed by a boring traversal sequence followed by a boss fight which is just slightly different than the boss fight in chapter 6. [/spoiler] All in all if during a boss fight I have to run more often than fight or shoot I don't like it. So I don't like the ending fight either. But the end cinematic for the chapter with the bond theme is just chef's kiss, perfect.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
So all in all its a mixed bag with some amazing chapters and some mid to bad chapters. But I enjoyed the heck out of the game and cannot wait to complete all the challenges and get all the achievements.

Anyways, 007 First Light, is a really good, sometimes great, action stealth game. IO Interactive was the perfect studio to make a Bond game, and they brought to this game the great level design and atmosphere of the HItman franchise. The story is good, with the voice acting in particular being great for all the major characters. He is, thankfully, not sanitized and his character has some edge and personality. The story gets a little convoluted and cliche near the end, but it's still enjoyable.

The game needed one or two more classic infiltration missions and a tighter conclusion to the story to push it into that coveted 9/10 range. Overall a really good genre-blending action game and something all Bond fans should play.

[h1]Absolutely a candidate for GOTY.[/h1]

[h1]Story[/h1]
I decided to give the game a chance out of no reason. I was never a James Bond fan—did not even watch a single movie from the franchise—yet still, the game managed to hook me with its story. I was expecting somewhat good gameplay, but this kind of a compelling story with great presentation and excellent voice acting? I was not expecting that at all. I'd love to see Patrick Gibson's James Bond on the big screen now.

[h1]Combat & Gameplay[/h1]
Moving on to the gameplay, melee combat is so fun! At first, I thought it would be simple and situational, but no: throwing enemies, cracking their heads into objects, and watching the environment collapse... the environmental interaction is at a maximum level, which really makes the combat system shine. Gunplay is not as strong as melee, but you can still have some cool and satisfying moments with it; the feedback and feeling of the weapons are solid.

[h1]Stealth & Gadgets[/h1]
Stealth is also surprisingly fun. It's mostly dependent on distracting enemies to clear your path or luring them into isolated areas for clean take-downs. There is a good amount of gadgets (you can bring 3 or 4 of them into each main mission) and they all have distinct uses, adding great versatility to both stealth and combat.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Overall, we absolutely need games like this, especially in a world where the industry is flooded with online service games or Ubisoft-style open-world games where you do the same boring things over and over again.

As long as you aren't expecting HITMAN (which, admittedly, for a spy-game developed by IOI, I wouldn't fault you for expecting), First LIght is a solid game.  The gameplay has several parts: gunplay, open-puzzle and driving are the main ones.
The open-world puzzles feel like a dialed-down version of HITMAN: WoA - usually having a couple of solutions revealed to you through eavesdropping - and a couple others to find yourself. There is also a lot of the boring "yellow-paint" parkour sections where you vault, climb, hang and shimmy like every other modern 3rd-person adventure game. There are also some decent sections of social stealth, although the [i]Bluff[/i] button and several of the gadgets can trivialise most of them.
The gunplay feels alright, but isn't exactly Max Payne. The fluid movement, quick TTK and ability to (temporarily) slow time feel pretty badass at times, and I would recommend playing on [i]Purist[/i] difficulty, and resisting the urge to play the game as a cover shooter unless you're stuck. The difficulty still feels a bit easy, even on Purist.
The driving is a bit dull, the cars all handle like you can't crash/fail, but there aren't too many vehicle sections in the game, and they usually have some gimmick to at least mix things up.
There are challenges and collectibles, but I feel no need to replay the main story and earn 100%,

[h1]⭐ Recommended — Earn the Number[/h1]
IO Interactive nailed the feeling of [i]becoming[/i] Bond, and after spending real time with it, this is an easy thumbs up.

[h2]🔫 Gunplay & Combat[/h2]
The shooting feels [b]fantastic[/b]. The hit feedback is satisfying, and firefights stay snappy and responsive instead of floaty. What really makes the combat stand out, though, is how seamlessly you can flow between [b]melee and firearms[/b] — switching from a hand-to-hand takedown straight into a gunfight is smooth and intuitive, and the animations tying it all together are [b]gorgeous[/b]. On top of that, the environment is interactive and weaves naturally into the fight, so you can use what's around you mid-encounter without it ever feeling clunky.

[h2]🥷 Stealth & Player Freedom[/h2]
Stealth is there if you want it, but it's [b]very optional[/b]. You can always boil any situation down to:
[list]
[*]a satisfying brawl
[*]a fun shootout
[*]or all of it at once — your call
[/list]
To be clear, this isn't an open-ended sandbox like [i]HITMAN[/i]; it's a more linear, directed experience. But that [b]absolutely doesn't make it any less fun[/b] — if anything, it keeps the pacing tight and the action constantly flowing.

[h2]💥 Action & Set Pieces[/h2]
The action is [b]brilliantly directed[/b]. The big sequences are choreographed with a real cinematic touch — they escalate at the right pace, never overstay their welcome, and keep that pulse-pounding momentum a Bond game lives and dies by.

[h2]🎬 Atmosphere & Presentation[/h2]
It absolutely sells the "young, reckless recruit climbing through MI6" fantasy. The espionage tone, the polish, and the overall production values are top-tier, and it runs smoothly.

[h2]✅ Verdict[/h2]

Стрельба ощущается [b]превосходно[/b]. Фидбэк от попаданий приятный, а перестрелки остаются чёткими и отзывчивыми, без «ватного» ощущения. Но по-настоящему выделяет боевую систему то, насколько плавно можно переключаться между [b]ближним боем и огнестрелом[/b] — перейти от рукопашного добивания сразу в перестрелку легко и интуитивно, а связывающие всё это анимации просто [b]шикарны[/b]. Вдобавок окружение интерактивно и органично вплетается в сражение, так что прямо посреди схватки можно использовать всё, что вокруг, и это нигде не ощущается топорно.

[h2]🥷 Стелс и свобода игрока[/h2]
Стелс есть, если хочется, но он [b]очень опционален[/b]. Любую ситуацию всегда можно свести к:
[list]
[*]смачной рукопашной
[*]весёлой перестрелке
[*]или ко всему сразу — как пожелаешь
[/list]
Сразу скажу: это не открытая песочница, как [i]HITMAN[/i], а более линейный, срежиссированный опыт. Но это [b]абсолютно не делает игру менее весёлой[/b] — наоборот, держит темп плотным, а экшен в постоянном потоке.

[h2]💥 Экшен и постановка[/h2]
Экшен поставлен [b]блестяще[/b]. Крупные сцены срежиссированы с настоящим кинематографичным размахом — они нарастают в нужном темпе, не затягиваются и держат тот самый напряжённый драйв, без которого Бонд немыслим.

[h2]🎬 Атмосфера и подача[/h2]
Игра полностью передаёт фантазию о «молодом, дерзком новобранце, пробивающемся через ряды MI6». Шпионский тон, вылизанность и общий уровень продакшена — на высшем уровне, и всё работает плавно.

[h2]✅ Итог[/h2]
Уверенный, стильный и по-настоящему увлекательный взгляд на историю становления Бонда. Отзывчивая стрельба, текучая боевая система с переходами между ближним боем и огнестрелом, красивые анимации и хорошо поставленный экшен с настоящим шпионским привкусом — однозначно рекомендую.

It's been a long, LONG time since we had an awesome spy game. But when I first heard about IO kicking the tires on a 007 game, I was 100% in for the ride.

After experiencing it first-hand now for over 20 hours, I can say that First Light was indeed awesome, and over the course of playing, it brought back memories of playing Goldeneye on the N64 during my childhood. And then when I saw the introduction to the game from Lana Del Rey... That's when I was really in for the ride. 

First Light's story felt like I was watching one of the Bond films on the big screen, with several different variations of gameplay inspired by the likes of Hitman and Uncharted, just to name a couple. By the way, the fake surrendering, bluffing and complying mechanics of the game were incredibly clever, yet brilliant.

This game was nothing like Hitman (although there are some people people that seem to be disappointed by this aspect), and that's okay, because First Light did what it set out to do - to tell another story in the Bond saga at its own pace. 

The performances by Patrick Gibson and Lennie James as Bond and Greenway, respectively, were outstanding, and it was really awesome to see that chemistry really blossom as the game advanced further along. But what really did it for me was the cinematography and the music. Perhaps the most stunningly beautiful scenery, and mood-setting sound in a game in quite some time. Again, felt like watching Bond on the big screen all over again. 

It's incredibly difficult to not become charmed over this phenomenal entry IO has provided us. Although a lot of folks were a bit skeptical about First Light at first, but I definitely was more than pleased with how it turned out.

I'll be looking forward to what's next.

There were some severe disappointments. 
The OST is up front as the biggest offender, I felt like I was waiting the entire game for a crescendo that never came.

Entire sequences that are just lengthy in-engine cutscenes kill replayability/speedrunning. Despite a driving sequence in the tutorial, there are 2? chase sequences in the game (largely scripted cinematic set pieces) and the singular moment in the spy car it's deployed in a little box... well, and a mission that isn't in the game yet. 

Speaking of missions in the game, post-story, there are 5 "Escalations" these are three-tiered missions that are very limited in scope: the first two (Advanced Tactical Training, Advanced Close Combat Training) are expansions on the tutorials, and the other three are: clear a modified single encounter from the story (Lords of Rust/Aleph's Port, Arctic Skies/The gandries, The Assault/... they actually have the same name) 

Honestly, I wouldn't mind this very much, but the two available "Operations" (Clean Infiltration, The Garden Party) are also just single encounters in a larger room.
If you've played any of the Arkham games, they're very similar to the "Predator Missions" and then the challenges ask you to do sub-tasks (Don't get seen, No Gadgets, Hack a Laptop)

SIDE NOTE: I LIKE THE IDEA OF ASSET REUSE, I WOULD LIKE TO BE ABLE TO PLAY THE GAMEPLAY PARTS OF THE GAME EASILY. WHY ONLY THE 3?

There's also like... no reward for clearing all the challenges? It's just something to do to earn points for the TacSim. Completion rewards you with the story mission outfits, but I'm still at 18/39? Now I could be at 22, if I bought the deluxe edition for the gaudy gold gadgets, but half of the outfits in the game are earned outside of the game? Alienware? A physical copy is the only way to get the classic tux?

Purchasable in TacSim: 
Tacsim Outfit
Event Staff Uniform
Chessmaster Suit
8 Weapons
1 skin for the pistol
15 upgrades for the gadgets (size, duration, resource cost)
3 gadget skins (guys what are we doing here)

All those for 7 missions, and an upcoming mission that won't even use those unlocks? 
The progression is such that I don't even think you unlock the last gadget at 100% right now?

Either way, this framework of a progression system is a more free-form way of unlocking things than Hitman where you have to wipe your left cheek in the third stall on a specific level to unlock the best gun in the game if you don't want to swipe credit card, so that MIGHT be good if they add stuff in, but I kinda regret spending my time on this currently as there's no meaningful reward.

So instead of more levels where you can approach things your own way, they padded the playtime with busywork and stretched things that should've been one tight, short level. The game can be a bit of a slog at times because of it.

Combat is fun, and once you finally get let loose with the gadgets and the different ways to take down enemies, it's great. But that's exactly the problem, a lot of the time you are not let loose. Half the game feels like tutorials or very hand-held levels. I don't mind linearity, but let me play. And once you give me a gadget, stop trying to take it away from me multiple times.

Same issue with the villains, I'd have liked them to be a bit more Bond villains. They tried with one, but it comes mostly toward the end and it wasn't that exciting because it was slowly fed to you instead of letting it land.
Some people seem to dislike the driving. I actually enjoyed it, much better than other Bond games for sure. And it was cool to see all the references to the movies and games at MI6, especially QLab.

[b]In short:[/b] if you're a fan of James Bond movies, you will absolutely love this game. If you're a fan of Hitman, you will either love or hate this game. If you're not a particular fan of either, I don't know, maybe you'll like it?

[h2]Things I liked[/h2]
As a James Bond enjoyer, I am happy to say that this game nails EVERY single James Bond trope without making them feel shoehorned. It has the megalomaniacal supervillain, the intimidating foreign henchmen, Q, M, Moneypenny, the car, the gadgets, the brutal interrogation scene, TWO absurdly slow deathtraps, jetsetting trips to half a dozen exotic locales, set-piece fights in absurd locations and a preposterously well-equipped secret lair somewhere that has no business being so secret. All of this is accompanied by a soaring musical score that references the classics while integrating modern touches.

At the same time, the game doesn't treat the canon with fanboyish reverence. It's happy to make changes to characters and tropes when it wants to. This is 100% an origin story for Bond - an examination of how someone could get this way.

This game also has the most important aspect of the best Bond movies, which is the smooth ramping from sensible to insane. The first real mission starts with you infiltrating a Slovakian hotel, and ends with you trying to find a parachute as you're falling out of a plane, and at no point does the sequence of events that led to it feel like there was a sudden lurch towards absurdity. Everything feels smooth.

For all that I'm cynical about corporations, this doesn't feel like some cynical shareholder-approved cash-in. This feels like a James Bond game made by people who [i]love James Bond[/i], and [i]wanted[/i] to make a video game about James Bond.

[h2]Things I liked less[/h2]
As a person who has 200 hours in Hitman, I can't help but judge this game in that light. It isn't anywhere near as freeform as World of Assassination. Hitman WoA dumped you in a level, gave you a target and said "work it out yourself." 007 First Light is definitely a more on-rails experience - a sequence of set-pieces separated by small sections where you can mess about and explore a little before moving on. I could still feel the DNA of Hitman beneath the surface, and at some points it felt like IO were working against their own strengths as developers. This is even more notable given that a lot of features are clearly carried over from Hitman.

[h2]Things I did not like at all[/h2]
The CQB system needs a massive overhaul. Some enemies will just grab you and throw you into a wall, which will deal more than half your health in damage, then immediately grab you again without you being able to do anything about it. This is particularly notable in the Tactical Simulation missions.

An acceptable James Bond story with a genuinely fun (if not, at this point, very common) combat system, which distinguishes itself through satisfying environmental interactions. 
[hr][/hr]

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]
[hr] [/hr]

[b] What works: [/b]
The combat is easy to pick up, intuitive, and very fun. Though hardly blazing any new trails, the manner in which you can dispatch your enemies is both various and fluid, and I had a blast tearing through swathes of armed soldiers, barreling into cover, shooting the guns from their hands, and throwing myself neck deep into a pile of grunts to further take them to pieces with my bear hands. You will feel cool!!

The incorporation of bluffing into the stealth sequences is very in-character for the series, and the bespoke interactions are a joy to watch. The bluff/lure system is definitely the better of the game's two resource management systems -- Speaking of!

[b] What doesn't work: [/b]
The gadget ecosystem is tiny, and arduous to interact with, they will either be far too good to not use, or utterly useless. Once you decide which is which, you will more than likely stick with the same selection of three/four the entire game. Likely knowing the balancing of the gadgets would be an issue, the developers implemented a resource system, requiring that you break from whatever cool spy thing you're doing and scrounge for chemicals and batteries like a junkie stripping the copper wiring from a suburban home, eager for their next fix. It's a bad system, and more often than not resulted in bumping my head against the battery requirement to hack an object (necessary to continue!) and having to walk in circle waiting for the battery to recharge so that I could pick up the amount necessary to hack the object, and proceed. It kills the pacing, and while I really enjoy the various environmental interactions they open up in the stealth/gameplay I really wish they were more fleshed out.

While I want to give this game its laurels for its length, and quality of production, but its later level design comes off as a genuine dissapointment. Bond's first mission offers what turns out to be a false promise in terms of level design. It offers a large sandbox style level which, while you mostly progress through in a linear fashion, offers several routes to obtain information/access to subsequent areas. While playing I was excited for the tutorial to end, and for subsequent missions to offer further depth to this formula -- depth which never comes. In terms of open-endedness, the game's missions are funnel shaped, by the end you're locked to a single hallway, and a single means of progressing, and while the gameplay never stops being fun, I can't help but be dissapointed by the ghost of the promise those first few missions seemed to be giving me.

[h2] Story [h2]
[hr] [/hr]

Evokes classic Bond in spades, while introducing surprising and unique elements which still feel right at home in a spy thriller. Clearly made with a lot of love for the franchise, and the best moments are ones where the developers allude to classic elements of the franchise while squaring them in the world of the story they're telling. The character of Bond is superb, and manages to paint a picture of a fledgling agent without scuffing the character traits which Bond is so known for. Its weaknesses, meanwhile, perhaps feel elevated because so much is done well that it begins to feel less like a strong AAA story mode, and more like flawed screenplay. 

[b] Spoilers Below! [/b]

[spoiler] The core villain of the piece, Damien, is used far too sparingly, while I imagine his presence was diminished so that his role as a twist villain felt impactful, it manages to do the opposite, and I largely did not care for the stakes he presented, much as the game tried. I feel especially burned by the failure to establish his character particularly because he is so compelling, he mirrors Bond well as an antagonist, and his mask's Romanesque design is a genuinely cool, and unique element of the game. In post, you can feel the gaping void left by his character in the early hours of the game, and the fact that so few moments are dedicated to seeding his presence feels confusing, and frustrating, specifically because his potential was so rich. [/spoiler]

[hr] [/hr]

All in all I would recommend the game, if you can get it on sale all the better, I would love for the post-launch to be inundated with DLC -- preferably continuations of the story -- which deliver on the more open-ended experiences IO does best. (Alternatively, more in-depth Tactical Simulations that recreate classic Bond setpieces would be welcome too, either way, please don't let this game collect dust!)

I might extend my words a bit because of what I’m about to tell, but my goal isn’t to write a long review. I’ve been in love with the James Bond franchise ever since I was a kid. If I had the chance to be a character in this world, I would definitely want to be the Turkish version of James Bond. As someone who has watched all of his movies, I can easily say that his games are just as successful as his movies are high-quality and memorable.

The first James Bond game I ever played and beat in my life was 007 Nightfire on the PlayStation 2. Even though the PC port was a bit different from the console version, I finished the game on PC as well. 007 Nightfire is the only title that comes to my mind when thinking of a James Bond game, and it’s an experience I will never forget. With its music, characters, sense of stealth, and mission variety, I think it was the most solid game of its era, and it is still a title that can be played with great pleasure today.
(For those who are curious, I'm leaving the link to that amazing soundtrack right here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R-smxdsN-T4&list=RDR-smxdsN-T4&start_radio=1)

Now, let’s get to 007 FIRST LIGHT, presented to us by IO Interactive, which will highly likely be among the games of the year... I’ll keep it short, as I don’t really like writing long reviews.

First and foremost, the biggest element that sets this game apart from the movies and other games is that it delivers a story explaining how James actually became "007," and believe me, this concept is executed beautifully. I have absolutely no complaints about the storytelling or the plot progression; they’ve crafted a beautiful, cinematic, movie-like production. Kudos to IO Interactive. The level designs and gameplay also thoroughly satisfied us.

Slight Feeling of Repetition: In my opinion, some chapters tend to repeat themselves a bit; it barely saves itself, but there is still a slight sense of repetition.

Artificial Intelligence Issues: For instance, let’s say I’m fighting 10 people; there is another enemy just 8-9 meters away, and while we are brawling, he doesn't even notice a thing. Other than these issues, I can say it’s a flawless production. Kudos to IO Interactive once again.

Final Note: By the way, Pierce Brosnan is indisputably the best James Bond.

A great game. A Bond game. Is it a great James Bong game? I don't know. That is not really a fault of the game itself, but the modern interpretation of the character and IP. The iconic Bond theme does clash with the image and doesn't really fit, but that's been an issue for any Bond property this century. The only thing that works as an interpretation of the silliness of Bond in modern day is Archer - a satire. If "007", Bond character name and the music were to be removed from this game, then there's really nothing to distinguish from any other action/adventure property.

This is an incredible espionage game. though. The social stealth is rarely explored in games, so it's a joy to experience whenever possible. Hitman series is my favorite games ever, but I'll try to not compare too much even though control scheme, some gameplay, and even assets are reused from WoA game. This is it's own thing in the end.

The story is too long. Even though the intro and training missions are brief (the training montage is the best tutorial i can remember in any game), they still drag somewhat and final mission that seemed as if it's going to be some quick epilogue to wrap up the game's climax, turned out to be a massive action mission, that just dragged and offered nothing new to the experience.

The best I can describe the gameplay is that it is a fulfilled promise of what the original Splinter Cell Conviction was meant to be. A complete departure from the series established gameplay where instead of stealthing through shadows, it pivoted to social stealth and dynamic freeform CQC combat. I thought it looked like the most amazing thing ever, but fans hated it so Ubisoft pivoted back to series roots and that unique stealth experience did not materialize. Until First Light's gameplay was revealed - it immediately reminded of that original Conviction demo and was like a dream come true. Nothing's perfect, so there's some clunkiness in combat, but the rush one gets from mixing gunplay and melee combat is unmatched. Until a proper John Wick games comes along...

I do hope that this evolves similar to Hitman WoA, where the TacSim mode can expand, remix levels and missions and create more content than the main story. In Hitman the contracts, Arcade and Freelancer are more fun than just replaying the same story missions. The systems and mechanics are primed for having a  ton of different globe-trotting spy operations. Right now at release, the package is somewhat empty. Hopefully this is a success and IOI can grow this franchise to what it can be.

This first outing feels more like a statement of intent rather than a finished project, if that makes sense... great start to a long journey. It would be a tragedy if a game that plays and looks this good would just fizzle out here. (writing this a week after release).

Reading back, there's quite a lot of criticism, and yeah, for first outing with new mechanics and systems, the balancing is wobbly (yet not broken), but it is still a rush and a blast to play through. It is fun, but not dumb fun. Can be challenging at times. Tightly paced. The characters are believable and very well written and performed. The story flows well and makes sense within the world presented- the big plot twists are logically consistent. Actually thinking more about the story, it becomes better and better. Usually game stories are just a string of ideas clumsily put together through convolution and contrivances. 007 First Light is not some masterclass in storytelling, but is refreshingly solid. Over-the-top Bond-esque, yet consistent.

In the era of overpriced FOMO live service grid-a-thon forever games, a spectacle adventure with start, middle and end of this level of quality is to be cherished and celebrated!
