**007 First Light Review – 10/10**

*007 First Light* genuinely feels like the James Bond game fans have been waiting for. From the very beginning, it captures that classic 007 atmosphere: the charm, the danger, the style, and the feeling that you are stepping into the shoes of Bond himself.

What impressed me the most is how much the game clearly respects the source material. You can feel the inspiration from James Bond in almost every part of the experience. The story has that spy-thriller energy you want from a 007 game, and Bond himself is written with the perfect balance of confidence, charm, sharpness, and cool-headedness. He feels like Bond should feel.

The characters are also a big highlight. As the story goes on, you actually start building a connection with them, which makes the missions and the story moments feel more meaningful. It is not just action for the sake of action; the game gives you a reason to care.

Another thing I really appreciated is that the game keeps the spirit of James Bond intact. It feels stylish, classy, and focused on what makes 007 iconic, without trying too hard to become something it is not. It knows what kind of game it wants to be, and it fully delivers on that.

The pacing felt perfect to me. Nothing dragged, nothing felt rushed, and every section kept me engaged. I honestly struggled to find anything negative to say, because the whole experience just felt smooth, polished, and enjoyable from start to finish.

As a disabled gamer, I also want to give credit to the accessibility settings. The game was very playable for me, and that matters a lot. Accessibility can make the difference between simply watching a game and actually being able to experience it yourself. *007 First Light* made that possible, and I respect that a lot.

Overall, *007 First Light* is a fantastic Bond game. It understands the character, respects the franchise, delivers a strong story, and creates that real 007 feeling from beginning to end.

For me, this is a **10/10 Bond game** and an easy recommendation for any James Bond fan.

As a longtime James Bond fan, I had been looking forward to 007 First Light for a long time. After having completed half of the campaign, I can say that I really enjoyed it and would definitely recommend it to Bond fans. However, it didn't quite reach the exceptional level I was expecting.

The biggest strength of the game is its story and characters. The narrative is engaging, the characters are well-developed, and the voice acting and performances are top-notch throughout. It's clear that the developers have a great respect for the James Bond franchise. The iconic gadgets, exotic locations, and familiar Bond atmosphere are all present and handled with care. It genuinely feels like you're playing through a Bond adventure.

That said, there are a few things that held the game back for me.

First, the game starts very slowly. It took me more than five hours before I fired a gun for the first time. While I understand that Bond is a spy and not just an action hero, the opening sections focus heavily on infiltration and espionage. As someone who enjoys FPS games, I found the pacing a little too slow during those early hours.

The controls also felt strange at times, at least on a controller. Reloading is mapped to B instead of X, and steady aim/slow motion is assigned to LB instead of clicking the left joystick. I eventually got used to it, but it never felt completely natural. I also broke the flow of combat when being in "Liscense to kill" situations, since I was searching and pressing the wrong buttons.

Another issue is that the game does too much hand-holding. Almost every object you can interact with, climb, or jump to is highlighted in blue. This makes navigation incredibly easy, but it also removes much of the satisfaction of figuring things out yourself. I would have preferred fewer visual cues and more opportunities to explore and think.

Finally, I wish there had been more puzzles. Bond stories often involve investigation, deduction, and problem-solving, and I think the game could have benefited from a greater focus on that aspect of the character.

Overall, 007 First Light is a very good game with a strong story, excellent characters, and a faithful representation of the Bond universe. It just didn't quite live up to the incredibly high expectations I had going in. If you're a James Bond fan, there's still a lot here to enjoy. Otherwise, I still recommend that game, but I would suggest that you wait for it to be on sale.

Yeah... this is clearly not what I expected, and not what I thought IOI was.

Let me explain.

Every journalist and content creator kept shouting that this was "Uncharted and Hitman combined." The developers never pushed back against those claims, so to me that was essentially confirmation that they agreed with them. In practice, that became part of the marketing campaign, which is why I think the criticism that follows is completely justified.

Even from the trailers, something felt off. It looked like they ripped the soul out of Hitman and replaced it with this clunky, toy-like combat system. Every fight felt awkward and chaotic, like I was controlling an unstable person. Then they added the most stereotypical cinematic action-movie elements imaginable: explosions, shootouts, scripted set pieces.

I thought, "Okay, that's a pretty big red flag." But then again, these are the developers of Hitman, so I figured they had earned my trust.

Release day got closer. Reviewers handed out high scores, everything seemed normal. Early Access arrived, I played the game, and I was genuinely shocked by how stereotypical, scripted, and soulless it felt.

Unlike Hitman, which felt like a game made by talented people with a clear creative vision, this felt like an attempt to imitate something else instead of creating something original.

The game is full of random celebrity cameos. Khaby Lame? Seriously, why? It's such a lazy and lifeless form of fan service aimed at people who don't actually care about games and just want to see something recognizable or popular. Whether the game has soul, whether it was crafted by talented developers, whether it has a genuine vision — none of that seems to matter.

Surely humanity hasn't fallen so far that people genuinely eat this stuff up... right?

Then I checked the negative reviews. Almost all of them focused on technical issues. Hardly anyone talked about how painfully mediocre the game is or how desperately it tries to copy other franchises.

It honestly feels like the only people buying this game are casual gamers who have barely played any truly great games in their lives.

That's when I realized that this mediocrity wasn't accidental. It feels like IOI deliberately threw away its legacy, creativity, vision, and talent in order to appeal to the broadest and least demanding audience possible.

And it worked.

The game got over 90% positive reviews. They made quick money. But then what?

Around 70,000 people played it at launch. The player count is already stagnating, and it will probably continue to stagnate because this is a painfully average game with no real replayability or depth.

Hitman: World of Assassination is basically a collection of games that are nearly ten years old at this point. Even at its peak, it only had around 10,000 concurrent players. But here's the funny part: when I check SteamDB today, it still has over 5,000 players online. After all these years, it has only lost about half of its player base.

Why?

Because instead of chasing shallow cinematic spectacle, it offered realistic and detailed NPCs, memorable targets, incredible sandbox levels, and maps designed with genuine passion and vision.

I would not recommend this game to any Hitman fan.

As a mindless cinematic experience to play for a couple of evenings with a beer? If that's all you're looking for, it's probably a 5–6/10.

But if you're expecting the depth, creativity, and replayability that made Hitman special, you'll be disappointed.

Finally we got a James Bond game worth playing, and it took long enough. Nothing here is trying to break new ground, but everything works. The controls feel right, the pacing holds, the fun is everywhere, and the mix of stealth and action trade off at a rhythm that keeps things fresh without tipping into exhaustion.

The stealth especially has one thing going for it that most games in the genre get wrong. The detection radius behaves like an actual human operation. Getting spotted doesn't trigger a battalion-wide panic across the entire map knowing you exist. The alert stays local, stays logical, and suddenly the whole experience breathes differently.

The story sells you a clear premise up front, then pulls the rug on everything you assumed. It earns the twist. The Bond atmosphere is all there too. Beautiful woman, beautiful woman walking out of the water, beautiful woman who can match Bond at every step, the Aston Martin, and of course a villain headquarters so absurdly massive in the middle of nowhere that no functioning government could have possibly missed it.

When the credits rolled, it left a specific kind of empty that only comes from something that was completely, uncomplicatedly good. Miss this game already. Stealth games this well-made are rare now. The Tacsim is fine, but it can't replicate the pull of a story being told well for the first time.

IOI, make the sequel ASAP, please.

P.S. Patrick Gibson IS James Bond. Just hire him for the movie already, for god's sake.

As a lifelong James Bond fan, I absolutely loved 007 First Light and had a great time from start to finish. Playing in 4K made the experience even better. The visuals are generally clean, sharp, and stylish, with some fantastic environments and cinematic presentation that truly capture the Bond atmosphere. That said, there were occasional moments where the graphics and animations felt strangely dated, almost like a polished 2013-2014 game rather than a modern AAA title.

The biggest highlight for me was the gameplay. The stealth mechanics are excellent, rewarding patience and planning without becoming frustrating. Combat is equally satisfying, with fluid fights that make Bond feel capable without turning him into a superhero. The blend of stealth, action, gadgets, and cinematic set pieces kept me engaged throughout most of the campaign.

The first two-thirds of the game are fantastic. The pacing is strong, the missions are exciting, and every new location feels like a proper Bond adventure. I constantly looked forward to what came next.

Unfortunately, the final third loses some momentum. The story starts feeling stretched beyond what it needed to be, and certain plot developments come across as forced. In particular, the classic "supporting character sacrifices themselves to help the hero" trope felt predictable and emotionally unearned. The ending section could have been tighter and more impactful with less padding.

The mysterious woman plot (main female lead) was very well put and left with a good hang for further JB games continuation.

Pros:

* Excellent stealth gameplay
* Satisfying combat and takedowns
* Strong Bond atmosphere
* Great cinematic presentation
* Beautiful visuals in many areas

Cons:

* Occasional dated-looking graphics and animations
* Final act feels unnecessarily extended
* Some story beats rely on overused tropes

Despite its flaws, I had an amazing time. The incredible first two-thirds, fun gameplay, and authentic Bond feel easily outweigh the weaker ending. As a James Bond fan, this is exactly the kind of game I've wanted for years.

[h1]Yet Another Unfortunate Victim of the "should've just made a movie" Effect[/h1]

[h2]Why am I counter-signaling?[/h2]
Simply put: I love James Bond's videogames. Unoriginally, Goldeneye was one of the first three games my hands ever interacted with, and Nightfire remains among the greatest FPS games in my mind. Omitting the movies since this is a game review, I was obsessed with this franchise to the point of genuinely wanting to renounce my citizenship and become a British national, just in the hopes that I could go work for MI6 one day. This all came crashing down when they tried to "reinvent" Bond with the abysmal choice in actor that was Daniel Craig, and I assumed after Casino Royale that Hollywood was just going to drag this franchise through the modernization toilet until it died.

Then I saw the trailer for this game, and decided I'd give the franchise another shot. Yes, it's an origin story (trash), yes, they've "reimagined" most of the characters. Yes, the themes and personalities are sanitized for the sensibilities of a modern audience. But where it mattered: The presentation, action, and Bond himself? It looked like we were finally back on the right track, albeit a bit unnecessarily redone. Silly me.

[h2]IO Interactive[/h2]
You would think that the idea is genius: Get the guys best known for making one of the most famous assassination puzzle-solving sims of all time, and have them do a spy game all about reconnaissance and social-engineering. There's absolutely no way this could ever go wrong. Oh, but wait... right, the spy in question is James Bond, 007, one of the most famous movie spies in all of fiction. This is where the issues begin, because if you're a Hitman fan, you'll immediately notice that there's a lack of, well, problem-solving to do. Everything is laid out for you from the get-go, there are sections of the map where you are allowed to fist-fight, and sections of the map where you're allowed to use guns. There is never a moment where the game presents you with a problem, and then makes you figure out how you want to solve it. Instead, you are presented with a scenario in which Bond, the character, has a problem, and then immediately fed the solution by your UI. This is because, unlike Agent 47, Bond is not an emotionless psychopath, and in order to keep from breaking character, IO Interactive stuck the biggest training wheels they could find onto this game just to ensure you could never do anything that would compromise Bond's behaviors.

Which segways into the other issue: If you're a fan of classic Bond games, then you'll be stuck for hours with interactive cutscenes before the game ever puts a gun in your hand, and lets you blast away at badguys. They created a game that only just barely appeals to either of these core demographics: The free-agency problem solving of Hitman, and the high paced intense action of old Bond games. Why? Because once again the goal wasn't to make a videogame, it was to make a movie.

[h2]Closing Statement[/h2]
There is a positive review on this page that literally just says "Feels like playing a Bond movie." I honestly hate that notion, because I shouldn't be "playing a bond movie," I should be playing a Bond game. Certain stories are made to be told in a movie format, and there was a time when other stories were tailor made to be told through a videogame format. This is apparently a lost art, because now every single videogame is written and directed just like a movie, with sections that handhold the player heavily to make sure they don't do anything that compromises the morals or behaviors of the protagonist while being forced to navigate a bloated, scripted set piece. I cannot see myself replaying this after I finally beat it, simply because I am not looking forward to going through the exact same tedium and interactive cutscenes over and over again, all so I can brag about finding all the collectibles or challenges I of course missed on my first playthrough, and I genuinely cannot believe the idea that anyone else would be inclined to do so also.

It's serviceable as a Bond story, at least, it's better than any of the crap that came out of the Daniel Craig era, but it was very clearly written to be a movie, and that's what it should've been made into.

So I dont normally care to leave reviews on anything, just not something I like doing generally, but having just completed this games campaign I felt I had to say something. 

This game is... AMAZING!

I was hesitant to purchase this at first, due to the price tag, but I decided to "pull the trigger" being a fan of James Bond. This game may not be a long story, I completed it on normal difficulty in appx 14 hours, but it has replayability just like the hitman games. There is more than one way to go about each mission. There is also a TacSim game mode that I havent delved into yet, but its essentially just extra missions and challenges. The missions are fun and not boring, they dont feel like the same mission over and over again, some objectives are more obvious than others, but like I stated, more than one way to go about each one. There is stealth aspects and massive shootouts with tons of (optional) explosions, so it definitely captures the James Bond thrill.
 
The Story is fun and engaging, and its much like watching a movie, if im honest. Each chapter/mission left me wanting to go to the next one to see what happens in the story. Most singleplayer story games dont keep me engaged like that anymore due to boring writing or repetitiveness in the missions. If I had to compare, it is basically Hitman gameplay, meets Uncharted story and adventure. 

Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who wants a great story, fun and immersive missions, with tons of action, stealth and problem solving. 

Side note, I played with a controller and had no issues, there was some lag but that was due to my doodoo wifi, seeing as the game has online and offline modes, a simple restart of the game fixed all my issues.

I can’t really recommend 007 First Light right now. The biggest issue for me is the optimization. Compared to games like Hitman 3, the performance feels inconsistent and poorly polished. Even on strong hardware, the FPS can suddenly drop during certain scenes, which hurts the overall experience.

The gameplay also feels too simple and lacks depth. Stealth mechanics are decent at first, but after several missions it starts to feel repetitive and limited. The AI is still AI not as smart as The Last of us series and mission design don’t feel as creative or satisfying as other stealth games.

Another disappointing part is the graphics and overall presentation. The game doesn’t feel “next-gen” at all. In fact, it reminds me of older games in some ways. For example, Batman: Arkham Knight still looks smoother, more polished, and better optimized despite being a much older title. That game had fluid combat, beautiful visuals, and excellent performance, while 007 First Light often feels outdated in both gameplay and visuals.

The story is okay overall — not terrible, but nothing especially memorable either.

This game has me shaken & stirred!

- The presentation is brilliant, You can tell that the developers are huge fans of James Bond and as consequence this game just oozes with charisma and charm - Much like the Ian Fleming character himself. Everything from the UI design, to the locations in the world, to the music, the voice acting, and sound design. Everything comes together in a really exquisite package.

- The story has a topical modern edge to it, and at the same time 'breezy' feeling without overextending itself. And gives pause for heavier emotional moments - which I quite liked. Some of the twists are somewhat easy to predict if you've seen any espionage/action films before. However I would be lying if I said I wasn't enjoying myself the whole time. And some moments genuinely had me smiling from ear to ear. 

- Gunplay felt stiff and awkward to me at first, however toward the end of the game I was mowing down my enemies expediently, even on the hardest difficulty. (Though I did die quite a number of times - I kind of suck.)
You carry limited ammo on all firearms which forces you to play more strategically and think on your feet, 
(Plus you can throw your weapon at enemies which will always be funny to me.)  

- Stealth plays fantastically and can pose a serious challenge - If you're clever enough you can slip through whole levels without getting caught. I also appreciated the nods to the developers previous Hitman games with elements used here. (Such as social stealth, disguises, and other stealth options.) 

- The rest of the game has you moving around almost like Uncharted/Tomb raider, as in limited driving of vehicles, and climbing and navigating all sorts of structures. Most of these to get from place to place, or to position yourself for a stealthy take-down or two. Or many, many more of them.

- Overall, this is genuinely a fantastic game and an absolute banger of a James Bond game. I can't recommend it enough, even if you aren't a James Bond fan, and I will be watching for future news regarding this game and IOI with great interest.

007 First Light is a fine game with fantastic gameplay, a serviceable Bond origin story, and a decent start to (what I hope will be) IO's Bond series going forward. I am eager to see more and it was an absolute pleasure to play. As somebody who is a relatively casual fan of the 007 series (which puts it lightly amongst the titan this franchise is) I can safely say this game is a solid 8/10. Which is marked at a high 8 for sure! This game alone offers a lot for any level of fan of Bond's adventures, from punchy line deliveries and unsubtle references to moments in the legacy. I loved it and most (if not a large majority) of fans will appreciate will find something from this game.

PROS:
- Solid character work, dialogue, and direction! I did enjoy a lot of the characters we were presented with.
- Humor is delightfully witty and chock full of that dry British humor. Good stuff!
- Combat is hard hitting and offers many options for mix-ups in combat, this can be a detriment to some players but for me it added a lot of depth. 
- Gunplay is FANTASTIC. I love how mechanically it works. How fun and tightly knit it feels.
- The action is the game is just enough and in my humble opinion feels well balanced amidst the dialogue/story stuff.
- Puzzles are awesome, if even clever I dare say. I do hope they can ramp up the creativity on them in the next installment. Some silent hill/RE stuff would be nice honestly.
- Audio such as sfx and music are top notch. Brilliantly made
- Intro is SO Bond. AMAZING.
- I like how they tied the name of the game into the theme (somewhat)

CONS [PARTIAL SPOILERS BELOW]:
- Story wise it is serviceable! It is nigh bad at all...I personally would have [spoiler] liked to see a more profound look on Bond and his adventures, if they were hoping to modernize him. His dealings with loss and how that is always counteracts with him being a cold-blooded spy. How would that test him and eventually bring him further from humanity, especially if he loses touch with those that GAVE him a connectivity. Yes, Bond does indeed face loss and has a fire to seek..some justice for it. But I felt it was a bit unexplored and almost brushed aside? This may be also because, I do feel a tad jarred by Bond's underdog personality sometimes since I am so used to him being coldblooded and stonefaced 90% of the time..It is reminiscent to the raging sweep of protagonist attitudes you see in modern media today. Which is not inherently bad but just very strange sometimes HAHA.

- Story wise I think it would have done better to have Bond get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up a bit more to raise stakes.

- I felt certain story-beats/set pieces were...quite unnecessary and almost were irrelevant despite the important lore we are presented with? Simply put I found some characters/details came and went as fast as I was presented with them. Very well could have either left it to be developed more with time and intention and save it for something bigger...OR don't do it to begin with? I'm an already snobby sort when it comes to filmography and this is some issue that most Bond movies face so I suppose this is appropriate. Overall I wondered to myself if certain characters were gonna come back, be traitors, or die off because of how little they explained (as I viewed it as a Chekov's gun situation more or less)

- The villain, the son, and the AI debacle all felt very Bond-like...and for the most part I was giggling at the tropes they pulled for some scenes. I loved it. BUT I felt that because they try to modernize 007's world and giving it depth..This gave me the illusion there would be something relatively in-depth about the villain(s) and we would have had more build to THEIR presence before the (clearly intended) big reveal. Joining the pantheon of licensed games sure to spawn another decade of "it really makes you *feel* like James Bond" memes like the Arkham games before it, 007 First Light is easily the finest James Bond game ever made and proves that IOI is not just a one trick pony when it comes to game development. 

Fans of IO's Hitman series, particularly the recent World of Assassination trilogy, will find a lot of shared DNA here, but this is not a shadow Hitman sequel. Rather, First Light borrows design elements from the Hitman games while containing and, yes, simplifying them in a way that true Hitman fans may find restraining. But, in exchange for that tightening of the sandbox leash, you are given a tight cinematic experience with a robust combat sandbox the effortlessly ties hand to hand combat, gadgets, and shooting together that truly feels like something I've never played before. 

Fistfights are brutal, with all sorts of throws and environmental takedowns, where you scour the environment for coffee cups to throw at enemies and ledges to fling them off. When firearms are added to the mix (smartly, they aren't always an option) IO has made the wise decision to limit your ammo and make the combat AI aggressive. Rather than a traditional stop and pop 3rd person shooter, First Light forces you to stay mobile, only ever taking out one or two baddies with your firearm before you are fresh out of ammo and have to discard it for another, perhaps violently at someone's head. 

The animation work on display is absolutely stunning and combat encounters remain dynamic and fresh throughout. 

First Light also shows that IO has some serious writing chops, and tells a modern Bond story that balances the traditional camp and womanizing with modern themes and technology. You hit all the major beats you're hoping for, and a few you didn't expect. And the story creates interesting gameplay opportunities in nearly every mission. 

This story often takes center stage, and I think it's deserving of the spotlight, but some may find the game to be too on-rails. Overall I would say First Light is more open than a Call of Duty or Uncharted campaign, but the story is closer to those style of games than the true sandboxes of say a Hitman. 

If the story is overbearing, though, the TacSim mode will serve as a welcome addition. This is similar to the Arkham games challenge maps, where it plucks out gameplay scenarios from the campaign and provides certain challenges and modifiers, letting you experience the best bits of playing First Light after you've rolled credits (or during, though I would avoid it until after the game is done for fear of mild location and outfit spoilers). At launch, this mode is a little light on content but I'm excited to see what IO's post-launch support looks like. 

In summary, 007 First Light is an absolute triumph of a game and a worthy addition to the collection of any James Bond or AAA Action game fan.

007 First Light does something pretty unique: it captures the scale, cinematic feel, and storytelling style of a Bond film inside the package of a video game. Whether that works for you will depend heavily on what kind of experience you are looking for.

At its best, the game makes you feel like you are actively participating in a Bond movie. The presentation, pacing, voice acting, and set pieces all sell that fantasy really well. The actor playing young James Bond does a great job, and the story feels like a classic Bond setup. It does not necessarily push storytelling boundaries, but it is enjoyable and leaves room for a more episodic, ongoing Bond storyline, hopefully through future DLC or expansions.

The tradeoff is that some sections feel closer to a high-end interactive film or visual novel than a traditional game. There are moments that are very linear and almost impossible to truly fail, but those seem designed to create the feeling of being in a large-scale cinematic sequence rather than to challenge you mechanically. Personally, I enjoyed that, but it is worth knowing going in.

The gunplay is adequate. It is not exceptional, but it is also not bad. The limited ammo and constant push to disarm enemies, grab their weapons, and use whatever is available feels very on-brand for Bond. Throwing empty guns, objects, or environmental items at enemies also fits the style well. The platforming feels familiar, sitting somewhere in the Uncharted-style action adventure space.

Structurally, it feels a bit like a more casual Hitman. Many missions can be approached in multiple ways, but it never reaches the same level of systemic depth or “solve this however you want” freedom that Hitman offers. The complexity is reduced, which makes the game more approachable, but also limits how much experimentation there really is.

Overall, I enjoyed 007 First Light. It kept me engaged, the story was fun, and it succeeded at making me feel like Bond. I do think the current price is a little high for what it offers, but I do not regret playing it. The foundation is strong, and I hope future updates continue building on this world and version of James Bond.

Recommended, especially if you want a cinematic Bond experience more than a deeply complex stealth/action sandbox.

TLDR:
As it stands, 007 First Light sits in an awkward middle ground. It is not the tightly crafted linear adventure that Uncharted is, but it also does not offer the replayability or sandbox depth of HITMAN’s World of Assassination trilogy.

I genuinely loved the gameplay when I was allowed to mess around in the sandbox levels. Some set pieces were 
 fun to experience, but the linearity of certain sections killed a lot of my enthusiasm to keep playing.

The combat sections were, hands down, the most fun I had with the game. The open ended arenas were a blast to fight through, giving me room to experiment with stylish melee finishers and precise gunplay. At times, it felt more  John Wick than Bond, but the open ended combat is when the game was at its best.

That’s also why I was disappointed by the lack of replayability options. I had expected the tac-sim mode to include some kind of arena or survival mode that encouraged mastery of the combat system and let players experiment with different styles. At least the chapter select lets you jump back to specific checkpoints, so you can replay your favorite moments without having to redo entire missions.

Overall, I’m walking away from this game slightly disappointed. I expected more replayability from the missions, or at least a better tac-sim/freeplay kinda mode? Its why this doesn’t feel like a game from the same people who made the endlessly replayable World of Assassination trilogy.

IO Interactive's Bond origin story borrows liberally from Max Payne 3, Control, and Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory. It never quite out-does any of them, and it's still a thoroughly good time.

There's a particular pleasure in playing a game that wears its influences this openly. 007 First Light, IO Interactive's reimagined origin story for a younger, rougher James Bond, plays like a mixtape of the studio's favourite action and stealth games, and, to its enormous credit, most of the tracks land.

The Max Payne 3 DNA was the first thing I noticed. It's there in the gunplay, the way Bond can run two weapons at once, the weighty, cinematic feel of a firefight, but it's just as present in the character himself. This isn't the unflappable, martini-dry Bond of the films. He's younger, more reckless, more bruised, and the game leans into that the way Rockstar leaned into a sweaty, self-destructive Max. You're playing a man who isn't fully formed yet, and the rough edges suit him.

Then there are the environments, and this is where Control kept flashing through my mind. The Webb Industries buildings in particular share that same cold, monolithic, faintly oppressive architecture, clean lines and brutalist scale that make you feel small inside them. Wandering those interiors, I half-expected the walls to start rearranging themselves.

The stealth, meanwhile, is doing its best Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory impression. Let me be clear: it does not reach those heights. Chaos Theory is a high bar, and First Light's stealth is shallower, more forgiving, and less systemically rich. But it borrows the grammar, the shadows, the patient route-reading, the quiet satisfaction of slipping through a room nobody knew you were in, and it borrows it well enough to stand on its own. That's the through-line of the whole game, really: it takes a little from everything it admires, and even at a notch or two below the originals, the sum is genuinely satisfying.

The standout moments, for me, were the License to Kill sequences. When the game finally takes the leash off and clears you to go loud, the combat opens up beautifully, you can drop into a gunfight exactly how and when you want, and it feels fantastic every single time. Those stretches are where First Light stops imitating and starts feeling like its own confident, swaggering thing.

It isn't all smooth, though, and the cracks are worth naming. For all its set-piece spectacle, the moment-to-moment gameplay is restrictive in a lot of ways. The driving is the clearest example, serviceable at best, more rollercoaster than open road, with little of the freedom the films' chase scenes promise. Even exploration can feel boxed in; there are stretches where poking around a map you'd expect to be open turns out to be a narrow corridor dressed up as a sandbox. You can feel the Hitman skeleton underneath all of it, the level design, the disguises, the systemic plumbing, and at times First Light reads less like a fresh creation than a Bond-flavoured remix of IO's own house style. Which, given who made it, is hardly a surprise.

And yet. For every limitation, there was a sequence that pulled me right back in. First Light is a game assembled from other people's best ideas, executed a step below the source material across the board, and somehow that adds up to something I had a genuinely great time with. It's not the best stealth game, or the best shooter. It just happens to be a really, really fun game.

A great action-adventure game, a mix of Uncharted and Hitman, with a touch of Batman Arkham and Watch Dogs.

All aspects of the game are of the highest quality. The game has a very interesting, Bond-like story. Patrick Gibson plays James Bond very well, and the other actors also delivered excellent performances in their roles.

Every aspect of the gameplay is very good. We have excellent melee combat and gunplay, stealth, and platforming sections. Additionally, we can use a wide range of gadgets. There are very enjoyable action sequences, and in some of them we can control various vehicles. The game features both linear sections and small, open levels that usually offer a few paths to reach your objective.

Some people criticize the game for simplifications compared to Hitman, for example the lack of the ability to move bodies, but have you read the books or watched the films? Bond doesn’t operate like Hitman. Bond works as he does in this game - first gathering intelligence and acting stealthily, but then things inevitably go wrong, leading to shootouts, brawls, and chases. And it’s executed brilliantly in this game! Others complain that the game is too short (in my case: 17h for the story + 2h to get the additional achievements), but I prefer an intense, engaging experience over bloated open-world games filled with repetitive tasks. Additionally, the Polish price in PLN is quite reasonable compared to other new AAA titles.

The graphics are very nice, the cutscenes and animations are too. The game is well optimized on PC. The opening theme song by Lana Del Rey is really good and could easily feature in a Bond movie. The other tracks and the overall audio are also top-notch.

The game is packed with references to various Bond movies and books. I’m not usually a fan of collectibles, but here I found everything.

There are some minor bugs, but compared to other titles at launch, the state of 007 First Light is excellent. I didn’t experience any crashes or game-breaking issues, although I did notice some frame rate drops, which were fixed by restarting the game.

As a 007 fan, I recommend it and I’m looking forward to a sequel. I hope this becomes a full series, where we get to fight a well-known organization familiar to Bond fans :).

I don't really know what to say, I'm that speechless.

Let's start with the graphics. For my "underpowered" PC compared to what's recommended, the graphics are incredible. The texture settings have to be played on low but surprisingly that doesn't really take away from the graphics, the game still looks incredible. All other settings can be on high and the game can run on 60 fps, easily.

The story, when so deep into it, once it reaches the end it feels disappointing. The game, averaging on 16 hours gameplay depending how quick you learn things and play through levels, unusually feels short. That's probably just me that felt it was short. I personally enjoyed the story that it did feel sad when it ended. Twists at every turn, cool cars to drive, beautiful story locations - just wow. Personally, I was waiting to drive the DB5 or DB10 but I'm sure there's plans for that at some point. Luckily, Bond has his number now so we know there's much more to come for 007.

Don't get me started on the gameplay. The combat is literally insane. Throwing guns at people, slamming people into walls, pushing them over cliff edges, and even more than that. Overall, it's a tricky system to learn in the initial couple of hours but after that you get so used to it. I love the idea of you being able to throw something at an enemy before charging at him, punching him then grabbing him and power charging him into a wall to knock him out. Pure brilliance.

Only issue I had was characters not loading in on cutscenes sometimes and Bond or others would be talking to no one. The characters would load in eventually but this took away from the flow of the gameplay into cutscene sequences. Additionally (to avoid spoilers) I had to fight two versions of the same blonde twin in the hut fire scene as for some reason both character models appeared, the one with burns and without. To be honest, no clue if that's a graphics thing or if that's just a game bug because we all know what games are like on release for PC - they're usually buggy as hell.

Overall, for this to be the first game in what's looking to be a long 007 game series, it is brilliant. People say that the game is just a "Hitman and Uncharted mix" as if that's meant to be an insult. Comparing this to already 2 brilliant games is what has attracted everyone. Oh, along with the trailers too as they had everyone hooked and waiting to play.
I'd love to see DLC packs based on the movies such as Craig era missions or even Connery. I mean I'd love to see a new game already but I'm patient enough to wait a few more years for that.

007 First Light is the best Bond game since Everything or Nothing, and I do not say that lightly.

For context, I am a huge IO Interactive fan. I have been playing their games since Hitman: Codename 47 back in 2000, and I have finished and loved pretty much everything they have made. Mini Ninjas is the only real gap for me, and not because I disliked it, I just never got around to finishing it. From what I remember, it was a fine game.

I am also a James Bond fan, especially when it comes to the games. I am old enough to remember being right in the middle of the GoldenEye 007 zeitgeist on the N64, and for a while after that we got one disappointing Bond game after another. Agent Under Fire and Nightfire were solid, but it was not until Everything or Nothing came along that it felt like we finally got something truly special again. It did not quite hit the lightning-in-a-bottle highs of GoldenEye, but before 007 First Light, I still considered Everything or Nothing the second-best Bond game ever made.

That is the context I am bringing into 007 First Light. So when I say this is the best Bond game since Everything or Nothing, and that it might just be the best Bond game ever made, I mean it.

Despite how some of the gameplay and HUD elements might look, this is not just Hitman in a tuxedo. It has elements of an Uncharted game: exceptional storytelling, expertly crafted cutscenes, visceral combat, and extraordinary set pieces, filtered through IOI’s strengths: focused social stealth sandboxes, gadgets, improvisational combat, and just enough Kane & Lynch ugliness to make the violence feel impactful.

The combat is fantastic. The hand-to-hand system has a familiar Batman-style counter system, but the game really shines when you are mixing fists, gunplay, gadgets, hacking, instinct, limited ammo, stolen weapons, and pure improvisation. Using your watch to set off a trap or hack a distraction feels great. Tossing an empty gun into an enemy’s face and stealing his firearm never got old. It constantly feels tight, chaotic, stylish, and reactive, like you are winging it and thinking on your toes while doing it with the pizazz of James Bond.

The stealth is also excellent. Hitman fans will feel at home, but Bond is not Agent 47, and IOI clearly understands that. Agent 47 survives social spaces by blending in and becoming invisible, despite how hilariously suspicious he may look to us players. James Bond survives them by being cunning, sly, and exceptionally charming. The hacking watch gives the stealth a bit of a Watch Dogs or Cyberpunk 2077 flavour, while the instinct system lets Bond bluff his way through situations in a way that feels completely natural for the character. Also, shout out to the writers and Patrick Gibson for what feels like a billion lines of dialogue for the many situations Bond can find himself bluffing his way out of.

Bond's first real mission, infiltrating the chess event disguised as a chauffeur, is where the game figuratively gives you the keys to the Lamborghini. You drive a Jaguar in this section, but you get the idea. That is when the game truly fires on all cylinders for the first time. The nightclub section before it is a damn good appetizer, but the chess event introduces how the somewhat linear sandbox functions, and it shows off this version of Bond’s social stealth toolkit beautifully. There are several great sandbox-style areas later, but that mission does such an exceptional job of showing what this game is, and it made me excited to see where the story would go next.

Then there are the set pieces. The airplane sequence, where you are in combat while also controlling the roll of the hacked plane, is one of the coolest action-game moments I have played. The car chases are a blast too. The garbage truck section is not mechanically deep, sure, you can basically hold the gas pedal and win, but as a Bond moment it absolutely kicks ass. Making it to the truck by the skin of your teeth feels great, and the banter between Bond and the truck driver when he borrows it is a perfect little character moment. The spectacle, the music, and hearing the proper Bond theme kick in made that sequence stand out for me.

Patrick Gibson also deserves a ton of credit. A rookie twenty-something James Bond sounds like it could be a terrible idea, but he immediately and completely won me over. Right off the hop, his Bond is charming, reckless, stylish, and just rough enough around the edges to make the origin story work. I also really appreciate that IOI went closer to the novel-accurate Bond appearance, with the blue-grey eyes and cheek scar. It is a small detail, but I imagine longtime Bond fans will appreciate it. I never felt like I was playing as Nathan Drake or some other dude. It consistently felt like Bond, just younger and slightly less refined.

The story does the job perfectly too. I will avoid spoilers, but the writing and acting were just as good as, if not better than, some of the greatest Bond films. The pacing is exceptional. It took me around 15 or 16 hours to finish, but it felt like a tight campaign in the best possible way. Time flew, I wanted more, and I still felt like I got my money’s worth. For this kind of game, that length is basically perfect.

It also reminded me how refreshing it is to play a straightforward single-player game in 2026. No live-service nonsense. No microtransactions. No bloated filler. No pointless systems trying to waste your time. Just a damn solid solo campaign that knows exactly what it is trying to do and does it extremely well. The Tactical Simulation (TacSim) mode adds some replayability after the credits roll. It's where you can play challenges with modifiers, scoring, unlocks, and different ways to approach each scenario. It scratches some of that IOI mastery/replayability itch without bloating the main campaign. A New Game+ would have been nice, and hopefully IOI patches it in, because it would be fun to replay the story with all the gadgets unlocked.

I honestly do not remember any part of it dragging. I loved the story, the gameplay blend, the set pieces, the pacing, and the feeling of finally getting a proper modern Bond game again.

Strongly Recommended.

Overall, it's a great game and possibly the best James Bond game to date. The gameplay mechanics are solid, the visuals look great, and the story is engaging. You can sneak through missions like a real agent, use a variety of gadgets, engage in hand-to-hand combat, or rely on firearms when necessary.

However, the first 1,5 hours feel like an extended tutorial, as they are almost entirely focused on James Bond's training. The game only really starts to open up after that. While this isn't necessarily a major issue, it does mean that the game takes some time before it truly gets going.

My biggest criticism is the price. €70 is simply too much for the amount of content offered. The game is a fairly linear experience with a playtime of around 11 hours and very little replay value. While the single playthrough is enjoyable, I don't think it justifies the full asking price. If the game included a multiplayer mode or more Hitman-style missions with multiple approaches and higher replayability, I would gladly pay €70 for it.

For that reason, I'll be refunding the game and waiting for a sale. Despite my criticism, it's still a good game that I can recommend, which is why I'm leaving a positive review.

I went into 007 First Light expecting a fairly standard James Bond game, but I ended up having a lot more fun than I anticipated.

What stood out most was how well the game balances classic Bond-style espionage with modern action. You're not just running around shooting everything that moves—there's actual stealth, gadget usage, investigation, and decision-making involved. It really feels like you're playing as a spy rather than a generic action hero.

The story does a good job of showing Bond before he became the polished 007 everyone knows. Seeing him make mistakes and grow into the role made the character feel more human and interesting. The locations are gorgeous, and the soundtrack absolutely nails that Bond atmosphere.

Combat isn't revolutionary, but it's solid enough and doesn't overstay its welcome. Some missions are stronger than others, and there are a few moments where the pacing slows down, but overall I stayed invested from start to finish.

I played on PC and was pleasantly surprised by how well it ran. Performance was smooth throughout my playthrough, with no major bugs, crashes, or technical issues getting in the way. It's always nice when a new release launches in a polished state, and this one delivered for me.

If you're a Bond fan, this is an easy recommendation. Even if you're not, there's enough here for fans of stealth-action games to enjoy. It may not reinvent the genre, but it captures the fantasy of being James Bond better than most games have in years.

007 First Light delivers a confident and engaging take on the iconic spy formula, blending action, intrigue, and cinematic presentation into a polished package. The game captures the essence of the James Bond universe while carving out its own identity through a fresh narrative direction. Its pacing remains consistently entertaining, ensuring that missions rarely lose momentum. There is a strong sense of adventure throughout, making each new location feel worthwhile.
The story serves as a compelling origin-style tale that explores the early stages of Bond's career. Political conspiracies, dangerous adversaries, and globe-trotting espionage combine to create a narrative filled with tension and excitement. Character interactions are well written, adding depth to both allies and enemies. The plot maintains interest from beginning to end with several memorable twists along the way.
Gameplay strikes an enjoyable balance between stealth, gunplay, and gadget-driven problem solving. Missions provide players with multiple approaches, encouraging experimentation rather than forcing a single solution. The controls feel responsive, and progression systems offer meaningful rewards without becoming overly complicated. A variety of mission objectives helps prevent repetition and keeps the experience fresh.
Visually, the game is impressive, featuring detailed environments and strong environmental variety. From luxurious urban settings to hostile remote locations, each area is presented with a high level of craftsmanship. Character models are expressive, while lighting effects contribute significantly to the atmosphere. The cinematic presentation enhances key moments and helps reinforce the game's spy-thriller tone.
Overall, 007 First Light succeeds as an entertaining espionage adventure that combines a strong narrative, enjoyable gameplay mechanics, and impressive visual design. Its effective use of the James Bond licence creates an experience that feels authentic while still offering something new. Although a few elements could have benefited from additional refinement, the overall quality remains consistently high. Fans of action-adventure games and spy thrillers alike will find plenty to enjoy.

The game is decent, but certainly not worth its full retail price.

Pros: The storyline is top tier for a solo campaign. Production for the signature style Bond opening theme was incredible. The Q Lab is really cool to run around, too.  Soundtrack is great and graphics are pretty solid. There are some areas they clearly spent more time on than others, but overall the graphics for this game are legit. 

Cons: Although the story is great, the entire campaign can be completed easily in about 10-12 hours.  The game is very repetitive, but not in a fun way. I did not think I would be playing a 007 game that limits by ability to use guns. Nearly every level requires you to fist-fight your way through and you can only shoot under certain circumstances. Despite being a 00 Agent, or at least a trainee under the management of Mi6, Bond almost never starts with any meaningful firepower. Even when you do secure firearms, your ammunition will be severely limited throughout the level. Your choices for firearms will be limited to whatever NPCs are using and the selection of those are also limited. With most of the game revolving around hand-to-hand combat, you would think those mechanics were airtight: they are not. NPC mobs can be easily led around with something as running in circles around a table -- they will just play ring-around-the-rosie with you into perpetuity. I am all for the realism of "secret agent subterfuge" but in a game that allows me to fire a missile at enemies by pouring window cleaner into my watch, its a bit much. There are also some parts of the game that a literal chimpanzee could play and complete. For example, the level with the garbage truck -- you literally just hold down forward and you complete it. $70, mind you. 

Overall, I do not recommend purchasing this game unless you can do so while it is on sale. It is not worth its full price. If you can get it for under $35, then I would say it is worth it.

I bought First Light less than a week ago. I have had a great experience so far and enjoying every minute. I found the story intriguing and found myself saying "Bond, James Bond" whenever he would introduce himself. here is my review so far of each aspect of the game.

Gameplay 7/10: When you are first learning the controls it can be a little unintuitive for some of the actions. However, the gameplay rewards mastering the controls and using both the environment, gadgets, and weapons as tools. When you start to get the hang of things gameplay overall feels a lot better. I will say that the game feels to be in a gray area between open and linear style missions. While I don't necessarily dislike this. I believe it will affect the replay ability of the story. Additionally, I found some of the "puzzle" sections of missions where you would have to find a specific route to get to the other side of a door to have unintuitive answers. this is not to be confused with the slightly more open sections that you usually encounter.

Story 8.5/10: As I had said before, I overall enjoyed the story. The story is cinematic like you would expect from a 007 movie while doing its best to maintain player agency. Many of the side characters had a unique personality that contrast with Bond and other characters leaving minimal overlap. Bond himself doesn't undergo much in the way of character development but you can see how the supporting cast changes throughout the story which makes up for that. I also believe that the fact that bond doesn't change in much is part of his character in that he remains as himself.

Graphics 9/10: I should mention for context that I ran on Ultra settings with HDR and V-sync. I found the sets were beautiful overall with plenty of cinematic shots accentuating the scenery. characters were very detailed and lighting was applied well. The cinematic scenes felt like they were straight out of a movie.

Overall, I would rate this game a 8.5 overall. This game is definitely worth it if you are a fan of the 007 franchise or  a general action game enjoyer. I can not however recommend the deluxe edition even for the minimal 10$ price increase I believe the benefits are too minimal for a deluxe edition especially since you will not really be looking at the "gleaming pack" items as they will be put away immediately after their use. only consider it if you want the outfits.

I'm something of James bond fan, the 2006 Casino Royale is my favourite if you want to gauge my judgment based of off that, so when this game was announced I was excited but a little worried.
Further still when I booted the game up and saw the yellow paint stuff in the tutorial but its pretty seamless and by the time they take the leash off, that kind of direction isn't need and it lets you decide how you want to take on encounters. Turns out 007 First Light really has "it"

First and foremost this is a cinematic game, I don't mean that as a dirty word, they clearly understood what that should actually be, a simple blend of stealth, gunplay, and cinematic action.
The game starts up in Iceland on a pre-MI6 mission, it's a bit of a slow build up, the tutorial is long but it leans into that cinematic nature before everything really comes together. For example there is a montage sequence made up of gameplay, switching between shooting, driving, parkour, fist fighting, and stealth, that's cut between seamlessly, no loading or breaks, all while teaching you what the game expects of you.
While not as open as Hitman or as linear as [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/reimuisbest2hu/recommended/28000/] Kane & Lynch [/url] [spoiler] which I am a big fan of [/spoiler] it finds a nice balance of what I'll call a "directed sandbox" giving you broad objectives with several fleshed out options on how to complete them. For example a later mission requires you to access a restricted area at a gala jammed full of people, you can investigate the guards and pose as one of them to get through using context clues in the level, or you can trick a PR person into giving you a press pass, steal a camera, and walk right in! You can probably knock everyone out as well but it felt like a waste to me. 

You get a great sense of scale in this game, the first time you drive down the mountain side in chapter 3 you can see the upcoming sandbox. A pirate city in the desert, a level set in Q lab that lets you set off gadgets on guards, a secret Antarctic base full of robots so ludicrously huge I can only assume it's here because it was considered too ridiculous for a Hitman level. All of these are great, they made me excited to play, excited to engage with the game's systems, but sometimes it pulls back.
In chapter 8 Bond travels to a holiday resort in Vietnam, it has all the bells and whistles of a real luxury resort. When tasked with infiltrating a party the super spy has to dress the part, up to this point we've seen bond take down multiple enemies, defuse bombs, jump from planes, make incredible leaps, but despite his ability he doesn't know how to tie his bowtie. What follows is a simple button pressing sequence where the games suitable dapper Q guides Bond on dressing the part, it sets it up so well. I think you have to play it to see what a great character moment it is, its not just an "X to Jason" or "F to pay respects". but the game isn't afraid to build on those ideas.
IO interactive committed to some pretty big set pieces and locations, I found that all of them paid off.
Also there is an [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2IyjDtp7sJQ] IO mandated nightclub level. [/url]

Graphically the game is very smooth, instead of chasing the bleeding edge of graphically fidelity they opted for much great visual clarity and honestly I prefer it to the temporal shimmer of certain big budget AAA games. There are a few textures here and there that look a bit rough, sometimes the occlusion is a bit aggressive. But the overall image looks fantastic, its never murky even when playing around with DLSS.

Perhaps I should have touched on this earlier but as a Bond entry I think this stacks up really well. There's a brevity to the witty remarks between action segments that don't make the characters seems too smarmy. Bond is charming, Patrick Gibson plays an excellent young Bond, confident enough to sell the role. There's a few good one liners and [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PGtRCL5nUOg] classic bond moments [/url] that I really appreciated. Don't let that undersell the other performances, I thought [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bRJxNpPj6Zc] Lennie James [/url] gave a standout performance as former 00 and mentor figure John Greenway, every scene with him is a delight! 

All in all an entertaining set piece romp, I'd like to think the game industry should be making more of these but it did take [url=https://www.ign.com/articles/007-first-light-budget-reportedly-more-than-200-million] 7 years, [/url] one of the most experienced dev teams in the industry, and the capital reserve of one of the [url=https://companiesmarketcap.com/gbp/largest-companies-by-revenue/] biggest companies in the world [/url] to make.

I don’t even know where to start, because at the end of the day, James Bond 007: First Light is a really good game.

For me, it was absolutely worth the money. I got around 22 to 23 hours of constant fun without rushing, and the game feels like a mix between Uncharted and Hitman. It has surprisingly good missions, interesting characters, and some great interactions.

There are definitely more good things than bad things here. The optimization is excellent. The game ran perfectly for me, with no frame rate issues, no graphical problems, and surprisingly, I did not encounter any bugs.

The story is exactly what you would expect from a James Bond game. It is exciting, clear, and not too over the top, at least by Bond standards. You always understand who the enemy is, and the story keeps moving at a good pace.

The gameplay is a strong mix of adventure, reflexes, light thinking, stealth, and shooting. I really liked the shooting because you do not have unlimited ammo. You need to find weapons, use what is available, and move through the levels carefully. I also appreciated that enemies are not bullet sponges. They go down quickly, which makes the action feel much better.

Visually, the game can be very impressive. Most levels are well designed and fun to play through. Some indoor areas can become a bit bland and repetitive, but overall the level design is strong. There are also collectibles for players who enjoy that kind of thing.

My main criticism is that some story moments and cutscenes make no sense. For example, there are moments where a whole army is shooting at you, but the second you reach a helicopter and fly away, everyone suddenly stops shooting. These moments break the immersion, and there are several scenes like that where it feels like the logic of the scene was simply ignored.

Still, despite these problems, I had a great time with the game. I think it deserves its price tag, and you do not even need to be a huge James Bond fan to enjoy it.

Great game, great fun, and I really hope we get a sequel.

I do somewhat have mixed feelings about this game… My perspective on it comes from a few angles and as such it’s tricky for me to nail down how I would “rate” the game.

I love the Hitman games, especially the most recent World of Assassination games. In my opinion they are basically the best stealth games ever made. The open kind of “emergent gameplay” in them is something I enjoy immensely. They are heaven if you like sneaking about and messing around with testing the possibilities…

I also am a fan of James Bond for sure, both the games and the movies. GoldenEye 007 on the N64 is a significant core memory for me. I like the GoldenEye movie too. Goldfinger, You Only Live Twice, Live and Let Die, The Man with the Golden Gun, Moonraker, Tomorrow Never Dies, Casino Royal, Skyfall, all movies I enjoy a lot. I do feel the last couple of Bond movies have lost their way a bit, especially the one where he [spoiler] (maybe) dies at the end [/spoiler]. To put it simply I like when James Bond is a bit of simple, not too deep, silly, glitzy fun.

So when I heard that IOI are making a James Bond game I was excited. Two things I like coming together. But quite different things really. Sure, James Bond is a secret agent, a spy, he does some sneaking and infiltrating, but I would never really describe that as his strength. Could IOI capture the action and fun vibe of James Bond in a way I would enjoy?

Well, the answer is yes, 007 First Light definitely feels like the kind of James Bond I like. It’s fun. There are gun fights galore, explosions, exciting fist fights, cool car chases, exotic locations, hot girls, nifty gadgets and lots of quirky British people and humour…

It plays a lot like Uncharted or the modern Tomb Raider games. A linear cinematic action game. There are some elements that remind of the Hitman games. Like solving this kind of how you get through the locked or guarded door kind of puzzle, or the ability to sneak and stealth kill. But instead of letting it all be open ended and giving you twenty different options it gives you maybe two or three options and pushes you forwards. Things inevitably boiled down to shooting or beating up a lot of PMC guys or security guard goons, especially in the second half of the game.

Don’t get me wrong, I like linear cinematic games. I like exciting action. But I also am some one who likes a game that gives me options, allows me to experiment, makes me think at least a bit. I mean, I know a lot of people love the Uncharted games, but I’ve never really been a fan, as I feel they essentially boil down to shooting up the fiftieth wave of these uninteresting bad guys. I’m also just not really a huge fan of Nathan Drake’s particular brand of dude-bro vibes. I like the modern Tomb Raider games though... I guess, it’s a fine line with these types of games. I feel like 007 First Light is good in that kind of way, but not exceptional. I would have liked a bit more variety, a few more options, a little bit less pushing me forwards. I did like this depiction of James Bond though. He’s a bit of rebel, a bit of a lad, but not in a way that I found off putting. He’s likeable, like the kind of guy you’re routing for to succeed.

The plot was enjoyable in a not too serious kind of way. The rich AI tech genius, is, big surprise, [spoiler]not such a nice guy[/spoiler], and his infallible miracle machine is [spoiler]not so infallible[/spoiler]. I mean, it was predictable, I saw the twist coming from a mile away. But still it was fun and I enjoyed it for what it was. It was certainly appropriately topical. The story is also about James Bond’s journey from being a nobody aircrew man, to going through training and then eventually being the indispensable 007 who proves himself and saves the day. One could really kind of look at the story and say it’s stupid and full of plot holes, but at the end of the day I thought it was fun in a not too serious kind of way. I feel like it got the James Bond vibe mostly right. However, I could’ve done without the classic [spoiler]you thought this baddie was dead but actually he’s still alive and you’ve got to kill him again[/spoiler] trope.

The graphics in the game are good. There’s nicely detailed environments and a nice variety of interesting locations. It has RTGI (Ray-Traced Global Illumination), which is a software based technology that is meant to add depth to environments. It looked pleasant enough in my opinion, the lighting and shadows and reflections are pretty good, but not anything amazing. Character models are ok, maybe slightly kind of cartoonish or lacking in variety, especially on the none main character models. The music was enjoyable, appropriately James Bond-ish, it adds to the cinematic vibe of the game nicely. Sound effects were good. Voice acting was really good. Performance was ok, it ran at about 80-110fps for me, 1440p, max settings, not using any upscaling or frame generation. I couldn’t really anyway, it has FSR but I think it is only FSR3 which did look a bit grainy and there is no option for native AA or FrameGen with it. There is no FSR4 which is a shame. But like I say, the game ran well enough for me and looked decent. I do though feel it has a little bit of a sharpness issue, FSR4 would’ve helped with this. There were a few minor bugs, but nothing really significant. No crashes, or loading issues or significant stutters. I know that some are a little bit upset about it not launching with path tracing or ray reconstruction, which is apparently going to come in a future update. It's unlikely I would be able to run that great on my 9070 XT anyway, if the game even allows the option on AMD cards anyway that is, so I mean, can't really say I'm super fussed. Like I stated, the game looks decent, like the graphics could've been better in certain ways, but I wouldn't of said the game desperately needed better visuals to be enjoyable. I can though understand how it might bother the sort of player who has a 5090 or similar. In my mind path tracing is certainly interesting, but we are still a few years away from it being a truly mainstream technology.

Is the game worth the money? I think it really depends how much you like James Bond, or this particular way of portraying him. I paid £44 for it from a key reseller, which included the deluxe edition stuff. It’s £60 for the standard or £70 for the deluxe version here on Steam. I am not really a fan of IOI’s shenanigans to get you to pre-order to get the deluxe stuff cheaper. I mean, IOI are infamous for this type of nonsense, they just can’t help themselves. I really don’t like it. Just sell the game in a no nonsense way for crying out loud. But I digress… It took me about 15 hours to beat the story and I spent a few hours messing about in the Tacsim mode, which is a bit like the Freelance roguelike mode in Hitman, but not nearly as serious or content filled. I think it maybe has potential and I might go back to it a bit, but it was all just a little bit whatever to me. I feel the game was an appropriate length for the type of game it is, but I think it’s unlikely I would play through it again. I feel like for me, the game was ok value for money, but it could’ve been a little bit cheaper if I’m honest. 

So, like I wrote at the start of this review, my feelings about this game are mixed. I really enjoyed how it captured the spirit of James Bond in a way that I enjoy. Frankly, it’s the best James Bond movie I’ve seen in years. But the gameplay was just kind of alright. It had moments that I really enjoyed, like the exciting cinematic moments, or the more freedom of choice based moments that reminded me of Hitman. But it overall just left me a little bit wanting gameplay wise. But, this is a James Bond game, an exciting, fun, cinematic action game, and credit where credit is due, this is definitely a successful James Bond game in that way, and that is easier said than done, and something I am definitely happy to see happen.

Like so many have said before, this game plays just like a movie, and I mean that as a compliment. For years developers have tried to make a video game that gives you the idea you are playing through a movie, but to me this is probably the first game that does it right. It puts you right into the shoes of James Bond and lets you experience all of the thrilling action that you would feel like watching a new Bond film.

While the story feels like the start of a new Bond film series, the gameplay carries its weight throughout the entire adventure. This mix of Hitman x Uncharted with sprinkles of LA Noire in it makes this game a real treat to play through. The brawling combat feels so satisfying to just fight your way through a room of enemies, and the gunplay feels satisfying, making each shot you land feel impactful. My only gripes is that I wish it could be a bit more forgiving, Bond feels like a wet paper towel, going down in three hits, I get that its to punish you for getting caught or in over your head, but it can get annoying sometimes when things take you by surprise and your forced back to the last checkpoint near the end of a mission. That said the core gameplay is still the highlight of the show and I am excited to see how they refine it in future entries.

The biggest issue I have with this game is the PC version is a bit of a buggy mess at times. My PC is no slouch, sporting an RTX 4070ti Super with a 9800X3D CPU, and the game would run into numerous bugs such as Bond getting frozen solid in certain situations after bluffing an enemy, leading to him getting caught, getting stuck in slow mo segments despite pressing the buttons the game wants you to press, and the funniest is Bond turning into a pacifist when he has the License to Kill and just....won't pull out his gun no matter how many times I pressed the aim button. Most of these bugs would fix themselves after reloading the checkpoint, but it still got annoying. This is on top of the crashing this game can experience at times. Oh right, and a good chunk of the Steam Achievements are just broken too.

Maybe if I played this game on PS5 I would give this game a 9? But the technical issues really took me out of a very engrossing and enjoyable experience. This game may be a hard sell at $70, but personally I got my money's worth with the game, and if you can find it on sale for $50 or $60, this game would be worth every penny. The developers got Bond right in this game, his charm, his story and the world around him. I am excited to see where this new Bond trilogy goes next.

The game has a little bit of a slow start but as soon as you start doing proper missions it gets so good. Don't get me wrong. The beginning also isn't bad but the game starts with a mission with very basic stealth and climbing that you would see in million other AAA games and it gives the wrong impression of what you are going to get. But after that when you go through the training missions the real game starts. And it is pretty obvious why was IOI such a great pick for the game. Instead of it just being a shooter with sneaking and some gadgets it has that Hitman sauce. You gather information by talking to people, listening to conversations and there are always multiple solutions how to tackle the problem. Which also gives the game a great replayability. The big difference between this and Hitman is that when you have to start shooting and fighting with people in a Hitman game it means  then you are in trouble, here the action is an important part. The shooting feels good, the close combat as well with a lot of options to use your environment. Actually when it comes to using your environment it feels very immersive sim, just like Hitman. Whether it is about trying to sneak around or combat there are so many things around you to distract or take out enemies.
Beside the not that impressive start the only thing I wasn't blown away by is the driving sections. A lot of them feel like a filler and even the more action-y ones are not really the highlight of the game but luckily they don't overdo them.
Another thing I need to mention: TacSim. Basically a challenge mode where you level up and complete levels with different challenges, buy new equipment, use modifiers to make it easier or harder. It is a great way to enjoy more of the stellar combat and imsim elements of the game. And it seems like they are going to keep updating the TacSim with new content just how Hitman is constantly getting free updates.

TLDR: A great game that feels like a combination of an Uncharted and a Hitman. If you like the Hitman games or if you want to play a game with light immersive sim elements, if you are a James Bond fan then this is a huge recommendation. Hell, if you are not a Hitman fan or found it overwhelming I would still recommend this game since it feels like a Hitman light when it comes to the similar elements (not in a derogatory way).

I had a good time with the game overall. It looks great, the varied locations you visit are awesome, the set pieces are cool and the occasional humour made me actually grin at times. The combat is fairly simple, both in hand-to-hand & gunfights, but it feels smooth, responsive and fun with the animations also being amazing. The gadgets also add variety to the gameplay and I think they are implemented well. Oh and, CLASSY intro B)

While I like most of the cast, the story didn't do it for me although I was invested in it up to a certain point. There is too much going on with the plot, and I think it would have been better with a more focused cast of characters. Even so, I can appreciate the direction the developers were aiming for. My biggest criticism is the pacing. The first half of the game is significantly stronger than the second half in my opinion. Some chapters involve a lot of walking around, and I felt a little bored at the start of chapter 7 especially.

While the game borrows elements from the Hitman formula, the infiltration mechanics are quite simplified. Many objectives have very obvious solutions; most of the time you can find a keycard or required item near where it needs to be used. That being said, there is one level that truly felt like I was playing in a small-scale Hitman map. If you are looking for true Hitman-style gameplay, you won't find it here. Then again, this isn't supposed to be Hitman. I wanted the infiltration to be more challenging than it is. Hopefully, next game :)

There are also a few escalations, just like in the newer Hitman games. They were fun to complete, but I don't really see much incentive to fully complete their challenges because there isn't anything worthwhile to unlock apart from rewards that help you get a higher score on the leaderboards. 

In summary, despite its pacing issues and being a bit simplistic, I had a great time with the game. It has strong presentation, enjoyable combat with fun gadgets, excellent environments and a cinematic atmosphere. If you're a fan of story-driven action games, you'll probably enjoy it.
