[h3]TL;DR[/h3]
This review is spoiler-free. I played on "intended" difficulty on both PC and PS5. Detailed pros and cons listed further below.

Overall, an extremely solid game with quite linear gameplay that feels a lot like a playable Bond movie (with LOTS of visual and textual references to the Bond movies and Hitman). There are slow and more stealthy sections that get mixed up with huge action sequences that might feel a bit overwhelming at first, mainly if you're a casual gamer, but with some practice, none of the levels is impossible or overly frustrating. If you let the game stand on its own and give it a chance to be what it attempts to be, it's [b]VERY good[/b] and certainly brings with it a lot of potential for future Bond games. I'd rate it [b]9.5 out of 10[/b] and am very much looking forward to where IOI will take the franchise in the future.

Admittedly, I had a bit of a hard time liking the game in the first couple of chapters, however, it grew a lot on me as the story progressed (and I'm very glad I gave it a chance tbh). I think it had to with the limited field of view that takes getting used to and the atrocious default keyboard settings (I started playing it with mouse/keyboard), and the default film grain which felt off to me. Once I switched to controller and turned film grain off, wow... THEN it turned into an experience that I now can't get enough of. 

[h3]Pros:[/h3]
[list]
[*]IOI - need I say more? They did their homework on the franchise, and they delivered bigtime. 
[*]Bond's relationship with the main secondary character, while antagonistic at first, turns out to have a lot of heart
[*]While referencing all of the other Bond actors/mannerisms, Gibson gets to be his own Bond, so to speak. That's a good thing. 
[*]The story overall, quite Bond-like in its grandeur and setpieces (and some of those setpieces are just... wow)
[*]Graphics are pretty darn good (my 3070Ti/64 GB RAM gets a steady 50-60 FPS in 4k resolution during gameplay; I do have FPS limited to 60 for all games, and 60 FPS works just fine for me. No stutters. I do have some graphics details turned to low, but overall, I'm quite happy that the game runs smoothly even on my rather mid graphics card). So better graphics cards will likely get you an even better visual experiene. Don't believe anyone if they claim that the graphics suck. They do not. 
[*]While feeling like a cardboard cutout dude at first, Bond did grow on me throughout the game. Well done, IOI and Patrick Gibson. 
[*]IOI managed to capture that Bond movie grandeur quite nicely, and there are a LOT of references to the movies (as well as to Agent 47, of course), and I'm certain to the books as well (I haven't read them, so I can't tell)
[*]Some interesting side character interactions early on.
[*]Lots of settings for graphics - I turned off film grain and preferred that over the default 
[*]Gadgets feel appropriately Bond-like 
[*]The TacSim part - use this early on to get a better feel for fist fights and gunfights. There's unlimited potential in the TacSim if IOI decides to add more levels to it.
[*]Expect to move a lot during gunfights. You won't be able to just fire from one cover due to the limited ammo. I hated this at first, but it actually grew on me during gameplay. 
[*]The Bond references big and small (such as Bond adjusting his cuffs or dusting off his suit, his swagger and ability to charm/bluff). This studio knew EXACTLY what they were doing, and they integrated more easter eggs/references than people will realize at first (from dialogue to visuals, to specific action scenes). 
[*]The set pieces! Some of them are so huge and detailed and only visible for a minute or so, but OMG, they are awesome!
[*]Adaptive trigger on PS5 - I know it's not unique to this game, but since I played with an XBox 360 controller on PC, the difference to the PS5 controller is huge. 
[*]And yes, Bond gets to be a ladies' man :) (As a gay woman, I see nothing wrong with that)
[*]A diverse set of characters (yes, that's a good thing!), where all of them get to shine in their own ways. 
[*]The story itself isn't overly long, but a new TacSim level has already been announced, so I'm sure IOI will be adding more content as time goes on.
[/list]

[h3]Cons:[/h3]
[list][*]Forced, very limited field of view during dialogue scenes (in each of which you're prompted to look around for some reason but then can't because all you get is the same limited FOV); even on repeated playthroughs, I find this highly annoying.
[*]Forced breaking of stealth over and over (I understand that it serves the story but it would still be nice if it didn't happen)
[*]Interactions with surroundings are extremely limited (e.g. you can't  pick up a hammer in order to throw it later, these types of things will only ever be available during and/or for fight sequences)
[*]You constantly have to "reload" your gadgets with battery power and/or any chemicals you can find everywhere on the levels (this feels weird, though I understand that otherwise the gadgets would be OP)
[*]Very VERY limited ammo (you can do the gunfights with what's there, and the game is pretty generous with the hitboxes on NPCs, though) - so expect to pick up guns all over the place
[*]Can't see what guns you're picking up from a gun crate so you end up cycling endlessly through the guns that are there until you have the one with the most ammo (if that's what you're looking for)
[*]EXTREMELY linear gameplay which includes literal arrows painted on the floor on some levels and extremely heavily marked jump areas/tarps/color pointers
[*]On the levels, there's no space for creativity, you follow the arrow and/or the ONE route that the game wants you to take, you break stealth when the game requires you to, you leave a frickton of bodies in your wake because of it 
[*]sounds of fist fights or takedowns don't carry even three meters to the next dude... until they do when you don't expect them to
[*]during gunfights, sometimes you'll have the sight dot, sometimes you don't
[*]your movement in gunfights may be limited EVEN IF there's free space behind you, and your aim may very much be affected by that
[*]You can't point your gun unless the game permits you to
[*]Loading times are really bad, even on the PS5. 
[*]Default keyboard controls are absolutely finger-breakingly atrocious
[*]Forced slow walking in many scenes
[*]The story itself isn't overly long. 
[/list]

[h3]Other stuff:[/h3]
[list][*]Apparently, MI6 doesn't include first aid in their trainings, 'cause doing chest compressions on a dude who's clearly still breathing (and bleeding out) is absolutely counterproductive. 
[*]Current equipped gun isn't represented in cutscenes (it's always the pistol)
[*]Expect to switch weapons A LOT due to the limited ammo
[*]Don't expect to carry a gun from one chapter to another. Bond will drop any weapon you had when you enter specific areas (except for his service weapon). This is quite different to the unlimited pocket space that seem to be available in most other action shooters. I found this quite annoying at first but in the end, it does make sense. You can't hide an SMG or a pumpgun under a light jacket, after all.
[/list]

After finishing James Bond 007: First Light, I have mixed feelings about it.

The music and gameplay are both quite good, and I genuinely enjoyed most of my time with the game. The gunplay, stealth sections, and overall presentation do a decent job of capturing the spy-action fantasy that you'd expect from a Bond title.

That said, the game often feels longer than it needs to be. A lot of the playtime seems artificially extended through repetitive puzzles, constant hunts for keycards, and similar objective loops that start to wear thin after a while. Had some of this padding been reduced, the game could probably have delivered a tighter and more enjoyable 8–9 hour experience.

My biggest disappointment was the story. The AI-centric plot feels generic and lacks the intrigue, mystery, and memorable twists that usually define great spy thrillers. Throughout the entire game, I never really connected with any of the characters. Nobody stood out, nobody felt particularly memorable, and by the time the credits rolled, I wasn't emotionally invested in any of them.

The female side character also felt overly familiar, coming across as a clear attempt at recreating the mysterious femme fatale archetype popularized by characters like Ada Wong. Unfortunately, she never develops enough of her own identity to become memorable in her own right.

The ending was another letdown. After spending hours with the story, the payoff didn't feel satisfying and left me feeling surprisingly indifferent. A Bond game should leave you with memorable characters, iconic moments, and a sense of adventure. This one simply didn't.

On the technical side, however, credit where it's due. I didn't encounter any major bugs, crashes, or game-breaking issues during my entire playthrough. The game was stable from start to finish, which is becoming increasingly rare these days.

Overall, James Bond 007: First Light is a competent action-adventure game with enjoyable gameplay, solid music, and good technical performance. However, its repetitive padding, forgettable story, weak cast of characters, and underwhelming ending prevent it from becoming anything truly special.

Final Score: 6.5/10

Three days, no breaks by choice. First Light is a tight origin story that earns its place, carried by confident writing, strong performances, and a cast that clearly understood what they were making. Watching someone become Bond rather than Bond simply being Bond is a harder trick than it looks, and it lands.

Gameplay is solid if undemanding in places, and a few gadgets are overpowered enough to drain tension from sections built around them. Neither issue actually broke anything. The fundamentals hold, and the story does the heavy lifting well enough that the rougher edges don't matter much.

007 First Light is a third-person shooter Espionage game set in it's own universe, telling it's own narrative of a young James Bond being recruited to MI6 from the Royal Navy and tracking his journey from a young, naive recruit to the superspy we all know and love.
This game gives the feeling I've been looking for in a James Bond game for years, the feeling of being *in* the action itself, not just watching it on the big screen(although the Bond films are some of my favorites to this day). 
Everything about this game is peak, 10/10 in my humble opinion.
The combat is fluid, fast paced action packed goodness. There's always options to deal with enemies whether it's the silent assassin approach or going in straight up guns blazing triggering explosives.
The espionage portion requires quite a bit of outside-the-box thinking, meaning you really do have to think like a 00 in the heat of the moment and make snapshot decisions that either make or break missions.
The story though? Oh my god the story is PEAK James Bond.
MGM studios really cooked with the story on this! As somebody who was raised watching James Bond films and subsequently playing some of the games throughout my childhood it was a genuine pleasure experiencing in the modern day a properly written, unique to gaming storyline that fits the tradition and idea of what Ian Fleming had for 007 James Bond. The little achievements are callbacks to older Bond films and made me chuckle at how on point they were, Bond's little snarky quips were well timed and executed by Patrick Gibson's portrayal of the secret agent.
The cast selection for mocap and the story is absolutely superb, again MGM really cooked here! 
And the graphics? Well, it's 2026 and this is arguably a triple A competitor of a story based game, there isn't much else to say except they're phenomenal.

All in all, this is a solid 10/10 game and I absolutely positively can't wait until the follow on games! This is one of my favorites of this year, I'd even rank it as beating Resident Evil Requiem, and I absolutely loved Requiem as well!

First Light is basically Hitman + Uncharted. It combines open-ended, social stealth infiltration and recon levels with more bombastic action set-pieces, as well as hybrid levels where stealth and combat are equally viable. Thankfully, both stealth and combat are well-executed.

Combat is a mix of brawling and shooting. Your melee arsenal is surprisingly expansive. You've got punches, tackles, dodges, grabs, parries and throws. Grabbing someone and repeatedly smashing their head into random objects is always fun and charging into someone so they get knocked over a ledge and fall to their death never gets old. I wouldn't say the melee is particularly deep or challenging, as you can use the same sequence of attacks to defeat practically every enemy even on the highest difficulty. However, like the hard-hitting combat in Mad Max, brawling in First Light is just fun.

Shooting is pretty conventional but still enjoyable. You can shoot the enemy's weapon to disarm them, shoot them in the legs to stagger them, etc. This is useful against armored enemies that can't be dispatched in a single headshot. Otherwise, ranged combat mostly boils down to headshots and the occasional explosive barrel.

Stealth borrows a lot of systems and mechanics from Hitman, though it isn't as open-ended. You can hide in tall grass and crowds, occasionally wear disguises, throw objects to knock people out, use emetic poison darts to make them sick, etc. However, you can't move or hide bodies nor can you carry a practically endless number of items to throw as distractions. Instead, you rely on your Q-Watch to aid in stealth by creating distractions, setting off traps or creating cover to block enemy line of sight. It's definitely more rigid than Hitman's stealth but given that this isn't a pure stealth game, it feels flexible enough to make stealth interesting.

The game's story and presentation are well done. I was always interested in finding out where the story was going and which exotic locale I'd visit next. Supporting characters are memorable and well-developed. Bond has his usual wit and charm and the new actor does a great job.

All-in-all, First Light is everything you'd want from a Bond game. Social stealth, regular stealth, luxurious parties, pretty ladies, fancy cars, dramatic vehicle chases, explosive shootouts, messy brawls, elaborate conspiracies and Bond's iconic quips are all here. Depending on your difficulty level, playstyle and completionism, a single playthrough can last anywhere from 15-30 hours. There's a [i]lot[/i] of optional content like challenges, collectibles, unlockable outfits, VR missions and a ton of incidental NPC dialogue to eavesdrop on. If you're a Bond fan, this is an easy recommendation. If you enjoy stealth and/or action games, it's also an easy recommendation, though the slower-paced social stealth segments might be a turnoff if you just want action.

I just finished 007 First Light . As a fan of the franchise, I’m genuinely impressed overall. It successfully blends the spirit of classic Bond films with modern action-adventure gameplay. However, it’s not perfect — there are a few noticeable drawbacks.
Captivating Plot
The story follows a 26-year-old James Bond as he joins MI6’s 00 program after a heroic act as a naval aviator. It’s an origin tale done right — tense, smart, and emotionally grounded. The pacing is excellent, with espionage, high-stakes action, and meaningful character moments woven together like a condensed Bond movie. There are clever twists and a strong narrative drive that kept me hooked for the full ~20-hour campaign.
Excellent Character Portrayal
Young Bond is portrayed as intelligent, charming, and occasionally reckless — a complex, believable person rather than just a suave icon. The supporting cast, including reimagined versions of M, Q, and Miss Moneypenny, are brought to life with strong voice acting and natural dialogue full of wit and tension. The character work is one of the game’s biggest strengths.
Fun and Engaging Gameplay
Gameplay is genuinely enjoyable and varied for the most part. It mixes stealth infiltration, fluid melee combat, gunfights, vehicle chases, and creative gadget use. Missions offer real freedom in how you approach objectives. Levels are well-designed and visually striking, with cinematic set pieces that capture the Bond fantasy. However, some wall-based traversal sections (hanging, dropping, mantling, and climbing) can feel tricky and occasionally laggy. These moments break the flow more than they should and require more precision than the rest of the game.
Mostly Smooth Controls with Some Friction
The third-person controls are responsive and intuitive in combat, shooting, and general movement. Stealth mechanics are fair and well-designed. That said, the same wall traversal issues mentioned above make certain platforming or climbing sequences feel less polished than the rest of the game. It’s not game-breaking, but it’s noticeable enough to pull you out of the moment.
Final Verdict
007 First Light is still a confident and enjoyable James Bond game that nails the story, characters, and core gameplay loop. The wall traversal issues are the main weak point, but they don’t overshadow the rest of the experience.

I played it on two different PCs — one with a 7950X + 5070 Ti and another with a 14600KF + 3060. On the high-end rig at 2K it looks and runs really well. On the 3060 it’s still playable on low settings, but you do get some occasional lag and stuttering, especially in heavier scenes or during those wall sections.

As someone who grew up watching 007 movies, from Sean Connery to Roger Moore to Pierce Brosnan and of course the newest movies with Daniel Craig, I've always loved this franchise. Sure they're a bit ridiculous at times but you know that going into it. High tension, high action spy thrillers with a charismatic James Bond at the lead, seemingly untouchable until he lets his love for beautiful women cloud his judgement, barely pulling out a win at the end. It's formulaic but if you love it, then you really love it. This game takes that feeling from the movies and puts it into your hands. You really do feel like a young, modern James Bond learning how to be a spy and the thin line between following orders and committing treason.

The game is very fun, the shooting is smooth, the melee combat is simple but still satisfying. The energy system with Bluffs is very fun, stealthily taking down 1 hostile while another comes around the corner just for Bond to somehow talk his way out of it. Absolutely has plot armor but so does every version of 007 to exist. The gadgets you get throughout the game are also very fun to have at your disposal. You'll unlock more gadgets as you get through the first few missions but being able to hack, laser, smoke bomb, missile pen, and more gives so much variety to what you can do. You can also only bring 4 gadgets on a mission, with the hacking one being required in the main story. So you have to decide what gadgets you enjoy and want to bring and through this, can make each mission feel a little different from player to player.

The story itself is captivating enough to keep your attention. I wouldn't say anything oscar-worthy but still good and keeps you wanting more to figure out the mystery behind what's going on and who is the mastermind. Also, the "Hitman-like" design in its levels is really cool. It does feel like there are several ways to complete your next objective and it is up to you as the player how you want to do it. I wouldn't say it's as in-depth as Hitman, obviously, but it always gives you at least 2-4 options of how you want to handle each situation. Anywhere from having to find someone's Press ID to pose as a journalist for access to areas, climbing up the side of the building and in through a window, down to just beating up everyone who gets in your way if you get spotted. It feels very natural however you decide to tackle that objective. Now once you get into the final about quarter to a third of the game, that feeling goes away a little bit as it becomes more linear in its design. Would've liked to see it keep more of that interesting, multi-layered design, but it doesn't ruin the game by any means.

Also, yes, it is a shorter game. You could probably complete the main story in about 10-12 hours, even less if you're really rushing through all the encounters. Whether it's worth the $70 to you to experience about 10 hours of a 007 movie with you at the driver's seat, well that's for you to decide. For me, I would say that it was worth it but I also love the 007 franchise. Beyond that, there's also challenges to complete throughout the main story and its side mode, "Tactical Simulations". This is a composition of levels that you would have seen throughout the main story while giving you specific objectives. Relatively short, each one of the "Escalations" can be fully completed with all challenges in about, 20-30 minutes give or take. And there's 5 of them. Then there's Operations which are more difficult but the same idea, there's only 2 of those right now. However, it seems like this TacSIM mode is going to have further content updates added to it. So over time, there will be more to do here, just not a whole lot right now.

Some issues I did have, some graphical bugs. Weird blurring around character models, especially with any bright light behind them. Weird ghosting where the side of their face and ear would double, not something I've seen much of. Despite that, performance itself was pretty good. I run an ultra-wide monitor at 5120 x 1440p, had all the settings at high, DLSS on Performance, Frame Generation x2. With that, I ran anywhere from 80fps at the lowest up to about 110fps at the highest. I'm attaching my specs so you can see how yours might compare. Also in terms of the story, seems like some characters were just completely forgotten about by the end. They appeared like they might have had some importance early on but were kinda written off instead. Again, nothing too big, but noticeable. 

All in all, 007 First Light is an amazing callback to the 007 franchise and everything that people like me love about it.

Solid game that gives you a great spectacle with everything you like about 007 from the movies using Hitman-Lite features. Stealth is solid with Bond's gadgets, making it to where you can possibly get through an entire section without sounding alarms or taking out guards. Combat system is simple, but effective as it challenges you to not just rely on your guns, but also your gadgets, environment and good ole' fisticuffs. The game will also throw in a random wrench in at times and put Bond through scenarios from interrogations, car chases, and many other manner of scenarios to break the pace up. Characters are very charming as they have their own distinct personalities and the voice acting really shines through to make these characters dislikeable/likeable (in the appropriate way of the character of course)

I think the main issue i have is that it focuses on more of being a Jack of All Trades rather than focusing on a few key elements and really nailing them on the head. Yes you do have a great framework in terms of gameplay loop. Usually consisting of get thrown into a new area, find your bearings by gaining info on your objective, stealth and possibly go loud and then progress the story to unravel something new. It is my belief that they could have gone deeper with consequences of going loud versus stealth, added more intuitive driving sections that involve more sporty cars, alternate routes that resulted in different cutscenes, or bosses that could have used a little more time in the oven.

However, I'm a big spectacle guy and First Light delivers on that front ten fold with solid graphics and set pieces, some stuttering will be prevalent though and I did have one crash. You'll go from jumping out of planes in European countries to sailing boats in Vietnam for your next mission objective. Variety is the edge that really takes this entry to the next level in the triple AAA space, though that might be at the sacrifice of the story. While having great dialogue and voice acting, the story might've ended a bit faster than some would like or some things felt out of place to pad runtime. Feels like the game will push you into the next thing a little too quickly rather than let you sit with what you just unraveled/experienced. Sometimes the opposite will be true as you have to get through at leats 2 doors as a chore just to get through to the end of a hall.

Despite this, I believe 007 is a GREAT first swing for IOI interactive to get their feet wet with this IP. I'm curious to see the improvements that they'll maker in the sequel. While I personally feel it could have used a bit more time to REALLY flesh out the mechanics and story, this game checks every box you want out of a 007 game from IO Interactive. Very little now do we get a game that is just beginning, middle and end. Thankfully one of the best games of the year so far is just that. Just wish we could've gotten more like what a lot of the big critics are claiming it is.

It's "FIne". Not great, not terrible. If you like short linear games where you're railroaded and hand-held and guided in one direction then this is for you. It's got some great set pieces and little moments, but somewhere around the halfway mark it drops off a cliff. Characters disappear, plot points just end at a screeching halt, And you go from one story arc with one set of characters in one location to another location with entirely new characters and a new plot that seems disconnected from what you did 10 minutes ago. Around this time, the plot also becomes predictable and I immediately guessed what was going to happen next, who the villain was when a new character appeared, and what their motives were. 

It's stuck between wanting to be a 007 game and a cinematic game, but fails at both because it refuses to commit to either. So what you get is an incredibly clunky stealth game where stealth is encouraged but not practical because of little things like being unable to drag or hide bodies and levels being so linear you can sneak around enemies as much as you're able to sneak around a very narrow corridor with no alternative route because that's the way the game wants you to go, and an action game that wants you to be creative by limiting your ammo (like having 5 bullets left in your gun, that's how limited we're talking) and using your gadgets and environment. But, the enemies are far too dumb and aggressive who rush you relentlessly giving you no time to analyse your surroundings to even use them to your advantage, so it's better to focus on the gunplay instead and play it like a traditional third-person shooter rather than a tactical action game with gadgets because it is unrelenting in giving you no space to breathe or process. Great for intense firefights that require situational awareness if this was a dedicated TPS, but it's not and your ammo is limited, so it's think fast or die. Stay in one place, you're dead. break cover, you're dead. don't have enough charges left for your gadgets to stun/neutralise enemies advancing on you, create a distraction or something like smoke to cover you; you're dead. Oh look, there's a pipe there. want to blow it up? too late, by the time you noticed you already have enemies Infront of you, to the left of you, to the right of you, behind you, on top of you, and below you, and there are already 3 grenades flying in your direction while you have no gadgets left and only 2 bullets left in your gun. The action segments in this game can be VERY punishing in an unfair and almost dare i say untested way where the devs overestimate how many you can handle at once. These issues kill the idea of being smart and playing smarter instead of harder because it forces you into scripted action segments, so there's no way to possibly avoid it. 

Going back to what i mentioned about railroading; the game also sets up very deliberate ways to deal with enemies that take a lot of your freedom away because this isn't how the devs want YOU to get around a problem, it's how THEY want you to get around a problem. Like in hitman you could set up very intricate chains of events or distractions to move targets or enemies around to set up creative traps in different ways, but not here. in 007, enemies will conveniently stand next to objects encouraging you to use that one specific way to neutralise them, or one specific way to distract them and have them look in one direction so you can get past them or steal something. There's no figuring things out for yourself, it's just "oh they're stood next to an electrical device. i better use that to electrocute them". 
Your agency as a player is very limited. 

I'm trying not to be one of those "hitman" people because i went into this game forcing myself to have an open mind, but after finishing it, i can't help it... Hitman was better. You'll notice my review time that i have 20 hours; well my hitman time is in the 200 hours. If hitman is an ocean you can swim in for hundreds of hours, then 007 is a puddle you can splash your feet in for a few hours like a toddler. There's just no depth or breadth, it's a short kinda sweet game which might be good for some players, but for more ambitious players who want something to sink your teeth into, this will disappoint you. I have just beaten 007 First Light in it's entirety and I'll cut to this chase. This game is phenomenal it is not a perfect game but it comes pretty close to it.

First off, the story and I happy to say they nailed it. This feels like a proper James Bond adventure down to an incredible title sequence and song. It features many twists and turns that I will not spoil here. It can be a little slow to start but the pay off is worth it. Moneypenny, Q, and Greenway I feel are standout characters. Patrick Gibson does an excellent job as a younger Bond slowly morphing into the James Bond we are all familiar with by the end of the game.

Gameplay: This is not a copy/paste of Hitman. As you play you will see that the combat system is kind of it's own thing. The basic punch and jab combos remind me of Arkham but not as detailed, this is my least favorite part of the combat system but it helps in a pinch. The gunplay I really enjoyed, but it is limited MI6 only grants a "license to kill" when the enemies have the express purpose of killing Bond. Were the majority of the game's combat system really excels is in it's stealth. Similar to Hitman, you will find yourself trying to take down enemies quietly though stealth. Q has also provided many gadgets to assist along the way.  A favorite of mine happened to be the laser strap.

Cons: I found the AI to be wildly inconsistent. I played on the normal difficulty. Sometimes the AI would be dumb as rocks and wouldn't notice me "stealthily" take out a enemy right in front of their line of sight. Sometimes the AI would be incredibly efficient and deadly. There was also a level midway though the game I wasn't super fond of but it improved and these sections were few and far between. I also wish the game was longer but I feel this is a nitpick because the story presented here was so well done I rather it not be padded out.

Overall Rating: 9/10 A phenomenal Game I enjoyed from beginning to end. I hope many more Bond games come out of IO they clearly have a love for the IP.

TL/DR:   If you're even the slightest bit of a James Bond fan, this game will [i]more[/i] than scratch that itch. The narrative is tight and well written, the characters are endlessly entertaining, the gameplay is easy to learn with an endless ceiling for making cool moments happen. Highly recommended.

   007 First Light hits every narrative beat you'd expect from a James Bond story; cool gadgets, quippy dialogue, high-flying stunts and plenty of plot twists. Patrick Gibson does a great job portraying a young and naive Bond cutting his teeth in the world of spycraft. Players should expect a slow burn with plenty of time devoted to Bond's training and his introduction to MI6. Once the narrative really opens up, however, you'll already be so invested you won't be able to put the game down.

   It was only until around the third act that I really got a handle on how I felt about the gameplay. For about half of my time playing I found myself frustrated by how much this game railroads the player into following a specific path. The one thing I'd recommend to someone first starting this game is to remember that

   [i]This is NOT Hitman[/i]

   I have [i]hours[/i] in Hitman World of Assassination, so I couldn't help but, during the more open sections of each chapter, try to do things that First Light simply wouldn't accommodate. Attacking certain NPC's, swapping disguises (which happens about three times in the story), taking alternate routes or employing certain tactics that feel natural to Agent 47 but would be [i]completely[/i] out of character for James Bond. Once I accepted what this game set out to be, I was more than able to enjoy it.

   This is first and foremost a narrative-based, linear game. Some sections offer the player a choice in how they want to accomplish a certain goal, but the goal will be met regardless. If you accept this, you'll find this game has plenty to keep you entertained. For one thing, the combat is spectacular. As opposed to Hitman, in which I couldn't help but save-scum as soon as my cover was blown, IOI did a fantastic job making firefights and hand-to-hand feel punchy and satisfying. More importantly, this game avoids the stealth game trap of tempting the player with the goal of never being detected in order to achieve a higher mission rating or score. You will be detected and enter combat many times during a level but it never feels like you've done something wrong.  I was often looking forward to the gameplay sections where I had "license to kill" and could freely dispatch hostiles at my leisure.

   Special credit to the score. This game is conservative with it's use of Bond's theme, so when it finally kicks in the player [i]really[/i] feels it.

   The story leaves itself open to what I'm hoping are many sequels to come, with what I theorize is a hint at Spectre becoming the over-arching "villain" to a multi-part series. I can't wait for more.

I enjoyed it from beginning to end. IOI did a great job with the IP, and I can't wait for more.
I'm impressed that this game was able to add something that older James Bond games were lacking in: acting like a spy.
While older games from previous generations of consoles tended to go straight for the FPS or cover-based shooter route, it was wildly refreshing to get a game like First Light where you weren't forced to rely on gunplay. Of course there are well crafted action sequences where shooting a gun is fun, but you will also be utilizing the gadget mechanics as clear those moments. Admittedly the gadgets are pretty simple and somewhat limited, it really does feel like IOI's other Hitman games when you're activating steam pipes, or messing with pulleys to drop a light rig onto enemies. But generally, it is satisfying to use the Q-watch to help sneak through levels.
I was initially a little disappointed when I heard that IOI was going to be in charge of making the new James Bond game, because Hitman has in recent years been pretty rigid in terms of gameplay and combat. Of course I knew that IOI would do an amazing job with level design, that would never be an issue, because the maps in Hitman felt open-ended and sprawling. However IOI has never proven that they can perform combat better than just picking up and using a gun, or throwing a briefcase at a target. Yet they proved me wrong. The hand-to-hand combat is fast and exciting. Being able to counter and grab enemies, throwing them off ledges, and effortlessly chucking loose objects at foes to stun them was extremely fun.

Overall, I like the direction 007 First Light went, and I like what IOI has done with the 007 IP.

If you like James Bond at all this feels like the modern version of that vibe done right. It’s fast, stylish, and actually tells a story that feels grounded instead of just “generic villain with a doomsday toy.” The shooting is solid, but the CQC is so satisfying I ditched guns half the time, very “Bond brawling his way through a facility” energy. The gadgets are top-tier too (missile pen is elite), giving off strong Q-branch-from-GoldenEye vibes, and the spy gameplay finally leans into that whole “sneak, improvise, and charm your way through trouble” feel Pierce Brosnan’s Bond nailed. Bond himself is spot-on—smooth, witty, a little reckless—and the mix of exotic locations, slick action, and slightly over-the-top villains feels straight out of that GoldenEye era. Complaining about “too much stealth” in a Bond game is like complaining about satellite weapons in GoldenEye and that’s literally the point. Only real nitpicks are the limited gadget loadout (let me carry everything, I’m Bond) and a slightly awkward camera in tight fights, but overall this finally feels like the closest thing we’ve gotten to capturing that GoldenEye magic—pour a martini (shaken, not stirred) and enjoy.

I'm a lifelong Bond fan who has read the books as a kid, and loves all the movies. This game nails the feeling of the 007 stories, while modernising them. Sure, its not winning any awards for writing, but the plot is suitable. The hand to hand combat is simple but flows well and really feels like scrappy fist fight. After dumping about 37 hours, I can safely say that this game is an absolute gem and could be one of my games of the year so far.

The big highlight of the game and what I was most excited for going in was the combat. In my opinion, it rivals the original F.E.A.R. as some of the most satisfying combat I've played, because in so many ways, you can just get really silly and creative when taking out enemies. The big feature with the combat for me was the ability to throw your gun, as well as any random objects off a table or something, because it makes for some very funny moments amidst the chaos. I constantly found myself shooting the guns out of enemy hands, closing the distance, and engaging in hand to hand fights right smack in the middle of a large gun battle because it was just that fun. And combine that with the gadgets in your arsenal, I have nothing to complain about in this aspect.

This being 007 and also an IOI game, what carried over from Hitman were the stealth, espionage, and immersive sim aspects, and IOI once again proves that they know how to tackle social stealth. Each mission has you tackling objectives in unconventional ways, and you are encouraged to explore and find as many opportunities as possible: gathering intel, sneaking through restricted areas, eavesdropping on conversations, using your gadgets carefully and creatively, and bluffing your way through confrontations. It makes for some very satisfying spy fantasy and scratches that itch for some good stealth. However, keep your expectations in check because it is admittedly more simplified and streamlined compared to Hitman's stealth. This is a linear story-focused game, so you don't get as much freedom as you would as Agent 47.

The voice acting is top-notch across the board, especially this new younger iteration of James Bond by Patrick Gibson, who managed to put his own spin on the character while also harnessing traits from previous versions of Bond. The side characters were also very good and had their own moments to shine, especially Q who is always a blessing to see.

The soundtrack is just *chef's kiss* perfection. Lana Del Rey's 'First Light" song during the title sequence will go down as one of my top 007 sequences, up there with Casino Royale and Skyfall.

It's also just a very pretty looking game, with some beautiful locations and backdrops, realistic facial capture from all the main characters, and some really fun action set pieces sprinkled throughout.

Now the game is not perfect, and I do have complaints. Some can be fixed with updates, and others not so much.

The story, while fun, was very predictable and clichéd. It's not bad, but it's nothing you haven't seen before, and I found myself questioning some of the writing, especially in the latter half when it got super silly even for 007. I also felt there wasn't enough development between some character relationships for me to buy into them, and felt kind of rushed. The villains were also pretty weak and weren't very compelling or intimidating. [spoiler]Nicholas Webb being a twist villain was fine, but he ultimately became the typical boring businessman who wants power with the whole AI computer ruling the world plotline. His son Damien Webb was cartoonishly evil, but he was at least entertaining to watch with his hammy performance.[/spoiler] It wasn't enough to deter the overall experience, but it's something I do hope IOI improves upon for the next 007 game.

I was unfortunately a little disappointed by some of the vehicle sections because it felt like a missed opportunity for IOI to do something cool with them. Other than a handful of cool chase sequences as well as [spoiler]the sick as hell Aston Martin cameo at the end of the game[/spoiler], it was mainly just driving slowly down a long path with some dialogue, occasionally getting out and push some buttons, driving some more down another path, and that's it; at that point, it should've just been a cutscene. It felt like they were there just to pad out the playtime.

Enemy AI can be kind of all over the place at times. Sometimes they're brutal and can overpower you in combat, and other times they're either stupid and can't hit anything or just become BS and snipe you through walls and smoke screens.

You can't move or hide bodies, which was a very odd thing to omit, considering a large part of the game is stealth. Way too often, I would stealthily take down enemies from behind only for their bodies to be discovered minutes later by a random patrolling guard because they were just left out in the open, which causes every enemy nearby to become alerted, and I risk blowing my cover because of that.

Checkpoints were kind of inconsistent, where sometimes when I restart from a checkpoint, it backtracks me way further than necessary, and I lose upwards of nearly 30 minutes of progress, and I have to do it all again just to get back to where I was before.

I ran into some performance issues occasionally, where the FPS would randomly drop to unplayable framerates and would stay like that until I had to drop the graphics settings.

So yeah, despite its shortcomings, this is a very solid game with some excellent gameplay and a nice treat, especially for 007 fans. Easily an 8/10 and can even be a 9/10 once some of the glitches and bugs are fixed.

007: First Light is a downgrade in many ways from the Hitman games, with its now-constrained maps and light systems. But it is a massive upgrade in story, dialog, music, cinematics and combat, especially melee combat. While it’s no God of War or Last of Us, it’s much better than last year’s Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. If you like the Bond movies, and you like big budget action titles, you’ll like this game.  

–

We’re given a wonderful origin story for 007. After an explosive opening mission, we’re recruited into the newly re-opened double-0 training program. We make friends with the other agents, and are treated to a cinematic training montage that doubles as an actual training for you as a player.

We grow to like our new friends, and dislike our overbearing boss. And, well, the story goes on, with drama, stakes, deaths, love affairs, and even some big questions about AI, government, and how much we should trust the system.

The story is fantastic. It dragged a bit in the midgame, before the stakes were fully revealed. But the beginning and especially the end are wonderful. I felt the emotions the game was trying to pull out of me, to a greater degree than even the Daniel Craig movies.

–

This is not a Hitman game, and does not feature the gigantic open maps and NPC schedules. These maps are claustrophobic by comparison. You are not free to approach a level any way you like. It’s sliced up into constrained smaller, linear areas composed of a few rooms.

These areas are dedicated to one of three types of gameplay: One, gun violence where killing is allowed, two, stealth where no guns are allowed, or, three, eavesdropping and light questing. The game alternates between one and the other, and just as soon as you’re getting bored of one, it throws another at you. (And between them, it's lots of walking and vaulting and climbing.)

To help you succeed, you’re given the choice of two spy gadgets (or three, at the end of the game). You can recharge these gadgets with power-ups located throughout a level. For gun-violence sections, you can also pick up enemy weapons briefly, but aren’t generally allowed to carry them with you for long.

My favorite part of the game was fisticuffs. There’s a fantastic melee combat system that is super cinematic and also comfortably challenging. Towards the end, I was opting to always use melee if I could, it was just that much fun. There are two ways to avoid attacks (parrying and dodging), a light combo system, multiple attacks, contextual attacks (such as bashing with a nearby coffee cup). It’s delightful.

–

As much as I like 007, it has its dull moments. The game is a bit like modern prestige television, in that there's a lot of downtime between the interesting parts. I found myself bored of walking and conversations in interstitial spaces, just waiting for the next time I get to make an interesting decision.

There’s no experience system, nor character customization. No items other than the gadgets. No branching dialog or branching choices. There isn’t that much value to exploring, and levels are extremely linear. 007 doesn’t ask very much of you. But it is fun. And by the end, I found myself looking forward to playing the next installment someday.

Recommended.

It is undeniable just how perfect the combat is--while [i]Batman[/i] is more melee-focused, and [i]Uncharted[/i] is more gun-focused, this game strikes the perfect 50/50 balance of both. It's a stark departure from the quieter, strategic assassinations of [i]Hitman[/i], though gadgets still remain essential when going stealth. I'd say the closest parallel is [i]Indiana Jones[/i], thanks to its globe-trotting adventure through similarly exotic locales, though it's a more melee-heavy and less linear immersive FPS.

This young Bond lacks the characteristic misogyny of his predecessors, but I think they missed the opportunity for a creative way to address it such that he could grow in sequels. Though impulsive and quippy, Bond is extremely emotionally mature for his youth and never loses his temper. Conversely, this incarnation of M seems rather naive, and MI6 appears to be severely understaffed, sending seven rookie trainees after a dangerous rogue double-O when it would have made far more sense to deploy experienced agents instead. Everyone else, like Moneypenny and Q, however, has extremely well-written dialogue, which also applies to the crowd NPCs.

At maxed settings, OptiScaler FSR 4 Native 1440p, performance averages in the 100s, never dropping below 70 FPS in busy scenes, while scaling down well to my ROG Ally X at lowest settings, staying far north of 30. Though dropping to TAA yields more performance, I strongly recommend against it due to the lack of sharpening, muddying the picture. Don't use the built-in FSR 3.1 Quality because it struggles to resolve hair cleanly. Most action-adventures are designed around controller play, but First Light offers separate binds on keyboard for things like takedowns so you can guarantee your inputs.

[h2]Cinematic Brilliance with Room to Grow[/h2]

007 First Light has left me completely torn. On one hand, it features some of the best storytelling, acting, and world-building of the year, making it a legitimate Game of the Year contender. On the other hand, its core gameplay mechanics are so unpolished and frustrating that they constantly drag the experience down. When buying a single-player, story-driven game like this, the baseline expectation is that the core gameplay should be average or above average. IO Interactive has crafted an incredible cinematic experience, but the actual act of playing it is a mixed bag that comes with heavy caveats.

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Cinematic Brilliance, Brief Story[/h3]
The absolute strength of this game lies in its production value. The story, acting, animation, graphics, locations, and music all combine beautifully to create an immaculate James Bond atmosphere. It feels like a premium, big-budget spy thriller from start to finish. The only real letdown on this front is that the narrative is disappointingly short, leaving you wanting more of this world before it abruptly wraps up.

[h3]Subpar Combat and Restricted Gadgets[/h3]
While the presentation shines, the combat reveals some significant mechanical weaknesses. The melee system is incredibly basic, and though it is passable, it feels subpar and needs a lot more work. The shooting fares slightly better, but it is crippled by a cover system that is barely functional. Forcing the player out of cover is a fine design choice, but it only works if the actual cover mechanics function properly, like the smooth snapping found in games like [i]Gears of War[/i].

The gadgets themselves are highly entertaining, but you are severely limited by your inventory. The developers should have allowed a larger limit of four or more active tools, along with a dedicated spare slot for situational mission items like lighters. Expanding the gadget pool would have naturally enhanced the weak melee and cover systems, giving players reliable tactical options like smoke grenades when caught out in the open.

[h3]"IGN-Safe" Driving and Plot Armor[/h3]
The driving sections are an absolute shambles. The only interactive advancement this game has over a basic sequence like [i]Mixtape[/i] is that you actually have to press the accelerate button. The vehicles themselves seem like they are modeled to be perfectly functional for actual gameplay, making it incredibly disappointing that the developers chose to turn these segments into glorified, self-driving set pieces just to keep them safe for IGN and other reviewers.

Nothing encapsulates this frustration better than the boat chase. Watching a massive, metaphorical "no entry" sign pop up over your target just to enforce blatant plot armor is a baffling design choice that completely breaks immersion.

[h3]The Painful Damien Interrogation[/h3]
To add insult to mechanical injury, the game suffers from some frustrating script bugs. The Damien interrogation sequence is downright painful. On my first attempt, the initial options I selected were entirely correct, but the game glitched and decided to register it as a failure. After multiple annoying tries and eventually looking it up online, I was surprised to see I should have passed it on the very first go.

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Final Verdict[/h3]
I still like 007 First Light for its incredible atmosphere, top-tier acting, and gorgeous world. I can still recommend it, but only with massive caveats. If IO Interactive can tighten up the melee, put some serious polish on the shooting, and actually let the player drive the cars, their future Bond titles will be unstoppable. For now, it remains a heavily flawed title that just misses its true Game of the Year potential.

It's playable, but it lacks the smoothness I'd expect from a modern AAA title. You can definitely feel the frame rate dips during action sequences, which breaks immersion .

Very good 007 game out of IOI, although some of its constrained design choices and fledgling gameplay systems prevent true greatness. This game shares a TON of DNA with the Hitman: World of Assassination games, but it is not a sandbox like those games. It is much more an on-rails, narrative experience borrowing a lot of gameplay elements (stealth, traversal, gadgets, takedowns, disguises), plus some new/refined ones (CQC system comparable to the Arkham games, better gunplay), with Hitman.

To put a numbered score, I give this game 7.5/10.

It's not really an apples-to-apples comparison, but this is probably the best Bond game I've ever played. But it's not going to replace any nostalgic GoldenEye multiplayer memories you have, since it isn't multiplayer. It looks great and ran perfectly on my system. Zero crashes, super stable framerate.

Campaign length is about 15-20 hours, depending on how many resets/respawns you do.

TacSim, a smaller challenge mode, has about 2 hours of content to clear right now, and the rest is challenge grinding the same content.

The story is pretty good, with some highs and lows, but I'll let you experience that for yourself. As an origin story, it's better than most.

The gameplay is pretty neat, there's 3 major "modes" to it. Secret agent/Stealth mode where you aren't in a fight, and you're either sneaking around restricted areas, taking down guards, or blending into civilians and gathering intel. There are a few disguises in the game, but a tiny amount compared to Hitman WoA. Still, THIS portion of the game feels almost exactly like Hitman WoA. I know this game ISN'T trying to be Hitman 4, but not being able to drag bodies for improved stealth is crazy. I'll die on that hill.

As soon as you get caught, or start a fight, there are the two escalating modes. Close Quarter Combat (CQC), and this is essentially a 007 fistfight scene. You can strike or grapple in a few different ways, and it's mainly about parrying or dodging enemy attacks, then attacking in an opening. You can also use the environment quite a bit. Edges, walls, and throwables are all over, and often allow for instant takedowns, or at least long stuns. Having to enemy lock-on feature seemed a little weird.

You can end up in a fistfight without the entire level becoming hostile, however. Enemies are often found in relatively small groups, and if you beat up 2-4 of them in a room, the game will downshift to the stealth/civilian mode with "Situation Contained".

The final mode is called Licensed to Kill. Once enemies pull lethal weapons on you, or you get cleared to put enemies down (narratively), you can pull your guns and start popping heads. The cover system took some getting used to, but it's essential for staying safe in firefights. Nothing overly difficult or innovative here. Enemies perform basic flank, search, and grenade throws to try to get you out of cover, and some cover is destructible. The gunplay feels much improved over Hitman WoA, but it's not best-in-class.

There are a handful of short, simple driving sequences with a driving model that I would call... serviceable. It won't offend you, but it might jar you if you've been playing Forza recently.

In all 3 modes, you can make use of Gadgets, and these are both fun and powerful. I will let you discover these on your own, but you can stun, nauseate, smoke bomb (and more!) your way out of every conceivable encounter. The real meat of the gameplay comes with learning to blend the stealth, gunplay, and gadgets all together as one to prosper.

What about the "constrained design choices" I mentioned? You can think of this game as a 20-hour romp of 100 different arenas. Some arenas are small, medium, or large. Some give a lot of freedom in how your Bond approaches the solution to progress to the next arena. Some arenas are extremely biased, the designers decided "No, THIS ONE IS A GUN FIGHT!" I think the game design was a bit too heavy-handed in biasing a lot of these arenas toward one gameplay mode or another. They could have loosened up a little.

A brief example: I reached a spot where Bond had been "made" during an infiltration, and kill teams are deployed to put him down. The arena begins in stealth and Licensed to Kill mode. The kill teams are searching the area, slowly closing the net around Bond's position. The intensity is great, but despite the difficulty, I managed to stealth past all of the kill teams and reach the exit door to the next arena. Nope! "Hostiles nearby", I HAD to kill the guards. As soon as I took down one guard with a stealth takedown, every enemy instantly knew my position and started shooting. This is an example of the "heavy-handed decision", now imagine that for roughly half of the arenas in the game.

007 First Light is at its best when it sets up the game board, but lets YOU choose what Bond succeeds. Ninja Bond? John Wick Bond? Batman Bond? Let the player decide as often as possible. First Light decides for you, just slightly too often, I think out of a misplaced notion of "A proper Bond movie is 30% infiltration, 30% CQC, 30% gunplay, and 10% banging Bond Girls, and our game must be this ratio too!" 

I disagree.

If the idea of a somewhat Hitman-y, narrative focused 007 game excites you, then this game is a good buy for you.

If you want more sandbox freedom, play Hitman: World of Assassination instead. It's better at that.

If you're a bit so-so on all this, I'd wait for sale.

IO ended up being a great choice for the first Bond game in over a decade. I love the Hitman games and believed in them, but they really nailed this one.

Compared to the Hitman WoA trilogy, this is more linear with sections that branch out into having multiple options to solve your objectives. The stealth feels great, and if you get caught, it doesn't feel like you've ruined your run. You can just dispatch the enemies in that vicinity, and as long as you don't allow anyone to radio for help, it'll resolve the conflict and you can stay in stealth. I also really enjoyed the bluffing mechanic that lets you lie to enemies while in a restricted area, and make a quick escape before they come back around to being hostile to you.

The shooting is better than Hitman's, but it's not stellar by any means. If you're a half-decent shot, it does end up becoming a bit of a headshot simulator. The integration of Q gadgets into combat (both shooting and melee) is fun, and fits the theme of using your tools and the environment to your advantage. You don't have to fight fair, since the enemies outnumber you.

The story and dialogue are well written, if maybe not the best in the world. I cared about most of the main cast, although some relationships feel like they build too quickly or have some conflicts resolved very suddenly. Overall, though it wasn't much of an issue.

Patrick Gibson does a great job as a young Bond, and I also liked M and especially Moneypenny in this. The acting overall was excellent.

The pacing of everything stays pretty high, and other than the initial load, and deaths, the game is pretty much seamless between cutscenes, stealth, action, driving, etc. from beginning to end. 

Graphics and art design of the locations are great (which isn't surprising since Hitman WoA is also a globe-trotting adventure) and the game ran well for me maxed out -though I have a high end rig, YMMV there. It has some pretty great set pieces as well, though for a game that's a mix of Hitman and Uncharted, they don't quite hit the same insane quality of set pieces that Naughty Dog has in their games. That said, it's overall a very impressive game. (and I think I've seen they're adding Path Tracing in an update?)

Overall I very much enjoyed this game. A great 007 game. The gameplay is a mix of Hitman The World of Assassination Trilogy-lite open world sandbox and tight cinematic linear gameplay. The melee system is basic but competent and the interactivity with the environment while throwing punches and yanking enemies into the walls actually feels fantastic. The gunplay takes some getting used to but with practice, you will mow down hordes of soldiers with a single headshot the way a James Bond would be expected to. 

The high point of the game is the cinematics. Visuals are gorgeous with the help of good lighting and style, even if the graphics are not cutting edge. The intro song and menu theme and the rest of the music works much better in the game than on YouTube so take that into account.

I really liked the characters in this game, more than I expected. I was annoyed by the characters that I was supposed to be irritated by, I was enjoying the characters I was meant to form a bond with, I hated the villains when it was time to hate them, I was ambivalent on the characters that Bond was ambivalent with. The game did a great job steering my emotions where it intended to be steered. The two characters that grew the most in the game are Bond and Greenway and I found their banter to be pretty fun. I do wish we had more closure on different characters that left the story for one reason or another, the game felt maybe 30 minutes short on cutscenes to better tie together the story.

The game moves slower than you think at first with the intro level and the absolutely massive 2 hour tutorial levels, Then it speeds up faster than you expect at the end in pacing. I finished the last 3 missions in a row, and it felt exactly like a Bond movie. After sitting with the ending for a few hours, my opinion has only improved on this game. It says that my playthrough lasted 23 hours but in reality, I left the game paused for 3 hours so I got 20 hours out of the game, exploring everything, since I got pretty immersed in this game. If you rush through just the main points of the story, it will be less than 15 hours.

There is a repeatable challenge mode in the game, letting you try different scenarios as part of Bond's training. I expect the developers to add to this mode in the future but I have not tried it out. It looks like a smaller more focused version of the Hitman modes, not as detailed or comprehensive or free-form but similar in style.

TLDR = A solid entertaining and stylish foundation for a promising series of 007 games. Perfect for those who like James Bond or want a cinematic spy game that lasts 15-20 hours, depending on how much you explore.

This is absolutely the best [u]Bond[/u] game ever made. (The only reason GoldenEye still has an argument is because of Oddjob in four-player multiplayer.)
IO Interactive nailed the source material. The Bond vibe was just enough to feel authentic (Not enough casual Seksism tbh), and everything they added to the universe feels believable and plausible rather than forced.

That said, it's also clear that the game could have used more playtesting time. Considering it was delayed from January, I can only imagine what state it was in before the delay, so I'm glad IOI took the extra time instead of simply pushing it out the door. As you progress further into the game, the rough edges become more noticeable. Objective directions can be unclear, vault and interaction points sometimes feel inconsistent, and there were multiple moments where I found myself asking, "Wait, what am I supposed to be doing?" Most of these are relatively minor issues that I would [b]expect[/b] will be addressed in post-launch updates.

Ironically, my biggest gripe isn't really with First Light itself, it's with me. After more than 20 years of playing Hitman, IOI has basically programmed me to hate chaos. First Light is not Hitman, and it shouldn't be. It's Bond. The game wants you to embrace action, improvisation, and situations spiralling out of control. But my Hitman instincts constantly had me looking for the perfect silent solution, and the game forces chaos a little too often for my liking. That's not necessarily a flaw in the design, but it's something I struggled with throughout the experience.

The acting is outstanding across the board, and credit has to go to the entire cast. It was also a very brave move by IOI to take one of gaming's most beloved franchises, secure the Bond licence, and then fully commit to making a Bond game rather than just reskinning Hitman. They took a risk, and for me, it paid off.

How this game has received so many positive reviews... It's Sonic Frontiers all over again. People are so desperate to get a somewhat playable game in the franchise they love, and they start hailing it as the second coming of Christ. And unfortunately, I fell for it and shelled out the 70 bucks.

I'll start with the good: the voice acting is top notch. The cutscenes are well done and the cinematography is excellent. The game itself is also very well optimized. I'm getting a consistent 120+ FPS on 1440P with all settings maxed, with only DLSS enabled and without frame generation. This day and age, that is extremely rare in a triple A game. The way this game handled the basic tutorial is also something that I haven't seen in any game before, and it was really well done.

The flipside of this optimization is that the graphics aren't exactly... stellar. They're servicable, sure, but there's so many corners cut - likely to get the optimization to where it is - that they're pretty obvious while playing, and it makes for some [i]interesting[/i] immersion breaks. My personal favorite is where Greenway lost all of his teeth while talking to me in Aleph. Another contender is the laughably short draw distance in some high-speed areas.
Aside from that, the character models also give me a bit of "uncanny valley" vibe while in-game. Remember folks, this is on all settings maxed and with DLSS set to Quality. You can tell that most of the graphical effort went into the cutscenes.

And maybe that's a good thing too, because there are [i]a lot of them[/i]. And you've got to think that the developers realized this, because a lot of the time, you'll just be playing a walking simulator from one cutscene to the next. As if the developers thought that me pressing forward for two minutes would somehow break the feeling that some of these cutscenes just go on for way too long. But hey, if you're a hardcore Bond fan, you'll probably like that. If you're like me and only casually interested in the franchise, you will get bored of them rather quickly.

That brings us to gameplay. Now let me start out by saying that I bought the game based on what the store page right here on Steam told me. There's an "action" tag, there's plenty of action and cool setpieces in the videos and screenshots on display, and even the store page description explicitly states that you can "go in quiet or go in loud".

Should I have maybe done more research? Probably, yeah. But I think the consumer can be pardoned if the store is actively making you think you're buying a full-on action game, and then not getting said full-on action game. Because make no mistake, this game is a stealth-game first and foremost. There's some action segments in here, sure, but they are very much defined in isolated segments of the story. Trying to go in guns blazing in any other part is simply not a viable option.

So sure, a little miffed that, [i]at fours hours in[/i], I hadn't yet shot a single bullet outside of a shooting range, but hey, I like a good stealth game too, so I gave it a shot anyway. 

The problem is that this is not a good stealth game either.

Most of the mechanics the game throws at you will not work when you expect them to, even when the game explicitly tells you they should work in those situations. Keep in mind that, once you're getting the more advanced tutorials, the game throws [i]a lot[/i] of mechanics at you. Some of these are overengineered takedown mechanics for when you get spotted which are usually completely useless, and some would actually be useful if they worked reliably. In fact, the only reason I was able to pass some areas was because the game's AI is laughably stupid and can be easily fooled into them not seeing you where any reasonable human would. In fact, I spent 10 minutes longer during a certain tutorial stealth area thinking of a way to get past two guards because I was giving the AI way too much credit. Eventually I just climbed out of a window in full view of one of the guards, and nothing happened. Just to give one of many examples. Also not unimportant: why in the hell is it impossible to move or drag unconscious bodies out of sight [i]IN A STEALTH GAME[/i]? That is basic stealth 101, and it's simply not here. But hey, good thing you can do a completely unnecessary 3-button combination for a takedown mechanic if a guard spots you!

Other types of gameplay include driving segments and shooting segments. Both play fine for the most part, but as far as the driving specifically goes, they managed to do something truly impressive: they managed to make a high-speed car chase down a mountain road, including jumps and off-roading, the whole shebang... feel boring and slow. That's honestly impressive, but not in the good way. Similarly, the shooting may be less boring, but enemies seem to spawn seemingly out of nowhere, and the cover system that is clearly developed for the stealth segments, is horribly broken when it comes to the shooting, and you [i]will[/i] pop out from behind your cover without meaning to.

On the gameplay overall, there's also some sort of input lag. I barely clocked in at 15 ms frame latency, but still Bond felt like he moved a split second slower than my button presses, and it made controlling him feel sluggish and just... [i]off[/i]. I've played games with literally ten times that amount of latency that felt less sluggish than this. I don't know what's going on there.

Aside from the gameplay, the game is also rife with bugs, both visually and mechanically. In every single driving segment, you can wheel the camera around to see inside the car, and every single time, Bond is holding his hands either in front of, or behind the steering wheel, but never on them. Greenway losing his teeth mid-conversation was another. A closed window popping into existence where there previously was none after vaulting out of the previously open window, barring my way back.  Bottles floating in mid-air in the night club level. The list goes on.

Since Steam refuses to refund this for me since the training area alone made me go well past the refund window, I will probably keep playing this to the end to get at least [i]some[/i] value for my money.

So is this game worth the 70 bucks? Not even close. Even at half that price, I would have second thoughts, knowing what I know now. I think this game is solely for the diehard Bond fans that don't mind a fundamentally flawed gameplay experience. But for anyone else, save your money. There's far better stuff out there.

I enjoyed 007 First Light more than I expected. While it clearly takes inspiration from Hitman, it does a good job of building its own identity through the James Bond setting, story, and presentation.

The campaign is engaging, the production quality is high, and the Bond atmosphere is captured very well. However, I felt the game could have benefited from giving players more freedom. I would have liked to see more opportunities to fail, more meaningful consequences, and alternative ways to approach or complete missions.

The challenge system didn't really appeal to me. Personally, I'm not a fan of replaying missions multiple times just to complete challenges or manipulate specific outcomes. If I replay a game, I prefer doing so because I want to experience the story again and explore different choices naturally, not because I'm chasing checklists. That's why I enjoy replayability in strategy games like Civilization much more than in mission-based games built around repeated runs.

That said, the core experience is still solid. The story kept me interested, the Bond theme is used effectively, and I had a good time throughout the campaign. It's not a game I'd replay over and over, but it's one I'd gladly recommend to fans of action-adventure games and James Bond.

Overall: 6.5/10.

I’m a 59-year-old father and Afghanistan War veteran, probably older than a lot of people who will be playing James Bond 007: First Light. I’ve always enjoyed story-driven games, but I wasn’t expecting this one to have such a personal impact on me. I’m a single father, and my son is now 21 years old. Like many parents of grown children, I found it harder and harder to spend quality time with him. He’s usually out with friends, working, or watching videos online. A few weeks ago, he told me about James Bond 007: First Light and couldn’t stop talking about it. He had already put more than 20 hours into the game in just a couple of days. Wanting to see what all the excitement was about—and hoping it might give us something to share—I picked up the game myself. At first, I was completely lost. The mechanics, objectives, and gadgets took some getting used to. I asked my son for help, and before long we were spending hours together working through missions, discussing strategies, and enjoying the story. What started as me trying to understand a video game turned into some of the best time I’ve spent with my son in years. Since losing my wife, those moments have meant more than I can put into words. This game gave us a reason to connect again, not just online but in real life as well. We talk more, spend more time together, and even make plans outside the house now. As a game, James Bond 007: First Light delivers a fun spy adventure with exciting missions and plenty of memorable moments. But for me, its greatest achievement was something I never expected: it helped bring my son and me closer together. It reminded me that you’re never too old to enjoy a great game, and that sometimes the most meaningful experiences come from sharing them with the people you love. Thank you for the memories.

Across gaming media, one quote keeps appearing whenever [i]007 First Light[/i] is mentioned: “The best 007 game yet.” That's a bold statement, and one that inevitably raises expectations.

For me, James Bond has always been something of a mixed bag. I've never really had the patience for the novels, and despite being a huge fan of espionage stories, the Bond films never quite clicked with me. The games were another matter: they were always hugely popular, yet I never felt drawn to them. To me, this kind of action-heavy experience always seemed better suited to a PC than a console.

So perhaps [i]007 First Light[/i] was destined to be the Bond game that finally won me over. And after playing it, I can honestly say that the praise is well deserved.

The story introduces a young James Bond during his time in the Royal Air Force, where a daring maneuver catches the attention of MI6 and leads to his recruitment. From there, the game delivers everything you could hope for from a classic spy thriller. You undergo combat training, experiment with cutting-edge gadgets, embark on dangerous missions, face betrayal, meet a compelling love interest, and experience emotional moments involving the people closest to Bond.

What truly elevates the experience, however, is the world itself. Every location is beautifully crafted and, on capable hardware, often looks remarkably realistic. Whether you're exploring MI6 headquarters in London, traversing the deserts of Mauritania, operating in Vietnam, or braving the icy landscapes of Antarctica, the game constantly presents breathtaking environments and memorable set pieces.

Gameplay offers enough flexibility to suit different playstyles. You can approach situations carefully and stealthily or engage enemies head-on. The difficulty remains accessible throughout, meaning even players without extensive shooter or combat experience can comfortably make their way through the campaign without excessive frustration.

Without exaggeration, [i]007 First Light[/i] is the finest spy game I have ever played. It captures everything that makes the espionage genre exciting - suspense, style, action, intrigue - and adventure, and delivers it with confidence from beginning to end.

007 First Light might be the best Hitman-adjacent game IO Interactive has ever made.

Unfortunately, it also feels less like a true Bond experience and more like a second-rate Uncharted with 007 seasoning sprinkled on top like someone got nervous in a focus test.

To be fair, the presentation is excellent. The environments, lighting, and performances are genuinely impressive. There is polish here. Real craft. The kind that makes you nod respectfully before immediately asking why the rest of the experience is wearing a fake moustache.

The bigger issue is the interpretation of Bond.

A younger Bond was a great opportunity to lean into something closer to Casino Royale: brash, brutish, reckless, dangerous, and in desperate need of refinement. A blunt instrument slowly becoming a scalpel.

Instead, we get something that feels closer to Gen Z Rick Astley in a tactical turtleneck.

The result is a Bond who looks expensive but rarely feels iconic.

Mechanically, the game leans too heavily on gadgets while not offering enough meaningful variety in combat. The stealth systems are serviceable but thin, often repeating the same beats without the depth or improvisational freedom IO is normally known for.

Which is where I kept thinking about the original teams behind Splinter Cell Conviction and Blacklist.

Those games understood how to make stealth-action feel aggressive, readable, stylish, and player-driven without turning every encounter into a designer’s little puzzle box of obedience.

In their hands, this probably would have been properly shaken and not stirred.

The scripted moments are where First Light stumbles hardest. Too often, success feels less like reading the scene naturally and more like failing three times until you understand exactly what the designer wanted you to do.

That is not player-centric design. That is “please step on the clearly marked fun square.”

And that is a shame, because the ingredients are here: strong production values, solid performances, beautiful spaces, and a studio that absolutely knows how to build tension through systems.

But Bond needs more than polish. Bond needs danger, style, intelligence, and player fantasy.

First Light has the suit. It just doesn’t always know how to wear it.

All that said, if you are looking for a polished, adequate stealth-action romp and have 10 hours to burn, there are far worse ways to spend them.

If you are a die-hard 007 fan, maybe bring a martini and lower expectations.
