007 First Light is a fantastic game with an engaging story that kept me invested from beginning to end. The plot features several well-executed twists that make you want to keep playing to see what happens next.

The combat is fun and satisfying, and one of the game's biggest strengths is the variety in its level design. Some missions are more linear and story-focused, while others are much more open-ended. These larger levels allow you to approach objectives in your own way, with multiple routes and solutions instead of forcing you down a single path. This freedom fits the spy theme perfectly and makes each mission feel unique.

My biggest criticism is that the game is simply too short. It took me around 16 hours to complete, and I would have happily played for much longer. Another minor issue is the melee combat in tight spaces. The camera can zoom in too much when fighting near walls or in corners, making it harder to see what's happening and occasionally causing frustration.

Despite these issues, 007 First Light is an excellent experience with a compelling story, enjoyable combat, and great mission variety. It captures the feeling of being a secret agent exceptionally well, and I am already looking forward to the next game in the series.

007 First Light is easily the best, most polished, and most AAA-feeling Bond game released so far. Patrick Gibson does an outstanding job portraying James Bond, he has the charm, the looks, and the charisma that fans would expect from the character.

It's worth noting that this is an origin story, so Bond is intentionally portrayed as inexperienced and somewhat naive. That aspect of the character is completely by design and fits the narrative well.

The story is engaging, easy to follow, and feels like a classic Bond adventure. The graphics are good overall, although there is still some room for improvement. Gameplay is mostly linear, with a few mechanics from the Hitman 3. If you're expecting the open-ended, highly non-linear approach of Hitman, this game won't fully deliver that experience. However, IO Interactive included Escalations and Operations modes to provide additional replayability and satisfy Hitman fans (myself included).

Performance is generally very good. However, on GPUs with 8 GB of VRAM, the game can develop an issue after extended play sessions or multiple scene reloads. Despite running smoothly on Ultra settings initially, the game sometimes appears to stop utilizing the GPU properly or fails to clear VRAM usage, causing the frame rate to drop to around 10–12 FPS. Fortunately, restarting the game resolves the issue, so hopefully IO Interactive addresses this apparent VRAM leak in a future update.

Overall, 007 First Light is a very good Bond game with excellent story, writing, and presentation. It's highly polished, largely free of bugs, and delivers a memorable experience that I would recommend to anyone who enjoys story-driven action games.

Face à la prolifération des mondes ouverts standardisés, 007 : Premier Éclat se distingue comme un excellent jeu d’action-espionnage linéaire de haute qualité. Développé par IO Interactive, il s’affranchit du schéma de Hitman pour restituer parfaitement l’esprit de la licence 007, avec une immersion digne d’un film, et s’impose comme l’une des meilleures adaptations de la franchise ces dernières années.
Le jeu retrace le parcours du jeune James Bond, agent débutant à la fois fougueux et novice. L’intrigue d’espionnage est tendue et bien construite, sans remplissage inutile. La caractérisation est soignée et montre parfaitement les origines et l’évolution du futur agent 007, pour un rendu très fidèle et plein de charme.
Le gameplay est très réussi, avec une double approche furtive / combat entièrement libre. Dans des niveaux en boîte bien conçus, vous pouvez soit passer inaperçu grâce aux déguisements et aux gadgets, soit engager des fusillades dynamiques en cas d’alerte. Fin et fluide, le système évite la lassitude des jeux d’infiltration classiques et s’adapte à tous les styles de jeu.
La partie sonore et visuelle est irréprochable : des environnements détaillés, une lumière soignée, la bande-son emblématique de 007 et une mise en scène cinématographique qui renforce l’ambiance des poursuites, infiltrations et combats pour une immersion totale.
Cependant, le jeu a quelques défauts : structure linéaire sans grande liberté d’exploration, faible rejouabilité, IA ennemie parfois agressive et certains dialogues un peu longs.
Malgré ces petits défauts, les 15 heures de campagne sont intenses et sans temps mort. Que vous soyez fan de 007 ou amateur d’infiltration cinématographique et d’action linéaire, ce titre est un excellent cru et l’une des meilleures surprises du genre.

IO Interactive absolutely nailed the vibe with 007 First Light. If you are looking for a true James Bond experience, this is it.

The Good:

Gripping Story: The narrative is fantastic. It hooks you right from the opening scene and keeps you gripped until the very end.

True Bond Atmosphere: It feels like a genuine Bond game through and through. While you can definitely notice some subtle Hitman influences here and there, it completely stands on its own feet.

Stunning Visuals & Performance: The game looks absolutely gorgeous. The locations are incredibly detailed, varied, and beautifully crafted. On top of that, the optimization is top-notch—it runs incredibly smooth on my PC at 4K Ultra settings. It just plays like a dream.

Cinematic Driving: The driving sequences look spectacular and feel like they walked straight out of a high-budget Bond movie.

The Catch:

More Linear than Hitman: You don't get the same level of sandbox freedom as you do in the recent Hitman games. It's a more guided experience, though the gameplay itself is highly satisfying.

Driving Controls: While the driving segments look incredibly cinematic, the handling and vehicle controls could definitely have been better. They feel a bit clunky compared to the rest of the polished gameplay.

Verdict:
It’s an incredibly fun, well-optimized, and atmospheric spy thriller. Despite some minor flaws with the driving controls, it is an absolute must-buy if you love James Bond or just want a stellar action-stealth game that looks breathtaking. High recommendations!

[b]Rating: [/b] ★★★★★ - Amazing
[b]Time Played:[/b] 15 hours
[b]Difficulty:[/b] Intended

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
- Linear, mission-based structure with roughly 11 missions. Don't come in expecting Hitman's sandbox freedom, this is a curated Uncharted-esk action-adventure and it commits to that fully.
- Destructible cover and aggressive grenade use from enemies mean you can't turtle behind walls, which keeps gunfights genuinely tense and dynamic.
- Stealth sections are the best the game has to offer. Focused, readable, and rewarding when they click; the gadget use feels purposeful rather than gimmicky.
- Driving mechanics are noticeably weaker than the on-foot sections. Car chases look great but feel slippery and undercooked compared to the rest of the package.

[b]Story\Dialogue:[/b]
- A young Bond who still has rough edges. Arrogant and reckless in ways that feel earned rather than performed, and the voice actor sells it.
- Original story not tied to any film. Bond joins the Double 0 program after a heroic act, then gets entangled in a conspiracy after a mission goes wrong; it's a clean premise that doesn't need movie knowledge to work.
- The Bond fantasy is translated to gameplay rather than just referenced. The humour, the romance, and the spectacle are baked into missions.
- IO clearly understands why Bond works across every era. This doesn't feel like a licensed cash grab, it feels like people who genuinely care about the character.

[b]Graphics\Music:[/b]
- Technically solid graphics for 2026 but not pushing boundaries. The lighting and image quality are impressive.
- Where it earns its praise is artistic direction. Mission environments are dense, detailed, and feel lived-in rather than dressed for a game level.
- Cinematic framing is confidently done. IO knows how to stage a moment and the camera work supports the Bond aesthetic without being showy about it.
- Score leans into classic Bond orchestration with modern production. It works and it knows when to stay out of the way.

[b]Before you Play:[/b]
- Don't play this expecting Hitman. The sandbox is gone and while there is some replayability loop in the Tactical Simulations, it's best treated like a tightly authored single-player experience.
- Stealth is worth the patience. Alerts aren't punishing but clean runs feel far more Bond than going loud, and the level design rewards it.
- Don't rush the dialogue or the atmosphere of the levels. The character writing is sharp and the side conversations flesh out Bond's relationships in ways the main plot doesn't always have time for.

IO Interactive just reminded everyone why Bond matters.
I wasn't sure what to expect going in. After 14 years without a proper James Bond game, the hype was real but so was the skepticism. I finished it, and I can say without hesitation — this was worth every bit of the wait.
The story genuinely surprised me. I went in expecting a loose framing device around sandbox missions, but First Light commits hard to its narrative. Young Bond is compelling, the writing feels like a proper spy thriller, and the pacing keeps you hooked from the opening chapter to the credits. Some of Bond's best storytelling in years, game or film.
Gameplay-wise, IO brought everything they refined through the Hitman series and then some. The stealth sandbox sections feel great — multiple routes, the Bond Instinct mechanic for crowd manipulation, and that smooth-talking bluff system that just feels like 007. You can go loud or stay ghost. Both are satisfying. The set-piece moments land with real cinematic weight without overstaying their welcome.
Visually it's stunning. The lighting in particular is impressive throughout.
Is it perfect? No. Some loading times drag a bit, and a couple of mission segments feel more linear than I'd like. But these are minor gripes on an otherwise excellent package.
If you're a Bond fan, a Hitman fan, or just someone who wants a well-crafted action-adventure with real story bones — buy it. This is the Bond game we deserved.
"Earn the Number." — and they did.

[h1]The name's Bland, James Bland[/h1]
First Light is IOI's first venture into a cinematic action hybrid, and I wish I could say it was anything other than mediocre. At its best, the game carries the feeling of being a decent spy thriller with the rise and fall in action you expect from a Bond flick, but a monotonous rhythm quickly sets in, and the experience quickly feels artificial and machine-like, with very little in the way of soul. I'll briefly summarize my dissatisfaction with the three pillars of the game: stealth, action, and story.

[h2]Diet Hitman[/h2]
The stealth based gameplay of First Light borrows heavily from IOI's Hitman: World of Assassination trilogy. Every mission places you in a social situation, and you're given a problem for Bond to stealth through, along with multiple paths to get through it. The problem lies in how little these options actually impact the mission. Choosing to bypass guards by finding a back entrance or walk by them under a false identity are functionally identical solutions, and they're always the ONLY solutions. Worse still, the game doesn't even let you fail via getting caught in the tiny restricted zones you can wander into. Add in the utter lack of reactivity to the endlessly repititive task of shooting lasers from your watch into someone's eye to steal their keys, and you have an experience that feels like a childproofed take on a spy drama. It doesn't help that the maps, unlike Hitman's sprawling levels, are pitifully tiny.

The dedicated stealth segments against enemies intent on finding Bond don't fare much better. Think of any big budget game with a tacked on stealth system, and First Light fits that mold to a T. Enemies have poor sight, poor hearing, and even worse memories. You're inexplicably barred from hiding bodies, even though that would be a top priority for a stealth operative that wants to remain undetected. Not that it matters too much -- enemies that discover the unconscious bodies of their friends don't wake them up, don't alert any of their comrades, and only radio for reinforcements if they discover a second body. 

The real silver bullet that destroys the stealth system, however, is the utter lack of consequence for ignoring it. There are zero gameplay and narrative consequences for playing this game like a brainless shooter, which leaves you zero reason to engage with the stealth mechanics whatsoever. But is that action any good? Well...

[h2]Diet Uncharted[/h2]

The shooting is bog-standard third person shooter fare. The guns sound weak, enemies barely react to anything but leg and headshots, and the integration of melee combat leaves a lot to be desired. Guns are treated as disposable, having very little ammo, which encourages you to run around and beat up guys for more guns. The problem is that you're running at men with machine guns covered by snipers, which often leaves you at critical health constantly, and if your aim is good enough, you can just headshot an entire room before running out of ammo with one gun. The melee system is very barebones, with basic counters and throws dominating the weak line-up of enemies. Whereas games like Uncharted 3 and The Last of Us spiced up their melee systems with several dynamic animations, First Light chooses to reuse the knee to the head animation CONSTANTLY. It gets old. Fast.

Cinematic set pieces are meant to make you excited for a small slice of gameplay, but First Light disappoints on that front too. Car chases are laughably railroaded, with even slight deviations triggering a swift mission fail. Everything else are just some variation of running an obstable course while someone shoots at you, and that one plane mission that was shown off at the demo years ago. They're all uninspired and bland.

[h2]Bond and the Spy Crew[/h2]

That just leaves the narrative, and it's another mixed bag, leaning towards bad. The opening starts off strong by showing Bond's career prior to his induction into MI6, but where it really careens off a cliff is the long, boring, bloated act 1 that is devoted entirely to his training and first field operation. The game throws a small cast of thoroughly unlikable trainees at you, and far too much screentime is devoted to these people. It'd be like if Indiana Jones was forced to be accompanied by a team of junior archeologists that we're supposed to pretend are his equals. When the story abruptly kicks these characters out of the story, you're left to wonder what the point of them even was.

After that harrowing introduction, the game improves by settling into a pace of mediocrity. The tone of the story is a weird mix of the grounded Craig-Bond era films and the fantastical goofiness of the Brosnan -Bond era, but its failure to commit to either just leaves it feeling...bland. Bond himself is a flatline of a character, his quips and smarminess coming off as hollow and vacuous. The Bond girl has such a lack of presence that his biggest degree of chemistry lies with a random NPC he meets in 1 mission. His mentor is such a stock character that you can predict his entire arc the moment he shows up on screen. M, Moneypenny, and Q all feel like people reading a script rather than actual characters.

It's just bland. Bland, bland, bland. There's no spice, no excitement, no wish fulfillment that is key to the fantasy of a Bond story. You can feel the hands of a HR department monitoring the story for "problematic" writing and keeping things as risk-free as possible. 

If you really need a Bond fix, just watch the movies again, or emulate the older games. Get this one when it's heavily discounted.

I've encountered a number of minor bugs and had 3 crashes in the first 10 hours, but I'm still recommending this game because it's an absolute thrillride.

The closest game I can compare this to is Splinter Cell: Conviction. I was a huge fan of that game back in the day, so I fell in love with this one pretty quick. It's a mostly linear blend of stealth and action with very big, open levels.

The action is every bit as bombastic and intense as the films, with some truly jaw-dropping setpieces even in the first couple of missions. The stealth portions are great, as well. It's not quite as "open" as Hitman, but there's definitely multiple ways to approach most of the objectives. The combat is fantastic. Punches feel hard and weighty, the brawling is cool, and the gunplay is solid. Having limited ammo keeps you on your toes, as you'll be strategically picking up new guns mid-firefight or using your surroundings to your advantage. There's also, of course, car chases and the driving works here, too. It's not the best driving in a video game, but it's more than serviceable and def fun.

The story is well-written, and the dialogue is mostly solid aside from a couple quips that fall flat and NPCs being hilariously candid about hints. There's not a ton of humor, but Bond is a bit quippy and most of his jokes land well, at least for me. The tone is mostly pretty serious, though, and it does a good job of balancing drama and lightheartedness. Pacing is good overall, but almost a little too much at times, because you don't often get any little breathers between levels--it's just go, go, go. It works for the story, but it can also feel tiring.

I like this new guy as Bond. His interpretation feels to me like a blend between Sean Connery and Daniel Craig, plus a bit of his own thing. All of the characters within MI6 are great here, actually. Some of the bosses/bad guys are pretty interesting, too! The main cast is all well-acted and likeable. The NPC performances have a pretty big range in terms of acting quality, but they all get their jobs done. 

The music is *excellent*, and Lana Del Rey's theme song for this game kicks ass.

Performance is pretty good. Aside from a couple of crashes, I haven't experienced any slowdown or major frame drops or anything. It's very stable, and the presentation is beautiful.

Overall, I was a little worried going in that it wasn't going to feel enough like a proper James Bond game as it's kind of a pre-00 origin story for him, but it is very much a James Bond game--an excellent one, in fact. This is the best Bond game yet, and I'm really excited for the future of the franchise now. This is a must-play for anyone who likes Bond flicks, stealth games like Splinter Cell, or big, flashy AAA games.

My Review of 007 First Light

After finishing 007 First Light four times, I can confidently say that this is one of the best James Bond games ever made.

What impressed me the most is how much the game feels like playing through a real 007 movie. The story is engaging from start to finish, the characters are memorable, and the pacing is excellent. The game never feels stretched out or filled with unnecessary content—it is exactly as long as it needs to be.

The story itself was fantastic, with several great plot twists that kept me invested throughout the entire campaign. Seeing Bond's journey before becoming the legendary 007 was a great choice by the developers, and by the end of the game, it genuinely feels like you have earned that iconic status.

The action is where the game truly shines. The combat system is incredibly satisfying, especially with the parries, dodges, and unique environmental executions. Every fight feels cinematic and makes you feel like a skilled secret agent rather than just another action game protagonist. The variety of locations and set pieces also helps keep the experience fresh throughout the campaign.

One thing I don't understand is some of the hate the game receives online. In my opinion, a lot of the criticism feels forced. No game is perfect, but 007 First Light delivers exactly what many Bond fans have wanted for years: a cinematic Bond adventure with great action, an engaging story, memorable characters, and the feeling of starring in your own James Bond movie. It deserves far more appreciation than it gets.

My only criticism concerns the Operations mode. After finishing the main story and officially becoming 007, I would have loved to see additional missions outside of the TacSim system. Something more similar to Hitman-style operations would have been amazing—missions with multiple approaches, different outcomes, replayability, and opportunities to complete objectives in creative ways. That extra content could have added hundreds of hours of replay value for players who wanted to continue their career as 007.

Even with that minor complaint, 007 First Light is an outstanding game. It delivers everything a Bond fan could want: a great story, excellent plot twists, thrilling action, memorable missions, and the feeling of starring in your own James Bond movie. If you're a fan of James Bond or action-adventure games in general, it is absolutely worth playing.

Final Score: 9.5/10

007 First Light Review – Bond Is Back

There was a lot riding on 007 First Light. Bond games have had a mixed history over the years, and after spending time with IO Interactive’s take on the world’s most famous spy, I can safely say this shaken-not-stirred reboot absolutely delivers.

From start to finish, 007 First Light is fantastic.

What immediately stands out is that this version of James Bond actually feels like Bond. This is a younger, rougher 007, but crucially, he still has the charm, confidence, recklessness and womanising swagger fans expect. He is not the fully polished superspy yet, and that is exactly why the story works so well.

The origin story is handled brilliantly. Watching Bond get recruited into MI6 feels earned rather than forced, and the Malta training sequence is one of the highlights of the entire game. The montage-style progression gives the story real momentum while showing Bond slowly developing into the legendary agent we know he will eventually become.

One thing the game does particularly well is showing Bond making believable mistakes as a trainee. Small details make a huge difference. Throughout the game, Bond repeatedly has a habit of instinctively touching his ear while using his earpiece — a subtle but obvious tell that eventually gets noticed and called out by one of the trainers. In another moment, he casually accepts a drink from a stranger… which ends about as well as you would expect for a rookie spy. These imperfections make him feel human rather than invincible and add genuine charm to the character development.

The chemistry between the trainee agents is also excellent. Monroe and Cressida are both strong supporting characters without ever overshadowing Bond himself. Their interactions feel natural, and the banter between agents helps the world feel lived in rather than just another parade of mission briefings and explosions.

Speaking of explosions — the set pieces are superb.

The level design throughout the game is outstanding, taking players across some genuinely breathtaking locations. The influence of Hitman can definitely be felt in the mission structure and level design, and that is a very good thing. Levels are larger, more open and encourage experimentation, giving missions replay value without ever losing the identity of a Bond adventure. Crucially, you never feel like Agent 47 in a tuxedo. Bond operates differently — more improvisation, more charisma, more chaos — and the game understands that distinction perfectly.

Technically, the game is excellent too. The graphics are beautiful, performance is smooth, and the cinematic presentation feels worthy of the Bond name. Whether it is a neon-lit casino, a luxury yacht, or a dusty Mediterranean safehouse, the environments constantly look stunning.

Perhaps most refreshing of all, though, is that the game simply focuses on telling an entertaining Bond story. There is no heavy-handed messaging, no endless moral lecturing, and no feeling that the player is being bludgeoned over the head with a political agenda. The game remembers the most important thing: James Bond stories are supposed to be fun, stylish escapism. Thankfully, 007 First Light understands the assignment.

And after years of uncertainty surrounding the franchise, that may be the biggest victory of all.

Bond is back.

Final Verdict:
007 First Light successfully modernises Bond without losing what made the character iconic in the first place. It blends cinematic storytelling, strong character chemistry, smart level design and classic spy fantasy into one highly enjoyable package. It may not reinvent the wheel, but like Bond himself, it knows exactly how to make an entrance.

Licence to thrill: granted.

Where do I even start? If you're a 007 fan, this game is a massive love letter to you. Honestly, it’s arguably the best James Bond game we’ve ever had. It’s insanely fun and fast-paced from start to finish, but it still manages to keep you hooked on a story that actually feels super relevant to what's going on in the real world right now.

Let's talk about the combat. The gunplay is really solid, but the Close Quarters Combat (CQC) is where this game truly shines. I constantly found myself ditching my guns just to engage in hand-to-hand combat because it's so satisfying. You can literally feel every hit your enemy takes through the vibrations in the controller, it makes the combat feel incredibly heavy and engaging. Add in the amazing gadgets (the missile pen is the absolute GOAT), and you literally feel like you are James Bond.
The spying parts deserve their own massive shoutout. Bluffing your way past guards and out of tight situations is such a good, funny feature, and it makes the game feel super interactive. The devs also clearly anticipated players doing dumb stuff, because there’s unique dialogue for almost every weird thing you try to do in the levels.
The characters are written really well too. I admit I mostly just cared about Bond, but they didn't sideline the supporting cast at all; everyone got wonderful treatment. More importantly, they absolutely nail Bond himself. He has the charm, wit, confidence, and occasional recklessness you'd expect, and the humor throughout the game feels very true to the franchise without ever feeling forced
What really makes this feel like a love letter to 007 fans is how well it balances espionage and action. You're gathering intel, bluffing your way through situations, using gadgets creatively, and relying on actual spycraft. It captures the fantasy of being James Bond. The villains, exotic locations, and adventures all feel authentically Bond as well, and fans will catch plenty of nods to classic films and different eras of the character. The soundtrack is the absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cherry on top. Also, the brand placements actually fit the luxurious world of James Bond and didn't feel out of place at all (Unlike Leon and his Porsche in RE9... still a goated game, but you get what I mean)

Some of these complaints about the game deserve a spot right next to "too much water" in Subnautica, "too much driving" in Forza, or "too many cowboys" in Red Dead Redemption 
Apparently a James Bond game having stealth, gadgets, and espionage was a shocking plot twist for some people.

If I had to nitpick a couple of cons:
The gadgets and weapons are so cool that it genuinely hurts you can't carry everything at once in your loadout. The inventory limit makes sense for realism, but I just wanted to play with all the toys

The camera can get slightly wonky if you're doing CQC in a really tight corner or hallway

But honestly, these are super minor problems that don't ruin the experience at all and can easily be fixed in a sequel. It perfectly captures everything that makes the franchise great and serves it up on a fast-paced platter. Get it, grab a martini (shaken not stirred, obviously), and ENJOY!!

TL;DR: I get to throw guns and soda cans at bad guys? 10/10. This feels like one for the favorites list:


-Gameplay has a strong core with great pacing and clear goals with variable approach.

-Graphics were beautiful while retaining their own unique style and lighting.

-Voice-acting had me completely immersed during critical scenes and felt natural.

-Melee combat flow feels great and offered a ton of variability for each encounter.

-Gun combat feels super smooth and precise if you get decent FPS.

-Difficulty felt balanced - excited to replay this on hardest difficulty for a new experience.

-Progression felt meaningful - combat flows well without, but upgrades contribute to variability late-game.

-Lots of extras with the Simulation options - the game has life beyond the main story and replay value alone.


In true IO Interactive fashion, there's multiple ways to complete certain tasks in most missions, which offers high replay value overall. The overall polish and performance of the title was great, I experienced two instances of heavy frame-drop when alt-tabbing - which needed a reboot to correct - but the game ran a lot better than I expected on my aging 3080 fully cranked with DLSS. Gun combat feels smooth and snappy with sufficient FPS, DLSS really helps here if you're struggling to retain a 60 FPS target framerate. 

This was a wonderful spin on 007 in the 21st century and true Bond fans will appreciate tons of nods to previous titles and films. My only complaint would be the price, creeping into that 70 dollar range for the standard game is a bit crazy, but that's just the new trend of game prices overall at this point. The game is also a lot smaller than I expected - at around 50 GB, it crammed a lot of story into that size. Kudos to the Devs for not having a 100 GB+ title which seems to be the new norm. Great game, great story, great experience - I'd say picking it up at full price is still worth it if you're a true 007 fan - this is the best Bond experience we've had in a long time.

I feel it is important to get one thing out of the way given how, when First Light was revealed, nearly everyone saw IOI was behind it as completely unsurprising. 
Out of the many games that have clear inspiration from Ian Fleming’s seminal spy series, the Hitman games (particularly World Of Assassination) clearly had some fanboys in the studio. From the fine suits, to the greater than life villains and socialite infiltration, it’s so easy to see why they were given the chance to make a brand new story in this world.

But this absolutely does [u]not [/u] play like Hitman, and you will be disappointed if that is what you’re after. This is an Uncharted 2-esque story oriented game that happens to give more options to progress the story, but has a structured pace, setpieces and intended flow. 

If you are cool with it, I guarantee you’ll enjoy this game, regardless if you are a fan or not of the IP, because this game was a total blast to play through.

This is just a great take on the material in nearly every front, and best of all it’s clear this is absolutely a new continuity in the service of original videogames, rather than a simple imitation of a specific film. Nearly all of the cast bring their A game, with the main antagonist being a particular highlight with how much you can tell the actor is loving chewing the scenery. MI6 regulars Q and Moneypenny are easily in the top 3 takes on the characters with how they bounce back of our titular man, who I must say truly manages to be a worthy iteration of the iconic character. 
Gibson’s portrayal is a wonderful combination of other actors' traits (such as Dalton’s lethality or Brosnan’s magnificent smugness) that still manages to be fresh thanks to his endless underserved self-confidence that remains enjoyable instead of grating due to the constant butting against other strong-headed characters.

Almost all chapters have a solid structure that involves setting up the mission, exploration with some options to complete objectives, to slowly funnel you into situations that allow stealth or combat, and finally we reach set piece mode where stuff explodes. This constantly keeps the pacing at a good rhythm, and allows good downtime to not exhaust. 

The spy and sneaking will be familiar to anyone who played modern stealth games, but don’t expect as much versatility or lethality. Bond is trying to remain undetected after all, so use of different gadgets with the environment, seeking alternative routes, or using the bluffing mechanic to walk in and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your way around is the name of the game, and while it works well, it does feel a bit limited overall.

It’s a good thing then that when the game ramps up, it goes all out with no breaks. Gunplay is smooth and the gadgets work great in combat situations if you know how to best use them, with the weapon throws in particular being both mechanically satisfying, while keeping you mobile. To me the highlight is the melee combat, it just clicks incredibly well, and always somehow creates moments of total slapstick comedy, while sounding and looking great thanks to reactive scenery and the animation work.

Everything works in service of the narrative, which was overall compelling, had a lot of unexpected twists, and kept me interested in what would happen next. I just lament that the postgame, TacSim, feels a bit barren overall, mostly due to the lack of user-made challenges like Contracts mode from Hitman. This mode is still really fun to mess around with, and hopefully new content will be added soon.

I really cannot think of any serious issues with the game as is, it’s very clear this was a passion project for the developers, and you can feel the dedication to the craft in every regard. Maybe I would wish the game had more options to disable accessibility features (such as waypoints) inside intended difficulty.

If this is the start of a new trilogy, then I personally am totally sold on whatever comes next.

Fantastic game all around. My only issue is the input lag i was experiencing despite my high spec pc. To be fair, I was playing on a 4k monitor, but even then and with DLSS performance turned on the input lag was egregious. I'll likely play the game again at some point, but when I do I think i'll just play at 1080 and cross my fingers there's no input lag.

Beyond that, the characters were well fleshed out, the story was engaging and it certainly holds up as a Bond story. The gadgets were fun, but I found myself only really taking the same 2 gadgets with me to every level (the laser and the darts). Combat took me a little bit to figure out, but once i got into a good flow it really made me feel like a badass 007.

The levels were really fun, though I'll admit I was hoping for a little more options to reach my objectives. However, it makes sense story wise as to why it's designed linearly and being a game developer myself it really didn't bother me as much after I broke it all down from my own perspective. Having as many options to pursue an objective like in the Hitman series would have made the levels a bit overwhelming and frustrating to follow. Sometimes more of a good thing can become a bad thing. They had to tell a linear James Bond story and the best way was honestly the way they approached it.

What was also really impressive was how there are NO LOADING SCREENS! Outside of the pre-caching shaders and restarting from checkpoint of course, but that really can't be helped. I loved how they hid the loading in such a natural and cinematic way. There wasn't a moment of boredom between levels.

The actors killed it for sure. I was feeling a bit emotional during specific times (you'll know when you see them).

The art was well done and though I could tell where they had to optimize in places, it didn't detract from the overall atmosphere and aesthetics. I think the art team did a great job and a lot of the set pieces were pretty cool and fun to look at!

The music hits. When that nightclub level started up, I was in it! Bringing in Chase and Status for that banger was chef's kiss! I can't wait to get my hands on that track if/when they release it! As for the title song and sequence, it was wonderfully done. The rest of the soundtrack blended in so well that it wasn't obnoxious to listen to, it was music that totally fit in with the Bond universe. Fantastic job all around!

I'll definitely play this again at some point and I hope they make a sequel after leaving all of those story threads hanging about! Great work all around!

007 First Light is the definitive James Bond game.

It combines IOI’s signature gameplay with elements reminiscent of Uncharted, although many other games make similar comparisons. If you enjoy story-driven experiences with focused gameplay and a degree of creative freedom, this game is definitely worth your time.

One standout feature is Tactical Mode, which many reviews don't seem to emphasize enough. It adds another layer of depth and replayability to the experience.

For those looking for more gameplay without replaying the entire story, there are several challenges and additional objectives to complete. Perhaps most importantly, IOI has a strong track record of supporting its single-player games long after launch. That means players can likely expect new content in the future, giving the game even more longevity and value.

So! I just finished the game.

Pre ordered it because I am a huge Hitman fan and believed in IoI, and I did right.

Do I recommend the game at 70 or 80 euro? No, except for spoilers, you should wait for a sale.
Do I regret buying the game? Also no, the Deluxe Edition is not worth your money, it doesn't add anything significant which is a shame, but I did want to support IoI.

So then, how is the game?

It is not hitman 4. Many people come here, expecting the sandbox and freedom of hitman, but it is a James Bond game. It is trying to tell a story and it has to railroad you from time to time to achieve it, which is fine. It borrows some assets from hitman, metaphorically and literally, and makes good uses of them. I am glad there is no AI used in this game (not to my knowledge). I'd rather have them reuse assets than generate some. Big thumbs up. 

The good :

The cast is charming, great voice acting, interesting story. It made me actually interested in watching a Bond movie now (Never saw one). 

I enjoy this Bond, he is funny, charismatic but also caring, I love his humour. 

Guns feel fine to use, I think it's an improvement over Hitman. 

Graphics are obviously great, so are the cutscenes, it really is eye candy.

The bad :
Bugs. As much as I don't mind minor bugs, some break the game. Especially if you alt tab a lot, the game keeps going at 7fps and you have to restart it. Some bugs here and there, bugged dialogue, bugged behaviour. Standard stuff. They aren't that consistent or extremely game breaking to make a fuss about, but worth a mention.

Checkpoints. Checkpoints at some areas are really strange. If you restart, you get spawned way further back than if you just get yourself killed. Since there are no saves, I dread how i am going to 100% the game, unlike in hitman where it's quite easy.

IO's take on an Uncharted style adventure romp, taking lessons from their own experience with the Hitman series and heavy notes from the recent Indiana Jones outing. I love this take on young James, combining the good humoured, cool-headed OHMSS Lazenby Bond with Craig's cold, clinical physicality and just a smidge of Roger Moore silliness. 007 First Light has a thrilling, true to brand, classic, James Bond story with characters I actually felt attachment to. This game had a good balance between stealth and action combat up to your choosing; both systems feeling pretty nice. As someone who usually gets frustrated playing stealthfully in games, I appreciated the mix of more choreographed stealth that made me feel like a bad a** spy and the open stealth that allowed me to go loud any time I wanted without punishment. The level design is brilliant and had great lively environnments throughout the game.

The only real criticism I have for the game is it crashed once during the car chase in the hotel mission, the camera can get a bit wonky during hand to hand combat, and I feel the game is a bit pricy for the kind of game it is. I'd feel much better paying at around $40-$50 so maybe wait for a sale. None the less, if you are a 007 fan this game is great and a must try. Hopefully it is just the first entry in a series.

I'm familiar with the 007 series but I've never watched a movie in full and I've only ever played Goldeneye and it's Wii remake as a kid, but it's tropes are so prevalent in pop culture that you'd be hard pressed to find someone who didn't know the name "Bond, James Bond". From my perspective this game does an incredible job of being an entry in the world of 007 and a great entry point for someone with a mild interest. It's story rarely surprises due to following that classic Bond formula and making sure it hits almost every mark but it also does it in a usually satisfying way, and never felt tacky. To be honest, there were moments I forgot this was meant to be a James Bond game and I think that's actually good. I was able to be immersed in the the story and characters without the legacy of over 60 years hanging over the games head. I've heard some people complain about what felt like "padding" in the story but I enjoyed every moment and honestly wished there was more. I'd absolutely play a sequel to get further to the bottom of everything.

Gameplay wise I knew this was in good hands but my god is it wonderful. I loved 2016's Hitman and it's subsequent sequels and felt this was a perfect fit. Luckily the game doesn't play exactly like Hitman which I now realize is a good thing. Instead of having a target or two that you need to find ways to eliminate, it's more like a bunch of targets in the form of mission objectives that you explore to figure out how to get done. It's also a lot more action focused than Hitman with a great free flow combat system. In a lot of ways it reminds me of uncharted, yakuza, arkham, and sleeping dogs. A lot of interaction in the environment whether it's throwing a mug at a guy in the middle of a fight or ramming a dude into a pipe causing it to explode. It always feels like I'm directing a real natural fight scene and not just playing a game. I think all the gadgets are good though I did personally neglect them in my playthrough, only really using them when I really needed to. 

I played both on my 32:9 monitor with mouse and keyboard and on my steam deck and it was a great experience both ways. The game really pushed my 3070 to it's limit at 5120x1440 all low settings but I felt like the game still looked good and performed well. I was especially surprised to find that the game ran very well on the steam deck, though it did have a massive visual downgrade to achieve that. Still, I put multiple hours in on the steam deck, particular playing through the Vietnam section that way which seems like a very intensive level. I think the default controller controls are a little odd but over all good and I really liked playing mouse and keyboard. I've always preferred Hitman with mouse and keyboard (or vr) so it doesn't surprise me that i prefer it here, but this definitely feels like a sit back and play with controller kind of game.

I think my only real complaint is that some moments in the game had unclear solutions or methods to move on and I kind of just walked around a room staring at everything with my Q-lens to figure it out, but that's likely on me and how dumb I can be. 

Overall, this is the exact type of game I love to play and I'd play any DLC or sequel in a heartbeat. 8/10

I am a MASSIVE Bond fan, have seen all 25 films multiple times, and have played many of the games and have loved the franchise since I was a child. So yeah this review is gonna be LONG.

Leading up to this game's release, I did a marathon of all the 3D James Bond games (excluding 007 Racing). I got to experience them through all the highs and lows of their respective eras and replay some that I played as a child. I'm saying all of this because I can confidently say that 007 First Light is the best James Bond game ever made. 

I have been looking forward to this since it was revealed as Project 007 nearly 6 years ago, and we finally got the trailers and gameplay in 2025. I knew IO Interactive were the studio behind the acclaimed Hitman series (one that I MUST get on asap - always been meaning to and in prep for this game I did play 75% of Hitman 2016) but I knew they were pretty much meant to make a 007 game.

Patrick Gibson is someone who I have seen play another young version of an iconic character in Dexter Morgan and he was brilliant in Original Sin, so I had faith in him delivering as a much younger Bond - he definitely did a great job here and I really found myself attached to his portayal.

What truly impressed me was the scale and the scope of this game, it really does feel like an epic James Bond film - it opens with the pre title sequence which we get to play through, and then we get the titles sung by Lana Del Ray!! It just felt so authentic to the franchise, and then the first couple of missions slows things down as we see Bond go through his MI6 training with other recruits whom we are supposed to get attached to, and the game actually does a good job with this too.

BTW this may have the best tutorial I have ever seen, as it is masterfully interwoven with the actual narrative, and the way its structured as a montage was actual genius.

The actual game's story only really starts nearly halfway through and we are only really introduced to the actual villain at this point too. It is a slow burn but I will say the story got more interesting later but at least it did, and got quite invested towards the end - but in the early stages I wasn't so sure how I felt.

I really liked the portrayal of our MI6 regulars such as M, Q and Moneypenny - they all felt authentic to the franchise. The standout was certainly Lenny James as Greenway - a great character.

The levels are actually surprisingly lengthy, and the game itself is quite meaty - I mean it took me about 13 hours to beat without rushing through, and it is a linear experience so that's pretty impressive and is already the longest Bond game ever too.

IOI put so much love and care into this one, you really can tell they are HUGE Bond fans, I caught quite the fair share of references to some of the films - but it was done in a nice subtle way rather than blatant nostalgia baiting, and man I was so happy to see Bond being a womaniser and flirting with multiple characters in the story - felt so refreshing coming off the Daniel Craig era - this version of JB had fun, charm, witty one liners, is a bad ass and stylish too.

I love the variety of locations visited, again it just feels like a Bond movie experience, we go from Iceland to Malta to London to Slovakia to Mauritania to Vietnam and even Antarctica! They are all beautifully represented too. Even the fact we get to walk around the MI6 building and FULLY walk around Q Labs and again see some references to older films while also feeling like it belongs - it just made me so happy as a huge Bond fan.

I haven't even spoken about the gameplay yet but man the melee combat is so much fun. It may be simple but its just undeniably fun and addictive. The gunplay is solid, Bond can't take too much damage and also can't carry much ammo so a lot of swapping will be done. The game definitely does feel open in that you can go full stealth mode if you want or just go crazy and shoot everyone down. There are plenty of explosions and opportunities to use the Q watch to mess with enemies and dispose of them in fun and interactive ways - it just gels together so nicely. It feels like a combat sandbox and that's perfect for a 007 game. There are also driving segments and they are quite short overall but they provide a nice bit of variety so again can't complain! I will be honest, the levels are not as open or well thought out as Hitman's but thats okay because there is a lot of variety here and even mechanics such as parkour, gadget use, the bluffing, much more advanced melee system, driving and much more cinematic story helps big time. This feels like a new Uncharted game in terms of its action set pieces and gameplay.

I do have some small criticism and that is to do with pacing. It felt like there was a fair bit of padding for paddings sake just to get the game to be longer - this is done usually with walking segments and exploring ' and there was one mission that was very much just pure padding in this sense. I do think that the sequel will fare better as all characters have now been established and also they will take feedback on board.

I was worried that this game would feature too much of the over-analyzing, bifurcating, surreptitious stealth that the Hitman franchise is known for, and I was pleasantly surprised to be proven wrong.

This game is a delightful mix between engaging gameplay, over-the-top action and innovative design. The stealth that is present is very approachable in the way that your modes of attack are presented. They are basically spoon-fed to you via HUD-icons when activating your watch. You are then offered somewhere around three different approaches of different viabilities depending on your current loadout and mood - an excellent design choice for replayability.

The combat actually requires some effort and adaptation for you to prevail, but still offers the sweet sensation of power and might when you understand it. Most encounters can either be skillfully avoided by sneaking and using your tools, softened by the ability to enter combat upon being discovered. The game has an excellent feature called "Situation Contained", meaning that you can resume stealth after having incapacitated all alerted enemies in the area (which never encompasses the whole map and is very forgiving). Entering combat almost never fails a given mission or sequence, which has been a long-standing problem for generations of games until now. 

The bosses vary in design from traditional combat to environmental stealth, but are rather forgiving on the intended difficulty and were never a source of irritation or repeated failure.

If I had to remark on something in this otherwise excellent game, it would be that the distraction mechanic can be a bit immersion-ruining. In order to pickpocket an essential item or interact with an item being observed by a watcher, the NPC in question needs to be "distracted". This often consists of the player, in plain view of the above mentioned NPC or others, shooting a poison dart or sabotaging a laptop in close proximity to the target, causing them to have amaurosis fugax for 20 seconds, rendering them completely oblivious to any and all actions by the player, before resuming normal duties. Whilst being an excellent mechanic to reduce tedium and frustration, it is very bare-bones and not at all as polished as the rest of the game is.

I'm thoroughly looking forward to trying out the TacSim in my sleek, golden suit and hubris from the campaign! This game has truly been a reason to wake up every morning for me, and I can't wait to see if it persists.

Where to begin...

First of all, whoever casted this motherf***er as James Bond should be keel hauled and then tied between two ships where he (or probably a she) is ripped in half. Bond has this constant smirk throughout the entire game no matter the circumstances, and it does not reflect the Bond we know and love from the source material. I.e. he has no aura, he's a simp (more on that later), and his dialogue seems to have been written by ChatGPT.

The entire point of James Bond is to be a gentlemanly figure, that persuades by his very presence, has his way with words, and handles situations professionally. None of that is present in this game, and thus greatly shifts from the source material. I know this is meant to be an origin story, where you play as a younger Bond, but the differences are too extreme in my opinion. I was pleasantly surprised to see that they indeed had a "Bond-girl" encounter in this game, but the way Bond handles this encounter is more like a horny school-boy with an erection tucked up his stomach rather than a gentleman. He literally simps for the girl, and so seems everyone else reviewing this game...

In terms of story, it is extremely lackluster, and offers very little nuance. It's a basic off-the-shelf spy plot, so nothing to write home about there. This by itself would be fine, so long as the gameplay element would be great, which is what we've come to expect from IOI in Hitman 2 and 3. In the Hitman games, we simply make due with the fact that the story is ♥♥♥♥, because the gameplay makes up for it. However, in the case of 007 First Light the gameplay is not even near that of Hitman. It's as if IOI couldn't decide on which direction to go; i.e. story-driven or Hitman-esque gameplay galore.

The entirety of the open-ended and free mission structure is completely eradicated, opting instead for a totally LINEAR progression system throughout the game. This means that you have no freedom in how you approach missions whatsoever, meaning that the entire creative and FUN element of planning your approach is gone. IOI seems to forget that THIS is what made Hitman the major success that it is. 007 First Light does give you nice combat in terms of the VISUAL aspect, but functionally it is not a deep combat system, since you can only push, punch and shove your way through every combat encounter. You literally become immortal when you are shoving an enemy, meaning that you can just shove your way through missions.

Furthermore, the entire stealth system should be thrown in a ditch a burned, since it serves no purpose. It does not matter if you approach a mission stealthily, since if you are seen it just results in a brief 10 second combat encounter, where you again push, punch and shove your way through until the situation is deemed "controlled" again. It is extremely repetitive, and many combat encounters in the game are forced shooting galleries, and they never stop coming. The boss fights are even worse (yes there are boss fights for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason), where the ONLY way to damage the boss is to use your hacking abilities on objects in the environment. Which sounds fun on paper, but in practice coupled with a ludicrously bad stealth system, it just becomes a chore.

It is objectively incorrect to say that this game is bad, it's not, it's just okay. But I think that given the way they've marketed the game as essentially being a "Hitman meets Uncharted" game is really overselling it, since the final product is neither of those two. If you're expecting a game with the depth of Hitman and the story of Uncharted you're unfortunately going to be just as disappointed as I was. That being said, the game at least offers some amount of enjoyment, much like eating a sloppy hamburger from Burger King; it's not good, but it's not outright disgusting either...

Final Score: 6/10

Probably the best game I've played in a long time. It's like a weird blend of Uncharted, Hitman and definitely takes inspiration form a few other games (The Valhalla scene really brought me back to Arkham Knight), but it works beautifully.

 There were a few issues here and there, like falling through the road on the drive to Carpathia, sometimes enemies punch you with no animation playing so you just take emotional damage (which on the hardest difficulty can be a pain) and some sections are... more frustrating that others. Also Bond gets a few too many last minute saves where someone shows up in the nick of time and bails him out. I know it's a convenient tension builder, but it was used a tad too liberally I feel. Not to mention the fight a certain duo of assassins was quite annoying because sometimes Bond blocks the camera and you can't make enough space from them to be able to see properly.

The positives - 

1. The writing is decent and the characters are definitely likeable and impactful.
2. The gunplay and fighting was highly enjoyable. 
3. A couple cameos here and there gave me a chuckle.
4. NPC reactions to your strange behaviour is both well done and Bond actually tries to bluff his way out of it. 
5. They incorporated the aspect of social stealth and disguises quite well. 
6. YOU CAN PLAY OFFLINE. This was a massive ball breaker in Hitman WOA, and I'm so glad they didn't make that same mistake.
7. A decent selection of gadgets that can affect different things in different ways. I was kinda hoping there would be a few more classic spy gadgets in there, but I was happy with what we got.

There are many more that I can think of, but all in all, whether you're a fan of the Bond films or not, this game really scratches an itch. Very, very well done. 10/10.

If the older 007 games are a Bond film, this game is a Bond Novel, the writing does a lot to turn Ian Fleming's 007 from a wise-cracking and quick witted ball of tropes into a well-rounded fully fleshed out and dare I say, complex character with depth. 

This game takes place in a rebooted spy universe and modern world, you play as James Bond AKA 007 but the game is less shooty-power-fantasy and more bonafide Spy Thriller, the characters are witty and funny and the writing has a real charm and endearing quality to it that makes the cast really stand out.

Unlike other James Bond Games where the most compelling thing about them is the gunplay and the dumb one liners that come out from whatever actor's playing Bond in the latest line of movies, in this game, you aren't an action man, you're an actual MI6 agent who has to infiltrate by lying, bluffing and sneaking your way through areas, you aren't some one-man-army capable of gunning down every mook and hired gun, as a matter of fact, some of the best sequences in this game are reserved for moments in which you improvise and find creative solutions, so, while you have one, Guns feel so much less rewarding in this game as guns are tied closer to you failing to infiltrate stealthily.

The sandbox is genuinely compelling and full of sequences where you can solve problems creatively with a bit of lateral thinking, though, I do wish that the Gadget costs were a bit lower on some of them and some of the Gadget Choices a bit less obvious as to what the "Best at all times" options were.

I also don't like how the final segments of the game are all action and shooty with very little stealth, creativity or... any Spywork, as "License to kill" is always active and you don't have your gadgets, but, you're given more bullets than you'd know what to do with.
The game pushes you to the point that stealth isn't an option and you HAVE to blast your way out.
Despite bearing the 3rd Person Shooter Genre, this game is NOT a shooter, this game is actually at it's weakest when you are shooting, and it is my hope that if we get a DLC or Sequel, that we get a climax to that story in which we eliminate the Villains in a more classic James Bond fashion.

Performance wise, this game is INCREDIBLE, it is optimized like a dream, I got a pretty consistent 60 FPS despite my computer showing it's age a little and despite there being a few freezes under the strain from me literally playing this game for almost 10 hours uninterrupted with very few breaks since I got it, the game didn't crash once or have any real notable dips in some of the more wide-open and spacious levels with lots of eye-candy, which, for a game Releasing in 2026, is actually quite rare and a wonderful change of pace.

IO Interactive did something great here and if this is the start of a big James Bond resurgence, I hope they keep the pace they set.

There's so many things that are wrong with this game. I'm not sure how they even made it to the final product.

 Knowing IOI they're a company who's known for their work regarding the Hitman series. You'd expect that same quality to be brought forth, heck you might even expect similar aspects. But this game is backwards. Even by the standards of the older hitman games: Absolution is the one that comes to mind, and it feels worse than that.

 I'll give some positives, but only a few: there a few cinematic sequences that are I guess you could say "cool", the gunplay is fast and feels great, the game seems to run okayish. However, these are the "expected" standards any AAA game should have. 

 This game is way too cinematic, not in the good way. Way too much repetitive and boring walking sequences that should've been cut or at least skipped. You know what's funny? The WOA (World of Assassination) had this problem solved in their menus. Why didn't they do that? Why does this game try to copy so much from Uncharted than if anything?

 Major gripe that comes to mind is the horrendous level design. This is somewhat unexpected. Especially, knowing IOI. You guys had Blood Money to WOA. What went wrong? Again, why go backwards from Absolution of all things. You have so many "choices" but what's the point? They're too linear! They lack any sort of depth, and lose all replayability.

 To top it all off: the mechanics they do have, are somehow made worse from their previous iterations. Especially the stealth and its systems tied to it. Why can't you drag bodies? Why can't you hide them either? Why are there so few weapons? When the previous IOI games had huge arsenals. Don't get me started on the AI, because they're just brain-dead, to be fair the WOA trilogy had some of these issues, but not this bad. Completely unacceptable!

Ultimately I'm going to recommend this game, but not without several serious, almost game-breaking drawbacks for me. 

The good: it really does feel like I'm playing through a Bond movie. Some early frustrations with extended onboarding and tutorial sections actually pay off story-wise as you progress through the game, and I really appreciate that the game takes its time. The graphics are often excellent and the story is about what you'd expect - it feel like if Uncharted was rebuilt within the constraints of a James Bond game. The performances and writing are excellent, and many of the characters feel like real people. Also, when the gameplay works, the action and traversal are thrilling. The climbing and platforming sections work for the most part, and the stealth works well. I wish there was more of it!

The bad: The combat (outside of stealth) ranges from functional, to tedious, to frustrating, to terrible. First, the hand-to hand-combat is an atrocity. There are the bones of a good system here, but the camera and lack of a lock-on system completely handicap any satisfaction you feel from actually landing punches and navigating the parrying/dodging system. Also, James is WEAK. Sometimes I feel like I'm wailing away on people for far too long and they just keep coming at you, whereas (even on medium difficulty), you get like 3-4 punches before you're dead. This is mitigated in larger stealth-action sections by takedown opportunities that trigger after a few hits, but the more cinematic, story-driven fights with stronger enemies and without takedowns can be infuriating. The parry system actually works better on mouse and keyboard than controller, which is weird. And - the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ camera. It's rarely where you want it to be - it's too close, or at a terrible angle, or actually obstructing the parry/dodge prompts. The camera is inexcusable, and the fact that a lock-on system that could have really helped is completely absent is unforgivable. This is probably my biggest complaint: the camera is hot garbage.

Then the gunfights. There really isn't much to them, and they end up going on for way too long. I like the inclusion of environmental triggers like explosives that mix it up, but every single section drags on for like 2-3 encounters too long. Ammo is way too limited, and there's no way to compare the guns lying around to what you currently have. I do like how your sense-effects can impact the gunfights, but they often, and inexplicably, don't work. For example: you're in cover behind a metal crate facing three enemies that are all facing you, and there's a beam above them that looks like it could be triggered to fall and crush them. I activate the instinct ability, and yes- it's highlighted with an "explode" text box with one of your abilities. But then...it just doesn't work. That happens ALL the time. I've died a few times standing there trying to get something to trigger that just won't work.

Third, the boss fights are simply not good. They sound cool on paper, their designs are interesting, but in execution they're cumbersome, awkward to play, and annoying. One boss fight mid-way has you using the environment to take down a boss because you're not strong enough to fight them hand-to-hand (it doesn't matter that you fought this same guy like 3 hours ago and beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of him before losing because a story cutscene gets triggered), and it's just a stupid slog to get through. When I won, it felt more of an accident than anything else.

Lastly, some of the bespoke gameplay moments are far more tedious than they are interesting. Environmental prompts sometimes fail to trigger during these moments, like a box that you're supposed to be able to vault over to avoid a series of laser traps that just won't activate. I'm also coming across regular bugs, like a full 2-3 minutes of loading from a checkpoint after dying.

I think 007 First Light has a lot going for it, and I'm still working my way through it. When it shines, it's an excellent and thrilling experience that lives up to the source material. But I keep coming up against moments and gameplay frustrations that completely take me out of it. Sometimes, 007 First Light can't get out of its own way. I read in a review about how while a game like Uncharted, despite its jank, comes together in a way that makes it greater than the sum of its parts, 007 First Light is the opposite. I completely agree. It has so much going for it, and its highs are truly excellent, but with all the things its trying to do and amongst all of its systems and gameplay elements, the final package is disappointingly less.

[b]-- Positives --[/b]

• Great visuals
• Great sound design
• Great acting
• Funny character banter
• Solid gameplay, and great variety in gameplay (car chases, stealth sections, detective work, gunfights, etc.)

[b]-- Negatives --[/b]

• Some of the story could be solved by James simply shooting the person he's pointing his gun at in a cutscene, and it becomes "yell at the screen" levels of frustrating.
• Keyboard and mouse controls are a bit iffy, and could do with a makeover.
• No way to change Anti-Aliasing type, and TAA is very bad near reflective surfaces.


[b]-- Notes --[/b]

• The campaign itself is about 15 hours long, but there's many hours of side-content that you can play both mid-campaign and post-campaign.
• I've not been able to play this side content due to a bug in the menu for it, so I can't comment on it.

[b]-- Review --[/b]

007 First Light is funnily enough the first new James Bond we've seen since Daniel Craig made his bombastic exit in No Time To Die in 2021. This game features a new Bond, and so it also serves as a new origin story for the role of 007 at MI6, so you'll get re-aquainted with all the familiar characters from the Bond mythos, like Moneypenny, M, Q, and so on. And while they are played by new people, they are familiar enough in their roles that you recognize them instantly.

Because First Light is made by the same people who make the Hitman series, there's a lot of that DNA from that series in this game, and that is by no means a bad thing. First Light is a lot more on-rails and a curated experience than the new Hitman trilogy, but that just means IO Interactive were free to create spectacular set pieces with various car chases, roof top runs, firefights, and so on. That being said, there's a very fine balance between this and the more open areas where you get to do some social deduction and sleuthing in order to obtain vital information on targets and gaining access to inaccessible areas. That's when the game feels the most like Hitman, but it's also the moments that feel like you can really explore what Bond is capable of as a gentleman spy in-training. You can talk to various people standing around and acquire information that way, you can pretend to be someone else, you can overhear conversations, or pickpocket people to obtain access cards, etc. There are often many different ways to solve the same problem, it's just a matter of stumbling upon them. This also makes it so that repeat playthroughs don't always play out the same.

This is accompanied by some excellent banter between Bond, his fellow agents, his girl-in-the-chair, the bad guys, and so on, which will give you some good laughs along the way. The story is also engaging all the way through, though it does feel a little disjointed between the very start of the game, and then the rest. Without saying too much, something happens a couple of hours into the game that basically switches up most of the character roster you interact with, and it almost feels like a completely different game as a result. It's a bit jarring, but I also think that's kind of the point, narratively.

The spy gadgets you gain access to are very quintessential Bond-like, with a laser watch, a phone with a poison dart, earphones that double as a flash grenade, and more. And when you have to find ways through locked doors, or sneak past people, they come in really handy, and you get plenty of opportunities to use them.

One thing I did NOT like about the gameplay was the fact that Bond's issued firearm, the signature Walther PPK pistol, doesn't come with a few spare mags, and is therefore discarded as soon as the one mag you have runs out. It does incentivize you to pick up and use other weapons, but I think it's annoying you can't actually use Bond's signature gun for more than a few seconds before it's tossed to the side.

In terms of performance, the game runs great on my machine, which is a strong AMD machine running Fedora Linux. I had 100+ FPS, so I can confirm it runs fine on Linux, and it runs fine on AMD. It is a bit strange that it doesn't have AMD FSR 4 or higher, and it's also quite frustrating that you can't change the type of anti-aliasing the game uses, especially because the TAA implementation has some really ugly artifacting around reflective surfaces. Outside of that, the game looks absolutely stunning.

The main story takes roughly 15-18 hours to complete, depending on how much you restart, and how much of the TacSim stuff you play during the story. I have not personally played any of the TacSim extra content, because as of writing this, I can't access it due to a bug in the menu. So I can't say anything about the quality of this part of the game. I hope IO has a patch on the way so I can try that out as well.

But yeah, this James Bond adventure gets a hearty recommendation from me.

[h1]IOI have earned the number[/h1]

Up until this point none of the previous 007 games had made me feel like I was Bond. I've got a lot of fondness for the EA era which definitely had their moments but these and what came before and after always ended up going down the 'Bond is a mass murderer' route which you could argue is adapting the movies of the time.

First Light feels like a true reinvention of the character of Bond and you could almost see this existing in a world without the movies. The gameplay focuses heavily on spycraft and stealth and aside from forced combat sections having to shoot an enemy down almost feels like you've failed and that's your last resort which I really like, this is exactly what the character should be. 

The story has some predictable beats [i](which is a problem the modern movies also have)[/i] but it does put a unique spin on things that only could be done in a video game. The absolute standout for me is the cast, I really care about Bond and the MI6 regulars so seeing them brush off with danger always had me nervous, especially since there really aren't any rules with what IOI can do here - this is their continuity and all bets are off.

The system specs for this game are hefty, I always knew I would be on the lower end due to my hardware but my first few hours with the game were a little disappointing because of how it performed. I realised I wasn't fully taking in the game, story and mechanics at first because I was constantly fiddling with settings trying to get to a level which I deemed acceptable. My target was a stable ~45fps but no matter what I did I couldn't get close with FPS tanking to the low 20's in action heavy scenes. Because this was hurting my enjoyment of the game I ended up streaming this from GeForce NOW which was much better. If you've got a strong rig you likely won't have any problems, but a word of warning for anyone who's looking at it thinking "eh it should run ok".

[b]Overall, a solid 8.5/10[/b] from me and based on the sales figures I think we'll be in for at least another entry in the next few years. My hope is that First Light is the Arkham Asylum of the series, a solid game in its own right but something that keeps pushing the gameplay and world in each new entry until we get that definitive Bond experience.

[b] Synopsis:[/b] "007: First Light" is a wonderfully written game with beautiful visuals, fun gameplay, but terrible performance/optimization. You might want to wait for a sale.

[b]Story 10/10:[/b] The plot of the game is really great, rivaling the likes of "Everything or Nothing," "Goldeneye" (the movie), and "Casino Royale." It does a great job at establishing the elements we know while sprinkling in new elements throughout. In general, the story feels like a love letter to the franchise without feeling like it leans on those elements as a crutch.

[b]Gameplay 7/10:[/b] Like most, when I first heard that IO Interactive was making a James Bond videogame, my mind jumped  to Hitman but with spies. However, it's important to note that this game is NOT a sandbox with linear elements. Instead, this game is a linear experience with sandbox elements sprinkled throughout.

For Example: In Hitman, you actively get to choose different mission stories to pursue. However, in this game, each mission has one mission story, but different ways to approach it. It's still fun, but you don't have as much freedom to explore as you might in Hitman.

[b]Combat/License to Kill mode 9/10:[/b] If you're worried about the gun combat in the game, or lack thereof, let me alleviate your concerns. There's no point in the game where you can't shoot an enemy if they're trying to shoot you. The only restriction is that you can't take out your gun anytime you wish, or to take out guards who are only trying to punch you.

To make up for the restrictions, I can honestly say that the melee combat feels really fun. It isn't too difficult, enemies don't have a health bar over their head, and it isn't just attack/counterattack gameplay. It's a nice balance, moreso akin to Uncharted 4 than Hitman.

[b]Optimization/Performance 2/10:[/b] This is my main gripe with the game. The performance/optimization is really bad, even on the lowest settings. The load times are terrible, particularly when reloading checkpoints. Characters have issues loading and unloading, (which includes their audio, interestingly enough), and I've had moments where my control over the character and camera have become desynced, (aka, I move the camera, then it moves 10 seconds later).

The last level in particular has had some of the worst issues. Idk why, (whether it's the snow, amount of enemies, size of the environment, etc.), I've had to restart the game twice to simply make it through certain areas without dying and needing to reload a checkpoint.

- Only a handfull of gadgets. most are redundant, with two being essential. you can only bring four items and you have no reason to ever think about picking anything other than the obvious choices

- Fake choices everywhere. Early on you get a quicktime event to triugger an explosion. let it pass and bond triggers it anyway. And this continues through all gameplay. 
You might think you have a choice in how to get past someone, but all gadets work the same. its all the same.
- There are plenty of good liniar games, to the point where people miss them and dislike open world games etc. This is not one of them. This would be a prime example of why people came to despise liniar games.

+ Combat is good. Its not really as good as in some other games, but in comparison to hitman the gun and hand to hand combat are great. Hell these are the only segments that feel like they play out how they were supposed to.
