TL:DR – The Names Game. Movie Game.

This review is from the perspective of a Bond fan, and a big I.O interactive game fan. I will be comparing this game to older Bond games a little bit. 

PROS:

.Brilliant acting makes for an immersive story.

.Likeable characters all around. I would have preferred a seasoned, Mature Bond, but Young Bond is brilliant too.

.Graphics look incredible, even on 1080P Medium settings, 60 FPS, achievable on a Ryzen 5 5600 G paired with an RTX 4060.

.Melee combat feedback is brutal and visceral, feels great to punch up enemies.

.Gunplay is quite unlike a conventional Third Person Shooter. Ammo almost as scarce as Resident Evil, if you can believe that. This means you have to be tactical in every fight. I didn’t like this at first, but it makes for more inventive gameplay as you are not sitting behind cover all day expending hundreds of ammo.

.I.O’s signature game engine Glacier 2 very smooth, bonus points for not being a U.E 5 game. Many, many NPC’s can be on screen at once.

.Truly well thought out Accessibility Options, including Subtitle enlargement which I needed because my PC’s fans drown out the voices

.When  the music motifs of the Bond theme hits, the Dopimine releases

CONS:

Extremely scripted, railroaded gaming experience. All the trimmings of AAA gaming cliche’s are here. Gaps to squeeze through, chasing character who you can never catch up to, etc.

Somewhat boring downtime moments. Sifting through large crowds of people, climbing ledges, etc.

Stealth doesn’t felt fair. Enemies crowd around each other, blocking routes from all angles making clever gadget use a necessity, but restarting checkpoint after death removes your gadget ammo, and sometimes you may not have the right gadget. This screwed me over when I could no longer break the lock on a vent at the start of a checkpoint. Thankfully, stealth is mostly entirely optional, aside from some very brief, easy gameplay moments.

Driving feels perfunctory, and doesn’t live up to its full potential.

The controls take some getting used to.

AAA gaming cliche of late game heavy armoured soldiers who become boring to fight.

Brahma was hyped up in marketing as the big bad of this game, but he has laughably little screen time and is later replaced with other villains. Why the marketing push?

Bond theme seldom plays compared to other Bond games. 

OVERALL:

It took me roughly 15 hours spread across 5 days to finish. Steam timer is wrong, because I played some of it offline.  I only recommend when in the future it goes on sale, UNLESS you are a massive Bond fan, you like interactive movie style games, and you are interested in a 007 origin story.  If so, then come right in, you will not be disappointed.

One of 007 First Light's biggest strengths is its story. The narrative is engaging, well-paced, and does a solid job of keeping players invested in what comes next. Visually, the game is also impressive, with polished presentation and a modern AAA feel throughout.

That said, the gameplay and some of its core mechanics are only decent in my opinion. They work well enough, but they rarely feel innovative or fully realized.

---{ Gameplay }---

I'm not sure how many gameplay "toys" the Hitman series gives players to experiment with, but while playing 007 First Light, I couldn't shake the feeling that there was still a lot of untapped potential.

One example is enemy melee weaponry. It feels strange that security guards in heavily protected facilities almost always rush at you with their bare fists once things go loud. Even something as simple as batons, stun batons, or other basic melee weapons would add more variety and tension to close-quarters encounters.

The hand-to-hand combat system also starts to feel repetitive after a while. Most encounters revolve around the same set of actions: punching, kicking, shoving enemies, and performing takedowns. Occasionally, you can throw objects, but I think the game could have pushed this much further.

Instead of using environmental objects solely as throwable items, why not let players pick them up and use them as one-time melee weapons or even for distraction purposes? This would be especially useful when you've run out of Chemicals or Batteries. Simple objects like glass bottles, wrenches, or folding chairs could become valuable tools for maintaining a stealthy playstyle without forcing players into a firefight or exposing their position.

---{ Missed Potential with the Robots }--- 

Another aspect that felt underutilized was the robot gameplay.

In the section featuring the boxing robot, its function is simply only for smashing through a glass barrier to open a path forward. Personally, I think this concept had far more potential.

It would've been great to see sections where players could control or manipulate the robot as a tool for eliminating enemies. It doesn't need to turn into a full-on killing machine, but even a few creative scenarios built around using the robot to deal with targets could have created some genuinely memorable moments.

---{ And on a completely different note... }---  

I was genuinely surprised that a portion of the game takes place in Ha Long Bay, yet nearly every employee, staff member, and security guard seems to be a foreigner.

Obviously, this doesn't affect the gameplay in any meaningful way, but it was still a little funny to see one of Vietnam's most iconic locations represented without seemingly running into any actual Vietnamese people during my playthrough.

Short answer: the vibes are excellent, the humour is spot on, and the actors sell it all so well. Paired with top-notch visuals and a well-paced, topical, story, this is a wonderful entry for a new generation of James Bond media.

For a longer example of something that truly stood out to me, I'd like to point out a particular aspect of environment design. Something that always stood out about the James Bond movies was their dedication to practical, physical effects - where these were missing, it generally stood out like a sore thumb (see the later Brosnan films). This game manages to replicate the feeling of gun battles, car chases, and other practical stunts in a virtual medium in no small part because of how interactive the environments are. Cars break and shove obstacles, enemies are thrown through windows or tumble over desks, James can grab mugs or keyboards to pelt and stun opponents with, and gunfire and explosions scatter sheets of paper, shards of glass, and other assorted shrapnel all over a room through a pall of smoke. At its best, the game evokes some of the best moments of all James Bond films (along with a bit of John Woo for good measure).

There are also, of course, many references throughout the game for James Bond fans to enjoy. All in all, I strongly recommend this game to anyone looking for an excellent modern take on the action adventure film genre, delivered in an interactive format.

All the combat animations flow nicely with each other, movement while dodging and combining world elements to attack your foes feels amazing. Especially when you get into a flow state.

Bond this time around is far younger, and it was an amazing touch seeing the scar on his face like described in the books. His charm, whit, and the funny one-liners are still here, albeit maybe not as much as I'd like.

During a mission where you're escaping a valley with one of your teammates, they cued in what sounded to be like a remade version of On Her Majesty's Secret Service's theme from the Lazenby film. An amazing touch here, and I wish they had more nods to the old compositions like this.

Unfortunately, this is where the good ends for me. This game has been such a love/hate relationship to play, and hopefully these issues will help explain that. There's a lot here, so I will be listing them.
- the camera FOV is sometimes TOO CLOSE (ended up installing a mod for it)
- the driving mechanics aren't fleshed out, wish there was a way to turn auto steer off
- dialogue options don't actually change the outcome
- not enough "007" themed/inspired music cues
- setting up too many villains/characters (they did nothing with Bawma, so rip)
- a cutscene where an agent you're trapped with, escapes but it's done right in front of the guards POV (how do they not see her?)
- stealth sections / guard patterns feel very intentional/linear
- wish they did a different story, the whole "axing the 00 programme" has been used in the last 3 movies
- whenever they finally let you go guns blazing, by the time you actually get into a grove with the enemies, you've already finished them all. (I want more!)
- game will randomly remove weapons from you arbitrarily based on whether it not the game thinks bond should have a gun in that specific scene or not
- they gave bond the white suit, and absolutely massacred it. The classic white tux suit is always a black bowtie with a red flower. they fumbled this and just did a white bowtie.
- A scene where Damien (one of the villains) is being perused by bond, he sneaks up on bond by LOUDLY stomping behind him (on concrete w/ tactical boots) and jabbing his liver with his fist. (how does a highly trained agent not hear someone stomping?)
- The whole Damien boss fight was a waste of time, it's made purely of 3 separate gimmick boss fights. No actual fighting happens in these boss fights.
- why the f*** does Greenway (bonds mentor figure) get done in by a random grunt? (his death could've been far more meaningful)
- M16 HQ isn't where it normally is London?
- there's a section where you're forced to talk to random engineers when infiltrating a base. This feels like it was designed purely to pad out run time. The information they give you/stuff they have you do doesn't aid you at all in the later sections (with one exception)
- I thought this one was funny, there's a section where you're sneaking into a base with someone and that person guns down 2 guards. Bond started to say "there's always another way", I think the developers forget that Bond as a character dispatches random grunts for entertainment? He's never had a kill or not kill moral code.
- Certain sections I've noticed I've been shot through walls

All in all, I could've completed this game in 12-13 hours if I didn't accidentally leave my PC on with the game running. This game is NOT worth $90, as much as it pains me to say that. Despite all the cons on this review, and my thumbs down, I really want this game to work, and I want this franchise to work. So I really hope IOI takes some time to fine-tune the formula for bond games, I feel like they're so close.

007: First Light is an amazing game from start to finish, and easily one of the best times I've had with a spy game in years. 

The biggest win here is the level design. It drops you into these massive, sandbox-lite chapters that feel straight out of a Hitman game, giving you freedom to figure out your own approach. You can sneak through the shadows using classic Bond gadgets, or just go loud and flex that signature 007 charisma. When things inevitably blow up, the game seamlessly transitions into these insane, cinematic sequences that I can only really compare to some parts of Uncharted but i wouldn't go as far as to say that they are just as good but still great. Plus, the boss fights sprinkled throughout give the whole campaign a really distinct flavor and keep the pacing tight. 

My only real gripe is that I wish the developers had been just a tiny bit more ambitious with all that structural freedom. When a game gives you this many choices in how to tackle a level, you naturally want those choices to mean something bigger. It would have been next level if your actions actually had a ripple effect on the narrative, or if the enemy AI dynamically adapted to your specific playstyle to counter your moves and make you improv.

But honestly? That’s just a nit pick because the core game is already so good. It’s an incredibly fun ride that never feels like its dragging. Solid 9/10, no real complaints here. Do yourself a favor and pick this one up.

[h1]007: First Light[/h1]
[b]Cinematic storytelling expertise[/b]

This game surprised me in all the right ways. I've never been a huge Bond fan. I think, like most people, I've enjoyed some of the movies and had a good time with them, but never really cared much beyond that. So when the game got announced, I thought, "Cool," and didn't think much more of it.

I watched the first hour or so on a stream, and the game grabbed my attention enough that I figured I could buy it, try it, and refund it if it didn't click. And boy, did it click! I've never played a Hitman or Splinter Cell game before, so I wasn't sure if the genre was for me, but I was pleasantly surprised almost immediately.

The game is very linear — that's the one complaint I've heard from Hitman fans, that it's much more linear than the developers' previous titles. That said, the linearity makes room for a structured narrative, so it feels necessary in this case. You often get options on how to handle situations, usually 2–3, and that opens the door for a bit of exploration and out-of-the-box thinking. Find a guest pass to enter the private lounge, or look for an "alternative" route? It's up to you. I love how the game gives you small hints, but the characters rarely tell you exactly what to do. In many games, objectives are practically spelled out for you. Here, I had to look around, explore, and figure things out for myself — or at least it felt that way. The gameplay is fun, and so is the gunplay when push comes to shove and Bond has to shoot his way out. Personally, I enjoyed the spy-focused sections just as much as the action scenes, and the game does a great job of balancing the two.

While the game does give you options on how to approach things, it's often boiled down to following a checklist. Do A first, followed by B, then C, and so on. For me, that kind of gameplay can potentially get boring. It relies heavily on the narrative being strong enough to keep my attention. Thankfully, it absolutely is.

007: First Light is a genuine spy thriller. A reimagined, modern (in the best way, not the bad kind of way) origin story for James Bond, with everything that should include: cool gadgets, awesome cars, interesting villains, and mysterious, dangerous women. The story is full of heart and memorable characters. They absolutely nail Bond's charm and cheekiness while still making him a capable, suave badass — something you can't take for granted in 2026.

The standout character for me, however, was Bond's mentor, Greenway. Unraveling his motivations and understanding why he acts the way he does was genuinely gripping. I think his story is among my favorites in recent gaming memory. Add in some effective twists, and you have a narrative that's cleverly written with strong character development. I'm already excited to see where this saga goes next.

The narrative is bolstered by the cinematic feeling of it all. I honestly think that was one of IOI's primary goals, given Bond's roots in cinema. The way scenes shift and blend together while you're still playing, almost like a quick-cut movie sequence with no loading screens, impressed me immensely. The character animations are gorgeous, and the facial animations in particular bring everyone to life. Driving through the mountainous Slovakian forests, with their incredible view distances, only adds to the experience. The game is simply stunning — and it runs great, too.

I beat the game on the hardest difficulty in about 17 hours, which feels like the perfect length for the story it's trying to tell. It doesn't overstay its welcome, nor does it feel too short. You can also replay missions to complete challenges, collect items, and experience different approaches if you want more of the gameplay. I probably won't, but I'll definitely return if story DLC or a sequel arrives.

Honestly, judging by the reviews and considering this is a 2026 release, I expected a lot more. The game definitely deserves credit for the movie references and little details, but everything else falls flat.

The dialogue is weak, the hand-to-hand combat is mediocre, and it's a shame that most enemies start their attack combinations the same way. Maybe they all trained at the same karate club.

Even though it's supposed to be a stealth game (or at least that's how it presents itself), it's much more effective to provoke enemies into using firearms and then brute-force your way through levels, because gunplay is ridiculously easy and the weapons have virtually no recoil.

Not to mention that you can't initiate combat with a firearm yourself—you have to wait for an enemy to pull out a gun first, which is just stupid, especially considering these are supposed to be special forces operatives. The place is full of people carrying AKs, but you can't draw your weapon "just in case" because apparently they don't yet have the intention of killing you. XD

Driving vehicles in this game is a complete disaster, and the camera swings around like it's having a seizure.

Even in the very first mission there were countless things that made no sense. You're sent to the world's biggest arms-trading hub, where massive weapons deals are taking place, and somehow a government agency with access to a powerful supercomputer never thought you might need money for the mission, so you have to come up with the funds yourself. And of course everyone is more than happy to help and immediately point you in the right direction.

It doesn't feel like dealing with an organized criminal network—it feels more like a local farmers' market.

Disarming traps on the ship was also incredibly frustrating because there were plenty of other ways to get through that section, but the developers only thought of one solution, so you're forced to do it exactly the way they intended.

And nothing beats the 5-centimeter-thick wooden plank that a highly trained spy wasn't able to remove, despite there being several obvious alternatives. Instead, he needed help from someone with a broken arm. The best part is that when the door finally opened, the plank wouldn't have interfered with it in any way anyway. XD

These are relatively small issues, but to me they're important because, on one hand, the game expects you to think intelligently and find solutions to problems, while on the other hand it throws such poorly thought-out design decisions at you that they completely break immersion.

I expected a lot more from a AAA game released in 2026.

I don't often review games on Steam but I felt inclined to do so here.

First of all the elephant in the room. Yes that was IOI developing the game and whilst there are a lot of similarities it has two very clear distinctions. This is a story driven game so its on the rails more than a Hitman mission. Secondly Bond is an MI6 spy not a hitman, so its not about killing and hiding bodies. It stays true to the movies in the "PG13" style violence against the bad guys.

Those who aren't keen on the casting of Bond, two words, Daniel Craig. How many didn't like Craig being given the role coming off the back of the suave Bond portrayed by Brosnan? As a backdrop to Bond's induction as a 00 I think this serves very well and I'm really keen to see a sequel.

I actually enjoyed the combat in the game, without spoiling the story I had run through a group of enemies and had around 10 and I found myself dodging, punching in one direction, then the other, dodging again, grabbing and subduing.

The AI isn't the greatest but then it never really has with Hitman titles either "Huh???? What was that" before walking over to investigate whilst it looks like the player's head is peeking over a wooden crate nearby.

If you had flawless enemy AI you'd need to severely reduce the numbers of enemies otherwise you'd constantly be reloading after dying dozens of times, the idea here is you are a superspy, so you're 

I experienced 1 crash in the 21 hours played and I had the Jag X type go through the map as I was bringing it around to park, but other than that it played well with a few framedrops along the way. 

One thing about this game, and gaming in general, please stop forcing the yellow (or blue in some cases) indicators of where to go, jump, hang or squeeze through. I get that some players will want this but many don't and I've love to see it more as an accessibility aid that can be switched off. Along a similar point its ok to just have the player navigate a maintenance area of a building without ducking or squeezing every few steps, it won't be any less engaging with fewer of these.

I found myself only using the Q watch for the gadgets and nothing else, such as seeing where enemies are, interactive objects etc. Though I wouldn't criticise anyone for using it as these are fictional spy gadgets, its kind of the point of them being OP.

All in all I thoroughly enjoyed playing this and as I said before I am looking forward to more coming in the future.

The Laser is the only one I would call useful in a way that changes how you access certain places, but even then it isn't needed. And the game will force the correct gadget on you anyway in places where it's needed to progress the story the way they want it progressed.
    [*]Very predictable story beats, "twists" and outcomes.
    [*]Boss fights are very underwhelming and quite clunky.
    [*]Vehicle sections are terrible. They handle awfully, and there's virtually 0 way to fail them. "Hold accelerate to win". They throw in a few enemy vehicles and explosions to try and make it seem like something is happening, but it's all set dressing, no substance or real effect on the outcome.
    [*]Very little distinction or feel between different guns.
    [*]Zero choice of gun or guns on ANY mission. You get what you're given or what you find.
    [*]So many forced stealth (non-lethal) and hand-to-hand combat sections, even in places where it makes no sense based on what's just happened in the game/story.
    [*]Hand-to-hand combat amounts to blocking when Yellow light, dodging when Red light, grapple when they're blocking, punch them until they go down. It's fine the first few times you do it, but it gets old very quickly, and is unfortunately required a lot throughout the game.
    [*]Many sections, especially earlier on in the game, where you aren't really playing a game. You're watching a cutscene, walking for a minute, and then back into another cutscene. I get that they want to establish characters and the story, but the connective tissue to tie it together in a "I'm actually doing something" way isn't there.
    [*]Playing on the normal/recommended difficulty, the game is very easy. There aren't many places where you're ever going to risk dying or failing.
    [*]Most of the puzzles aren't worthy of the name, and amount to nothing more than walking a few meters to the thing that gives you the answer/code.
    [*]Too many modern day references, at least for my liking, that make it seem like it's desperately trying to be trendy and appeal to that part of the brain that goes "Hey, remember that thing you've heard about?". Crypto, AI, social influencing, etc.
    [*]You'll spend a lot of the game being told by other characters how bad you are at your job, despite all the evidence to the contrary that actually it's everyone else who's making bad decisions.
    [*]The writers will forget established game mechanics for the sake of the plot, and then suddenly remember them for the plot a few minutes later. E.g. being able to shoot a gun out of someone's hand, which would be very useful in a cutscene I won't spoil, but he doesn't, then a few minutes later with another character, does it easily.
[/list]

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Might be worth it on a sale, but you're not missing much otherwise. People are saying it's like Hitman and Uncharted, but I'd say it's inferior to both. The others do what they do much better. Hitman offers you much more freedom and choice about how you play, with a true sandbox to approach your challenge. Uncharted offers you a much better story and adventure, with more engaging puzzles and narrative drive. If you haven't played those before, I'd play those instead.

I really wanted to love this game. As a Bond origin story, IO Interactive absolutely nailed the narrative, the music, and the overall cinematic vibe. It genuinely feels like you’re playing through a gritty, well-written espionage film.

But my god, the gameplay balancing in the second half of the game is an absolute trainwreck.

Excellent writing. A fantastic, fresh look at a 26-year-old James Bond earning his 00 status. Great music, cool locations (Antarctica and Vietnam look stunning).

Even playing on lower difficulties, the ammo economy is a joke. You carry next to nothing, and weapons barely give you any spare mags when you pick them up. Meanwhile, standard enemies act like they have infinite bottomless clips and will blindly spray at you forever. You spend half your time scrambling for a single bullet.

Near the end of the campaign, the game completely loses its identity. It throws heavily armored robots at you that can literally corner you in tight spaces and gang up on you all at once. If they trap you, there is zero escape.

Your standard guns do absolutely nothing against these late-game bullet sponges. You're forced to rely on heavy explosions to crack their armor open, which means relying on your Q-Watch gadgets. However, the game doesn't give you any resources to replenish your gadget ammo during these fights. You are essentially left completely defenseless because of bad design.

Play it for the story and the early-to-mid game stealth, but be prepared to pull your hair out by the finale. IO Interactive desperately needs to release a balancing patch for the endgame, because right now, the artificial difficulty ruins what could have been a masterpiece.

Overall this is a wonderful game I think everyone needs to play. But it is loaded with long stretches of some of the least enjoyable gameplay put into games in a decade.

Let's start with what is consistently good:
- Story
- Characters
- Story Telling
- Pacing of plot

The mixed bag items are
- Sneaking missions
- Combat missions
- Traversal
- Level Design
- Boss encounters

The always bad are
- CQC (Easily the worst close quarters combat system put into a video game in a very long time.)
- Interactions

So the game will give you this long beautiful stretch of story and sneaking... And then drop you into a required CQC/Combat section. And just completely fall apart. One of the worst cameras in the past 20 years, combined with the worst cover system ever equal combat is never good or fun. The system just are not there. And about 1/4 of the game is loooooong stretches of combat. So you have to combat the urge to unplug your console and go outside and do yardwork or try and slog through it and hope the next level is a good one. 

And when they are good. They are BRILLIANT! Some of the best I have ever seen. Thought provoking and fun. When they are bad you feel like you are playing a point and click adventure mixed with "where's Waldo" But no one told you what Waldo looks like. So you just have to interact with everything till you find the one random thing that moves the story forward. Infuriating wastes of time. 

It also feels like the level layout was changed part way through production. Mid leta game you end up in a few EXTREMELY hand holding, very tutorial like sneaking and combat sections. Where you are being told the controls again as well having lots of assistance to get through it... Something that would have been welcome early on.

Because the game has what feels like a robust tutorial section, when later on you find that many of the situations it trained you for never occur and there are many more situations it never gave you tools to work with.

Only to later find those tools in a mid game tutorial or worse. Opening up the optional side content and finding a full tutorial on CQC the game easily could have duplicated in the opening parts. And SHOULD have. Hell the CHALLENGE mission was 10x easier than the actual tutorial and taught me 10x more!

But now we have the controls and interactions. They just do not work 10% of the time and some almost never work. You will try it 20x to get through a tutorial and then NEVER accomplish said action ever again.

And do not get me started on interacting with items and ledges. This is one of those games where you need to find the exact right spot to stand and aim the camera for the interaction prompt to appear. Making traversal a constant nightmare and never reliable in a fight.

Set pieces are OK. Some are glorified "Hold forward" moments that are ok. Others are QTE and moronic nightmares. "How was I supposed to go left vs right there?" By going right, dying, and needing to redo the entire section... That's how.

And do not get me started on the dog crap check point system and unskippable cut scenes.

Can you skip cutscenes... Yes! Almost always.. Unless it is a cutscene right before a boss fight. Then you get the classic issue of needing to re-watch the same crap over and over before getting to re-try difficult sections and moments.

Which brings me to the boss fights. What an absolute mess. You are either running around, trying not to die, trying to find the 1 thing that damages the boss. Or the boss dies in 10 seconds. No in between.

What is worse is once you learn the trick to a boss, they are completely trivialized. The only challenge provided was obscurity with some minor trial and error... That's not fun. It's the opposite.

Not to mention the visual language of the game is another area of brilliance or stupidity. Combined with mixed messages. One moment you are traversing smoothly through areas marked in creative ways that do not break the flow of the level then you are in an area where everything is marked with yellow tape and there is no way anyone could have seen that hidden spot without it... WHY!?

It honestly feels like a game designed by 2 teams who later came and put their levels together. Sometimes you play levels by Team A and other times you want to delete the game when playing levels by Team B.

Let me be clear. I love this game. It is so brilliant. They just showed up Uncharted in how to do almost everything (Except combat and Gunplay. They failed there.) Mixed with some of the least enjoyable and most infuriating moments in any game in 10 years.

The good is good enough to over come the bad. But it is not good enough to give this game a high score. 6.5/10

IO interactive have struck gold with first light. I’ve been following this one since they first announced it as project 007, roughly five years ago, and seeing it finally come to fruition is deeply satisfying.

james bond and IO interactive always sounded like a match made in heaven, and first light proves that instinct right. their years with hitman have clearly sharpened their understanding of what makes an IP like 007 tick. the levels blend linearity with open-ended sandbox sections in a way that feels familiar yet distinct from their previous work; it works brilliantly.

the combat is where this game really sings. the gunplay is responsive and satisfying; pair it with the melee system and you have something genuinely special. each punch lands with real weight, countering feels rewarding, and the dodging is slick without ever feeling cheap. you can shoot enemies in the legs to briefly incapacitate them, opening up takedowns; when you run dry on ammo, you can hurl the gun itself to stun them. it’s the kind of system that just clicks; smooth, inventive, and endlessly fun to play with.

the creativity extends to how you handle entire encounters. you have the q-watch, the q-lens, and several other gadgets that let you interact with the environment in all sorts of ways: blowing things up, stunning enemies, electrocuting them. combine that with the variety of takedowns available in stealth and the whole thing opens up beautifully. at a certain point, you stop playing tactically and start toying with people. you throw things to stagger them, send them off railings, use everything around you. the environment becomes an accomplice. Everything feels improvisable in the best way.

stealth is encouraged throughout, and the game handles 007’s reluctance to kill with real care. he isn’t a stone-cold killer; firearms aren’t always on the table. in most scenarios, you’re working with your gadgets: knocking enemies out, distracting them, slipping past without leaving a trail. when you do have your licence to kill, it opens up its own layer of creativity. kill, move, distract; there’s so much nuance in how you approach any given situation, and the game never forces you into one way of playing.

the story is engaging, the set pieces are spectacular, the driving sequences are tense and exhilarating. structurally, it’s a good old-fashioned video game: clear, linear, purposeful. that’s not a criticism. fhe social stealth sections deserve a special mention too; they’re executed with a confidence that feels very IO.

first light is stunning. that opening segment is one of the most striking environments I’ve seen in a game in years: iceland rendered in extraordinary fidelity, bond’s face detailed to an almost unsettling degree, topped off by lana del rey delivering the theme. it’s so unbelievably cinematic. the final three missions scale up so dramatically that each one feels like a finale in its own right.

patrick gibson as 007 is a revelation. he’s charismatic, likeable, and genuinely fun to watch work. the voice acting across the board is stellar; the pauses mid-conversation feel natural, unhurried, real. IO have clearly thought hard about how these characters should sound, not just what they should say.

the choice to tell an origin story is commendable. we’ve almost always encountered bond at an established point in his career: composed, assured, untouchable. here, we see him in his twenties, striving toward becoming 007, still becoming the man we know. it’s a perspective on the character that’s rarely been explored, and first light earns it.

this is one of the most fun I’ve had with a video game in a long time. it’s my favourite game of 2026 and a very strong recommendation from me. it’s been years since Bond had a proper outing in games; I played blood stone as a child and loved it, and first light feels like a worthy, overdue return.

IO interactive have teased more to come with this IP, and I genuinely cannot wait. they understand 007 in a way that feels earned rather than licensed, and I’m fully along for the ride.

until next time; I’ll be diving into the tacsim mode in the meantime.

007 First Light was a blast from start to finish. The gameplay feels fantastic, especially the combat, and I loved the Hitman-style approach to missions where you're encouraged to find multiple ways to complete objectives. It really captures the feeling of being a resourceful spy and taking time to plan and gather information from the surroundings rather than just running from one point to the next.

The visuals are absolutely gorgeous as well, from the environments to the lighting and character animations, the game consistently looks stunning and helps sell the cinematic experience.

There's also a decent amount of replay value. The variety of approaches, hidden opportunities, and alternative ways to complete objectives makes you want to revisit missions and see what you may have missed the first time around. And the Tactical Simulations, which are replayable scenario's with challenges and simulations, really help that value to keep coming back as well.

If you enjoy player freedom, creative problem-solving, and satisfying action, this is an easy recommendation.

I want to say, I had a pretty fun time with this game. There was a lot to love but there was also a lot of grievances that I had with this game. 

The Good:
It's definitely an action-packed, spy adventure. I really liked sneaking around stealthily and being able to have at least a few options in how to solve a mission/problem. It's pretty easy to get immersed and the gadgets and gizmos are pretty intuitive. They really nailed James Bond's charisma and personality down to a T. The characters are also very likable, minus the villains in this game.

The Bad:
The story is... alright I guess. One thing I had an annoyance with at the beginning was how the characters and the story tries to convince you that James is somehow still lacking as a recruit. Even though his spontaneity and quick deduction skills has done wonders in solving certain cases. Greenway also just starts off as your stereotypical, grumpy old fart who somehow hates James at the start. Even though, he really doesn't have any reason to. He does grow on James over time, but it's really stupid how he just doesn't like James right at the start. The transitions in the story are also very abrupt. One minute you are in a very serious and precarious situation and then the next? "Oh naw, we cool now." Like what? There's just no time to digest what's going on. You are plummeted straight into one thing after the next. The final boss is just very underwhelming as well. It's not the only boss to do that. Most other 1v1 fights can be very lackluster. You have to use your environments and use gadgets to stun them, to then be able to get close to attack them. It's very rinse and repeat. The villains are also very one-note. Their reasoning for being bad is just... ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid. The twist of what's been going on is pretty good though. However, it's the same "AI can make mistakes too" kinda sh-peal. And then the good guys are still acting like James is incompetent, when he figured who the bad guys were, and their secrets. It's mildly infuriating. The story does kinda take a dive into the absurd and outlandish when a character supposedly "dies," but then comes back with a powered up Armored Suit. Then facing psuedo-Terminators in a later segment which was kinda funny too.

The Jank:
The combat can be quite good, but it can also be VERY janky. For instance, the fist fights can sometimes make you clip through walls if you grab someone. It happened to me in a boss fight and it was just very awkward to see the QTE under the map. Super jarring. Then there is a skydiving segment that just happens out of nowhere. It's very abrupt and plays out like the skydiving event in Saints Row the Third. It was super weird and funny. Jame's player model can also get stuck on walls and objects during combat. I remember clipping to a punching bag and just could not move. Had to restart and do that segment all over again. Wasting 30 minutes of figuring out what to do next. Yeah, the checkpoints are not good in this game. If you try to restart from checkpoint, it does not save your progress. So if you flub in a stealth section and hit retry? You get sent back like 25-40 minutes. It's absurd. 

My personal consensus:
It's still a fun experience though. Is it worth full price with DLC? Absolutely not. The performance wasn't bad, and I was able to play at 80-90 FPS with all settings set to Ultra with DLAA enabled. I used Frame Gen x2 for the extra frames and the latency was pretty good at just 4-7ms. Bumping up my FPS upwards to 200 FPS. The game is a fun ride that is very reminiscent of Tomb Raider and Uncharted. Despite my rants about the negatives, I still had a fantastic experience with this game. Didn't take me long to finish at just around 14 hours or so. There's a gauntlet type VR sim mode that i just not tried yet. Cosmetics can only be used in those VR missions, so you can't even use them in the main story. So don't bother with purchasing the DLC. I would say, just wait until the game goes on sale to get it. It's fun, but not a life-changing experience. Just enjoy the game for what it is and you will have an amazing time with it. I still think ppl should play it, and i hope they improve on the next game, if it ever comes out. 

P.S.:

MIXED REVEIW - MIXED REVIEW

007 First Light is a refreshing breath of fresh air in the modern AAA gaming landscape. From the moment the campaign begins, you're greeted with stunning visuals, crisp graphics, and a beautifully crafted world filled with striking scenery and memorable locations.

The gameplay is engaging from the outset, supported by a strong story and solid character development that keeps you invested in uncovering the mysteries surrounding Bond and MI6. The cast is memorable, and Bond's quippy one-liners are delivered with just the right amount of charm—enough to make you smile without crossing into overly cheesy territory.

One of my favorite aspects of the game is its subtle respect for the classic Bond films. Q Branch is filled with amusing gadget references, and conversations with scientists contain clever nods to iconic moments from the movie franchise. These little details add a lot of personality and help make the world feel authentic.

I also thoroughly enjoyed being able to freely explore MI6 headquarters and interact with various staff members. These conversations often add extra context and depth to the story, making the world feel more alive. This sense of exploration extends into the missions themselves. While the objectives are generally linear, the game does a great job of giving players multiple ways to approach situations. Whether you're eavesdropping to uncover a security weakness, creating a distraction, or pickpocketing a keycard, the game frequently makes you feel like you're forging your own path rather than simply following a predetermined route.

That said, the game isn't without its flaws.

My biggest disappointment was the lack of vehicle-focused missions. Prior to release, many of the trailers and promotional materials seemed to heavily feature car chases and high-speed action sequences. In reality, these moments are surprisingly rare. Even when the game does put you behind the wheel, the experience feels heavily scripted and restrictive, often amounting to little more than driving at a controlled speed while listening to dialogue. For a Bond game, this felt like a missed opportunity.

The two mechanics that frustrated me the most, however, were the hand-to-hand combat system and the "Licence to Kill" mechanic.

The combat system relies heavily on a hit-parry-dodge rhythm, with visual indicators appearing on enemies to signal incoming attacks. Unfortunately, it often feels unreliable. To rule out hardware issues, I tested the game using a keyboard and mouse, Xbox controller, PlayStation controller, and Steam controller, and encountered the same problems across all of them.

Frequently, after successfully parrying one or two attacks, the system would simply stop responding correctly—especially when dealing with multiple enemies. Inputs often failed to register consistently, causing combat encounters to feel frustrating rather than skill-based. Considering that a large portion of the game revolves around hand-to-hand combat, these issues become increasingly noticeable and, at times, infuriating.

My second major issue is the Licence to Kill system itself. Throughout missions, the game tracks threat levels and attempts to encourage stealth and restraint, which is a fine concept on paper. However, I repeatedly found myself in situations where I was heavily outnumbered and still unable to draw my weapon because enemies hadn't drawn theirs first.

Initially, I assumed this was a bug, but it eventually became clear that it was an intentional design choice. Unfortunately, it never felt natural. James Bond is a licensed secret agent with a licence to kill—not Batman. Being forced into prolonged melee encounters against overwhelming odds while waiting for enemies to escalate the situation often felt ridiculous and undermined the fantasy of playing as Bond. More than any other feature, this mechanic became a constant source of frustration and ultimately hurt my overall enjoyment of the game.

Overall, 007 First Light delivers a compelling story, strong character development, impressive visuals, and a beautifully realized world that is genuinely enjoyable to explore. However, the lack of meaningful vehicle sequences, some misleading expectations set by pre-release marketing, and several frustrating gameplay mechanics prevent it from reaching its full potential.

Despite its flaws, there's still a lot to like here, and Bond fans will likely find plenty to enjoy. I just wish some of the game's more questionable design decisions hadn't gotten in the way of what could have been a truly exceptional Bond experience..

Amazing rendition of 007. I highly recommend it for anyone that is a fan of both action adventure games and open-ended gameplay.
It is a highly dynamic set of mechanics. The game includes some specific types of sections. 
The "social" section, where you, as Bond, is tasked to achieve an objective in a semi-open environment that presents multiple approaches. This is the most Hitman-like of the bunch, while also being very much Hitman-lite. The gadgets can provide interesting ways to solve these sections, however they are still very limited in emergent gameplay opportunities. I would prefered if the gadgets need to be aimed actively instead of automatically aim at an interactible target. Could be less hand-holdy, allow the player to think more about their own approach. 

There are the "stealth" sections, in which you can hide from enemies in an arena and can distract them with the environemnt by using your gadgets, take them out in different ways or even initiate the "punching" section. This one is activated either during the stealth sections or the "shooting" sections, and it is basically a hand-to-hand combat section, a mix between Batman Arkham series, early Assassin's Creeds and a very strong influence from 3D beat-em-ups like Sleeping Dogs. The hand-to-hand feels spectacular, and the stealth feels good and relatively fair. I really like the option of "bluffing" to convince some lesser enemies that they should ignore you.

The shooting might start when the "license to kill" is activated, and it happens in specific areans with enemies that are either actively seeking you or when they are passive but armed and you blow your cover. 

There are also the "action" sections, in which you are put inside a rollercoaster ride with very little control, but bombastic action-pumped scenes happening all around you. These are fun, but very straight forward, like any action scenes in Uncharted, for example.
And finally, there are the "traversal/climbing" sections, which can be either straightforward hand-holdy follow the yellow/blue paint or weak puzzles. I think these are the weakest and most unnecessary sections of the game. They feel like set-pieces but with no actual gameplay. I never liked this kind of thing in games such as Uncharted or the modern Tomb Raiders. I would prefer way more if these sections really included platforming labirinths or puzzles to complete.

The story is a typical 007 tale, but it really leans in on the super high tech, which I really like. I liked some of the character development and how some of the relationships were built, although very superficial, like any other James Bond movies.

All in all this is the most solid version of a 007 as a game that I have ever played and I really hope they can expand and more creatively improve some of the more simple aspects of the game. I would really like to see the traversal/climbing sections be more thoughtful and interesting to solve than to climb in the only specific paths that are laid out by the devs. 

I was surprised by the art-direction, graphics and the performance. I played it on high, 1080p DLSS, and it stayed above 60fps most of the time. Explosive sections dropped the frames a lot, but these were very quick and sparse sections and did not bother that much. I was impressed by the characters rendering in cutscenes and about the lighting in the social sections. 

Highly recommended.

007: Last Light is a strange one for me, because I both enjoyed it and kept noticing how safe it feels.

Let’s start with the obvious good part: performance. The game runs beautifully. No DLSS, no heavy post-processing trickery, no weird stutters, no sudden frame drops. I was sitting comfortably above 80 FPS the entire time, and from a technical standpoint it is rock solid. Visually, it looks good, but I would not call it graphically innovative. It is polished, clean, and perfectly fine, but it is not trying to reinvent anything visually. That is not really the point, though.

The real question is: does it feel like James Bond?

Yes. Absolutely. It gives you that “playable Bond movie” feeling. The tone, the locations, the action set pieces, the espionage flavor, the stylish presentation, it all lands. If you came here wanting James Bond, you are going to get James Bond.

Where the game starts to lose me a bit is the gameplay. It is not bad, but it is repetitive. You can technically approach situations in different ways, especially in stealth sections, but the enemy AI is far too predictable. Even on the highest difficulty, enemies do not really force you to improvise or adapt much. For a stealth-focused game, it rarely feels like you are outsmarting a dangerous system. Most of the time, you are just moving through very readable patterns.

The other big thing is that this game really, really wants to be Uncharted. It is honestly hard not to see it. The movement, the pacing, the set pieces, the exotic locations, the banter, the cinematic action, even this version of Bond himself, it all feels very Nathan Drake-adjacent. In fact, this Bond often comes across as Nathan Drake with a British accent and an intelligence agency behind him. Obviously the characters are not literally the same, one is a spy and the other is more of a treasure-hunting mercenary type, but the vibe is very close.

That said, I still recommend it.

It is a good game. It is polished, fun, stylish, and it understands the fantasy it is selling. The replayability is limited, but there is enough there if you want to revisit missions or try slightly different approaches. It also feels like a strong foundation for future games in the franchise.

So, final verdict: if you want a deep stealth sandbox, this probably will not blow your mind. If you want a slick, cinematic, technically excellent James Bond adventure, then yes, this absolutely delivers.

As soon as I've heard "IO Interactive is making a 007 Bond game" several years ago, I realized that fewer things in the industry made as much as sense as that sentence, and now that the game has hit the shelves everything makes even more sense. 

A must-play banger, especially for people that are adjacent to Bond movies and/or games. 
IOI went full prime mode on the Hitman reboot series and it is absolutely ecstatic to see a release of a different IP from them, not to mention that Hitman reboot took quite a lot from Bond.

And of course, this Bond took a lot from the Hitman in turn. 
If anyone remembers Hitman Absolution - this and 007 First Light are quite structurally similar (for e.g level segmentation through doors that transition you to other portions of the location, the linearity of the choices you can make inside those segments, etc). 
I loved Hitman Absolution dearly back in the day, but I get to see clearly how others did not, or they've expected better. 

First Light doesn't have nearly as much of a systemic, freeroamy-sandbox gameplay loop as the latest Hitmen, and it is quite linear, quite scripted at times (not to its own benefit I'd say), and it does not challenge you enough, but damn -- does it deliver within these constraints, with its story, characters, combat (which makes for some of the best third-person shooting that you can get your hands on nowadays), level design is an absolute blast. This is THE single-player experience that does not compromise within the industry full of multiplayer slop, which is exactly how IOI operated for years up until this point. I've savored this game throughout the 20+ hours that I've spent in it, absolutely wanting more.

There are a few things that I would like improved for the 007 Second Light or whatever the sequel could possible be called (and yes, this one appears to be a trilogy going forward... God I love it):

- Less scripted sequences - if you're making a QTE within a cutscene that provides choices - let me fail it and pick incorrectly, let me figure things out and don't resolve the QTEs for me just to create a frictionless, uninterrupted cinematic experience. 
- Don't steer my wheel when I'm driving the car, ever. And don't create smooth collisions that hug the barriers of the driving sequences - let me actually hit the obstacles and fail a chase/race. 
- I would definitely strive for just a bit more non-linearity and way more challenge. Although on Hard it was a fine experience, as well as enemy placements within the levels were actually top notch, it was never really easy -- I would still like more challenge.
- Personally, I'd make an experience like that longer, say 30-40 hours if possible, but that's my personal single-player fanboy mentality. 

All else was an absolute joyride, after waiting for this game it actually delivers with colors.

And yet one question remains unanswered:
IOI, Freedom Fighters 2 when?

I ain't gonna call this game a 10/10 chef kiss muach muach kind of game. It obviously have some flaws and would definitely disappoint people who have been following this game for 5 years, only to find that this game is basically a refined version of Hitman: Absolution.

If you have played a video game in your life before, the way you can complete some of the more open levels are very obvious and straightforward (yes, just like Absolution). There are alternate routes that checks off a challenge list, but if you're not into that, why even bother with the alternate routes? I guess IOI needs to add more incentives for the players to do the alternate routes than checking off a list. Some immediate reward would be nice, instead of having to complete the level several times and check them all out to unlock... an outfit that you can use in TacSim... Yay...

My biggest disappointment is that the game showed all of its cards wayyy too soon. After the peak that is the hotel level, pretty much every level after that never lived up to it, even setpieces-wise. It's either a compact version of the hotel level, or an on-rails section with little variations. I do like to replay the hotel level a lot, but the other levels, ehhh....

The game has two different combat mechanics, hand-to-hand and shootouts. More often than not you'll engage in hand-to-hands, like 80% of your encounters.

The hand-to-hand combat is pretty basic. You have a punch button, a dodge button, and a parry button. The combat is cool and flows really well if you know your buttons, but sometimes the AI twerked like crazy, like a brute who kept spamming throws, a specialist who dodge kicks even when I'm not hitting him, etc. It's more funny than annoying for me tbh.

The gunplay is pretty much serviceable, but I like how you don't have a lot of ammo, even for your pistol, so you have to tactically use the environment to take out multiple enemies, and scavenge for weapons from dead bodies. Throwing your guns to get a guaranteed daze and knockback is also really cool and funny. I got a lot of cool kills from that. Sad that you don't get a lot of these sequences.

I'd say the hallmark of this game's gameplay is the gadgets. The way you can creatively use the gadgets to distract enemies and take them out tactically is so cool. I'd say they nailed this aspect of Bond perfectly. You can also use them in combat, which adds so much layer to the very basic combat system.

The thing that I don't like about this game is how it hides some of the explanation of its mechanics behind TacSim. Like they don't even tell you that shooting both kneecaps counts as a non-lethal, or that there's a "Strong Attack" move that guard breaks by holding down the attack button. It's not necessary to finish the game, but it would've been helpful to know, right?

Story is pretty much meh. I don't hate it, but I don't love it either. It's a very safe story, and it felt more like Mission Impossible than 007, but the thing that sells me on the story is the vibes, music, and the main characters. 

Moneypenny and M did an amazing job selling themselves as handler and boss respectively with their actors' performances, and I don't care what the racists say, this might be one of the best depiction of them. Lennie James as Greenway literally carried the whole first half of the game with his stellar performance. And I never wanna shoot a Bond girl so bad until I met this game's Bond girl (for reasons I will not spoil). These characters did a great job in shaping Bond on his journey.

Bond itself, though, is a cheeky smug bastard that a lot of Bond fans would raise their eyebrows at for how different he is compared to the older Bonds we see in the movies and books. But then again, he's 26 in this game (same age as me at the time of this review's writing lmao). He's young, troubled, and rebellious, very much unlike his other depictions.

An inexperienced Bond is pretty much what people are interested to see. "How can this Bond be transformed into the Bond that we knew and loved" is the challenge this game has to face, and I'd say... it did a so-so job at it.

On one hand, this Bond is pretty much the Bond we know and love, just more youthful and quippy. The dry humor, the love for women and guns, and quick thinking to bluff his way out of any situation (shown even in the gameplay with the Bluff mechanic), is pretty much spot-on James Bond. They even got the scar for him, which no movies has ever done.

Though despite pretty much getting everything else right about Bond (except that annoyingly permanent smirk of his lmao), my biggest irk with this depiction of Bond is despite his youth, brashness, and rebellious streak, somehow he's always in the right. Ngl I wanted this Bond to fail. A lot. Get effed on by not just the villains, but also his employers and friends. I'm not saying he should be Spider-Man miserable. I'm saying, as an inexperienced agent who should make a lot of mistake, they should let Bond make more mistakes, and rise up to it. The grit to never give up despite the odds being stacked against him is what we like to see in James Bond, not this perfect git who somehow got his way despite going rogue like THREE TIMES ALREADY.

The antagonists are pretty much predictable, you can see them coming from a mile away, as well as their motivations. My only grievance is that there's no build up to them. They don't get a lot of screen time, and they felt awkward when revealed as the villains of the game. Now if they built them up like Irons in Advanced Warfare, the story might be better in my opinion.

All in all, why did I give it a thumbs up, despite my obvious mixed opinion? Again, I love this game despite its obvious flaws. I paid $30 for this game (regional pricing ftw bish), so I didn't really felt cheated on. I got my money's worth. I see the potential this game has, and I would like to see another game like this. Though maybe next time, take some more inspirations from WOA than Absolution, please.

7.5/10. Get it on sale if they sold you this game $70. Still a pretty solid game despite its flaws.

 Pretty much sums up my overall thoughts on this game. The story is phenomenal. The voice acting is impeccable. The graphics is stunningly detailed. This is so far my favorite cinematic game experience of the year. I cannot get over how good the game is. Sure it has its flaws. Its not the best action adventure game nor the best puzzle, stealth or driving game but it has all the bits and pieces to make it a mosaic of a masterpiece. Its dialogues feel authentic, because its voice acting feel very natural. Overall, its one of the best games I've ever played the only downside is there isn't enough of it to play.

So, I played this. I don't know what I was expecting, but it wasn't this.

The game is technically sound for the most part. Combat is dead simple, essentially a timing mini-game with little to no strategy to it. 

The stealth is... rudimentary at best. Enemy AI is similar to games we'd see in the early 2000's. Dumb as bricks, deaf, blind, etc. until you're very close to them. 

My main problem with this game is that it's more of a movie than a game. It's a "cinematic experience" that holds little to no challenge. In fact, the game holds the player's hand all the way to the end, with very few instances where the player has freedom to actually choose what they do. 

The music is pretty good, I'll give them that. The characters are very difficult to take seriously. 

The idea that a newbie like Bond would be capable of taking down entire groups of seasoned soldiers and mercenaries without breaking a sweat is ridiculous. Sure he gets some training, in a controlled environment, but that hardly explains how he can body groups of 5+ dudes going at him.

There are also so many deus-ex machina moments that are [b]necessary[/b] to keep the plot somewhat coherent. For example, there is a point where a dead agent leaves a message for someone, and it's such an obscure way of conveying the message that I don't believe it's realistic that this dead agent could predict who would come for him, that they would investigate the relevant items, and then put the pieces back together to [b]guess[/b] at the meaning. 

Spies have excellent cryptography that they can use to deliver a message. Are we truly to believe that spies would play guessing games, instead of plainly writing the message in encrypted form? 

There's also tons of platforming sections that don't make sense. Of all things, I don't believe for a second that any of the platforming is appropriate for the James Bond franchise. I also don't believe that it adds anything to the game. Just like all the walk-and-talk sections, the platforming is just another cut-scene.

It doesn't help that this game suffers immensely from yellow paint syndrome. Every. Single. Time. I can't even remember, off the top of my head, any instances where the obnoxious blue tarps/ arrow graffiti/ signage [b]didn't[/b] exist, and I had to actually [i]had to look around and orient myself in the space![/i]

I can't fathom how much contempt IOI must have for the average gamer. You know what they could have done? They could give us a MAP of the space. The Q-lens gadget is *perfect* for this. They could have had a feature in it which shows the interactible elements of the levels on demand, instead of putting blue tarps everywhere (including in places that realistically nobody would put a tarp, such as fused into a wall, concrete block, or other items. 

The highlight of the game is the Vietnam mission, which actually allows for a larger amount of freedom, and [i]nearly[/i] feels like a Hitman level. Still, it's rather short and consists mostly of cutscenes, which is disappointing. 

I won't speak of the story, it's the usual government/corporation conspiracy affair. It's fine. The characters suck, but the story itself is passable. 

In total, [b]while there is some game in 007 First Light, it is definitely more of a movie experience than a genuine game.[/b] The ratio of boring cutscenes/ walk-and-talk/ platforming/ following blue tarps and signage to objectives, vs. the actual gameplay, is just atrocious. 

Now, some may argue that platforming/ walking while exposition happens in dialogue, or even collecting evidence is something a spy may do, and it should be considered gameplay. 

Alas, I don't believe that it's so - the game takes control away in these instances, and forces the player to listen/ watch exposition like it's speaking to a 5-year-old.  Genuinely - if you play this game, all you have to do is follow the blue tarps and graffitti, and you'll easily get through the entire game without sweat. 

The only consistent failure states are in combat (reasonable, but it's way too easy) and a few QTE's which frankly shouldn't have been there in the first place.

If you're a Bond fan, get it. It's a completely fine entry for the franchise. But don't treat this as a game. It's by far more of a movie than a game, and the lack of challenge is genuinely painful. 

I believe that if 007: First Light was trimmed down, reduced the sit-down-and-listen exposition, and cut out large portions of """gameplay""" (walk-and-talks, platforming, puzzle sections), it would be a much better game, and ultimately a much better story, too. 

For me, 4/10, there's some game, but it's not much at all.

As a spy-action title centered on the early days of a young James Bond, 007: First Light delivers an authentic and engaging secret-agent experience.

The game blends stealth gameplay with intense gunfights, complemented by a cinematic narrative that feels straight out of a classic Bond film. High-tech gadgets developed by Q, Bond’s iconic watch, and brutal hand-to-hand combat allow players to fully step into the role of 007. Dynamic camera work and an immersive soundtrack create a gripping atmosphere throughout the adventure, while thrilling chase sequences, explosive set pieces, and satisfying stealth takedowns keep the action exciting from beginning to end.

The story follows a rookie Bond as he begins his career at MI6. His clashes with his mentor over differing ideals add depth to his character and make his development more compelling. The supporting cast is another highlight, bringing charisma and style to the narrative. Whether appearing in elegant evening wear or sleek field attire, the characters contribute to the sophisticated and glamorous atmosphere that has long been associated with the Bond franchise.

The main campaign spans roughly twenty hours, maintaining strong pacing throughout and avoiding unnecessary filler content.

Overall, 007: First Light stands as one of the finest Bond video game adaptations to date. It is highly recommended for longtime 007 fans as well as players who enjoy stealth-focused gameplay, espionage stories, and cinematic action adventures.

[h2]
Menu Design, Chapter Select & Aim Assist Toggle [/h2] 

The aim assist settings are oddly named and confusing. There is no simple option to completely disable aim assist.

Additionally, if you want to check which collectibles you've missed, you have to load into the game and view them from there. The menu only lets you view challenges. A Chapter Select feature exists to help with this, but it's just a list of text. Even a small image or screenshot for each chapter and checkpoint would make it much easier to understand where they actually take place.

The collectibles menu also has its own issues. It doesn't clearly show which area a missed collectible belongs to, and the items appear to be sorted randomly. For the final files, I had to search for the names of the collectibles I had already found and use that information to track down the ones I was missing.
[h2]

Forced letterboxed cutscenes.[/h2] 

I had to use ReShade to remove the black cinematic bars during cutscenes. I also removed  long startup logos with a mod. The game now reaches the main menu in about 3 seconds.

[h2]
DuaIsense Controller Bugged Features on PC [/h2]
 
Half of the features randomly stop working on their own and start behaving abnormally.

[h3]I solved the problem in time using a method I remembered from Jedi Survivor. If anyone's curious:  [/h3]

Go to Control Panel → Sound Settings → Show All Devices. Right-click the DualSense speaker device, select Configure Speakers, then click Next. On the following screen, check both boxes and save the settings.

After doing that, the haptics and audio worked properly. You can also increase vibration intensity and set it to Mechanical in-game. 

Switching the USB port or connecting it directly to a Thunderbolt port can also sometimes help.

[h2]

Audio crackling issues. [/h2]

I've seen reports about this on IO's website as well, so I assume it'll be fixed eventually.

[h2]
Sound and SFX[/h2]

Early in the game, I turned on the field radio to use it as a distraction and immediately recognized a copyright-free military radio sound effect I also use on YouTube, which was pretty amusing.

Sound effects such as bullet casings and suppressors feel very weak and are almost barely noticeable.
[h2]
Unstable Frame Generation & FPS Drops  [/h2]

Frame Generation is unstable, and there are massive FPS drops during explosion and fog effects.

[h2]Equipment selection is oddly restrictive.[/h2] 

Once you confirm your loadout from the equipment van, the menu closes and you can't make adjustments without backing out. Chapter Replay suffers from the same issue.
[h2]

Don't use DLSS or FSR override/swapper mods.[/h2] 

They conflict with the game's implementation and can create weird floating artifact clusters, especially around vegetation.
[h2]

Hitbox / collision issue and weak ai [/h2]

I frequently got shot through cover despite being completely behind walls. Smoke grenades also seem broken in many scripted encounters. If you throw one near yourself, enemies continue shooting you as if the smoke isn't there at all. The smoke grenade issue is annoying, but the wall penetration problem absolutely needs to be fixed.

[h2]

He Had Him… Then Left [/h2]

Another major issue is how often the game relies on the classic "villain doesn't kill the protagonist when they have the chance" trope.

I've watched every Bond movie, so I know this is basically a franchise tradition, and I normally don't mind it when it's used sparingly. For example, in No Time to Die, something like this only happens once or twice.

In this game, however, it's used way too often. After a certain point, Bond is practically walking around enemy strongholds with his hands in his pockets while the villains constantly choose to talk instead of finishing him off. It happens so frequently that the antagonists stop feeling threatening.

[h2]

Lecturing the side character 10 seconds before taking out four enemies with clean headshots from a suppressed pistol [/h2]

As for the story, there are several moments where the dialogue and the actual gameplay completely contradict each other.

For example, James talks about being careful regarding taking lives, and then literally ten seconds later we're mowing down four enemies.

Another example happens near the end of the game. Earlier, the game foreshadows Bond's ability to hold his breath underwater. Later, when [spoiler] James and Damien fall into the water, I expected Bond to survive using exactly that skill. Instead, he loses consciousness after what feels like ten seconds underwater. [/spoiler]
[h2]

The overall UI and the lack of a dynamic interface feel weak for an AAA production. [/h2]

The lack of dynamism in the UI and its overall design make the game feel somewhat cheap. For example, even in situations where they can't be used, prompts for Q Watch, Bluff, and Lure remain permanently on the screen, constantly displaying which buttons to presseven while driving. 
[h2]

Expectations and Reality [/h2]

In the promotional campaign, names like Lenny Kravitz and Gemma Chan were announced with great excitement, and some players even expected villain performances on the level of Raoul Silva. However, these characters end up saying little more than a single line before disappearing from the game entirely. It felt as though the celebrities were included mainly as a marketing tool to attract players. Bawma’s backstory, in particular, is reduced to a single brief explanation and never properly explored.

[h2]

For the next game, [/h2]

I hope IO keeps the storytelling style from the early sections instead of shifting it midway like in this one. 

I’d also like to see them introduce more varied mechanics and ideas beyond the “shoot, move forward, listen” structure and something closer to the chapter-based, long-form storytelling style of [b] Casino Royale.[/b]
[h2]

And start the second game with a 15-minute chase! [/h2]

Great experience, but I feel somewhat conflicted about its length. Let me explain:

The game and story are really good. Part of me wishes the campaign was longer, as the narrative, characters, and cutscenes are highly engaging. It leaves you wishing the game spent more time with characters like Cressida and Isola. On the other hand, the gameplay did feel a bit repetitive after a while. While some locations open up for a more Hitman-style approach with optional routes, the majority of the game is fairly linear. (Which is fine—after all, I feel the natural tradeoff for a lack of freedom is a stronger narrative and story). I played on the "intended" difficulty and found it way too easy. I mostly found myself brute-forcing my way through enemies; while it was fun, cinematic, and engaging, I never really felt like I had to break a sweat to beat large groups.

I was really hoping the TacSim mode would be the natural place to put more open-ended missions. Unfortunately, I found TacSim quite disappointing—it mostly consists of shorter, highly curated experiences on smaller maps. This would have been the perfect area to add what IO Interactive is known for: massive sandbox areas.

Overall, though, I am very happy with the game. My ideal version would be this linear campaign accompanied by a more open-ended, sandbox-style gameplay loop in TacSim, however, as of now, it falls a bit short of that.

[h2]9.5/10 - A Must Play for 2026[/h2]
[i]007 First Light[/i] is one of the best games of the year, and an absolute must-play for both Bond fans and IO Interactive fans alike.

Pretty much everything this game sets out to do, it does remarkably well. The action set pieces are fantastically crafted, full of tension, spectacle, and momentum in a way that genuinely makes you feel like you are inside a Bond film. The gameplay is incredible, the combat feels great, and the game constantly finds new ways to throw you into fresh situations that force you to improvise using the skills you have built up. It rarely feels boring or mundane, because every mission feels like some new spy caper with its own rhythm, challenge, and cinematic payoff. The story and cutscenes are a huge part of the experience. This is a very cinematic, story-heavy game, and for me, that is one of its biggest strengths. The cutscenes keep you hooked all the way through, and the whole thing feels like playing through a Bond film or one of Ian Fleming’s Bond novels. That said, if you do not enjoy cutscene or story-heavy games, this might honestly be a skip for you, because the entire experience kind of hinges on that cinematic storytelling.

The level variety is also excellent. The strongest missions for me are when the game leans into that IO Interactive/Hitman-style design: a large area to explore, multiple ways to approach objectives, and plenty of room to experiment. That is when the game is at its absolute best. A lot of the levels late in the game are more linear, which I personally did not mind, especially because the combat and presentation are so strong, but I do wish the game returned to that more open-ended style a little more often. Despite that, for me, this is peak game design. The gameplay, story, mission variety, action, and overall Bond atmosphere come together beautifully. There's also some side content for those interested. It's an easy recommendation for Bond fans, and an even easier recommendation for fans of IO Interactive.

Instead of just listing why it's great, I want to directly address some of the criticisms I’ve been hearing from people who seem to be missing the point:

1. "It's built for a modern audience / He's not womanizing"
People are complaining that it’s "not James Bond." 
Chambers, Moneypenny, the Woman in Red, Selina Tan, Charlotte Roth, and Theresa Lorca. Enough said. 

2. "It's not enough of a sandbox like Hitman / Too linear"
Last time I checked, the game is called 007, not Hitman 4. The story mode is intended to tell a cinematic story. The sandboxes are there, they feel very IO Interactive, there are just fewer of them. If you want pure sandbox replayability, the TacSim mode has you covered.

3. "Too expensive for a 20-hour game"
Let me put it this way: you can buy 10 meal deals at the grocery store for £4 each and technically have "more food," or you can go to a nice restaurant and get a premium steak for £40. Most people understand the difference in quality here. First Light is a production of the highest tier. The acting, the graphics, the soundtrack, the level design, and all the official licensing. It's a premium product. Honestly, if you play a game like this only once for 20 hours and never touch it again, that's on you. IO put their heart and soul into this, clearly. 

4. "It's just a movie game that plays itself"
This is plain wrong. The sandbox levels offer plenty of gameplay variety. The shooting sections are challenging on the intended difficulty, and the stealth requires consideration and resource planning. Plus, there are tons of unlocks and challenges that force you to go out of your way to play in interesting ways.
This game deserves your money way more than "Generic Open World No. 256" with its 1,000 mindless fetch quests.
