First of all: Wow. Just wow. OK, now that's off my chest, let me say I LOVE this game.

I understand people had certain expectations of it to play more like Hitman given the fact its developed by IOI but as someone completely unfamiliar with Hitman, and more with the Bond movies and books, as well as the games of days gone by, all I wanted was a new James Bond game and for it to be good (especially after the disaster that was 007 Legends).

And this game is phenomenal. I grew up with Agent Under Fire, NightFire, Everything or Nothing, GoldenEye: Rogue Agent, From Russia With Love, Quantum of Solace, GoldenEye: Reloaded, and to a lesser extent Blood Stone and 007 Legends. This game blows them all out of the water... Frankly it is, in my opinion, the definitive James Bond experience. Even better than GoldenEye on the N64.

From the start, it grabs you, pulls you into the world of a new James Bond, one still finding his feet, and it doesn't let go. The story is engaging and topical, and the characters feel real. From Bond himself, to his fellow trainees in the 00 program relaunch, authority characters like M, Greenway, Moneypenny, and Q (probably my favorite depiction of Q, other than the late Desmond Llewellyn himself!). And of course there are the Bond Girls. Couldn't have a Bond game without Bond Girls, and they are stunning. And the villains are better than some in the movies, some even undergoing minor character development as the game progresses.

The gameplay goes a long way in making you feel like you are James Bond, with multiple choices of how to execute your missions, the heavy reliance on gadgets from Q Branch, and not constantly on the weapons. A man who doesn't need a gun necessarily to get him out of a tricky situation. Needless to say, I think the game manages to balance the stealth combat, hand-to-hand combat, and weapon combat incredibly well.

It's a truly globetrotting adventure, going from Iceland to Malta, London to Slovakia, Mauritania to Vietnam, and even BLOODY ANTARCTICA (which somehow Bond of the movies and books never visited, so that's a first)! There's also the cars, plenty of Aston Martins, Land Rovers, and Jaguars for you to drive and appreciate.

I've followed this game since it was announced in November 2020, and it did not disappoint me. Now the big question is: Will there be post-launch DLC? Or will we have to wait for a sequel to see 007 again?

I had a blast playing this game. It's good to finally have a good fresh 007 game after many years of absence. IOI did a great job making a solid spy thriller based on 007. It's a fun action game with some fun cinematic set pieces and levels that are enjoyable to go through. That being said, don't go in expecting this to be like Hitman. There are parts of the formula there, but this game is far more linear and less of a playground than Hitman. It still gives you some freedom of how you do some objectives and approach obstacles throughout the game. Characters are done well, especially 007. The story is a solid James Bond story that doesn't necessarily do anything new, but is still enjoyable. Combat is open enough that you can handle fist fights and fire fights in a variety of manners with your gadgets' help. The gadgets also allow for different ways to handle objectives. It's not a perfect 10/10 like so many people are saying, in my opinion, but it's still a ton of fun.

STORY:
It's a James Bond story. If you're familiar with his past missions, this doesn't do anything new. It's solid, but nothing mind-blowing.

The characters, overall, are done well. I really enjoyed Bond's character in this. He's a snarky smartass with plenty of one-liners. Money Penny was a fine support character. M was also fine, though I don't think anyone anywhere will top Judi Dench. None of them were bad; outside of Bond they were just fine.

GAMEPLAY:
As stated above, if you go in expecting something on the level of hitman as far as freedom goes, you will be vastly disappointed. The game gives you a few ways to complete objectives on occasion, but it's all pretty straight forward with no sandbox fun. Completing the objectives though, can still be a lot of fun. Gadgets also allow you to implement different strategies to complete said objectives. Combat is solid, melee gives you some freedom with how to handle enemies. Gunplay is fine. The environment and gadgets give you plenty of different ways to approach encounters with the enemies. 

GRAPHICS:
The game looks great. My only complaint is that some of the facial animations just looked...off. Sometimes the characters looked like they were always smirking...when they VERY clearly shouldn't have been. Optimization is ok. I hate frame generation, but I will say it did bump my performance up a bit, a shame that I had to use that in order to get a variable 60-75FPS.

SOUND:
Sound design is great. It has the iconic sounds you'd expect. What I wasn't sure to expect was the fact that they have an original James Bond openening credits scene with a song. That made extremely happy!

REPLAYABILITY:
There is a system in the game that allows for some replayability and progression. The Tacsim system is fine. It lets you play various segments of missions with modifiers and objectives to complete. This allows you to level up and earn new gear to use in them. It's fine if you want a little extra gameplay to do.

THE ISSUES:
While I can glaze this game pretty heavily, it's not perfect. The story takes some predictable turns. The characters, while fine, can sometimes just kind of exist in the role they're supposed to. Gunplay is pretty basic. There did feel to be some unnecessary padding to some of the story sections. Again, optimization isn't great, but it was bearable for me.

OVERALL:
It's great to have Bond back in a solid experience. I do look forward to see where they go from here using this is a foundation to build on. It's worth it for a great action-adventure spy game that gives you a solid story that lasts long enough without overstaying it's welcome.

Let me be upfront: I was never a Bond guy. Never cared for that smug bloke in a tuxedo who saves entire continents with a single raised eyebrow. Then IO Interactive had the audacity to put 007 First Light in front of me — and now here I am, three days later, unshowered, surrounded by empty crisp bags, writing a review.

The Cinematics: Please Stop, I'm Already Crying.
Yes, I cried. No, I will not be confirming that. If anyone asks: it was dust. Very dramatic, orchestrally scored dust that falls in slow motion onto Patrick Gibson's exhausted face while a sunset detonates behind him in perfect cinematic time. IO Interactive apparently decided that "cinematic" was too low a bar and simply made a film and disguised it as cutscenes. The transitions between gameplay and story sequences are so seamless I forgot to pick up the controller again — twice.

The Title Song: Lana Del Rey Showed Zero Mercy.
In April 2026, First Light was released as the game's title song, performed by Lana Del Rey. Of course. Who else would step up and dismantle my entire emotional defense system in under three minutes? The song sounds like someone converted moonlight into audio, poured a string arrangement over it, and then quietly whispered: "You're never getting rid of this." Correct. My playlist will consist of exactly one song for the foreseeable future.

The Score Overall: A Composer With No Restraint Whatsoever.
The soundtrack is what happens when an orchestra collectively decides that subtlety is overrated. Every car chase, every stealth segment, every loaded glance between Bond and the next impossibly charismatic villain — all of it comes with its own perfectly tailored musical carpet. This game sounds more expensive than my entire apartment is worth. That is not a criticism. That is a diagnosis.

The Aura: Absolutely Unacceptable.
IO Interactive promised cinematic flair — from a covert operation at a high-profile chess tournament in Slovakia to the infiltration of a black-tie gala. What they delivered is a game that feels like you are starring in a Bond film, not merely watching one. The cinematography, the way light falls on a tuxedo lapel, the sheer entitlement with which Patrick Gibson walks into every room as though he owns it by birthright — this isn't game atmosphere. This is style as a state of matter.

Combat itself varies a lot — gadgets are almost always present, but the focus shifts between hand-to-hand fights, firearms (usually with limited ammo), and, in certain encounters, making use of the environment is almost essential

I really enjoyed the game, and I’d like to take this opportunity to thank everyone involved in making it. It’s not perfect, but it offered me a very enjoyable experience.

Fun gameplay, easy-to-learn controls, a very “Bond” story, plenty of action, hot babes, a suave spy, cool cars, and yes — we even get an epic montage.

The campaign took me about 20 hours, which honestly felt perfect. Compared to another game I’ve sunk 100+ hours into and still haven’t finished because it’s starting to drag, First Light doesn’t overstay its welcome. It stays enjoyable the whole way through.

There are still plenty of missed collectibles, challenges, and other things for me to go back and try. Pair that with the different ways you can route through each level, and I’m sure there’s still a lot more to do, see, and experiment with.

There’s also an entirely separate TacSim mode, though I’ve only tried the intro so far. From what I’ve seen, it acts as a hub for your campaign collectibles and has a ton of extra content. I’m excited to jump into that next.

My only real issues are that the game does hold your hand a bit, it could probably be optimized better, and it sometimes gives a false sense of choice. It looks fantastic even on medium textures and mostly high-to-ultra settings, but performance ranged anywhere from about 40 to 130 FPS on my build.

As for the “false sense of choice,” you can approach missions in different ways with your pathing, gadget choices, stealth, or guns-blazing playstyle. The issue is that progression is sometimes locked behind scripted events or required steps. So even if you discover something early, you may still need to complete another objective first before the game lets you move forward.

Overall though, I had a great time with it. Stylish, fun, cinematic, and exactly the kind of Bond-style spy game I wanted. Couldn't have asked for a better studio to make the game, IO Interactive did an incredible job, can't wait to play what comes next.

This game is chocked full of  references to the movies that range from "anyone will pick that reference up" to things really deep dive references.

As far as the overall game mechanics go, I wouldn't look to pick this up if your looking for a shooter, or Hitman clone, or stealth type game because it doesn't really play like that. There are obviously shooting and stealth mechanics in the game, but I wouldn't say those are really the highlights of the game. Not saying they're bad but I felt like the focus is very much the story (as I feel it should for a Bond game). Along with that, the story isn't overly long (which I don't feel like it [i]should[/i] be and though there is end-game content, I'm not really a fan. This is just because the story was the real highlight and not gun play or fist fighting.

 It is very much [i]not[/i] "Hitman in the 007 IP", if that's what you're after. There a many similarities and you'll certainly be reminded of Hitman if you're a fan, but in my own head, Agent for 47 dropped out of my thoughts about 5 minutes into the game. It brings a lot of freedom to how you accomplish your tasks and some disguise stuff (which, honestly, seemed a little off in the game), but it's similarities end there. Which is plus.

The story isn't overly long, and though there is certainly end-game content, I'm personally not very interested in playing it. Largely because, again, the story is what really shines in this game. If you're good with spending the money on a game you'll likely go through quickly, I'd very much recommend picking this up. If you're trying to stretch the return on your money though... you probably want to wait for a sale. (I'm at 23 hours writing this, but I'd say at least 5-6 of those were idle time).

Overall: I can't wait for the next one!

Ngl I love this game's more linear take on the Hitman formula. I get that a lot of people haven't vibed with its linearity, but Hitman feels imo a lot like a "best of" level pack, not like a complete package, and it's never held my attention very long as a result. First Light, on the other hand, puts a lot of effort into feeling like a complete game and making sure every level actually does something - and if linear design is what it takes to do that, so be it. (Besides, it does still open up on occasion, just in curated chunks where nonlinearity best fits the goal of the game.) Maybe that's just my opinion, and I've always been very much a "polished and tightly packed singleplayer campaign" kinda guy, but still.

Anyway, that's the part I most wanted to talk about, because that's where most of the criticism has come from. Imo First Light is an 8.5/10 - it's an awesome cinematic stealth-action game that I highly recommend (even if you're not a Bond fan - I genuinely couldn't care less about the guy), it's full of epic setpieces, awesome music, stellar art direction, and really fun gameplay, and you should maybe get it on PS5 or Xbox if possible (Denuvo doesn't really like to, you know, keep a stable framerate without stutters). If you're like me and Steam's all you have, though, then this version's perfectly serviceable, and lets you play KB&M to boot - just be wary of stutters and maybe some occasional visual glitches.

oh, one more thing: don't bother with the deluxe edition unless you REALLY like using nice cosmetics in optional side content. I literally only have it because it was free with every preorder.

This is probably the ultimate Bond gameplay experience:
- true to the character, respectful of the source material
- tons of references to Bond titles for people to catch
- has all the clichés and tropes people love about the series
- you can disable the QTE events to make the experience even more cinematic
- no "shove it in your throat" DEI stuff

It's truly a great, enjoyable adventure to play through, feels like you're playing a genuine Bond movie!

That being said, it comes with a lot of asterisks, so while I still [b]truly recommend people buy and play the game[/b], here are the things that some people will find irritating, infuriating or even potentially dealbreaking:
- this game is considerably more narrow in possibilities compared to the latest Hitman, it's not an open world sandbox, they changed it into a more scripted, linear design which works great for the story, but be aware of this before you buy, this is NOT a Hitman 4 game. Because of this, the replayability of this game is considerably more limited, it does have TacSim which is basically Escalations from Hitman but you can't simply load into a mission and have fun with it in the same manner as before
- manual saving is gone, you have to rely on auto-save feature which is a gut punch to all the "I want to make this playthrough perfect" people, I'm one of those people and I really didn't like it, it substantially limits experimentation and how you approach your gameplay, felt seriously restrictive compared to Hitman
- combat is substantially more action-focused and stealth is more limited because of this, again, comparing to Hitman (the combat does feel nice when you get into the rhythm of it though)
- there are some small moments in the gameplay where I'd straight up ask myself "why? who even thought this would be fun", my guess is they added a few moments like this for gameplay variety, not all of them are a hit, there are some misses, but few and far between, thankfully
- while there is no horrendous DEI, some characters are race-swapped (most notably Moneypenny and M), mentioning this just in case this is a dealbreaker for you, it doesn't feel bad or out of place in the game itself in my opinion

Really enjoyed the game, IOI did not disappoint.

The combat is really satisfying to pull off, shooting feels nice. Movement took a little bit to get used to so I had Bond moving like a drunk for the first couple missions while trying to sneak and get into cover. The gadgets are all really fun to use, even if they are maybe a little too strong (I don't see why me flashing a laser pointer in someone's face wouldn't alert them after it wears off). Them being a limited resource doesn't massively affect you as there's things to refill both meters everywhere. Bluffing is also a cool mechanic, and the fact there's an option to comply with people finding you trespassing instead of them aggroing on sight is much appreciated. NPCs do seem a bit more aware of you while sneaking around and more likely to check you if they catch a brief glimpse of you than they are in Hitman, and they do seem to fill up their suspicion meters a lot quicker.

Story was good (does end in some sequel bait which we probably wont hear anything about for 4 years), liked the characters and was generally well acted. There's also a lot of background details that you might not notice, especially in Q lab. (for example every time the story takes you there you can find the evolving prototypes for the exploding pen in one of the siderooms of the lab). Having lore in collectibles is always nice too.

There's not a huge amount of challenges to complete during missions, generally there's a couple of "Don't ever get seen", "Don't KO anyone" and "KO X amount of people" and then one or two that just involve interacting with a certain prop per level and that's about it, and there's not really much reward for doing it other than an outfit you probably wont wear because the twitch drops and ioi account bonus ones look better anyway, and for bragging rights ig. Feels like they were either a bit of an afterthought to give replayibility for people going back through to find all the collectibles, or they used to be part of a system that didn't make the final cut. At least in TacSim they give you the currency you use to upgrade your tools.

My main gripe with the game is the excessive hand holding. Even though I had tutorials turned off It felt like I was constantly being reminded about certain actions. There's also an insane amount of "yellow paint" syndrome present. Even in linear sections where there would be no other options for where to go, the whole place would still be lined with bright blue tarps, yellow pipes, tape that wouldn't make any sense why it was there. Some was more subtle, like areas of rock with yellow growths on, but most of it was very in your face and as soon as you notice it it does take you out of the immersion a little. I also feel like on the harder difficulty (or just give an option for it) it could've stopped pinging all the hints so I could have a chance to actually work out puzzles and find things. There may as well have been stickers on everything saying "Find Me" and "Come this way!"

Performance was pretty solid. A couple of frame drops here and there but generally smooth. Only crashed once in my 20h playthrough. Camera could be a little janky at times while locked while inspecting things or in real time "cutscenes", but generally not a problem. Majority of bugs I encountered just made me laugh if anything and then I would move on.

Also PSA to anyone getting the game: Do TacSim as soon as you get it after completing I believe the advanced training? They're basically extra tutorials that tell you things that the main game doesn't mention unless you're really looking through the menus like what combos you can do in combat and different ways to disarm enemies. I didn't know this was in the TacSim because when it was described to me by Gemma Chan doing a nerd accent it sounded like it was just in-game lore for replaying levels and not its own thing. It would've been really helpful to know the stuff from the advanced combat escalation about 12h earlier than I ended up doing it, and the combat on replaying the game to get the rest of the collectables feels so much better now I know what I'm doing rather than just spamming click and q.

[b]Summary:[/b] 007 First Light is a nice eight hour experience stretched into twenty by the skin of their teeth. While the ideas of tactics, espionage, cinematic action sets and shooting are there, they aren't really as impressive as the games they emulate. They want the set pieces of Uncharted but aren't quite there. They want solid shooting but cut short. They sacrifice gameplay and choice for hallway choices between going under an obstacle or over one, and they sacrifice creative open level design for a focused story which isn't interesting in the slightest.

[b]Story:[/b] The origin of James Bond. The start of his journey into spydom is a great idea, and we see how he gets his training and eventually masters the abilities he has learned. The game starts strong where you meet the other recruits to the program and progress through the game unravelling a conspiracy. Unfortunately, it is incredibly boring. The game makes some interesting choices that vastly cut down on the unique characters you interact with and focuses far too much on this story for how predictable it is. Every twist is seen a mile away, something which I'm not good at discovering myself and yet I could still see it. While 007 might not need a vastly complicated story, it does need to be fun and keep you on your toes. This does not do that, and by the end it felt like they didn't care either. I won't spoil much, but the part of the game where Bond is doing CPR on a guy who is not only breathing still, but moving and actively talking to him, is where I checked out because it was so laughably bad and just got worse.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] The shooting feels great. Walking around a gala while discovering clues sounds great. But it falls short. The game is laughably easy with really only three enemy types. Guys who will stand still, shoot at you, and maybe throw a grenade that die with one shot to the head, armored guys who will slowly approach or stand still to shoot you and die with two shots to the head, or heavily armored guys that do the same but, you guessed it, die with three shots to the head. Oh and snipers that have giant lasers, a giant flashlight, and also get one shot to the head. There is little recoil and no sway, so it makes it incredibly easy if you have decent aim to kill seven people with seven bullets and not even have a risk to missing. Enemies don't jostle or move fast to dodge, so you can kill them with ease. The melee combat is another feature which does feel better than the shooting, but there is little variance. Enemies do a three punch combo, or maybe try to taze you, or try to grab you which requires a dodge. That is it. There is simply not enough variety to make usage out of the environmental aspects and fighting them for it to feel replayable. I played the game on the hardest difficulty and it felt like easy mode with how simple it was to kill people and how much leeway you are given for mistakes.

The pacing is awful as well. Levels are typically slow walking sections with a little bit of dialogue, then you have to get somewhere and are given three very obvious options that the game tracks and tells you the progress on these, then a small stealth section where you can fight enemies on one side of the room, have them call in reinforcements, and when you finish the fight you can see their buddies are just relaxing on the other side of the room. They lose sight of you easily, and if you distract enemies with gadgets you can just immediately do what you need to do, even if they still are looking at you. The levels where you are doing your 'spywork' is essentially running around until you find the eavesdrop point. Coming from all the stories about creativity and different ways to take out targets in Hitman, it is laughably less here.

The gadgets are also kind of boring. The laser strap is required because it unlocks unique things that you can only get with that, and the rest of the gadgets are essentially the same flavoring of item that do not have any uniqueness like the laser strap. They feel mostly samey or underwhelming. They also didn't really try with them. You get a shockwave camera that looks like a shockwave, but Bond doesn't pull out the camera to use it. It just flashes. It doesn't feel like you have a wide spykit arsenal but one gadget that can do three slightly different things. Since this is your only spy tool it is a bit of a shame.

The pacing. My god. So much slow walking with nothing interesting, so much wasted time and going back and forth in spots that could've been easily removed, so many back sections with nothing interesting that adds nothing. The worst one was a minigame that was about five minutes of Q telling Bond how to tie a bowtie, with QTE's. I thought it was a joke because it isn't interesting dialogue, or something happening in the background, it is literally just tying a bowtie. Not even a good tutorial that could teach you how to either, just Hold M1 or M2 and stretched out for way too long. That's pretty much a great example of this game. It had a lot of fat that it could've trimmed, but was scared to do so in case people complained of paying this price for an eight hour game. Thing is, it would've been a better and more replayable game if that was the case. Something they excel at yet were scared with his one.

The TacSim mode is cool, and honestly more fun than the rest of the game. You can try out more gadgets, more creative stuff, and it gets rid of a lot of the boring stuff. The main campaign isn't replayable, but this certainly is.

[b]Music:[/b] Music is great. The bond song is great and the way it tenses and shows is great. I really liked this.

[b]Graphics:[/b] Top-notch, with faces looking like the actors and real for the most part. NPC's are duplicated a little more than my liking, but everything in the environment looks great with amazing lighting and animations. The fact that this game has WORKING MIRRORS without ray-tracing should earn it an award alone. It also ran relatively well, though I did get some frame stutters very rarely in smoke or with a lot of particle effects. I also had one crash during the game, but it worked fine on the next book.

[b]Overall:[/b] I enjoyed the game, but not for the price. It is good, it is fun, but there was a lot of it that could've been removed and I think it would've been better. It definitely is a game that I would wait for a sale on, but otherwise it still is a good entry and, while the standards are low, is probably the best Bond game out there. Just don't go into it expecting Hitman, or Uncharted, because you will be disappointed.

Pre-ordered and installed right away, I've already finished the main story and it's superbly crafted with a great script and voice acting. They really hit the high notes of the James Bond experience. I did a few of them but lost interest pretty quickly.

In my opinion the ultimate success of this franchise will greatly depend on extra content being developed and released. Thankfully IOI has a good track record of catering for this from the Hitman games, so I will keep faith that they will do something similar here.

007 First Light does a great job of making you feel like you're actually playing through a Bond movie. From the exotic locations to the spy gadgets and undercover missions, the game nails the secret agent fantasy better than I expected.

The story is good and kept me invested throughout. There are some nice plot twists and the ending felt satisfying. My only issue is that it feels like the game sets up certain characters early on and then does not fully use them later. For example, I kept expecting Cressida to return in a bigger role and assist MI6 in some meaningful way later in the story. It felt like there was more potential there that never got explored. Even with that, the overall plot is strong and delivers a proper Bond adventure.

Combat feels smooth and responsive. The shooting mechanics are solid, hand to hand combat gives you enough options to feel stylish, and the overall gameplay flows well. Enemy variety could have been better, but the game makes up for it with its spy mechanics. Stealth is a little too easy at times, and the enemy AI is not particularly smart. There were several moments where enemies seemed to intentionally miss Bond during certain animations, which made combat easy to manipulate once you noticed it. Despite that, I loved that you can talk your way out of situations instead of always fighting. That feature alone makes you feel much more like Bond than most spy games.

Visually, the game is excellent. Character models are highly detailed, environments look fantastic, and performance was great throughout my playthrough. Whether you are sneaking through luxury casinos, infiltrating secret facilities, or exploring international locations, the game always looks impressive.

The characters are good, but I wanted more from them. Greenway, Bond, Moneypenny, and Isola get most of the attention and have some great interactions throughout the story. The rest of the cast, however, often feels underused. There are several interesting characters who could have benefited from more screen time and development.

World and immersion are where the game really shines. Every location feels like it belongs in a Bond film, and I genuinely felt like I was part of a global spy thriller. Combined with the classic Bond style soundtrack, the game captures the atmosphere of the franchise perfectly.

The game is also fairly polished. I ran into a few bugs and some animation stutters during basic interactions, but nothing that seriously affected the experience.

Final thoughts

007 First Light succeeds because it understands what makes Bond fun. It delivers espionage, globe trotting adventures, smooth combat, and plenty of stylish spy moments. While some characters feel underdeveloped, the enemy AI is a bit too forgiving, and a few story opportunities are left on the table, the overall experience is highly enjoyable. If you have ever wanted to step into Bond's shoes and live through your own spy thriller, this game absolutely delivers. 8.5/10 final rating

Reviews for this game are weirdly polarised, but ignore those—it's really an OK game with some strengths and some weaknesses. I enjoyed it overall, but probably won't be spending much more time with it after finishing the main story.

Strengths:
- Absolutely phenomenal presentation aesthetically
- Engrossing story (with just one or two clunky moments)
- Good PC optimisation

Weaknesses:
- Tries so hard to be a movie, it fails to be a game—half the time feels like a walking simulator
- Tied in with the above, weird pacing—tries relentlessly to keep flowing into the next sequence, as though it expects you to play through the whole game in a single sitting, but it's a 15-20 h game, not a 2h movie!

Both stealth and combat are relatively unfun—many of us can't help comparing this to the phenomenal Hitman 2016+ series IOI developed beforehand, and it's a significant downgrade in gameplay:
- Open-ended puzzle-solving has been replaced with handholdy walking simulator type situations. 
- The simple but well-tuned gunplay has been converted into what I felt was an overcomplicated mix of melee and shooting. 
- Hitman's mix of movement and disguise-based stealth has been replaced by gadget-based (and dialog-based) stealth that again feels overcomplicated but at the same time repetitive to me personally.
- Movement in Hitman was effortless and responsive; here, agent 007 feels clunky to control and occasionally refuses to move the direction I press, which was frustrating

IOI has clearly tried to outdo Naughty Dog's Uncharted and the Last of Us in creating a story-rich experience, but unfortunately at the cost of gameplay and pacing. Overall, worth playing if you like action games, but maybe not at full price, and maybe not if you're too busy for games that are 'good' but not 'great'.

[h1] TLDR: [/h1]
All around amazing game. Good story, great gameplay/combat, fun level design, good graphics, and well optimized. If I had to give it a numerical score, I'd say 8–9/10 (roughly a B+ to A- on the American grading scale).

[h1] Expanded: [/h1]
Wow... nothing but respect for IO. You can really tell this game was a passion project for the team, and their experience making the Hitman franchise shines through. I didn't expect much from this title before release, a solid game at best, but it easily surpassed my expectations, especially in the story department. If I were to compare it to other titles, I'd say it's a beautiful mix of Uncharted, Hitman, Sleeping Dogs, and a touch of Batman: Arkham (I know that sounds weird).

The story follows Bond's origin, so don't expect to jump in as an already established Bond who's a master spy right from the start. The game gradually builds tension throughout the story, and it was really fun growing alongside Bond as he learns more and gains access to new tools that help him complete missions. Alongside that, the supporting cast is, for the most part, very well written and likable.

The gameplay is the best part of the game, in my opinion. I've read online that the person who designed the combat was also the combat animator for the old Batman: Arkham games, and you can definitely tell. The combat isn't exactly freeform, but it's similar. The best part is that everything, and I mean every object in the game has physics and can be interacted with. Nothing beats being in a room with six enemies, throwing one into the middle of the group, grabbing the next, bobbing and weaving, countering, and so on. You can really enter a flow state. On the stealth side, the gameplay is very similar to IO's Hitman games, albeit a bit watered down (for example, not being able to drag or move bodies).

I'm really excited to see what's next for this franchise, as there is definitely going to be a sequel somewhere down the line. IO has a great opportunity not only to bring back 007, but to create some of the best Bond games ever made.

[b]007 First Light is honestly one of the most impressive games I have played in a while.[/b]

The graphics are a genuine 10/10 for me. Some parts of this game are absolutely beautiful, and IO Interactive deserves serious praise for what they pulled off with the Glacier engine. Path tracing is not even available yet, and there were mirrors, reflections, lighting, and environments that looked better to me than games using much heavier RTX features.

It also played almost flawlessly for me over 26 hours. I ran into one save bug where a save would infinitely load, but I was able to load another save from the same chapter and continue without losing much progress.

It is not perfect. Picking up batteries to refill Bond's watch felt a little forced. I understand why the hacking abilities need to be limited, but I wish they had found a more natural way to do it. Collecting chemicals felt similar, and crouching or taking cover could feel awkward at times.

[b]Still, the positives outweigh those issues by a lot.[/b]

The world feels alive. NPCs are constantly talking, working, reacting, and having conversations that are actually worth stopping to listen to. The levels also give you so many unique ways to handle situations that it can almost feel overwhelming if, like me, you want to collect everything, do everything, and see every possible option. But that is also what gives it real replayability. I already know there are routes, interactions, and moments I missed.

The story is amazing, and my biggest complaint is honestly that I wanted more of it. Gameplay feels like IOI took what they do best with Hitman and turned it into a proper cinematic Bond game, with some Uncharted-style spectacle mixed in. It never felt like Hitman with a Bond skin. It felt like its own 007 experience.

Even if you are not already a Bond fan, this is an amazing game. If IOI ever builds a larger, more open-ended Bond game from this foundation, it would be insane.

[b]Highly recommended.[/b]

James Bond: Absolution... sorry, 007 First Light is not a bad game. It's a decent action-adventure game. But why the thumbs down? Because it doesn't commit to anything strongly enough to become a great game, something it really could have been and even intended to be. 

People wanted IO to make a James Bond game for the longest time because we loved the sandbox missions in Hitman, where you can use a wide variety of opportunities, gadgets, items, and environmental interactions to eliminate your targets. It's an experience you can't find anywhere else. And who else uses a wide variety of gadgets and creative methods to accomplish missions? James Bond.

However, IO's 007 game is far from what many of us imagined. There are stripped-down Hitman mechanics during stealth sections, and there are a limited number of gadgets you can use alongside the environment. But they're implemented in an extremely limited fashion, more akin to Splinter Cell: Conviction than Hitman. The gadgets, in particular, can be very disappointing. If you think you're going to use different gadgets to achieve your objectives in widely different ways, as you would in Hitman, you're gravely mistaken. I'm halfway through the game, and there are basically only two or three gadgets used in every stealth section, and all of them feel very similar.

Aside from the sections where you walk around, talk to people, and gather intel, the game consists of four main types of gameplay segments: 1. Stealth 2. Driving 3. Brawls 4. Gunfights

And they're all fine.
The overall experience is more reminiscent of Uncharted than Hitman, which isn't inherently a bad thing. However, it's nowhere near as polished or thrilling as a top-tier action-adventure game like Uncharted or The Last of Us. I'm not even a huge fan of those games, but 007 First Light cannot go far enough, due to so many reasons, to achieve the same level of engagement and quality.
At the same time, it has abandoned its classic sandbox formula, and the result is just a decent action-adventure game. A 6-7/10 game, if you will.

I think the core issue can be summed up as: unless you're specifically looking for a decent James Bond game (and there haven't been many of those in recent years), there are better games that do each of these four segments. That's why it's hard to recommend 007 First Light; it's ultimately a bland blend of mediocrity. I suppose the upside is that it feels oddly nostalgic, because the disappointment is very similar to what I felt as a teenager when I played Hitman: Absolution. Thankfully, the story and characters here aren't nearly as dreadful. That's not exactly high praise, though.

007:First Light greatly scratches the itch for more Bond, given we won't see a Bond 26 in the near future. It even goes beyond what the films could offer, giving us a cinematic spectacle with fun gameplay and remarakble visuals. 

For the most part, this game was a very linear, a very casualized, more forgiving version of modern Hitman's gameplay combined with the cinematic presentation and adventure elements from Uncharted. The cinematic Naughty Dog approach is very apparent, because a good portion of the game has a lot of these "walking dialogue" segments, where you don't do much, but walk around and a scene unfolds without doing much. Personally, I wasn't a fan of these moments, since they eat up a smidgen of what could've been more engaging gameplay, because it surprisingly packs more punch than IOI had clearly intended. There's no shortage of QTEs and On-rail segments , which honestly I didn't mind, IOI were aiming for the same variety of action and adventure some Bond games used to feature and it's serviceable. The game's a bit of a slow burner, but the moment Bond starts engaging in actual missions in character and is out of training, that's when the game truly shines. Lots of alternative ways to complete situations and puzzles  which is very appealing. There definitely is some replay value, if you'd like to complete all of the challenges and handle missions differently.  Nevertheless, the game in general is a great time guaranteed and you won't regret giving it a go. 

 The hand to hand combat is very Arkham-esque, no surprise here since the combat designer was the combat animator for that trilogy. Everything feels so seamless and natural in these fist fights. The Naughty Dog-isms don't stop at the cinematic presentation- there's a crazy attention to detail in this game, and not just on a visual level. There's more contextual animations in the combat that I could count, that make the otherwise simple hand to hand combat look like a million bucks. You throw enemies into random furniture, a urinal at a club, an expensive suit of armor, you name it and they simply break, selling the impact of the scuffle. You can tell that they've taken a lot of time to animate these things and set them up properly. 

The gunplay is pretty snappy. Bond's barely a year into his training as an MI6 agent and he's already a killing machine that barely feels the recoil of any gun in the game.

The story, for what it is, is great. It's the usual Bond epic - you've got an era-relevant theme,  Bond girls, crazy action sequences and a villain causing high stake situation after high stake situation. Personally, I really liked the time relevant angle with the villain and the twists, though I find the actual villains pretty forgettable, compared to, say, the Lenny Kravitz character in Aleph (He was a vibe through and through).

 Bond initially reminded me a lot of Eggsy Unwin before he became a Kingsman in the first film, but after a couple of missions, he's already emulating the 007 character know and love. He's got a ton of charisma, I swear Patrick Gibson would make a killer live action Bond. 

I hope the inevitable sequel leans into a more gameplay-heavy route next time around, since Bond finally becomes 007 in the end.

Takes some of the sandbox elements of Hitman but it's not supposed to be Hitman. This is just a good old fashioned, single-player campaign. 

The hand-to-hand combat is technical and satisfying. A lot of destructible objects littered around areas where you can start fights. There's few things in life more tactile than slamming a goon's head into a fire extinguisher. 

The shooting is dynamic, you're never using one weapon for long since they all have very limited ammunition and it's very easy to grab a new gun. The gadgets also give you a lot of opportunities to create chaos.

Stealth is essentially Hitman, but with the hacking of Watch Dogs. You can raise cover from the floor, distract enemies with radios from a distance, create smokescreens. Stealth is just one component of a much more action driven game, so you can't do anything like hide bodies or change disguises. You do get a very fun bluff system though and every time I used it there was some unique bit of dialogue which was appropriate for the section of the level I was in.

The game looks great. There's some graphical glitches I noticed with textures taking a while to load in, or level geometry disappearing due to some aggressive occlusion culling, but overall it looks and performs well on my rig. The cutscenes are all well directed and the performance capture is excellent. Some weird cameos but hey, it's James Bond. 

Speaking of being James Bond, don't go into this expecting a gritty Daniel Craig, Casino Royale style of Bond. This is much more inspired by older, goofier Bond movies. Bond himself is very well written. There's a lot of wit in his dialogue and he exudes charm. 

There's only a few sections which I thought were bad, one in particular was about mid-way through, where you're being interrorgated and you need to balance provoking and stalling your captor. As far as I can tell, there's only one correct sequence of "stalls" and "provokes" but the game doesn't really give you any hints. It was trial and error for me and I had to watch the sequence four times in total before guessing the right order. 

Overall though, this was an excellent game. I don't think I've played a game this much in such a short time period for a while now. It was really hard to put down, especially because the pacing was pretty much perfect the entire time. Really excellent game, can't wait for the next one.

All in all, game is not bad, but I thing "Very positive" and 70$ is too much.
In details:
- The game contains too much cutscenes and sections where you just go and listen for the exposition. I would say 60-70% of the game is not actually a game in this regard. And this content is not really necessary, can be easily cut in half.
- The story is okay. Not good or breathtaking, but also not really bad. Suits the modern Bond and that's just it.
- Melee combat feels clanky. Reaction of environment on your fight is pretty good and throwing guys over rails feels satisfying, but melee combat has zero evolution through the game. No new moves, no new enemies, no interesting combinations or arenas.
- Shooting gameplay is the best part, can be dynamic and good-looking, pushes you to rotate guns and can be switched to melee and back any moment, although it also doesn't have much evolution (just guys with more solid helmets appear), it is okay for one game due to visually interesting arenas.
- Gadgets balance is elegant. Limited resources  doesn't let you spam it, but it is pretty easy to restore them, so you don't afraid to actively play with new toys. Of course, some gadgets are more useful than others and balance is questionable, but still okay, it works.
- Stealth is cut bad. For some reason movement system is worse than in WoA trilogy, even if it use all the same base. No crouch-steal sprint and unintuitive cover system. Bluff and Fake surrender works good and balanced, but conventional stealth is a step back.
- Car scenes are not good. They are cinematic, but so linear and with so many auto helpers, you barely feel your participation.
- Characters have no-charisma. Bond might have 0.1 of it, but Moneypenny, M, your 00 buddies are mostly talking heads. Would be not a big deal in a context of video game, but as I said, most of the game is "pure cinema".
- Optimisation is okay. Game can maintain compromise 60FPS on 2k on High settings with RTX 4080 with dropping a little closer to the end. Graphics looks okay.

Almost every aspect is "okay" with obvious potential to make it really good. This game can get a feeling of "being Bond" and catch overall esthetics of 007 franchise, but take a turn to a completely linear experience, where you are the passive observer too often. I ran 007: Nightfire (2002) just for comparison and received a lot more dense experience, showing how short and straight to the point cutscenes could be, if you are making an actual game to play, not to watch. I hope IO will make conclusions and give a little bit more flavor to future releases.

007 First Light: The Ultimate Secret Agent Fantasy (9.5/10)

is hands down the best James Bond game ever made, and arguably one of the greatest stealth-action spy games in history. I completed all achievement requirements in 22 hours (though 6 of them are currently bugged—more on that below). It’s a near-perfect masterpiece that genuinely makes you feel like a Hollywood super-spy.

Here is my detailed breakdown:

Visuals & Optimization: Gorgeous, Smooth, and Alive
The Aesthetics: While it doesn’t quite hit the absolute technical peaks of Horizon Forbidden West or The Last of Us Part II in texture micro-details, the art direction, color palettes, and level designs are stunning. You will constantly find yourself slowing down just to soak in the atmosphere and explore every nook and cranny.

The Crowd Tech: The game achieves something truly spectacular—the sheer density of NPCs. Levels like nightclubs and museums feel packed and alive in a way we haven’t seen since Assassin's Creed Unity.

Performance: Impeccable optimization. At 1440p Max Settings with DLAA, I got a rock-solid 90–100 FPS. With Frame Generation on, it regularly cruised at 170–180 FPS. No stutters, no crashes—pure stability.

Narrative & Campaign: A Generous Origin Story
This is a brilliant 007 origin story. Bond here isn't brooding or miserable like Snake or Sam Fisher; he’s witty, charming, and charismatic—giving off major Nathan Drake vibes. All cutscenes use top-tier motion capture, making interactions feel natural and engaging.

Pacing: It starts a bit slow for the first few hours, but once it clicks, the stakes and action skyrocket.

Content Value: My first 100% collectible playthrough took 20 hours. The devs packed these 20 hours with pure sincerity across 17 chapters. Instead of reusing assets, almost every chapter introduces a massive, uniquely designed environment (the Vietnam resort late in the game blew me away).


ameplay: Hitman's DNA, But Masterfully Refined
As an IO Interactive title, the Hitman DNA is obvious, but they fixed the onboarding issues that casual players usually bounce off of. Levels flow beautifully through three distinct phases:

Intel Gathering (The Spy Phase): You blend into massive crowds, eavesdrop on conversations, steal key items, or disguise yourself to find a way inside. Unlike Hitman, the guidance here is smooth and intuitive, completely eliminating the frustration of "not knowing what to do."

Infiltration (The Stealth Phase): Classic stealth amplified by Bond gadgets. Your high-tech watch can hack cameras and laser-melt locks, while your phone can shoot distraction darts to make guards feel sick and leave their posts.

Action (The Combat Phase): Hand-to-hand combat is incredibly punchy and satisfying, built on a simple parry/evade system. When the guns inevitably come out, it transitions into a solid third-person cover shooter. Cover gets completely destroyed under fire, and ammo is scarce, forcing you to constantly move and scavenge weapons.

The chapters culminate in bombastic, cinematic set-pieces—car chases, glacier boat battles, mid-air skydiving—all blasting that iconic 007 theme. It’s an absolute adrenaline rush.


Achievement Hunting & Replayability (More than 20 Hours)
The Bugged Achievements: Currently, 6 achievements are glitched (4 for all collectibles, 1 for reaching TacSim Level 3, and the Final Platinum/Completion achievement). They don't pop naturally right now, though you can use SAM (Steam Achievement Manager) to unlock them manually if you've met the criteria, or wait for a patch.

Hunter Tips: Do not blind-play if you want 100%. The game doesn't track collectibles per chapter, so follow a guide (I highly recommend PowerPyx). The rest of the combat achievements are a breeze.

Merciful Design: The devs didn't tie achievements to the in-game level challenges, meaning you only need one single playthrough for the 100%.

Replay Value: Even after hitting full completion in 22 hours, I am immediately jumping into New Game+. Levels have 4 to 5 different routes to solve objectives, easily pushing the true lifespan of this game to 40+ hours.

Conclusion
Whether you are a die-hard James Bond fan or just someone who loves a phenomenal action-adventure game, Project 007 is a must-buy. It’s a 9.5/10 only because of personal preference regarding "emotional peak value," but objectively, the game is flawless. Even if you don't play it, watching a full playthrough movie-style is worth your time.

Highly recommended. Go buy it.

Having been a James Bond fan since I was a child, this game is fan`s dream come true I`ve watched all the movies countless times and played nearly all of the PS2 era games to death. There has been a serious drought of games for 007 in the last decade or so and I wasn`t sure if the transition to more modern gaming would be an easy task for IO Interactive but I`m happy to report that they have delivered and then some.

Coming off the heels of finishing the Hitman: World of Assassination trilogy, IO Interactive have tried to blend some of the social stealth elements from that game and the DNA definitely shows. Despite this they have managed to craft a unique Bond experience that plays to the strengths of the franchise while reinventing it all at the same time. Bond is no longer a “Cold-War dinosaur” as M once put it but a young and often reckless spy who always manages to pull through no matter the odds. I was a little skeptical in the first few missions with Bond having Gen Z pals but the writers managed to create a fantastic story full of highs and lows about on par or sometimes even exceeding the movies in terms of over the top, adrenaline fueled action.

Gameplay can feel on rails at times but I think this was necessary for the story to be conveyed effectively. If you are looking for Hitman-style large sandbox levels you might be a bit disappointed. Think of the levels more like Hitman: Absolution (but everything is actually good) in terms of scale. The combat feels impactful, you can almost feel the pain as you throw a guard over a table. The animation and sound design compliments everything and you can really sense the chaotic feel of every fight. IO Interactive have really done their homework on getting this part down to a tee.

My only real gripes are the lackluster driving segments as these are essentially on rails with you just pressing the accelerator while something cool happens in the background. The other problem is that there is not that much content for the tac-sim mode at this moment. I have heard that there will be more missions added (notably a set of driving missions) soon but we will see what happens.

Overall I would fully recommend this to anybody who has loved 007 over the years like me or anyone who just wants a good stealth action title to play over the weekend. The game just does almost everything smoothly while looking as cool as Bond himself.

007: First Light is exactly the kind of James Bond game we've been hoping for.

The storyline is strong and finally gives us a true James Bond origin story. More importantly, it feels like the beginning of something bigger. With the game's success, this appears poised to be the first entry in a trilogy, and after finishing it, I'm genuinely excited to see where the series goes next.

What impressed me most was how much respect the developers showed for the Bond franchise. This is classic James Bond through and through, filled with thoughtful nods to the films, novels, and previous games. In an era where many reboots seem determined to reinvent or disregard the source material, it's refreshing to see a developer honor the IP while still telling a new story.

If you've played the Hitman games, the inspiration is immediately obvious. That's not surprising considering they're made by the same developer. The result feels like a blend of Hitman and Uncharted. As others have noted, there isn't quite as much freedom in mission design as a traditional Hitman sandbox, but most missions still allow multiple approaches - typically stealth or loud - and the game is better for it.

The gameplay itself is consistently enjoyable. Missions mix stealth, puzzles, exploration, and action sequences in a way that keeps things feeling fresh. The melee combat is crisp and satisfying, and the gunplay feels equally polished.

One particularly innovative mechanic is the ability to bluff your way out of trouble using Bond's trademark charm. If a guard catches you somewhere suspicious, you're not always forced into an instant alarm state. Sometimes you can talk your way out of the situation. It's a simple idea, but it adds a lot to the experience and feels uniquely James Bond.

The gadgets are another highlight. They're clever nods to classic Bond films and games while also serving meaningful gameplay purposes. The laser watch, for example, can be used to cut locks open or temporarily blind enemies. These gadgets are integrated into both stealth and action gameplay and are genuinely fun to use.

Visually, the game delivers plenty of variety. You'll move between nightclubs, galas, tropical islands, snow-covered mountains, and elaborate villain lairs. Each location feels distinct and colorful, often paying tribute to iconic moments from Bond's history while still feeling fresh.

Technically, I had an excellent experience. I didn't encounter any bugs, glitches, or performance issues during my entire playthrough. The game feels well optimized and polished.

I finished the main story in roughly 20 hours on Normal difficulty. Players looking for more can easily push that to 30–35 hours by tackling the additional challenge content.

My only real criticism involves the vehicle sequences. They're largely cinematic set pieces with fairly basic mechanics and limited player freedom. They're still entertaining and fit the Bond fantasy, but they aren't nearly as deep as the rest of the gameplay.

If you're a James Bond fan, this is an easy recommendation and an instant buy. I'd also recommend it to anyone who enjoys well-crafted, single-player, story-driven games. There's no battle pass, no microtransaction nonsense, etc, just a complete, polished game. 

If your Steam backlog is already overflowing, waiting for a sale is perfectly reasonable. But if you're looking for a great Bond experience right now, I personally found it worth the $70. Supporting quality single-player games like this helps ensure we get more of them, and I'll be first in line when the sequel arrives.

Great Uncharted/Hitman/WatchDogs mashup. The missions are open levels but fairly linear, there is some replay value and the Tac Sim mode is great for additional fun on the side from the story levels. Most of the "Bond" stuff is there; crazy gadgets, extravagant locations and bombastic action sequences, although the music feels a little muted at times, or like the composer held themselves back.

James' life is saved by his female secret agent counterpart Isola Vale multiple times and she almost always gets the upper hand on him when they interact. He is just boring.
Of course, the game also ends with sequel bait and you do not get much closure.

[b]TLDR:[/b]
Overall, the game is a good interactive experience. It does not tell everything to the player which leaves some freedom of experimentation, it offers a little bit of replay value and different difficulty levels.
Don't go into it expecting good James Bond characters or story though.

[h2] Lingering is not something Bond is known for. And lingering is exactly what IO Interactive specializes in. [/h2] 

007 First Light isn't a half-bad spycraft experience per se, but it's definitely not a very good Bond experience either. It simply lacks the spontaneity and viscerality that usually entails a Bond IP.

Let me put it in terms of a Vesper Martini for better understanding: [i] it's three measures of protracted reconnaissance and chauffeuring, one measure of back-and-forth between tediously unstylish CQC and tepid gunplay, ½ measure of anticlimactic chases. Stirred, not shaken, with a large, thin slice of lemon peel for a plot. [/i] Now, although this concoction may come across as born of spite, in actuality, I might very well just be describing how spycraft in reality works under the guise of sardonic remarks.

But there lies my point: despite being the poster child of everything spycraft, James Bond is anything but lingering, as real-life espionage often is. Yet, the only real extravagance or spontaneity of a Bond IP this game delivers is at around 3-hour mark, when Bond hijacks a parachute midair after getting sucked out of an exploding plane (the exact segment in the gameplay trailer that made everyone and their grandmother fall for the game). Everything that comes after could easily be fed to a casual media enjoyer as, let's say, Ubisoft's newest stealth-action RPG, [i] Jim Bend 00ver: It's Your First Light [/i] —if not for the absolutely masterfully composed, iconic Bond score that kicks in during tense situations. Other than that, I absolutely loved the prologue—Against All Odds, along with the training montages. The music, as mentioned earlier, is absolutely stellar. Acting and dialogue delivery is another strong suit of this game. And last but not least, I've never seen such careful detailing put into NPC models in any other game.

Now to conclude this blistering passage, I will reiterate that this game is not by any means bad, nor is it an experience not worth having. It's just that, as a person who predominantly grew up on the Brosnan and Craig eras, the highest form of thrill I got out of this game was at the beginning, when M was standing a little too close to a slowly opening THEIA vault door, and I was losing my mind the whole time she spoke, fearing she was going to get crushed by the descending door! I might've giggled a bit too, at the thought of it. What can I say? I'm a silly Bond! Never felt so bad not recommending a game before; I wish Steam had a neutral option now more than ever.

I was able to get 45–90 FPS on a 1440p monitor with everything on Ultra, no Ray Tracing, with my rig. I ended up enabling DLSS Frame Generation (x2) to get a consistent 90 frames at least. [h1]The Highlights[/h1]
[list]
[*] [b]A Modern Bond:[/b] The shift to a younger, more reckless Bond is a masterstroke. Patrick Gibson’s portrayal feels grounded and gritty.
[*] [b]Visual Fidelity:[/b] The [b]Pirate King[/b] segment is the absolute standout, offering a stunning and mechanically deep playground.
[*] [b]The Gadgets:[/b] Using the classic watch laser and proximity mines to manipulate the environment feels incredibly satisfying.
[*] [b]Optimization:[/b] The game runs [u]flawlessly[/u]. No stuttering or frame drops—it's a rare, polished AAA launch.
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
If you’re looking for a cinematic action title that respects your time and your hardware, this is a must-play. IO has successfully modernized 007 for a new generation.

Hitman Absolution: 007 The Remake…
---

Short version:

The game is really OK. It does what it can to not be terrible. It could even be called good if you ignore its pedigree and throw away your expectations. If you look for reasons to like the game, you'll probably even find some.

I have to be honest and give the game a positive review, it does what a game should do and provide some hours of fun in a somewhat interesting storyline. I can even praise the voice acting quality, it's above average.

And that's where I should shut up, but I find myself unable to do so. If you don't care about comparing this to Hitman or classic James Bond; skip the rest of the review.
---

Long version:

I have to remind myself to judge things on their own merit, but I can't help but also mull through where things came from and how we got here. I've been watching Bond films since the 1970's and playing Hitman games since they started over a quarter of a century ago.

The first few Hitman games are considered classics for a reason, they really defined a genre and by the 4th one Blood Money, they were an iconic stand out. We had 6 good years from 2000 to 2006 with 4 great games in the franchise and it went dormant. Then came the corporate mergers and behind the scenes that redefined the developer (ioi) and jump to 2012 with the release of Hitman Absolution.

Absolution, under a new publisher (Square Enix) was the most cinematic, story focused, extensively voice acted and polished linear action game of the Hitman franchise up to that point. What it wasn't, was a good Hitman game. The story wasn't what fans wanted from the character, it didn't let you be a Hitman. It was an anti-hero story where your character used to be a hitman and now you're on some personal journey where you occasionally killed people.

Absolution was a good game, if you didn't want it to be a Hitman game. It was a bad game, if you were looking to be true to the Hitman franchise. Many people noted it could have been character-swapped into another franchise and it would have been fine.

Then came Hitman (2016) which eventually turned into a trilogy, which eventually got all merged into one game Hitman: World of Assassination. Why does any of this matter? Somewhere in those years ioi (the developer) becoming independent from Square Enix, losing the majority of the developers that worked on Hitman and growing into a massive corporation of its own (which now even publishes games for other developers) and taking on investors to grow who have demands of their own with the direction of where the company should go. And during that they get the rights to make a game with the 007 license.

What we had with Hitman WOA once the trilogy was complete was a return to the more Hitman feel of Blood Money, large sandbox set pieces, unlike Absolutions short linear pathways, while still keeping some of the cinema feel of Absolution. It has its flaws, but it is both a good game and a good Hitman game, something Absolution, wasn't.

One thing you could feel however was a strange Bond influence over the entire thing. You could already feel the influence of the company having the 007 brand. There's entire scenes that could be right at home in a James Bond film. So, maybe ioi is the right company to make a James Bond game?

And yet, the majority of developers who worked on Hitman over the previous years quit and went over to form their own company and; that's a story too long for this review. So who was left at ioi? Well, the head of the studio, several producers and management all of whom seem to have decided to use the pieces that they already had, hire 100's of new people and shovel out 007: First Light.

So what the hell did we end up with as a game?

Is it a Hitman game? No, but sort of. The story is not. You're not an assassin. But the world building tools are the same. It's the same engine they've been using since 2012. You can see the same assets, models and animations lifted directly from other missions of previous games. Does it matter? It probably shouldn't. But it can make it feel like you've been here before. You're walking through some of the same terrain, near some of the same buildings, with people doing the same idle animations that you may have seen many times in the  past Hitman games.

It it James Bond? Yes, but not the one you know. First off, throw away any expectations from the films. This isn't inspired by the movies, it's inspired by the books. Now for all you readers out there: throw away any expectations you have from the books, because this is only loosely inspired by the books and doesn't follow any specific book.

Instead it reimagines James Bond before joining mi6 and becomes the man you know. And realizing that is the key to getting any enjoyment from the story. Because that's the only unique part of the game that makes it stand out.

Graphically the game is borrowing the tool set from Hitman with set pieces that are on par with Absolution, linear and pushing you in the direction you need to be going. You can clearly see some models from WOA, you'll drive a boat that looks like it's from Sapienza and so on. Functionally you'll stealth or fight your way through trouble spots but you're mostly being shuffled from one cinematic moment to another with lots of banter.

And someone on that design team played Uncharted, because there's some Drake in the jungle vibes going on with the climbing and jumping where you can tell they wanted to make Bond a little less stoic than 47 is.

Bond looks the part of a young military man trying to come to terms with his new injuries, he gets the facial scar from the books that the movies never showed, while adjusting to being recruited into mi6. In contrast to the books and films where he's more mature, experienced and already earned his place as a spy.

And that's where we are. It's not a Hitman game, but it wasn't supposed to be. It's not Uncharted, but there's inspiration from it. And it is James Bond, just a new one.

Judge the game on its own merits: It's a reasonably fun action adventure that leans heavily on stealth that's been inspired by James Bond. The voice acting is good, the graphics are decent though not any better than Hitman (2016).

Beyond that, the main campaign is pretty linear and doesn't have much replay value. It's not big sandboxes, it's small set pieces. But it does offer TacSim mode that gives it some replay. In context it's a virtual training simulator that remixes the levels into challenges. Functionally these are identical to what escalations are in Hitman.

Additional notes: The timeline is modern, this isn't Bond in the past, it's now with a more diverse cast. The stealth can be wonky, some of the attacks look brutal and noisy but a guard two feet away facing the other direction won't hear you beating the snot out of his friend right next to him. Lack of blood in lethal kills can break immersion.

The biggest positives are a well presented story and Bond theme, the worst negatives are janky driving and melee combat with quick time event patterns.

This could have been game of the year 2012. It just feels like it's already a decade old and cobbled together with the bones of old Hitman games, the skin of James Bond ideas and the ghost of Uncharted lurking in the background. Or maybe I'm just old and cynical.

I don't often give number ratings, but this is a 7 out of 10. Maybe the company and the engine just come with too many years of baggage for me to judge it higher.
---

Bottom line: It's a James Bond stealth action adventure, if you can let go of the past and accept that it's a new version of Bond in a world that looks suspiciously like a Hitman remake without actually being one.
---

9/10 – A Strong Start for a New Bond Game

I've had a great time with 007 First Light. One of the things that stood out to me straight away was how easy the game is to get into. The controls are intuitive, the mechanics are explained well, and it doesn't take long before you're comfortable with everything the game has to offer.

The combat feels solid and well-balanced. Gunfights are fun, stealth is rewarding, and the gadgets add some variety without feeling overpowered. There are usually multiple ways to approach objectives, which helps keep missions interesting and makes you feel more like a spy rather than just running from one firefight to the next.

Visually, the game is impressive. The graphics are excellent, with detailed environments, strong character models, and great lighting throughout. Some scenes genuinely look cinematic, especially during story moments and larger set pieces.

The story does a good job of capturing the Bond atmosphere. It's engaging, has plenty of twists, and keeps you interested without becoming overly complicated. The characters are well-written, and the game strikes a nice balance between action, espionage, and storytelling.

What I appreciated most is how polished the overall experience feels. The pacing is good, missions offer enough variety, and the game rarely feels repetitive. While there are a few minor issues here and there, nothing really takes away from the experience.

Overall: 9/10

007 First Light is a fun, polished, and visually impressive Bond game that manages to be accessible for newcomers while still offering enough depth for experienced players. The combat is enjoyable, the story is engaging, and the presentation is top-notch. Definitely worth playing if you're a fan of action-adventure games or James Bond.
