[b]Minor spoilers for the story included in review.[/b]

[h1]Intro[/h1]
I'm not really a big fan of James Bond. Nothing against the character or spy theme, just never really got into it. I've seen very few movies, remember only one of them (Spectre), and I wasn't even really blown away by that one either. Also, this game costs $70. So I wasn't too interested when this was recently released. But then I heard that it was made by the same people behind the Hitman franchise (I really enjoyed Absolution), saw some clips of the gameplay and got too intrigued to pass up on it.

Safe to say I was not disappointed at all and I'm very glad I bought this. This game is amazing.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The combat, both melee and gunplay, is incredibly satisfying and fun. I think I actually found the guns more satisfying to shoot than the Hitman games I've played. I actually had so much trouble with the stealth (which is fun too), because I was just itching to start punching people, throw them into walls and just scrap with everybody. The destructible environments and contextual finishers (which can be pretty brutal) really make the melee combat super satisfying and tough to stay away from. James Bond is an absolute powerhouse in this game and some character dialogue even notes how almost scarily good he is.

The game gives you several gadgets throughout that you can use for combat or stealth, and they're all very fun to use. They give you even more variety and options to approach certain situations. I also really, really like the inclusion of the bluffing mechanic, where Bond just makes up something random on the spot to make an enemy turn a blind eye to you for a limited amount of time (even if there's a body on the ground).

Now, are there linear, scripted segments in the game which allow for far less variety (or none)? Yes, definitely. But the game makes up for it with its incredible environments, setpieces and scenarios. The dialogue between James and other characters make the slower, linear segments fun to experience as well.

This game isn't afraid to be a video game (much like something like Resident Evil 4) and it benefits from it greatly. There are some ridiculously fun setpieces and scenarios in this game. Are some (or most) of them unrealistic? Yes, sure. But the game isn't afraid to just go nuts and make exciting moments happen to make the Cinema really pop, and it's incredibly fun. I'm not looking for perfect realism or reasonability in video games. It's a spy game after all. It's realistic enough and doesn't go all the way 100% of the time, allowing some breathing room between the cinematic moments, so it doesn't get boring or tiresome. Same goes for the separation of stealth segments, where you can do as you please, and full on action segments where your only objective is kill everything in your way. Neither of those got boring for me because the game switches between them often.

Overall, the gameplay is incredibly fun, satisfying and engaging and I was never bored while playing.

[h1]Story / Characters[/h1]
The game is more story focused than the Hitman games I've played — I honestly couldn't tell you anything about the story from any Hitman game — and as such, the missions are way less sandbox-y and more linear than Hitman. But there's still a variety of approaches you can take in most missions that make the gameplay varied. But my main point is that I actually really like the story and characters, so the game being plot-focused didn't bother me at all. It's nothing mindblowing, but it actually has several twists and turns that surprised me. And even the stuff that was somewhat predictable was intriguing and engaging enough that I wasn't bored at all. As fun as the gameplay is, I enjoyed the story just as much.

James Bond in this game is a really likeable protagonist. He's reckless, endearing, heroic and quippy (which might or might not work for you, it did for me). He makes a few big mistakes throughout this game and is overly bold for his own good, at times requiring help from other people, but I like that as part of his origin story. I didn't expect Bond to be the full-fledged spy he is in the movies, and he isn't, and it's great. He's a brand new spy and it'd be boring if everything was effortless or a breeze for him, or if he was cool, calm and collected 100% of the time. However, despite his recklessness and the mistakes he sometimes makes, James is no pushover in this game's story, and his quick thinking and heart make up for his shortcomings. And I like all of the other characters too, I just wish some of them got more screentime. The ones who do get it, however, have a great dynamic with James and I had a great time watching him interact with them.

To share some of my favorite moments from James in this game would be too spoilery, so I'll reserve them, but my point is that I really liked playing as him and seeing his origin story unfold. Very intrigued to see how they're going to handle his growth in the (potential) sequel.

[h1]Criticisms[/h1]
Sometimes the dialogue does not match the subtitles. It didn't happen often to me, only a few specific lines, but either the line will not be 1:1 with what's being said (but have the same gist), or it will be completely different. This doesn't happen in cutscenes or very important dialogue, mostly just quick lines after combat or some minor NPC dialogue, but it's still a bit funny (and jarring) to see in a mainstream game.

I liked how the game handled pacing for the most part, but there are specific story bits that feel like they end a little bit too early or just don't get expanded on enough. Some cutscenes just fade out too early for my liking when I would've liked to see more, and it can sometimes come off handwavy (very few instances). This partly ties in to me wishing there was more content and that the game was longer (especially for $70).

For how many outfits this game has, they really should've included a customization for the story on subsequent playthroughs, sort of like an NG+ thing. You can only earn and equip specific story outfits in the arcade minigame mode, not in the story, which is a shame.

Sometimes, the dialogue of some characters reminds the player of the objective or backseats WAY too much, and this goes ESPECIALLY for James. Important to note, this isn't a criticism of James Bond as a character in this game, merely how the game handles hints. In several (not all) of the missions, James will speak out loud to tell the player about the objective or what they need to do. Sometimes you can't even listen to nearby NPC dialogue or stealth without James constantly telling the player that they need to do XYZ. It gets ridiculous in a few specific mission segments (including some combat ones too). This game has some stellar level design and in a few instances you can't even slow down to enjoy it without a character constantly nagging you about doing the objective. Could've been toned WAY down.

In melee combat, the camera can sometimes be very frustrating to control, especially when you're even slightly cornered or in close quarters. It didn't impact my ability to win fights too much, but it was still irritating at points.

And finally, this game has very little blood or bruising. I'm talking VERY little. eh

[h1]TLDR[/h1]
This game is great. While it has similarities and shares mechanics with the Hitman franchise by the same studio, to call this a "Hitman reskin" would be incredibly insulting, because there is much more to this game. The gameplay is incredibly fun, the story is engaging, James Bond is very likeable and fun to play as. Even with some of my criticisms and a few personal nitpicks not worth typing out, I am very, very glad I bought it and I really hope they make a sequel. Replayability isn't bad either, and the more arcade-esque mode is great if you're simply looking for gameplay without any story strings attached. 100% worth buying, even with its steep price.

This is a great James Bond game and, surprisingly, the first new Bond title in 13 years. For me, it ranks alongside GoldenEye (N64), Nightfire (PS2), and Everything or Nothing (PS2) as some of the best Bond games, while doing something very different with the formula. IO Interactive proves to be a perfect fit for the franchise, and their experience with Hitman is evident throughout.

The gameplay strikes a solid balance between espionage, stealth, and action, all supported by a cinematic story that feels genuinely film-quality. Fans will appreciate the various references to classic Bond films.

The level design and setpieces are standout highlights, clearly showcasing the craftsmanship also seen in Hitman: World of Assassination, with each location feeling distinct and memorable.

The combat loop is one of the game's biggest strengths. I found it fluid, engaging, and consistently moreish, thanks to the involvement of a developer well known for his work on the Batman: Arkham combat system. Unfortunately, the gunplay doesn't reach the same heights, feeling weightless and serviceable at best.

The soundtrack is tremendous, and I was pleasantly surprised to hear the iconic On Her Majesty's Secret Service theme, a fantastic callback that helps the game feel authentically Bond.

My biggest complaint is the excessive use of painted markers and environmental guidance. At times, the game even resorts to blatant "go here" arrows, which hurts immersion. I wasn’t a fan of the Q Lens either, though I understand this level of handholding is common in AAA games. Ideally, the painted markings could have been limited to the Q Lens or made optional.

I don’t enjoy the overly aggressive "modern audience" approach in any form of media, but this game manages to avoid that trap. While it has a modern feel, it respects the 007 IP and is far from the “woke” reinventions some might fear. Credit also goes to the cast, who do a stellar job bringing the characters to life.

Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed 007 First Light and look forward to what IO has planned next, especially with a potential trilogy on the horizon.

## Rating 5/5

Every few years, a game arrives that doesn’t just meet expectations but completely redefines what a licensed adaptation can achieve. 007 First Light is that game. Developer IO Interactive hasn't just built a phenomenal stealth-action experience; they have crafted the definitive James Bond simulator. It is a masterclass in how to fuse world-class technology with cinematic storytelling, resulting in an experience that makes you feel like you are genuinely becoming Bond rather than just controlling him.

## A Perfect Tapestry of Design & Tech

What elevates _First Light_ to legendary status is how flawlessly its core pillars are woven together into a single, breathtaking package:

* *The Graphics & Art Direction:* Powered by a heavily supercharged Glacier engine, the visuals are staggering. The contrast between global locations is beautifully handled. One moment you are soaking in the ultra-luxurious, reflective marble floors of a high-society European hotel, and the next you are lost in the atmospheric, densely packed, and vibrant neon-lit street markets. The character modeling—particularly Patrick Gibson’s brilliant portrayal of a younger, sharper James Bond—is strikingly lifelike, capturing every subtle facial tick and determined glare.

* *Immersive Gameplay & Physics:* Pulling from their unmatched stealth pedigree, the developers give you total player agency, but with a faster, more kinetic "Bond momentum." The physics engine plays a massive role here; every gadget, from Q-Branch's hacking tools to the laser-precision OMEGA Seamaster watch, interacts realistically with the environment. Throwing a smoke device forces guards to dynamically scatter and choke based on the room's geometry, while the crunchy, weighted hand-to-hand combat physics make every punch and environmental takedown feel immensely satisfying and grounded.

* *Meticulous Attention to Detail:* The game is a love letter to Ian Fleming’s original spy and decades of cinema. Hardcore fans will marvel at the extreme attention to detail—from the distinct literary vertical scar on Bond’s cheek to the tiny scratches on his retro 2006 Aston Martin. Even the way Bond casually adjusts his tuxedo cuffs after a brutal, chaotic fistfight screams pure, unadulterated 007 swagger.

* *A Cinematic, Sweeping Score:* The music is the final, gorgeous thread holding this masterpiece together. Composed beautifully by The Flight, the soundtrack masterfully balances tense, modern thriller beats during high-stakes infiltration with classic, swelling orchestral brass. When those iconic, traditional Bond chords subtly creep into the arrangement right as you successfully execute a perfect covert play, it delivers genuine goosebumps.

## The Verdict

_007 First Light_ is an breathtaking achievement. By perfectly balancing narrative freedom, cutting-edge technology, and a deep reverence for the source material, it easily takes the crown as the greatest spy game ever made. Whether you are a die-hard James Bond fan or just a lover of flawless game design, this is a mandatory, unforgettable experience.

IO Interactive, take a bow.

[b]007 First Light[/b] feels less like a routine licensed game and more like a confident reintroduction of Bond in interactive form. 007 First Light Review – The Best Bond Game in Years.

For years, James Bond games have struggled to truly capture what makes Bond special. Some focused too much on shooting, others felt like generic action games with a Bond skin. *007 First Light* finally understands the character and the world he belongs in.

This genuinely feels like stepping into a modern Bond film. The story is fantastic, filled with espionage, tension, stylish action, and memorable characters. Bond himself is incredibly well written here — confident, intelligent, charming, and human without losing that larger-than-life presence. Honestly, this might be one of the best portrayals of James Bond we’ve had in any form of media in years.

The supporting cast is also excellent. The villains are memorable, the allies are enjoyable, and the Bond girls are handled surprisingly well, actually feeling important to the story instead of just existing for style points.

Visually, the game is absolutely stunning. The environments, lighting, and cinematic presentation constantly make the game feel expensive and polished. Even on PC at 1080p, the game still looked fantastic. I played on mostly high-to-medium settings with DLSS set to Quality, and performance was excellent throughout. I had a locked 60 FPS with no frame drops, no stuttering, and no technical issues at all. Even without pushing ultra settings, the game still looked gorgeous.

One of the game’s biggest strengths is its focus on stealth and gadgets rather than nonstop shooting. Sneaking through areas, using Bond’s tools creatively, and thinking your way through missions feels incredibly satisfying. The gadgets actually matter here instead of feeling like gimmicks.

However, the game’s biggest weakness is definitely the combat difficulty. The stealth sections have tension, but the pure combat encounters are simply too easy. Enemy AI rarely feels threatening, and firefights lose intensity because of it. A tougher combat system could have elevated the entire experience.

My other issue is the Taxim mode. It’s a great idea with a lot of potential, but right now it feels underdeveloped. There are only two operations available, and after finishing them, there really isn’t much else to do. It feels like a foundation for something bigger that just needs more content.

Still, despite those issues, *007 First Light* absolutely succeeds as a Bond game. It understands the atmosphere, the style, the espionage, and the fantasy of being James Bond better than almost any game before it.

## Final Score: 8.5/10

I went into 007 First Light expecting something closer to HITMAN, and after finishing the game in about 11 hours, I can say that while you can definitely feel IO Interactive's DNA, this is not HITMAN with a James Bond skin.

The game does a great job capturing the Bond atmosphere. The locations are beautiful, the story is entertaining, and the gadgets are one of the highlights of the experience. There are several moments where the stealth gameplay and mission design remind you of HITMAN, and those sections were some of my favorite parts of the game.

However, if you're expecting the same level of freedom, sandbox gameplay, and replayability that made HITMAN special, you'll probably walk away disappointed. 007 First Light is much more linear and focused on delivering a cinematic story.

My biggest issue is the combat. It feels a bit too arcade-like and doesn't flow naturally. The stealth sections are generally more enjoyable, while the gunfights often feel less polished than the rest of the game. I found myself avoiding combat whenever possible because it simply wasn't as satisfying as the stealth gameplay.

Performance is another area worth discussing. The game looks great, but it is surprisingly demanding. You can really feel how heavy the game is on hardware. Looking at the official PC requirements and my own experience, it's clear that players with older or even some mid-range systems will need to make compromises. The game seems to be built primarily for relatively modern hardware, which may frustrate players who don't upgrade their PCs every generation.

My biggest criticism, though, is the value for money. I completed the game in roughly 11 hours, taking my time and enjoying the story. While those 11 hours were fun, I simply don't think the current price tag of around 110$ justifies the amount of content being offered. The quality is there, but the game ends just as it feels like it's getting started.

Overall, I enjoyed 007 First Light. It's a solid James Bond experience with great atmosphere, interesting gadgets, and some enjoyable stealth mechanics. But it's not the next HITMAN, the combat needs work, the hardware requirements are quite demanding, and the campaign feels too short for the asking price.

I recommend it, but only if you're a Bond fan or if you can get it on sale.

After almost seventeen hours, I finally finished this masterpiece.

My expectations weren't particularly high going in, mainly because I had seen quite a few "critics" trying to mock the game with rather cheap arguments, often focusing on minor issues like missing physics interactions here and there. After playing it myself, however, this game exceeded my expectations by a huge margin.

First of all, compared to the Hitman World of Assassination trilogy, this feels like a significant step forward for IO Interactive. The developers clearly experimented with many new ideas and mechanics, some of which will likely find their way into future Hitman titles.

Let's start with the protagonist. James Bond is charismatic, young, and full of personality. I know some people dislike the idea of a younger Bond, but I honestly think the actor's performance and the overall atmosphere of the game are absolutely top-notch. This version of Bond feels fresh while still capturing the spirit of the character.

The environments are another standout. Hitman's maps were already among the best in the industry, but the locations here feel even more detailed, alive, and immersive. Every area feels handcrafted, with an incredible amount of attention to detail.

The story kept me engaged from beginning to end. What made it work so well for me was how believable the characters and their emotions felt. You could genuinely feel their struggles, victories, fears, and motivations. The world felt alive, and the narrative never lost its momentum.

As a long-time IO Interactive fan who's been playing their games since Hitman: Codename 47, I've always bought their titles at full price. Not only because they've consistently delivered quality experiences, but also because I believe supporting an independent studio that continues to take creative risks is important.

One aspect that seems to divide opinion is the game's length, but I actually think it's perfect. A 15-20 hour campaign strikes a great balance. It's long enough to tell a compelling story, yet short enough that you'll happily revisit it a few years from now. Unlike some modern blockbusters that stretch their stories to 50+ hours, this game respects the player's time while still delivering a complete and memorable experience.

For me, this is easily one of the strongest games IO Interactive has ever made, and an excellent foundation for what I hope becomes a long-running James Bond series.

If you're an old-school Bond fan, a Hitman fan, or simply someone who enjoys story-driven action games, you're doing yourself a disservice by skipping this one.

9.5/10

P.S. It's honestly refreshing to play a game that feels complete on day one. No live-service nonsense, no endless checklist content, no padding, just a well-crafted single-player experience made by developers who clearly care about what they're creating.

The name's DARKER. Lucas DARKER.

 23 hours. Three shaken martinis. Countless bad decisions. One saved world.

 007 First Light is the closest I've come to feeling like Bond without risking a lawsuit, an international incident, or an awkward conversation with HR.

 What surprised me most is how natural it all feels. The action is great, the stealth is fun, and the story kept me invested the whole way through, but the charm is what really sells it. Bond doesn't just fight his way through problems—sometimes he smiles, says the right thing, and somehow walks away with both the information and a dinner date.

 What I loved most is that it understands the fantasy. You're not just a walking gun. You're a spy. Sometimes your greatest weapon is your brain. Sometimes it's your charm. Sometimes it's a watch that's definitely not approved by workplace safety regulations.

 I finished the story in 23 hours, and by the end I was genuinely disappointed there wasn't another mission waiting for me. The credits rolled and I felt like Bond at the end of a movie: slightly bruised, slightly smug, and already looking for the next adventure.

 Now if you'll excuse me, I'm off to introduce myself to strangers as "DARKER. Lucas DARKER." until security asks me to leave.

Highly recommended. Shaken, not stirred.

I am not a run and gun or combo/combo/combo fist fight kind of game player. I bought this game because of IOI and my love for the Hitman series as much as my love for 007 lore.

That said, there isn't a single element of this game I do not absolutely love - including the fighting and gunplay, which is just there enough to balance a great stealth and gadget-based exploration and puzzle game. In other words, this is everything a James Bond game should be. 

My other big concern was boss fights. I just finished one of the early ones and it felt so satisfying. It was EXACTLY how Bond would have done it (reminded me of a very particular fight in one of the movies) and it was EXACTLY as challenging/unique as I wanted it to be.

This isnt a stealth game. It isnt a car racing game. It isnt a fighting game. It isnt a first person shooter. It isnt a puzzle game. It isnt an exploration game. It is all of those things - done very well - in a single game.

And the story is amazing as well.

It’s anyone but James Bond. IOI, you let me down.

There isn’t even a “shaken, not stirred” martini in the entire game. There’s no driving an Aston Martin. Even the sidearm issued to Bond by Q Branch isn’t a PPK, but some generic tactical pistol, and then you want to tell me this is a 007 game? The game lacks Bond elements, but it certainly has plenty of random things like Khaby Lame easter egg in the Vietnam level. It’s just ridiculous. The whole time I felt like I was controlling a college student spy: first training, then team operations, then paired up with his mentor. He could be anyone, but he is absolutely not James Bond.

What I find mostly unacceptable is that Fleming’s Bond was educated at Eton, he has formal education at prestigious British boarding schools, the game starts with him serving in the Royal Navy, yet later Bond needs Q to instruct him through an earpiece how to tie a bow tie, with the player pressing certain keys step by step. What exactly are you testing me on here, my patience?

The game has serious problems with story structure. In Chapter 1 Bond can fight, stealth kill, climb walls and use ziplines, but starting from Chapter 2 it suddenly becomes a training camp and turns into over an hour of tutorial. Instead of story-driven missions, you’re playing capture the flag constantly in a simulated training facility, while other trainees watch from above. That completely destroys the pacing.

And the story is not fun enough. It’s the same few things over and over: crawling through pipes, walking through vents, eavesdropping, constantly using the watch gadget to activate devices. The content is highly repetitive. Some of the puzzles are vision tests, just checking whether you can spot a panel. The driving feels terrible. The plot is fairly shallow, a typical evil AI story just like how No Time to Die hid the Heracles nano virus inside the MI6 building, this game also lacks originality. 

I’m not saying you had to get Anthony Horowitz to write the story, but This one is not up to standard. There are too many plot holes, like Bond runs on a plane about to take off straight toward someone firing a machine gun at him, and got completely unscathed and uses the machine gun position to get into the plane; the entrance to a huge part of MI6 department is a coffee machine; Damien stabs Moneypenny but somehow does absolutely nothing to Bond who runs right past him; and he was poisoned twice in the game. There are very few genuinely good moments, though I did like the scene where Bond sits with Greenway and Greenway says “Don’t let it change you.” M’s voice acting isn’t good. I understand as the head of MI6 she is supposed to remain calm, but she sounds like reading a script with no emotion. Lennie James’s performance and voice work on the other hand, are excellent.

Some players may find the game fun, after all, every player is different, but don't forget this is James Bond, not just some random spy. I pre ordered the game because I really love James Bond, and I trusted IOI, I expected a game that matched the character. Instead, this game feels far too far removed from how I understand him. And don’t even get me started on the fact that you can’t change outfits in the singleplayer story. What was IOI thinking? I bought the deluxe edition skins just so I could look at them in the bedroom mirror?

The game also has a lot of bugs. I could walk straight off a platform and float in midair, and there was a door that wouldn’t open unless I reloaded a save. IOI really should have done more playtesting.

I finished the game on normal difficulty in 14.5 hours, deleted it immediately afterward, I probably will never touch it again. IOI really disappointed me this time. I grew up playing the Hitman games and loved them, I’ll keep buying Hitman games in the future, but this 007 title was a huge letdown. In my opinion, the best Bond game is still Blood Stone, the one Activision made many years ago.

Despite some shortcomings, 007 First Light is easily the best Bond game we've ever had. IO Interactive managed to deliver a remarkable and memorable James Bond experience and demonstrate very clearly that they're capable of more than just the Hitman franchise. I was admittedly a little skeptical of how an origin story would translate into quality gameplay, but the overall experience was quintessentially James Bond, even without his 00 status.

007 First Light is full of references and nods to past James Bond media, including the books, films, and games, but they never once feel too much, overbearing, or in-your-face. They're there in ways that make sense and each one brought a smile to my face. You do not need to be a James Bond enthusiast to appreciate and enjoy the game, but it definitely helps get more out of the experience.

The story is a semi-linear, narrative-driven one that does offer some freedom of approach. While it may not be the open sandbox that IO Interactive is known for, you do have a few different ways of completing objectives and navigating from one part of the level to the next, which is appreciated. Aside from specific key moments, it never really feels like the game is shoving you in a specific direction. The only issue I have with the story is that it starts to lose momentum during the last chapter and doesn't go out with the bang I was hoping for, which was disappointing.

Nearly every character, ranging from key figures to cameo appearances, are done well with excellent performances, and 007 First Light has some of my favorite people in any Bond media. While we'll never have anyone as good as Bernard Lee or Judi Dench, Priyanga Burford is an amazing M and I'm looking forward to seeing more of her in the next game.

The only issues I had with 007 First Light aside from the finale, is the overuse of recycled assets from Hitman: World of Assassination. It was sometimes hard to fully immerse in Bond's world when I kept seeing weapons, cars, and objects I recognized from the Hitman franchise. I understand it was probably done to save time and money using assets and resources they already had, but it hindered 007 First Light in establishing its own identity. Additionally, the driving sections left a lot to be desired; while it was, I believe, IO Interactive's first time doing driving segments, they did a good enough job. However, I just hope we have more car-related missions that are less "on rails" in the next game.

Either way, 007 First Light was a remarkable experience and, after 14 years since the last Bond game, need I say it was long overdue. I just hope they won't make us wait too long for the sequel.

007 First Light is perhaps the closest a game has ever come to making me feel like I’m starring in a Bond film. IO Interactive takes the stealth sandbox of Hitman, the intense thrills of Uncharted, and experimental spycraft of Batman: Arkham, and reshapes them into a globe-trotting cinematic spy thriller filled with covert missions, explosive action, and cool gadgets. While the immersiveness of the campaign occasionally lags, this stylish origin story still feels like a triumphant return for the most iconic secret agent.

When I heard IOI was building a Bond game, I was excited. Given their experience with the Hitman series, they were easily one of the best-suited studios to nail this type of game. And I'm glad to say they very much did. That being said, this is not going to appease someone who loves Hitman purely for the sandbox gameplay. 007 First Light is far more stripped-back and focuses heavily on its story and cinematic set-pieces. Still, it's a solid experience in a neat package with no unwanted surprises. I definitely recommend picking it up, whether at full price or later with a discount, and I look forward to the next iteration.

The narrative follows the origins of Bond and how he earned his legendary status. Instead of the manicured 007 we're used to seeing in the films, this version is young and more reckless, starting with MI6 recruiting him from the Royal Navy. You're initially introduced to a cast of very annoying, private-school-esque British spoilt brats, but thankfully, they disappear very quickly. Overall, the story is good and fun, though it hasn't changed the way I look at life or anything. It's not the greatest narrative I've ever seen, and the character deaths aren't the most impactful, but it serves the cinematic tone perfectly.

While I think the gameplay is generally solid, it is a bit of a mixed bag. On the positive side, the hand-to-hand melee is addictingly fun, and the gun mechanics are incredibly well thought out. Similar to Indiana Jones, you never have much ammo, which creates a great loop where you consistently have to steal enemy weapons on the fly.

However, I do think there needs to be more gadgets and a harsher punishment for taking the hard and loud approach. I kept nearly the exact same list of gadgets throughout my entire playthrough, only swapping one item at the end. There is no ability to upgrade them. Because there’s very little punishment for going loud, it's often easier to just shoot everyone in the room; stealth ends up feeling less like a rewarding spy tactic and more like an unnecessary time-sink.

As for performance, I played this game on a high-end PC with all settings on Ultra, DLAA, and frame generation enabled. I was sitting at a comfortable ~180fps with 1% lows dipping to around 100. The performance we saw in demos with framerates tanking to the 20s on the PS5 Pro thankfully did not come to fruition. It's not going to win any awards for cutting-edge visuals, but it's still undeniably pretty and doesn't suffer from the noisy visuals of many titles we've become accustomed to this generation.

As a life-long Bond fan, this is it. This is the perfect iteration of the super spy in interactive form.

IO has studied and emulated the flair and exotic thrill of the best James Bond films while bringing a brand new origin story to life. Patrick Gibson's performance as the British double-O is a real stand out among a crowd of great supporting characters. The world of James Bond is well represented in a young, modern context with beautiful locales, dangerous villains and mysterious women. Small nods and hints at previous Bond films, games and even the Hitman franchise are there to be found by eagle-eyed fans.

Bits and bobs of the Hitman franchise show through here making for frenetic combat that rewards improvisation as much as careful stealth. The multi-stage levels move the player through social engineering, shoot-outs, driving, platforming and cat-and-mouse stealth. The narrative keeps a good pace and the developers are eager to throw unique scenarios at players to keep things exciting. The final chapters especially pull out fresh ideas to keep the exhilaration high. A variety of level challenges and the optional TACSIM bring a good bit of replayability though don't expect anything as dense as the clockwork puzzles like Hitman's assassinations.

PC performance is excellent on Linux through Proton, another gold star for a great AAA title. Character models, texture work and environment design really bring this game to a movie-like quality. A few small animation and dialogue bugs popped up during my time along with one crash, nothing that should dissuade a purchase as patches roll out.

After one playthrough I am ready for more and eagerly anticipate more of this planned trilogy.

My childhood dream of finally getting a good 007 game has come true, at least partly. When I first heard about 007 First Light, I was genuinely excited and bought it at launch. As a huge fan of the Hitman series and Splinter Cell, and after how impressive the recent Hitman games have been, I expected something truly special.

Unfortunately, 007 First Light never fully lived up to that expectation.

**SPOILER WARNING**

To be fair, the game starts off very strong. The opening hours nail the Bond atmosphere, and the training sequence is fantastic. You immediately get a real sense of who Bond is supposed to be, and the hotel location from the previews is also excellent. For a while, it really feels like the Bond game fans have been waiting for.

But after that, the game starts to lose its identity.

Compared to Hitman, there is far less stealth depth and far less player freedom. I also have no wish to replay the missions. Most missions are extremely linear and often feel like narrow corridors disguised as larger levels. Even the more open sections give you only limited flexibility in the end. The game is much more of a third-person action-adventure than a true spy or stealth game.

That is also why the lack of core stealth mechanics bothered me so much. There are almost no meaningful systems involving surveillance cameras, counter-intelligence, or classic espionage gameplay. You cannot hide bodies, which immediately limits what you can do in stealth situations. Suppressed weapons only become available very late in the game and are barely relevant because the game constantly pushes you into large combat encounters anyway.

The AI is also extremely weak. Many stealth sections boil down to sneaking past a few guards before the game inevitably turns into another shooting gallery with dozens of enemies. These encounters become even less enjoyable when heavily armored opponents start appearing everywhere. Instead of carefully planning an infiltration, isolating targets, and managing risk, you usually end up fighting wave after wave of enemies.

The gadget design reinforces this problem. Instead of giving you tools for clever infiltration, most gadgets are offensive and action-focused. Smoke screens, micro rockets, and combat-oriented tools fit the game's direction, but they do little to support actual spy gameplay. Another thing I never expected to see in a Bond game were boss fights with extra armor and visible health bars. They felt completely out of place and made the game feel more like a generic action title.

There are still things I liked. The Bond-style one-liners and comments are very well done, and the exaggerated action sequences are easy to forgive because they are part of the franchise's DNA. The game also looks great, and some locations are genuinely memorable.

That said, I was hoping for something closer to Casino Royale: grounded, tense, and believable. Instead, the game often feels like it could have been a generic shooter with a Bond skin.

The "License to Kill" concept is also interesting, but in practice it does not add much. The system does not really discourage killing, instead it totally prevents shooting. As a result, many of the environmental interactions and distraction mechanics that make games like Hitman so interesting are missing. You can throw objects that are already in the environment, but you cannot collect and carry tools or items yourself. There are no situations where you find a screwdriver, or other item to unlock alternative approaches. The game rarely rewards creativity or experimentation.

In the end, 007 First Light is not a bad game. It is visually polished, stylish, and has plenty of Bond charm. However, it misses the grounded, intelligent spy gameplay that would have made it truly special. Instead of a true stealth sandbox, I got a heavily scripted action-adventure game with light stealth elements.

It's a solid game, but far from the masterpiece I was hoping for.

**Score: 6.5/10**

007 First Light is one of the most enjoyable action-adventure games I have played in recent years.

[h2]Stunning Graphics[/h2]

From the very beginning, I was impressed by the game's incredible visuals. Every location is beautifully detailed, and the graphics help bring the James Bond universe to life in a truly immersive way.

[h2]Smooth Controls and Great Combat Physics[/h2]

The controls feel responsive and intuitive, making every action satisfying to perform. The combat physics are another standout feature. Fights feel impactful and dynamic, adding realism and excitement to every encounter.

[h2]Excellent Stealth Gameplay[/h2]

Stealth plays a major role in the experience, and it is executed brilliantly. Sneaking through enemy areas, avoiding detection, and planning the perfect approach is both rewarding and fun.

[h2]A Wonderful Story[/h2]

The story is one of the game's greatest strengths. It captures the spirit of James Bond perfectly, with memorable characters, thrilling moments, and a narrative that kept me engaged from start to finish.

[h2]Multiple Ways to Complete Missions[/h2]

One thing I really appreciated was the freedom the game offers. Most objectives can be approached in different ways, allowing players to experiment and choose their preferred playstyle.

[h2]Pure Fun From Beginning to End[/h2]

Above all else, 007 First Light is simply fun to play. The combination of excellent gameplay, strong storytelling, stealth mechanics, combat, and visual presentation creates an unforgettable experience.

007 First Light – A Triumphant Return for James Bond in Video Games
After more than a decade without a proper James Bond game, 007 First Light feels like a long-awaited reunion with an old friend. And let me tell you — I absolutely loved every minute of it. From the opening moments to the final credits, this is the Bond game I’ve been craving for years.
The story stands out as one of the game’s biggest strengths. Instead of jumping straight into a super-experienced 007, we get to follow a young, rough-around-the-edges James Bond as he earns his double-O status. It’s a fresh origin tale that feels personal and grounded while still delivering the high-stakes espionage we expect. The narrative has real emotional weight, surprising twists, and some genuinely cinematic moments that rival the best Bond films.
The characters are fantastic across the board. Patrick Gibson brings a perfect mix of charm, recklessness, and vulnerability to a younger Bond. His dynamic with John Greenway (brilliantly played by Lennie James) feels like a true mentor-student relationship with real heart. Q, Moneypenny, and M all shine with strong personalities, and the villains are memorable and properly menacing. Every major character feels well-written and well-performed.
One of the things I loved most was the incredible variety of locations. The game takes you all over the world — from icy landscapes in Iceland, to sunny Malta for training, glamorous London nights, a sprawling Slovakian chateau, the deserts of Mauritania, the stunning beauty of Vietnam, and even the frozen expanse of Antarctica. Each location feels distinct, beautifully detailed, and perfect for the mix of stealth, action, and improvisation the game offers.
Mechanically, it’s a joy to play. The blend of Hitman-style sandbox freedom with proper James Bond gadgets, bluffing, and brutal close-quarters combat works incredibly well. It never feels repetitive, and the multiple ways to approach each mission kept me coming back.
Overall, 007 First Light is an absolute triumph. It’s refreshing, exciting, and respectful to the legacy while still feeling modern and bold. Playing a James Bond game again after so long reminded me exactly why this character has endured for decades. If you’re a fan of spy thrillers, stealth-action games, or just great storytelling, this one is a must-play.

The main story is called Earn The Number, but Bond is so slick that he doesn't need to earn anything; girls are dropping their phone numbers to him all the time.

If I hadn't played Hitman WOA before, I would think 007 First Light is a game from the developers of Watch Dogs Legion, and because of budget constraints, they had to get rid of the open-world. I liked both, but I never managed to finish Watch Dogs Legion, yet I finished 007 First Light in less than a week. If you like stealth, gadgets, and alternative routes via air vents, you'll like 007 First Light.

Since I have played Hitman WOA, 007 First Light felt very familiar to me, but at the same time, a huge improvement over Hitman WOA. It doesn't have all the Hitman features, most notably dragging bodies and using disguises, but it has many new things that Hitman doesn't. The biggest improvement, in my opinion, is the presentation; each mission fluidly continues into another, which seems to be all done with in-game cutscenes. It feels very much like Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, but with even smoother story transitions.

Another notable improvement is the incredible look of the main characters. Environment-aware melee combat is very easy to understand, yet challenging to master. Gunplay felt a lot like Max Payne 3, which means you have a limited amount of ammo and you need to keep moving to keep shooting - you can't just cover-shoot yourself out of a sticky situation. Just like Max Payne 3, you have slo-mo focus, which you earn for taking out enemies.

Great game!
I was worried that it will be a movie on rails or Hitman clone, but we've got an actual, original experience matching the 007 fantasy.
Missions are concentrated around: solving problems on open map (usually with people and sneaking), logic puzzles (rather simple) and fighting - both meele and with firearms.

Some maps are indeed hitman-like, you go to an open map and look for opportunities to achieve your goal. Flow is often more linear however as closed sections are blended seamlesly. There are many gadgets and ways to achieve an objective and you usually have to be creative. What is cool if you screw up and alert enemies, you can "handle them" before they call reinforcenments and contain the situations.

Puzzles are rather simple, often connected to "climb a color coded ledge/pipe" and use a gadget in a clever way. They are not bad, they are not very challenging either.

Probably the most controversial is fighting. You can clearly see that the main objectives of the creators was to make it exciting over actually making sense - which is actually faithful to 007's movies and books. There is a lot of interactions with environment, you can shoot something that will fall down on enemies, throw them over the ledge, when you run out of ammo (which happens quite often) you can just slam enemy with your gun in their face. Gadgets help, there is a lot of weapons, everything looks great and blows up. AI is not great however. They will try to take cover and flank you, but when they cannot reach you easily they will just walk towards you in a nice queue so you can headshot them easily. Sometimes I found it was better to charge 4 men with rifles and beat them with fists than try to shoot them - they go into a 80's action movie mode and fight you one at a time. Again, exciting and faithful, but not sometimes feels weird.

Game includes a lot of zones where you drive a motorboat, giant truck or solve some problem in a scenic, explosive way.

Main thing that positively suprised me was a roster of characters. This is young Bond, before achieving his 00 status and he is not yet the bitter loner we know. We are very often acompanied by other people, either in world or at least as a voice in the headset. Characters are build in an interesting way, with their unique identities, quirks and role in the story. Probably one of the stronger parts of the game. This includes enemies - while not very original - crazy power hungry Bond villains, they match the story and feel in place. While mostly crazy, they have clear motivations, not just doing evil for the sake of being evil.
Of course some of the characters are beautiful sexy ladies who inevitably fall for Bond sooner or later. As we all know, scientific conferences are full of sunbathing supermodel doctors who explain their mysterious experiments in a swimsuit. 

Story itself is well.. a Bond story. It is quite clear who the hidden villain is and that they will want to take over the world, but they were able to introduce some plot twists and keep me invested. Again, it was driven mostly by great characters, not the story itself.

Technically, game runs smoothly, no loading between maps with impressive transitions that made me feel it was a movie. 

While not perfect, it is one of the strongest titles released recently.

Very few games truly immerse you in the role of an iconic character, but 007 First Light excels at this. The game feels less like a typical action title and more like an interactive James Bond movie. Each set piece, high-speed chase, exotic location, and sharp line of dialogue captures that unmistakable Bond energy. It reflects the spirit of the franchise in an authentic, cinematic, and genuinely exciting way. 

I was most surprised by how much the game reminded me of my first experiences with Uncharted or even Half-Life. There’s a continuous sense of momentum and immersion that keeps pulling you forward. The pacing is exceptionally well done, mixing stealth, action, espionage, and storytelling into one smooth experience. The game knows when to slow down for tension and when to unleash pure spectacle. It consistently makes you feel part of something massive and rarely loses that momentum. 

Visually, 007 First Light is stunning. IO Interactive has crafted some of the most beautiful environments I’ve seen in a narrative-driven action game in years. Whether you are sneaking through luxurious casinos, infiltrating high-tech facilities, or escaping through chaotic war zones, every location is rich with detail and atmosphere. The lighting, facial animations, reflections, and environmental design combine to create a world that feels incredibly alive. The presentation has a consistently movie-like quality. 

The cast deserves high praise as well. The performances are excellent and enhance the overall experience. The writing gives characters genuine personality, and the actors deliver performances that make the relationships, betrayals, and tension feel real. Bond himself is charismatic, confident, and dangerous without being a mere imitation of past portrayals. The supporting cast brings just as much energy, making the story feel like a true blockbuster spy thriller. 

Of course, no Bond game would be complete without gadgets, and 007 First Light delivers in that area. Using Bond’s tools during missions genuinely makes you feel like the world’s greatest spy. Whether you are hacking security systems, distracting guards, using hidden tech to access restricted areas, or turning enemy gadgets against them, the gameplay reinforces the Bond fantasy. The gadgets are not just gimmicks; they are seamlessly integrated into the gameplay, enhancing the cleverness and style of the missions. 

However, the game is not without flaws. One of the biggest letdowns is how linear the overall mission structure can feel, especially considering IO Interactive's work on the open-ended Hitman series. In Hitman, players have significant freedom to approach objectives creatively, but 007 First Light often guides players down a more scripted path. While this structure benefits the cinematic pacing, there are moments when you long for more experimentation and player choice in missions. 

Hand-to-hand combat can also be frustrating, especially when facing multiple enemies. While the animations look impressive, the combat sometimes feels clunky and overwhelming under pressure. Encounters that should feel smooth and empowering can become awkward due to camera issues or enemies crowding the player too aggressively. 

Another problem is the game’s restriction on gun usage during specific sequences. There are moments when you want to go full action hero and shoot your way through enemies, but the game limits this until you reach designated “License to Kill” combat sections. While this design decision helps maintain Bond's stealth-and-spy identity, it can sometimes feel restrictive for players wanting more freedom in how they approach situations. 

Despite these shortcomings, 007 First Light is still an exceptional narrative-driven action game deserving immense praise. It accomplishes what many modern games struggle with: providing a focused, cinematic experience that feels handcrafted from start to finish. It is thrilling, stylish, visually stunning, and filled with memorable moments that truly make you feel like James Bond. Hopefully, the success of 007 First Light inspires more developers to create these types of cinematic, movie-like single-player experiences again. Games like this remind us how special narrative-driven action adventures can be when done well.

The Definitive Spy Experience of the Decade (8.5/10)
If you’re expecting a Hitman clone with a James Bond skin, you’ll be pleasantly surprised. IO Interactive has successfully taken their masterful stealth-sandbox DNA and fused it with the high-octane, cinematic pacing of a linear action game. The result is a gorgeous, respectful, and incredibly fun 007 origin story that actually encourages you to improvise when your master plan inevitably falls apart.

Instead of playing as an untouchable, polished super-spy, you play a reckless, raw, and cocky young Bond. It borrows Daniel Craig's physical brutality, Roger Moore's charm, and Timothy Dalton's cold edge, wrapped up in a substantial 20-hour global campaign.

🟢 The Good
Dynamic Gameplay Loop: The game drops you into massive, open-ended sandboxes (luxury hotels, hidden fortresses) where you can gather intel, pick your infiltration routes, and deploy classic spy gadgets.

Failsafe Action: Unlike Hitman, where being spotted means reloading a save, First Light shines when things go wrong. The gunplay is punchy, featuring an "Instinct" slow-mo mechanic for headshots, and the hand-to-hand combat handles chaotic brawls beautifully.

Unbelievable Atmosphere: From a stunning three-hour prologue training sequence to a full, stylized cinematic opening credits sequence (featuring an incredible, slow-burning original track by Lana Del Rey), this game nails the 007 vibe perfectly.

Deep Lore & Variety: The campaign keeps the pacing fast, shifting you across highly distinct global locales before any single environment or mechanic starts to feel repetitive.

🔴 The Bad
Identity Crisis: The transition between wide-open, player-driven stealth sandboxes and heavily scripted, linear action set-pieces can feel jarring at times.

Narrative Padding: While the story is high-stakes and engaging, stretching a cinematic spy plot over a 20-hour campaign results in some pacing dips and repetitive NPC dialogue in the middle chapters.

Clunky Melee: While the rhythm-based parrying and finishing moves look great, the physical hand-to-hand combat can occasionally feel a bit loose and messy during tight indoor skirmishes.

💻 PC Performance & Optimization
Running on IO's Glacier Engine, the game looks spectacular. The lighting, reflections, and dense crowd physics make the environments feel genuinely alive.

However, it is a resource-heavy title. While the stealth segments run incredibly smooth, the explosive action set-pieces will cause frame rates to dip on mid-range hardware. If you are targeting a stable 60+ FPS at 1440p or 4K, expect to rely heavily on DLSS or FSR upscaling to keep things buttery smooth.

Final Verdict
007 First Light is a gorgeous love letter to the franchise. It successfully delivers a rich, player-driven espionage playground that easily crowns itself the best James Bond game in over two decades. If you love stealth, cinematic action, or just want to feel like a lethal secret agent, this is a must-buy.

Overall I do believe this is a very solid game, and I've enjoyed my time with it so far very much. Giving it a number, I'd say 8.5 out of 10. IO have crafted something with a lot of Hitman's DNA but that is strongly borne of Uncharted as well. The levels aren't quite so one-path-only as Uncharted, as you do have several paths or means by which you can progress an area (different physical routes, violence vs stealth vs bluffing, etc) but you can't often abuse one more than the others, due to resource constraints both with your tech and your ability to socially influence others via bluffing or confronting. It isn't as super-wide open ended as your most recent Hitman titles - which is to be fair, I think, because IO wants to tell a specific story, and at that I think it greatly excels.

The character models are very well designed (to the point that if my eyes don't deceive me, Bond's hair jostles in real time as you walk around which I found to be a welcome bit of attention to detail), the motion capture for both facial expressions and body movements are smooth and seamless during anything resembling a cutscene, and controls are fluid and consistent throughout the experience. 

As for the story, you can make or break a story's quality just by the performances of the characters involved - and I'm pleased to say that in my opinion, First Light has a fantastic array of characters, almost without any exception. The initial cast you meet after the tutorial, M and Q, your handler, the side characters, the big bad and co., I found that I enjoyed just talking with everyone I got a chance to. It's succinct and condensed enough dialogue that it doesn't drag down the story's pacing with exposition but the dialog that IS there is nuanced and very much makes cutscenes and dialogue in this game feel like... well, like you're watching a Bond movie, that you find you kinda dig, y'know? Uncharted tries to be an action flick, and this game tries to be a Bond movie and I think they nailed it.

Aside from the main story, there are also 'simulations' that you can partake in to attempt bits of some levels with specific modifiers, like not being able to pick up enemy weapons and thus having almost no ammo, not having core kit components to make yourself more resourceful, etc, as well as challenges that you will find yourself completing (a handful of most likely at any rate) in the main campaign missions that require you take specific approaches or actions, which really really helps with the replayability.

All of that being said, there is a bit of graphical inconsistency with the environments in terms of lighting, specifically. More than once by turning the camera I'd get light shining in sections of the environment that should not have any light (like a sunbeam coming through a window over your shoulder, and then turning around to find a big shelf in front of it that correctly blocks light when it's observed, but doesn't when it's not). I also found in one instance a bit of the floor texture glitched inside a building and I could see through it, which considering it was quite a ways up was admittedly a bit amusing, but even still.

This game also crashed on me running at Ultra settings I believe on four occasions, and none of them were related to one another in terms of how long I'd spent playing, cutscene vs no cutscene, etc. All in all, the game is very well crafted but alas no game ships perfect out of the box these days, and this one is no exception. To be clear - this isn't, like, Cyberpunk-at-launch levels of jank, not even close - but if you keep your eyes open you will notice the odd bit of graphical inconsistency from time to time.

If I had to rate this game, I'd probably give it an 8.5 out of 10. The setting, the characters, the stakes, and the gameplay all work together really well to make this title a very cohesive experience, and I found it effortless to just keep going to see where the story would take me next. It was occasionally marred by the odd graphical glitch, and the handful of crashes when they did occur were pretty annoying I'm ngl, but I'm not too proud to admit that some of the puzzles initially seemed like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because I was too smoothbrain to realize what I could do with the kit I had available (forgetting you can vault over stuff b/c in a lot of games cover is only cover is a repeat offense of mine). 

TLDR, if you liked Uncharted and/or you enjoy Hitman, pick this game up, particularly if it ever finds itself on sale. I almost never buy games on release but this has been a thoroughly enjoyable experience.

** Strongly Recommended**

I really enjoyed *007 First Light*. The game was polished, top-tier in presentation, and I ran into minimal bugs. I enjoyed pretty much every second of it, and honestly, the fact that I wanted more by the end is a good sign. It did not overstay its welcome, and I would rather finish a game wanting more than feel like it dragged itself out just to justify the price.

I beat the game in about 17.9 hours, and that was with me taking a stealth approach whenever I could. While I originally thought the campaign could have been longer, thinking back on it, the pacing actually worked really well for the kind of experience the game was going for. It felt focused, polished, and intentional rather than stretched out for the sake of adding more hours.

The gameplay itself was excellent. I think IO Interactive found a really strong balance here. It has just enough of that flexible, thoughtful design philosophy you would expect from the studio, but it still feels like its own Bond game rather than *Hitman* in a Bond skin. The cinematic pacing, stealth, action, and overall mission flow all worked extremely well for me. Looking back, I actually think the gameplay formula was pretty much perfect for what this game was trying to be.

Story-wise, I wanted deeper storytelling for each character. The cast had a lot of potential, but I would have liked more time with some of the most interesting and likable characters before the story moved on from them. Some of these characters were so well-designed that I really wish they could have made it into a sequel. There was room to build them further, maybe even with scenes or smaller segments from their perspectives. That could have opened the door for stronger character development and emotional weight, similar to what games like *The Last of Us* achieved with Joel and Ellie — or potentially even better in its own Bond-style way.

I especially wanted to see more of the MI6 cast. That team dynamic is part of what gives Bond its identity, and I think the game could have spent more time building those relationships. M, Q, Moneypenny, and the rest of the team should feel like a real part of Bond’s world, not just characters who appear when the plot needs them. Imagine future games where we get short sections or missions from the perspective of some of these amazing characters, with each one playing completely differently. Their fighting style, aim, movement, gadgets, and overall approach could feel unique, giving the story more variety while also making the world and characters feel deeper.

Overall, I strongly recommend *007 First Light*. It is polished, fun, cinematic, and a strong foundation for a modern Bond game series. For a first entry, IO Interactive got a lot right. I just hope a sequel gives us deeper character writing, more time with the MI6 cast, and lets some of these relationships breathe a little more.

My only real gameplay nitpick is that, at times, the structure did feel a little **PS2-era linear**. There were moments where it felt like “go here, do this, move through the hallway, trigger the next section.” It never ruined the experience for me, but I do think future entries could keep the same cinematic Bond formula while giving certain areas just a little more room to breathe. Adding RPG elements like skills other than the watch would also be awesome. Fighting is good, but lock on and off with R3 should be a thing. Sometimes bond does this thing where he wants to touch everything he's around even in bad/tense situations where he should be a bit more locked in. 

For me, this is a very strong **8/10** — and with even deeper storytelling, stronger character development, and slightly wider mission flow in the future, IO could easily turn this formula into a **10/10 Bond experience**.

really good in some areas, maybe a little lopsided but rarely lacking in others. this is perhaps the best 007 game that's ever been made. it's like playing through the first season of a 007 show, and i mean that in a good way. this feels a lot like 007, and a fair bit of its own thing, because we've never seen this story done before for James Bond. 

there are largely 3 types of gameplay that occur throughout: traditional / social stealth, nonlethal combat, and lethal combat with guns out. I actually think the game is at its best in the lighter social stealth areas, and the lethal combat sections. it's a brawler in the nonlethal areas, which is a bit restrictive, and can get repetitive with how few actions there actually are to combat. sure you can use gadgets but it's not quite on the level of the arkham games or anything. it still manages to be very stylish with its combat with how interactive and destructive the environments are. when you are allowed to use guns, some of the sections are a blast, others feel a little underwhelming. if you actually use your full arsenal in the lethal sections, you really feel like a proper 00 agent. this is why I feel that the nonlethal sections are not as good, less opportunity to use some of the gadgets, environment, and guns.

the social stealth is well executed, being able to bluff your way through areas without watchers is nice, and can provide a welcome safety net to getting caught. the more strict stealth sections can be kind of annoying, particularly because of the vagueness of what will and won't get you caught. you have to experiment and come to understand what distance someone's going to see or hear you take out certain guards. some areas feel restrictive in the expression of how you advance through them, others are fairly open if you embrace using the tools at your disposal. Even if you do get caught, it just means more brawling for you. if there were more nonlethal options to take out enemies in open combat, it would be on par with the lethal combat.

the story overall is about par for a 007 story. it feels a little average in quality. the revelations and twists aren't especially great (serviceable for a 007 story), but do have some novelty to them with the subject matter, which I won't spoil. really, the writing pulls in both directions of quality. some dialogue feels really triple A slop / marvel (THINK JAMES! THINK!), and sometimes it manages to be fairly clever, and make the characters more likable. 

Largely bug-free, at least for stuff that matters. Never had a game crash, performed great, no game breaking bugs.

it can be a mixed bag at times, but a pretty fun one with some real high points. I'm definitely excited to see upcoming content, and the sequel(s) for this.

Honestly I thought it was fantastic. Definitely a lot more linear than I was expecting, but both the action and subtle parts of the game were done wonderfully, and it was just so cool, as a Bond fan to be able to finally play a modern Bond video game. I did think the final 5-ish hours dragged. Definitely way too much nonstop shooting, mostly because the third person shooting mechanics aren't great. But the other 15 hours were pretty fun. In particular, I LOVED the opening 3-ish missions, as well as the Vietnam mission and the Webb Gala mission. The rest of the missions were okay, but those were my personal standouts.

I will say though, all the people detracting it for not being "like Hitman" are kinda odd to me? I have hundreds of hours in Hitman WOA, and I love that game (as well as the originals), but I think it's really important to look at this as something *separate.* Just because IOI made it, doesn't necessarily mean it's going to be exactly like Hitman. Like, if IOI wanted to make another Hitman game, they would just do that. They wouldn't make another and reskin it as James Bond. To be honest, if they did that, I think that would feel pretty cheap. This is its own thing. Sure, they've DEFINITELY reused some mechanics from previous Hitman games (who would blame them?) but it is NOT a Hitman game. 

If you want this game to be a Hitman reskin, then this won't be for you. But if you're a fan of Bond (and spy movies in general) then this is for you. 

For an apt comparison, I've heard people say it's closer to Uncharted -- and I do agree. In particular, this reminded me a lot of Uncharted 4. Very streamlined action setpieces with more open, calmer areas in between. And while the game was streamlined, it never really felt like I was being "railroaded." The devs did an amazing job of allowing me to notice where I had to go, even when I was running at full sprint through gunfire. Actually incredible level design.

The Tactical Simulations and Challenges (paired with the post-game level selector) allow *some* semblance of replayability / "new game plus" but again, THIS IS NOT HITMAN. You are not going to be wandering through every level dozens (or hundreds) of times mastering a perfect run. Think of this as more akin to DOOM 2016, where every level has a few branching paths, easter eggs, and collectibles that you need to replay the levels to collect. That's basically it. TacSim is a little more complicated, basically a bare-bones new game plus mode with "escalations" where you complete different challenges in levels you've already played at different levels of difficulty, with tech / strategies you've worked out later in the game. 

Lastly, performance was okay but it definitely chugged quite a bit when there was a lot of particles / smoke on the screen. I was able to generally maintain a steady 60, but it routinely dropped closer to 45 or 50 through the heavy action parts.

I grew up loving James Bond. I've watched so many 007 movies that I know some scenes by heart. The classics had that secret-agent elegance that the more recent films, heavily inspired by Bourne, moved away from. Especially in the fight scenes. Bond was still elegant, but far more action-focused. This game takes that action-packed approach and runs with it.

It feels like you're playing a 007 blockbuster movie. Not quite James Bond as we know him, but the Bond he's slowly becoming. The story is good, but I feel like it lacks a bit of emotional weight and punch. For a spy game, there aren't many memorable twists, or at least none that left me genuinely surprised. Still, it's a solid story with a clear beginning, middle, and end.

Gameplay-wise, the game is fun and delivers the action you're expecting. I've seen people compare the combat to the Arkham games, but honestly, it feels much closer to Uncharted. That's probably the best comparison I can make having played all of them. It has a lot of the same DNA, with a small pinch of Watch Dogs thrown in. It's entertaining, though not as stealth-focused as I would've liked.

The levels are interactive to a point. If you're expecting Hitman-style sandbox design, you'll be disappointed. Some missions offer a little freedom, but this is first and foremost a linear single-player game. Most of the time you're on rails. Occasionally you'll get different ways to approach an objective, but they're usually minor variations rather than meaningful player choice.

A lot of people have talked about the new social mechanics and interactions. Honestly, they're pretty underwhelming. "Lackluster" is probably the best word for them. Most of the time you're just pressing a button to apologize, persuade someone, or get a few seconds to look around unnoticed. It's a neat idea, but it never feels particularly deep.

The gadgets are fun and allow for some experimentation. Since the environments are somewhat interactive, you can create a few memorable moments with them. However, they feel limited. You can only bring a couple of gadgets per mission, and while you eventually unlock another slot, you're still constantly looking around to recharge them. It's a cool concept, but I think the execution could've been better.

Now, you can't say "spy" without talking about stealth. Unfortunately, stealth here is very basic. You can sneak around, quietly take enemies down, and occasionally use the environment against them in ways that feel a very Hitman-inspired. Beyond that, there isn't much depth. If combat breaks out, only nearby enemies seem to care. Even when reinforcements are called, it rarely, if ever, escalates into a level-wide alarm. You can finish a firefight and immediately return to stealth as if nothing happened. Sound barely matters either. You can cause an explosion and enemies in the next room won't react. It disappointed me, but this is clearly an action game first and a stealth game second. With that said, combat is easy and very forgiving, I will be playing on the hardest difficulty later to see if it gets better.

There are collectibles to find, challenges to complete, and a tactical simulator that lets you compete for high scores. Right now, though, it feels somewhat limited. I'd love to see something similar to Hitman's Contracts mode or Freelancer, added in the future. The developers have said they'll expand the simulator over time, so I'll wait and see. For now, I'll play what's there and try to have fun.

As for the price, I've seen a lot of people asking whether it's worth buying at full price. The answer depends on what you're looking for. It's a complete narrative experience with a good story and enjoyable gameplay, but replayability just isn't there. Personally, I wouldn't say it's worth full price (not the 70 USD at least, thanks regional pricing), but it's still a great game. I finished it in 16 hours, at my own pace while exploring every nook and cranny. It could have been an even better game if it gave players more freedom and creativity, which in turn would've added more reasons to come back and try stuff out.

Overall, I liked it. As a 007 fan, it's a treat. Buy it if you enjoy high-action cinematic thrillers. Don't buy it if you're looking for something that'll keep you busy for hundreds of hours. At least not right now.

I expected something closer to a Hitman-style 007 game. It isn't that. Actually, they stripped many mechanics that they had in those games that gave you freedom. 

This is a fantastic James Bond game. The story, gadgets, dialogue, and overall presentation all feel exactly like a proper 007 adventure. The thing is, by building the game around Bond as a character, you're naturally limiting player freedom. The story and moral framework mean you can't just do whatever you want. This is a on rails experience. 

If you're expecting Hitman, don't expect to freely change disguises, take out anyone you want, or switch between going in guns blazing and stealth whenever you feel like it. The game is much more structured and narrative-driven. This is also a very easy game, with barely any challenge when it comes to stealth.

That said, IO improved the engine in a lot of ways, and holy moly, the driving sections were incredible. I honestly wish there were more of them because they were some of my favorite parts of the game.

2. Arsenal. If you want something where you just go guns blazing on everyone and nobody can stop you - play doom or uncharted. I’m only four hours into 007 First Light (currently on Mission 4: "The Past Never Dies"), and I can already say this is one of the best games I’ve played in years.  IO Interactive has managed to capture the essence of James Bond in a way that feels both fresh and nostalgically classic. 

The gameplay is incredibly compelling.  The seamless blend of stealth, social engineering, and chaotic combat makes every encounter feel like a scene from a movie. Whether I’m bluffing my way past guards, using gadgets to create distractions, or throwing an empty pistol at an enemy’s head before tackling them, the mechanics encourage improvisation and make me feel like a true spy. The "License to Kill" mechanic adds tension, forcing you to think before you shoot, while the melee combat feels visceral and impactful. 

The story has me completely hooked. Playing as a younger, less experienced Bond adds a layer of vulnerability and growth that is fascinating to watch.  The narrative moves at a breakneck pace, taking me from the streets of London to the black markets of Aleph, with twists and turns that keep me guessing. The mission structure strikes a perfect balance between linear set-pieces and open-ended sandbox exploration. 

But what really stands out are the characters.  The dynamic between Bond and his mentor, John Greenway, is fantastic—gruff, antagonistic, yet deeply human.  Supporting characters like M and Moneypenny feel authentic and well-written, adding emotional weight to the spy drama.  Even the villains, like the imposing Bawma in Mission 4, leave a strong impression. 

This game has successfully brought back the kid in me—the one who dreamed of being James Bond, complete with gadgets, fast cars, and narrow escapes. If you’re a fan of the franchise or just love a well-crafted action-adventure, 007 First Light is an absolute must-play.

I just finished 007 First Light by IOI, and as a huge Hitman fan, I think they did an incredible job with the James Bond license.

For 007 fans, this is a must-play. For Hitman fans, set your expectations appropriately—this is not Hitman, and it isn't trying to be. However, it still carries the quality, attention to detail, and design philosophy that IOI is known for. Supporting IOI in this new endeavor is important because what they've built here has a tremendous amount of potential, and I'm excited to see where they take it next.

What impressed me most was seeing the foundation of sandbox gameplay already present throughout the game. While this is a much more cinematic and story-driven experience than Hitman, there are moments where you can clearly see the DNA of IOI's previous work. I hope future updates, missions, and sequels continue to expand the tactical mission design and replayability in a way that resembles Hitman's mission structure. The mechanics are there. The systems are there. The potential is there.

The references were a great touch as well. Finding hidden ducks and nods to Agent 47 was a fun reward for longtime Hitman fans and showed that IOI hasn't forgotten the community that helped make them successful.

The entire experience reminded me of some of the best single-player games I've played, combining the adventure and character-driven moments of Uncharted and The Last of Us with the cinematic spectacle and pacing that Infinity Ward perfected in the Modern Warfare series. It was a masterclass in single-player storytelling, presentation, and immersion. The production values are excellent, the set pieces are memorable, and the campaign consistently kept me engaged.

I do have one criticism. There was a single mission that felt more like a way to pad the campaign's length than a meaningful gameplay experience. To avoid spoilers, I won't go into details, but it felt like a "walking simulator 2.0" section that slowed the pacing considerably and didn't need to be there. Fortunately, that's only one mission in an otherwise excellent campaign. The rest of the game is well-designed, entertaining, and genuinely fun from start to finish.

My biggest hope moving forward is that IOI leans further into the sandbox elements that made Hitman so special. More than anything, I want the freedom to truly feel like 007. Give me the tools, the gadgets, the opportunities, and the freedom to approach objectives my own way. Let me succeed brilliantly or fail spectacularly based on my decisions. Those systems already exist beneath the surface, and expanding them would add enormous replayability to future content.

As it stands today, this is one of the best single-player experiences I've played in years. It isn't Hitman, and it shouldn't be. It's 007. But it successfully establishes its own identity while still carrying the quality and craftsmanship that fans expect from IOI.

If future entries continue to develop the replayability and sandbox freedom that are already present, this could easily become my second-favorite franchise behind Hitman.

Thank you, IOI, for another fantastic game. I look forward to future updates, new missions, and whatever comes next for James Bond. The future of this series looks very promising.
