007 First Light is a really well-made game. It looks fantastic and runs very smoothly, which is exactly what I’ve come to expect from IO Interactive. I finished the main story in about 13 hours while exploring some of the choices during missions and picking up some collectibles along the way.

The game does a good job at telling an origin story for a younger, more reckless James Bond. During missions there are meaningful choices in how you gather information or complete objectives — whether through stealth, combat, gadgets, or dialogue — and experimenting with different approaches feels satisfying. However, the missions themselves generally conclude the same way no matter what path you take. It still has that signature IO Interactive polish and delivers a strong cinematic Bond experience on the first playthrough. It’s not quite as replayable as the Hitman games since the overall mission always ends the same way.

I’d recommend 007 First Light if you’re looking for a polished single-player action-adventure with a great story. That said, at full price (70€) it might feel a bit light on long-term content for some people, so waiting for a sale could be a smart move if you’re unsure.

I'm not a huge Bond fan, but I AM an Uncharted fan. And this feels like a spiritual successor to Uncharted 4 in a lot of ways, with a healthy sprinkling of Hitman. The gameplay isn't revolutionary or anything, but it's fun, the set pieces are exciting and the story is competently told and presented. The animation and graphics are impressive and the music swells in all the right places. The voice acting is extremely believable. There are a couple of spots where it feels like you're a bit too much on rails, but I didn't mind them too much. It's also extremely well optimized - I had no significant frame drops at any point. Just a really solid experience. 

Only thing that brings it down for me a notch is that it feels like everything about it apart from the gunplay was made for controller. The MKB configuration is just a bit clunky out of the box, so I'd suggest rebinding at least the gadget UI right away.

007 First Light is an exceptional experience that had me paying attention to every single detail. The story is crafted with genuine precision — playing it feels like being inside a big-budget cinematic film, not just a game.

On the gameplay side, the combat system is smooth and satisfying, giving you the freedom to approach situations in different ways, whether through direct confrontation or stealth, adding real depth to every mission. The game’s length feels just right, never making you feel bored or like you’re going through repetitive motions.

The visuals are among the game’s strongest points, especially with NVIDIA technology support, which takes the visual experience to a completely different level.

On the flip side, some missions lack variety in objectives, and certain players may find the difficulty level unbalanced in specific sections.

Overall, IO Interactive has delivered a mature and polished title that deserves recognition, and I hope they continue on this path with future installments. I also have a special message for the studio: a massive Arab audience is waiting for Arabic language support — this is a step that would open up a huge market you shouldn’t underestimate.

Ever since the days of Hitman (2016) began its first season with Paris: The Showstopper, IOI developing a game around Bond has been lingering in the back of my mind, and seemingly everyone else's. Thankfully, this latest entry into 007's video game catalog does not disappoint. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, man. I'm nearly speechless with how much I liked this game. It's like Uncharted, Mission: Impossible, and Hitman 3 had a baby.

I said on Twitter that this game is only really comparable to the last truly exceptional game starring Bond, that being 007: Nightfire, and that this succeeded where it failed and failed where it succeeded. What I mean by that is as such: this game is excellent at crafting the stealth-gadget-combat fantasy of Bond, has gameplay that doesn't strictly incentivize pure stealth the way Hitman did, has improvisation in both its sneaking and gunplay that feels incredibly rewarding regardless of if things go awry, and has a narrative that's actually fairly intriguing, but sags towards the middle, as well as questionable driving mechanics. Now, the driving is easily forgivable, as I'm pretty sure both 007: Agent Under Fire and 007: Nightfire had their respective driving sections worked on by the Need For Speed development team. The narrative, though, I'm a little less sure of. 

The campaign is only ten chapters long, but spends two of those ten chapters in a desert nation where you're mostly exploring renovated, rusty, old cargo ships. By about halfway through the second of those chapters, it got to be visually dull. As well as this, the chapter set inside the high rise office building and server farm also ran on just a tad too long. That's about it, really, which says quite a lot. I'm surprised at how well-paced and fresh the rest of the game felt, which constantly remained visually fresh with environments ranging from gala parties to luxury resorts to snowy escapes, etcetera etc. It's all very classically Bond, even if you can very easily tell which Hitman: World of Assassination levels were serving as direct visual & design inspiration. I will, however, knock off a point for how much the first third or so of this game borrows from Uncharted 3: Drake's Deception. No, I am not referring to that game's initial setting in London, but rather to its use of the "stowaway on the plane as it leaves the runway then diving through its cargo as it crashes to find a parachute" and "captured by pirates and traversing wrecked cargo ships" segments. Those two back-to-back felt a bit too similar for me to forgive.

There's really not much else to say about 007: First Light. Patrick Gibson does an incredible job playing a new and cocky yet suave and capable James Bond. This goes for the rest of the cast too, really. M, Q, Ms. Moneypenny, and even the small bit we get from Ms. Ponsonby is extremely true-to-form with the Bond franchise. I'm rather excited to see these characters in this form again, as seemingly teased by the "JAMES BOND WILL RETURN" preceding the credits. As I write this, the game has sold 1,500,000 copies and counting, so I'm confident IOI will continue with development of a sequel. Hopefully, with an experienced Bond leading the game, we can get back to the classic 007 mannerisms and plot structures, skipping the two to three hours this game had to spend on an origin entirely. On a final note, I do wish we got to see more of Cressida, though. She vanishes from the story and seemingly MI6 as a whole after the incident in Slovakia. Sheesh, M. You could've at least given her a desk job or something.

It's a good game. Just very AAA in design compared to what I know IOI can do.

[h3] The Good [/h3]
- Beautiful visuals. That includes things like the animation work which makes the world and characters feel alive in a way IOI haven't done before.
- Great acting. Patrick Gibson is great as Bond. Good amount of charm, cheekiness and that combination of being hot-headed whilst stubbornly holding on to a sense of righteousness. Acting across the board is great.
- Great writing. So much relationship building is done with dialogue that felt natural and the humour landed without feeling out of place or eye-roll inducing. I liked the relevance the overall plot has to our world at the moment.
- Combat feels amazing. Fluid, fast, chaotic. The melee combat isn't deep but it doesn't really have to be. It's just great with excellent animations for enemies bumping into different environmental objects. Shooting was my greatest concern because Hitman's is really bad but here the weapons are accurate, aiming is snappy, feedback is good, ragdolls look great, particle effects and explosions are super satisfying. The flow of combat when you're constantly moving between cover and rummaging for another gun reminds me of games like Max Payne 3 and Doom Eternal that encourage constant movement. 

[h3] The Bad [/h3]
- The driving sections are terribly boring except for a final section right at the end of the game. 
- Bosses are basically short versions of the Mr Freeze fight from Arkham City. 
- Performance in a few areas drops significantly.
- The espionage sections are pretty much on the rails. You're shown an area to infiltrate and 2 or 3 solutions are all found equal distance from the entrance. There's no actual sense of finding anything out on your own. Even eavesdropping on a conversation has to be done with a button press to prompt the next part of the script instead of it being seamless like Hitman. 
- AAA-style prompting. A few moments use yellow objects where it feels unnecessary but it's not too bad at signposting. Objective markers can't be removed and even at times where an entire item or section is marked Bond will still say out loud what needs to be done. It makes the game feel like it was made for a more casual audience which is surprising given how many sales the newest Hitman trilogy has managed. I would say what IOI do doesn't have to appease to a wider audience. I hope a sequel tones this aspect down.

TL:DR

 007 First Light is easily one of the best Bond experiences I’ve had in years. IO Interactive perfectly understood what makes James Bond special and combined cinematic storytelling, clever mission design, fantastic gunfights, strong music, and immersive spy mechanics into something that truly feels worthy of the legendary IP.

Despite taking clear inspiration from games like Max Payne, Hitman, and Uncharted, the game still manages to build its own identity instead of feeling like a cheap imitation. Sure, it has some flaws. The melee combat can feel a little clunky, and the ending feels somewhat rushed, but none of those issues stopped me from having an absolute blast from start to finish.

As for Steam Deck, while performance stability can sometimes be rough and certain areas push the hardware very hard, 007 is still surprisingly playable and visually impressive for such a demanding AAA title. With some tweaking and realistic expectations, it delivers a genuinely enjoyable handheld Bond experience that feels great to play on the go.

I was someone who fell for the hype on this game early on. Growing up watching all the Bond movies with my dad definitely has made me a lifelong fan, and when I saw IO Interactive were the ones fronting the game I knew I had to give it a go. I already beat the game, and to avoid spoilers I will just say I am look forward to the future of this title. I will start with some PROS on the game.

PROS: 
-Beautiful environments from beginning to end, 
-The voice actors were all fantastic especially the early interactions with Bond and his fellow recruits.
-Great stealth gameplay, almost Splinter Cell/Uncharted like
-Story was exactly what I would take as a Bond origin story and his come of age experience to be the double 0 we all know and love.
-Controls and mechanics are very easy to learn.
-TacSim offers a lot of replay-ability 

CONS:
-If you have any experience in Uncharted, Splinter Cell, Metal Gear, etc. Just start off in Purist difficulty. The AI enemies as so dumb that playing on normal almost got boring
-Even though IO interactive prides itself in approachability and letting the player decide how they want to complete the mission, First Light definitely is not as robust as the Hitman series. Its more streamlined to keep the story going.
-Driving missions were incredibly lackluster considering that high speed chases, and escapes are one of the things that highlight any bond story. Action packed as they were, they were glorified cut scenes.

Overall I think the game is great, and I dont regret falling for the hype and pre ordering. IO Interactive has started a great foundation to build on, and if you want a great 007 game that checks all the boxes of a good single player experience, then I highly recommend this for you. If youre expecting a robust Hitman game with Bond instead of Agent 47, then maybe wait until a sale comes out because you might be disappointed.

Personal Score: 8.5

As the first James Bond game in a long, long time, 007 First Light delivers beautifuly in a superb blend of classic James Bond infiltration, satisfying combat and unexpected, but well thought, puzzles weaved between each other. The gameplay itself is fluid and responsive, giving you ample tools to do cool, James Bond stuff.

The main story is quite predictable, but again, so are most Bond movies. You play as James Bond, the newest recruit of the reinstated 00 program. A rogue agent resurfaces and your training is cut short as the 00 recruits are required to help apprehend him, eventually leading to a bigger-than-life plotline as any Bond movie does.

The good stuff doesn't end there either. You have quite likeable characters (especially Q), despite their presence in the story being cut a bit short. You also get the usual Bond stuff: cool gadgets, exotic locales, beautiful and dangerous women and plenty of references from the movies and novels. I especially liked seeing the neurotoxin shoeblades from SPECTRE in Q Lab.

The gameplay itself is great. Much like IOI's most popular IP, Hitman, you are given tools to get to your goals with. The maps themselves are, for the most part, open ended when it comes to infiltration sequences, with actions sequences being more railroaded. Said action sequences, aptly dubbed "License to kill" moments offer you limited amunitions, forcing you to use all the tools in your arsenal to get by. That includes using gadgets, hand to hand combat, throwing empty weapons on enemies and using the environment to your advantage. Overall, it's a load of fun.

The game, following Himan's formula, seem to bank most of the future content on Tactical Simulations, the secondary game mode, which allows you to take your own outfits, gadgets and firearms into missions. Although unlike Hitman, you don't seem to be able to go to any and all levels and redo them different ways.

However, it all comes with a pretty big hiccup: Performance.

The recommended specs mention a RTX 3060 TI but does not mention what resolution or framerate to expect to play at. Alas, I have a 2080 Super and it was very difficult to maintain 60FPS in 1440P. Forcing me to downgrade resolution to 1080P AND using DLSS Ultra Performance AND having every setting on low, making the game kind of ugly to play.

One could argue a 2080S isn't a 1440P card, but that's kind of a strawman, considering the same 2080S can run Hitman: WOA in native 1440P with light raytracing on. Hopefully, future updates will mitigate this issue.

What really stood out to me was the presentation. The music, the atmosphere, and the overall direction are genuinely stunning.

As for the price, I cannot say with complete confidence that it fully earns the 70 USD tag, although it comes close. There is side content such as the tactical simulations that I have not tried yet, so there is at least something beyond the main campaign for players who want more.

Overall, 007 First Light surprised me in the best way possible. It is stylish, polished, and consistently entertaining. I am already looking forward to a sequel. My final rating is a strong 9/10.

Recommended

Pros

Great game. Performance was excellent from the moment I launched it. I only experienced two crashes during my entire playthrough, both occurring during mission briefing transitions into the live-action style cutscenes.

It genuinely felt like playing through a Bond movie. The story is packed with twists, espionage, memorable set pieces, and all the spy work you'd expect from a 007 title. The campaign wraps up nicely while leaving clear room for a sequel in the same universe.

At roughly 14 hours played, that's about how long it took me to complete the campaign using a mix of stealth and going in guns blazing. Both approaches felt fun and viable because the combat is simply enjoyable. The developers absolutely nailed the feeling of being James Bond.

Cons

My biggest criticism is that the AI can be inconsistent at times. Without replaying certain sections, I can't say for sure whether some of what I experienced was pathing issues, bad luck, or intended behavior, but there were several moments where enemies were fairly easy to manipulate or exploit on the standard intended difficulty.

The TacSim mode, which serves as the game's replayable content, is made up of remixed sections from the campaign. You can tackle them in different ways while unlocking cosmetics and weapons you've already encountered. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but I would have liked to see a few more completely unique locations that weren't part of the main story. That said, this impression could change as I spend more time with the mode or as future updates are released.

Final Take

Honestly, this game knocks it out of the park. It feels like a return to form for big-budget single-player experiences, blending elements of Hitman and Uncharted in a way that works surprisingly well. If you're a Bond fan or simply enjoy story-driven action games with stealth, espionage, and cinematic set pieces, this is an easy recommendation.

IO Interactive seemed a logical choice for a James Bond game after the massive success of their Hitman games. And to give a short overview, I was not disappointed, this game is a truly exemplary James Bond game. 

Right away, if you are hoping for missions that demand the kind of intense exploration and trial and error that the Hitman games have, you will likely be somewhat disappointed, as the missions in First Light are quite linear, with most choices involving how you approach combat. The missions are great fun, but not strictly on the same level of sheer replayability as Hitman. 

What this means, however, is that the story can really shine because you spend an ample blend of time experiencing the story and playing the game, and it is quite a good story. I will not spoil it here, but the high points remind me of the best parts of the Brosnan Bond movies with the visceral punchiness of the Craig Bond movies. The only critiques I have of the story are ones I've leveled against the newer Bond movies, namely that they tend to overstay their welcome in a few places. There are a few sections that feel overly-drawn-out compared to their relative importance ([spoiler]The escape from the Gala comes to mind[/spoiler]), but on the whole, it's still a very good time. 

The characters are original interpretations of the core canonical characters (Q, M, Moneypenny, and of course James Bond himself), and the interpretations bring some real freshness to the story. Bond in particular strikes a nice balance between adept and wisecracking, while also not falling victim to the Austin Powers comparisons. I also really like the characterization of Moneypenny, as her role in the books and movies was often an office assistant to M, where here she's something more of a remote support person. Also as a nice nod to the books, M's secretary is named Ponsonby, a nice reference to book Bond's secretary Loelia Ponsonby.  

The singleplayer story took me about 18 hours to complete, but the journey doesn't have to end there. TacSim is this game's equivalent to the tweakable mission parameters that the Hitman games have, and even more. It's a really interesting game mode, and what IO Interactive does with it will be very interesting to see. 

On that note, the gameplay systems are a really clever mix of Hitman and Uncharted. This is definitely one of the most adrenaline-pumping games IOI has made, and it really suits the Bond licence. I think the most fascinating thing the developers have done is the mandatory training level. Instead of a bunch of training missions all in a row, you are given the benefit of playing the training [i]montage[/i]. It's genuinely really clever, and it's no wonder people harp on it because it is the sort of thing I want more games to play with going forward. 

The combat systems are a delight to play. Close-quarters combat in particular feels very visceral and powerful, much like the Arkham games. The gunplay feels like a nice variation on standard third-person combat, and being able to toss your empty gun at a foe then rush them to take them out feels really good. Plus, the gadgets are a really fun way to vary the missions in a few ways. The gadget loadout is a nice way to create fun scenarios where you might struggle with certain situations while others are dealt with ease. I also really like the way you can bluff your way out of some scenarios, because that is exactly what Bond would do, and the way they keep you from abusing it (an energy system that accumulates as you accomplish objectives, deal with enemies, etc) makes it feel really dynamic. I especially love being able to bluff myself out of a jam because of a mistake, which lets me keep up the thrill without devolving into combat I wasn't prepared for. These systems don't always work because some enemies are immune, but it's still great to have the option.

If you're a Bond fan, you know the music can sometimes make or break key moments, and the music here is truly delightful. The use of the classic James Bond theme is appropriate without being overused, and the opening credits in particular feels like the sort of thing you'd actually see in a Bond movie. 

As for bugs, there were a few times that my character got stuck in cover or died due to some sort of physics glitch, which isn't great, but on the whole it was a really solid experience. It runs beautifully on my computer, whose specs I have attached below, but I would be more surprised if it didn't run well. 

All in, 007 First Light is a brilliant Bond game, possibly the best one yet. It's also a tour de force for IO Interactive, with new elements that have been otherwise absent from their games such as drivable vehicles. The creative vision here is something that the Bond franchise has sorely needed, and I hope that we get another game or two from IO Interactive, because I would love to see more of this interpretation of the franchise they've created. I look forward to our next mission with 007, IO Interactive. You've definitely sold me on another go or two. For England, James.

007 First Light is not just a great James Bond game, but also a genuinely fantastic action-adventure game. Functionally, it feels like a mix of the Uncharted games and Hitman, all with the dressing of classic James Bond films. 

Gameplay loops feels similar to Hitman, with open levels to explore opportunities and secrets to continue through the level or reach a certain target, albeit with much more linearity and action set-pieces like Uncharted. Action and combat feels really good, especially melee combat which felt very snappy and it lets you to really utilize your environment to take out enemies (think Batman Arkham or Sleeping dogs). 

Story is really good and really feels like a Bond film, with some stellar performances from the cast. I think my only gripe with the narrative is the pacing, which felt slow and too quick at times. For example, almost the first half of the game follow Bond in what feels like "training", which really made the narrative feel patted out. Despite the pacing, the story is truly a delight.

Overall, I really enjoyed 007 First light and I look forward to what IO Interactive has planned next for the character and franchise.

I wanted to love this game, but 007 First Light is honestly one of the most broken and immersion-destroying experiences I’ve played in years.

The AI is completely brain-dead. Enemies either stand still staring at walls or magically spot you through objects from across the map. Stealth feels pointless because half the time the guards bug out and the other half they instantly know your location for no reason. For a James Bond game, the immersion is absolutely ruined by constant glitches, stiff animations, and terrible voice syncing.

The bugs are nonstop. Characters clipping through floors, missions failing randomly, cutscenes freezing, audio cutting out, objectives not updating, and crashes during important moments. I had to restart checkpoints multiple times because the game simply stopped functioning properly.

The driving sections feel unfinished, gunplay is clunky, and the controls somehow manage to feel both sluggish and overly sensitive at the same time. Instead of feeling like a smooth spy thriller, it feels like an early beta build that got pushed out way too soon.

What’s most disappointing is that the atmosphere and idea had potential, but everything is buried under technical problems and lazy polish. It completely kills any tension or excitement when the game is constantly reminding you it’s falling apart.

I'm recommending this game because It's a well made game with an amazing story. However, for me I was bored for 2/3 of it so only buy if the below is what you want. 

James is cool, the game looks beautiful, the amount of Easter eggs to find is great for a Bond fan, the gadgets are cool for the first few hours, and it genuinely feels like a proper Bond film. But the pacing and constant point and click walking really drag it down. If you want a slow, interactive version of a Daniel Craig James Bond movie with a great story, you’ll probably love this. If you’re looking for a rapid, run and gun shooter that keeps your heart racing, you’re only going to enjoy about 1/3 of the game.

The story itself is really great. A young Royal Navy cadet saves the day, MI6 recruits him to track a rogue agent and he uncovers a massive mystery. However, as a video game it’s basically an interactive walking simulator with occasional action. The gameplay loop gets repetitive fast. You go into an area, look for clues, and use the exact same few tricks (poisoning, blinding, distracting guards) to climb a ledge, shimmy to the next room, and look for more clues. It definitely feels like it was built for casual players who just want a spy vibe. The marketing made it look way more intense than it actually is. I wasn't expecting Hitman 4, obviously, but I did expect a lot more actual gameplay.

Coming from the guys who made Hitman, this feels like a massive step back in freedom. The "choices" they give are alright - pick two out of four possible ways to progress. Some of the choices seemed like an illusion though, a lot of the time it felt like choosing between a left or right door that both lead into the same exact hallway. Casual players might not care, but it got annoying for me.

On a more positive note, The TacSim mode plays like the challenge mode in the Arkham games, I enjoyed that a lot more because you get dropped right into the action. Quite a small amount of content currently though but obviously the game's only been out a couple days so looing forward to seeing where IOI take it. 

If you're cool with a casual, cinematic movie game, buy it. If you want fast action, maybe wait for a sale.

Man, what a mixed bag. All the stuff you'd expect the Hitman devs to do well is done VERY well, and everything else is even worse than you'd expect. Cars feel awful to drive, somehow boring AND frustrating at the same time. Fist-fights feel weighty but control terribly; square to punch and circle to parry, but you grab with... R2? Finishers are X plus square, and there's a tackle that I immediately forgot how to do. Apparently it's pretty important, so good thing there are no prompts for it after the tutorial. There's also a dodge input you can do by pushing left or right while pressing X, which makes the finisher input feel even more arbitrary AND never feels right because there's no lock-on mechanism whatsoever. Multiple times now I've tried to circle my opponent to reposition and just ended up turning and running, sometimes taking a fist to the back of the head in the process. Near the end of the first level you get into a boss fist-fight with two guys at the same time, and it's absolute agony to get through due to the aforementioned lack of lock-on and how little time you've had to really internalize the signals for parrying and dodging. Shooting feels only slightly better than Goldeneye 64, and your guns are constantly out of ammo. This is meant to impart a sense of forward momentum as you shoot until empty, throw your gun to stun an enemy, and pick up something else to continue the fight. In practice, however, it doesn't square up well against their shooting gallery level design, and I spent more time than I'd like in cover waiting for the strawberry jelly to get wiped off the screen so I could keep fighting. It's so, SO janky, but I grit my teeth and push through for the actual meat of the game, which is the free-form level exploration and story. 

All of the lessons IOI learned from the latest Hitman trilogy are on display here, along with homages to that franchise. The first *real* level, which occurs three hours in after WAY too much tutorial/training montage nonsense, feels like an incredible remix of the fashion show level in Hitman 2016. It's pared down to be more of a directed experience, but not in a way that actual feels linear. There are riffs on the "stories" system from Hitman 2016, and multiple ways of getting through the narrative. The sandbox gets traded away for a story that seems to be shaping up quite well, and it's delivered through some very well-acted characters. The dialogue brushes up against AAA Whedon-esque platitudes at times, but it all feels like a proper Bond experience. All of this is wrapped in level design that's top-notch, and visuals that are genuinely breath-taking at times. I love all of the attention to details in MI6, and it's genuinely great to spend time wandering around the Q Lab and looking at all the gadgets. Q is great, M is great, Moneypenny is excellent.. I can't say enough good things about the cast and their design.

If this second part of the game sounds good and you can grin and bear it whenever a car appears or James puts his fists up, you'll probably find it to be worth your time. But I would never recommend this game at full price, because it just doesn't feel ready for primetime. It's probably the best Bond game we've got, but that's quite a low bar to clear, and the game feels disappointingly close to being yet another bad franchise tie-in. For those reasons, I'm just barely giving it a "Not Recommended". If you get it on sale and get into the mindset of a PS2-era janky action game experience, you'll have a really good time. $70 for the game just makes the flaws feel too apparent.

Edit: I just beat the level with Lenny Kravitz, of all people. Two deus ex machinas right in a row, and yet another shooting gallery. There was no need for this. Bond doesn't have to end every level with a 40+ kill count, it's just something they felt like they had to have because it was in Uncharted. Don't buy this game, especially not for full price.

Second Edit: The final piece of gameplay is a QTE, a perfect ending to a game that takes so many cues from the worst games of the 2010s. IO, if you're reading this, throw away all of the shooting corridors and clunky driving sections; you can't make them fun, and they take way too much focus from the things you did well in this game. There's a reason the Hitman trilogy didn't make you straightforwardly fight hundreds of guys with guns and then QTE a boss to death, and you've seemingly forgotten why that was.

A little torn on this game, because while I think it's a great time for the most part, it hits some big snags along the way that might really hurt it for some. Knowing this is IOI really breaking from the playbook they're used to, it was bound to have some issues with polish or gameplay/story balance. Once again asking Steam to give us a more nuanced rating system, or at least just a 'Mixed' option. It's a very 7/10 kind of game.

In short before I go into a big ramble, it's a good narrative adventure/action game that uses the 007 license mostly quite well, even if it takes a few dud hours to get going and actually feel like a proper Bond game. I was a little let down by undercooked mechanics, pretty poor pacing and some of the choices made with characters, but the best gameplay sections really shone through.

For some positives, I liked the presentation. The graphics are quite nice for the most part even if they can look a bit dated here and there. The game has pretty damn fun combat too. It takes a while to get the hang of, but once you've got it down, you can chain some crazy combos and really use yourr environment to engage in some awesome fist-fights. The gunplay doesn't feel too shabby either, even if I'm not a big fan of the aggressive aim-assist that comes with using a controller. The sections where you're permitted to engage in combat or stealth feel nice and open to explore or improvise your approach a little, which I really loved even if it's not quite the sandbox you get with the Hitman games. Around the halfway mark of the game is where this combat really starts to feel great, and the story finally picks up in a big way to complement that.

And that's what leads me into the first critique. The first act, the opening four or five hours just flat out suck. The gameplay is boring and over-tutorialised, the supporting cast is strange and uninteresting, the general tone and atmosphere feels completely off-kilter from what I expected from a 007 game. It feels more akin to Kingsmen or like a weird spy Hogwarts soap opera. The prologue was cool, but then there's the long training chapter, and then you're doing your first mission and still getting tutorial prompts, it's just such a slow and arduous way to start a game, particularly when all the worst parts of it (including the villain!) just get binned entirely and the game suddenly changes course in a *very* positive way. I don't know if this was IOI trying to pad out the game's length or if they somehow realised too late how poor their opening was and had to just really work on improving the latter portion of the game, but they kind of messed up the opener here. And that's going to filter some people, which is sad. Especially when around 10 hours in the game really clicks into place with a much more interesting story thread and more gameplay variation. I almost wish they just cut out a decent portion of the game in the interest of better pacing.

Everything outside of those combat/stealth sections I mentioned earlier are not so great, and they plague the first good chunk of the game. You spend a good 70% of the game exploring, gathering clues to reveal a path through your current mission, or engaging in corridor-walking with other NPCs. Now I love my linear video games as much as the next guy as a life-long PlayStation gamer, but with how fun those combat and stealth sections are, to be shuttled back into these slow and ponderous periods where I'm not allowed to use any gadgets, use my gun, or even engage in stealth is a bit fatiguing in a 20 hour game. Some encounters that look like Bond should be sneaking around are weirdly non-consequential, you can pretty much stun someone in plain sight of a dozen other NPCs and pickpocket from them with no recourse. Stealth outside of combat areas basically does not exist. Again, wasn't expecting Hitman immersive sim elements all the way through, but some sections have the absolute minimum amount of gameplay scraped over them.

The driving sections are also a bit of a wash. Your speed is hard-programmed depending on the sequence, your steering is obnoxiously pulled from you constantly to trigger cutscenes or just keep you from going off the narrow invisible racing line. I fully accept they're there just to add excitement and introduce sweeping vistas as you enter each new country, but the driving sections have often been the best parts of any 007 game and they just didn't do anything worthwhile with it here. Not that I'm expecting the ability to crash into NPCs or drive around a massive open world area, but just some more variation on where I can drive or at least some illusion that my input is doing anything would be nice.

The presentation as I mentioned earlier is quite nice, with some great locations with big crowds and lots of incidental detail. There are some bafflingly low-resolution textures and set dressings that may or may not be the result of bugs, but some stuff comes out looking like they belong in a PS3 game at points. It means the game scales quite well with lower end hardware and consoles, but even at maxed out settings, it looks decidedly last-gen at the best of times. It's workable and the art direction is still very strong, but I never really had my mind blown either. It was never going to get the kind of polish a Naughty Dog game gets, but I wish they gave the textures in this game another pass at the very least.

For a sequel, I'd like for less hand-holding, and maybe more combat/stealth sections, because those were the best part of the game despite feeling like they only made up a few hours of the game in total. There's a lot that's good here, but there's also plenty that just drags it down as well. I have no complaints about this Bond or the story they finally managed to land on once that prologue gets tossed away, but IOI need to tighten up their game design on the next one.

But seriously though, what was the deal with Lenny Kravitz? Dude had like, two minutes of screentime then dipped.

The main story runs about 20 hours, while the TacSim missions add another 1–2 hours depending on whether you go for the extra challenges. The game doesn’t have much replay value once you finish the story, there isn’t a strong reason to come back. The main campaign offers “Black Box” style missions, which are different from the open-ended approach in Hitman. You do get a few entry points to choose from but the overall mission structure is still fairly linear. I enjoyed my time with the game, but my biggest disappointment was the TacSim mode. I expected larger, more open areas similar to Hitman, but instead they are more like small challenge rooms, similar to the Arkham games.

Overall, I’d say the game was worth playing and I’d give it an 8.5/10.
